source_title: release-notes 0.161.0 (Aug 18, 2026): bounded sub-agent nesting and truncated web results
author: Dex+others
quote: CodeLayer subagents now delegate at most three levels deep
claim: Version 0.161.0 (2026-08-18) caps sub-agent delegation at three levels to stop runaway fork chains, and truncates large web search and fetch results so one lookup cannot crowd out the session.
evidence_detail: Two release-note lines.
landing: Two caps to copy: a depth limit on nested agents and a size limit on tool output returned into context. FixFlow caps outputs already; nesting depth is not stated.

author: Dex
quote: You can't get 10x. It can't be done. Not today.
claim: For production work that must last, the ceiling is about 2-3x at roughly 99% of hand-written quality; 10x-100x is only for highly verifiable domains.
evidence_detail: Stated repeatedly; cites the Bun rewrite (tens of thousands of unit tests) as the verifiable-domain exception. No measurement.
landing: Expectation-setting for the ship plan's phase budget; nowhere obvious in config

author: Dex
quote: The PRs that take a long time to review are the ones that are bad.
claim: Review effort is a function of PR quality; well-designed, well-ordered PRs are quick to review, so effort belongs upstream.
evidence_detail: Stated as observation.
landing: Opus reviewer per PR; PR-size guidance

author: Dex
quote: You will find some things and you will raise the floor
claim: AI review bots (BugBot, Codex reviewing Claude) raise the floor and should catch small issues so human hours are not spent there, but they do not replace human code review for high-quality production code.
evidence_detail: Judgement, no measurement. Also: 'let Codex catch it and fix it for sure' for small issues.
landing: Role of the Opus reviewer: floor-raising filter, not the final gate; cross-model review idea

author: Dex
quote: there will be inefficiencies that are not bottlenecks.
claim: Apply Goldratt's Theory of Constraints: do not maximize utilisation of one station (token maxing, loops); fix the end-to-end bottleneck, which is currently human review/understanding.
evidence_detail: Based on The Goal; analogy to 1960s-70s factory MBAs optimising a single station.
landing: Harness investment prioritisation: spend on the bottleneck (review, verification), not on more parallel agents

author: Dex
quote: you need a metric and you need social proof.
claim: To drive AI adoption, pick a defensible directional metric (e.g. weighted PRs per dollar of token spend, or DX's metric divided by token spend) plus a team that visibly ships more without slop or more bugs.
evidence_detail: Says teams he talked to already measure this way; admits metrics are gameable and productivity has resisted measurement for 50 years.
landing: Measurement of whether the harness works: a directional per-phase metric (merged phases per cost) and a comparison arm; relates to skipped measurement pipeline

author: Dex
quote: I don't care what tools you use... but you have to hit that level.
claim: Manage by outcome bar, not by prescribing tools: a proven team sets the bar (e.g. double the numbers at same quality) and others get any route to it.
evidence_detail: Management advice.
landing: Harness-as-hypothesis: judge routine by outcomes, not compliance

author: Dex
quote: use tokens as many tokens as you can... then pull them back out
claim: Unconstrained token use pushes people into obsession ('AI psychosis'); once hooked, shift to efficiency and cost.
evidence_detail: Observed at companies whose budgets, set before Opus 4.5, were blown after the December shift.
landing: Phase of effort routing: explore at high effort then tune down

author: Dex
quote: get it working with the smartest, best model you can.
claim: Make it run, make it right, make it fast, maybe make it cheap: establish what works with the smartest model, then optimise cost later by trying cheaper models.
evidence_detail: Advice from a decade of practice; no measurements.
landing: Effort/model routing: default to strongest model, step verifiers down only after they demonstrably work

author: Dex
quote: I don't have time to fix Sonnet's work.
claim: Using the smartest model for implementation is faster and a better use of human time than fixing a cheaper model's errors; some enterprises mandate Opus for planning and Sonnet for implementation, and whether that works depends on subscription vs per-token billing.
evidence_detail: Personal experience; enterprise guidance reported second-hand; no quality numbers.
landing: Model-per-role routing (Opus planning / cheaper implementation, Haiku explorer); counterpoint to cheap models

author: Dex
quote: if you're just using Opus for everything and maxing out your subscription, you're probably doing too much
claim: Maxing a subscription on the top model for everything signals over-use; vibe-coding the whole universe of software is not productive in value terms.
evidence_detail: Opinion.
landing: Effort routing / budget guard for verifiers

author: Dex
quote: The plan has to be good enough that if it's 20% wrong, I know I'll be able to recover
claim: Build intuition for how much fits in one context window (with and without sub-agents) and size plans so errors are recoverable within one session; otherwise rewind further.
evidence_detail: Experience-based heuristic framed as stacking probabilities (fog of war).
landing: One phase per new session sizing rule

author: Dex
quote: 10X or 100X is reserved for very specific, very verifiable domains.
claim: Speedups above 2-3x appear only where verification is cheap and thorough, so verifiability, not model strength, sets the ceiling.
evidence_detail: Example: Bun rewrite with huge existing unit-test suite; compilers also called very verifiable.
landing: Verifier/backpressure investment: make FixFlow work verifiable (tests, scripts) before widening autonomy

author: Dex
quote: The biggest tell for me when it's like, all right, kill it now
claim: Kill the session and start fresh when the model struggles to get tests passing and starts trying weird things; it can forget how it got tests running 100k tokens ago.
evidence_detail: Personal heuristic.
landing: Phase routine abort/restart trigger; reviewer note that repeated test-fix flailing means restart

author: Dex
quote: we will give a warning around 100K tokens
claim: The dumb zone used to be about 40% of context (80-100K on 200K models); CodeLayer warns at ~100K on 200K windows and ~200K on 1M windows, and he regularly goes past 300K by judgement.
evidence_detail: Product warning thresholds; no benchmark data given.
landing: Context budget: concrete token thresholds for sessions; compare to one-phase-per-session

author: Dex
quote: it actually includes verbatim every user message that has been sent
claim: Compaction has improved: the summary now keeps every user message verbatim and points to the conversation history for grep, so earlier steering survives; the JSONL shows what was kept, though a hand-written markdown resume file stays editable.
evidence_detail: Observation from custom client reading the compaction user-message event.
landing: Compaction policy: reconsider avoiding compaction; inspect compaction output in JSONL

author: Dex
quote: sub-agents are map reduce.
claim: Sub-agents suit parallelisable, mostly read-only work that compresses a million tokens of context into 50k, and context-heavy loops (CI watch, log/Sentry/Datadog debugging) are best isolated in a sub-agent context.
evidence_detail: Used in own CI/CD optimisation and debugging; 'a little slower but better results'.
landing: Custom agents/skills: add CI-watch and log-reading agents beyond the Haiku explorer

author: Dex
quote: You're not allowed to read any files
claim: An 'RLM mode': prompt the parent to work only through sub-agents (no direct file reads), with one extra depth of sub-agent nesting, to keep the parent context clean.
evidence_detail: Exploratory in their custom harness; Claude Code can now allow nested sub-agents.
landing: Workflow-tool orchestration: parent-as-dispatcher pattern for context-heavy tasks

author: Dex
quote: figure out how you can make it as easy as possible for the model to check its own work.
claim: Learn backpressure: engineer small loops so the model can verify itself; this is the only way to leave work unattended longer and still get good results.
evidence_detail: His number-one advice to working engineers.
landing: Backpressure scripts / verification commands in phase routine; CI gates agents can run locally

author: Dex
quote: If you can express something as a linter you absolutely should
claim: Express every checkable rule as a linter so agents fix it themselves; judgement-only lessons (pain learned at 3am) cannot be linted and need human review.
evidence_detail: Host states the linter point and Dex agrees ('you can enforce some of this with linters, but a lot of it, you can't').
landing: Move CLAUDE.md prose invariants into lint/import-linter/test checks (supports W1 trim)

author: Dex
quote: Would you want to debug this code at two in the morning
claim: Agents cannot judge maintainability pain; a reviewer checklist question like 'would you want to debug this at 2am' needs a human who has felt the pain.
evidence_detail: Rule from a 2013-14 repo README at his first job.
landing: Reviewer prompt question; limit of agent-only review

author: Dex
quote: you vibe code the tools that help you improve the code quality
claim: Fight slop with slop: vibe-code throwaway tooling that improves production code quality, while keeping production code itself carefully read.
evidence_detail: Aside; he vibe-coded launch-video animations (2,000-line React files) unread.
landing: Unverified-OK zone for scripts/backpressure tooling versus verified zone for product code

author: Dex
quote: Vibe coding a side project... share almost no constraints worth naming.
claim: Vibe-coding side projects and maintaining a long-lived regulated system have different constraints; advice must be matched to the stakes (fintech with fines must read the code).
evidence_detail: Quotes Addy Osmani's Loop Engineering article; Dex adopts it.
landing: Risk-tiering of review depth (money/ledger paths vs UI)

author: Dex
quote: you can give it a really good architecture doc... but somehow the code is still garbage
claim: A perfect system-level spec is not enough: the model follows architecture to the letter yet produces leaky abstractions and tramp data, so planning must reach program design (interfaces, test seams, dependency injection).
evidence_detail: From six months of customer work and internal use; no numbers.
landing: Phase routine plan step / reviewer checklist: add a program-design level (interfaces, test seams) beyond slice boundaries

author: Dex
quote: Specs, then architecture, then program design: lights-off levels
claim: Levels of lights-off: (1) specs plus self-testing with browser/bash, (2) architecture knowledge, (3) program design (interfaces, seams); throwing more tokens improves but does not guarantee correctness and levels 1-2 proved insufficient.
evidence_detail: Paraphrase of his 'evolving thesis' from six months of customer and internal work; the quoted words are a label, not verbatim.
landing: Maturity ladder for how far to remove the human reader from the loop

author: Dex
quote: outer harness... feedback and testing and a browser
claim: Software-factory anatomy: sandbox orchestration, an outer harness (feedback, testing, browser), an inner harness (Claude Code/Codex), then testing, AI review bots, manual human testing and human code review before merge.
evidence_detail: Whiteboard description; classic SDLC plus AI layer.
landing: Vocabulary for the harness layers; where hooks and verifiers sit

author: Dex
quote: hand crafting my own memory so I can control every single token
claim: Context engineering is a thin layer: understand that everything assembles context windows and hand-build memory rather than adopting memory/RAG abstractions, since none has nailed it despite good benchmark results.
evidence_detail: Opinion; acknowledges memory vendors score well on benchmarks.
landing: Knowledge-store design: hand-curated rather than a memory product; supports building own

author: Dex
quote: you make it better than what the YOLO prompter can do.
claim: Do not wait for the bitter lesson: the edge is getting a model 20% better at tasks at the boundary of what it can do, and each new model makes part of the work irrelevant but invites more context engineering.
evidence_detail: Argument with NotebookLM quote; AI Engineer Miami slides.
landing: Expect harness pieces to expire with model upgrades; periodically retest whether each rule still earns its place

author: Dex
quote: have your personal eval that helps you understand how much better is this model
claim: Keep a personal eval of something AI could not do and retry it with each new model release to gauge improvement.
evidence_detail: Attributed advice from Simon Willison, which Dex endorses.
landing: Cheap regression eval for the harness itself (e.g. P1 cold-resume trial re-run per model)

author: Dex
quote: we had to update all our prompts to make Codex write like Opus
claim: Prompts and workflow artefacts are model-specific: Claude writes research docs in the desired readable form while Codex produced 200-bullet file-line lists, so artefact formats need per-model tuning.
evidence_detail: Experience porting CodeLayer to Codex; GPT more literal, Opus more expansive.
landing: Skill/agent prompts must be re-validated when changing models or effort

author: Dex
quote: you should send an agent off to spend 10 minutes reading code
claim: Design workflows so humans are pulled in only where their time is most valuable: send the agent to read/think for 10 minutes, riff, then let it build a first part, rather than synchronous back-and-forth.
evidence_detail: His answer on highest net benefit: 'leverage'.
landing: Phase routine human touchpoints (plan approval, closing message)

author: Dex
quote: you have to be comfortable throwing stuff out.
claim: Be willing to rewind and rebuild from scratch after understanding the constraints; the rebuilt feature is better, and plans are disposable.
evidence_detail: His own habit as an engineer.
landing: Rewind rule in phase routine; discard-and-restart a session rather than patching

author: Dex
quote: What I actually love is two people doing two things in parallel.
claim: Best throughput pattern is two humans each running two parallel agent tasks, pairing in person so one task covers blocking on the other while sharing prompts and tricks.
evidence_detail: Preference from observation; no numbers.
landing: Owner/agent working arrangement; limit parallel streams per person

author: Dex
quote: Go figure out why
claim: AI changes PR review pedagogy: comments that point where to look now just get pasted into Claude, so reviewers should say what is wrong and make the author work out why.
evidence_detail: Cites Mitchell Hashimoto's Ghostty comment threads; wording is a paraphrase of the practice.
landing: Reviewer prompt style; low relevance to a single-owner shop

author: Dex
quote: giving engineers permission to ship slop... collapse your codebase into ash much faster than you think
claim: The biggest company mistake is abandoning code and system quality; skipping quality burns the codebase down within months.
evidence_detail: Opinion based on customer observation; 'you will be throwing it out in six months'.
landing: Reviewer/closing-message gate; reinforces that review stays human-read for production code

author: Dex
quote: very high level one, your CLAUDE.md... more detailed you get the more churn
claim: Distil knowledge into layers by volatility: a stable top layer (CLAUDE.md: what it is and how it works) and increasingly detailed, higher-churn layers refreshed at a chosen cadence.
evidence_detail: Brief aside on onboarding to a codebase; framed as an optimisation problem.
landing: Supports trimming CLAUDE.md to stable facts and moving high-churn detail (migration head, counts) to a generated or on-demand store

author: Dex
quote: people are accidentally training on test.
claim: Public benchmarks are contaminated and gamed (secrets in system prompts on Terminal-Bench), so he looks at newer ones (SWE-Marathon, FrontierCode) instead.
evidence_detail: Brief agreement with host; no data.
landing: Caution when using benchmark claims (e.g. effort-level results) to set harness policy; prefer own evals

author: Dex
quote: they can read Sentry crashes and they can go change stuff
claim: Shipping is more than coding: aim for models that also read support tickets and Sentry crashes and iterate, and treat the engineer's job as producing working software however the code is written.
evidence_detail: Cites Guillermo Rauch's coding-vs-shipping distinction.
landing: Closing the loop from Sentry (just wired) into the phase routine

author: Dex
quote: we would much rather hire someone with really good software engineering fundamentals
claim: Hire fundamentals (systems, distributed systems) and teach AI use, since AI proficiency to the 99th percentile takes only a couple of months.
evidence_detail: Hiring stance.
landing: nowhere obvious

author: Dex
quote: I want to kill the pull request.
claim: Make review continuous and shift left: expose plan, design and code understanding as agents work rather than a discrete plan-build-review waterfall, with artifacts, sessions, tasks and streaming diffs as the data model.
evidence_detail: Product vision for CodeLayer; he posted 'should we kill the PR?'
landing: Draft-PR-first routine already moves this direction; nowhere new

author: Dex
quote: the spec is not about getting it perfect... optimizing your chance of success
claim: Spend about 10 minutes getting a plan 80% right, then re-steer at each zoom level, rather than an hour perfecting it; it should be good enough that a 20% error is recoverable and a 50% error means rewinding to the plan.
evidence_detail: Coaching experience; thresholds (20% recover, 50% throw out) given as heuristics.
landing: Phase routine: plan-then-re-steer thresholds, decisions journal / rewind rule in the draft PR

author: Dex
quote: It should let you read a 200 line markdown file and re-steer
claim: A spec's job is leverage: review and correct a short markdown artifact at 50k/25k/10k-foot levels instead of re-steering thousands of lines of code later.
evidence_detail: Stated as design principle; no numbers beyond 200 vs 2000 lines.
landing: Plan @ <sha> draft PR body as the short steerable artifact; owner one-page view

author: Dex
quote: If you are at a level of detail that you are guaranteeing every line... you've written code.
claim: A spec detailed enough to fix every line is just code; over-specifying wastes effort and a program is itself the most detailed spec.
evidence_detail: Attributed to a Haskell poster and Mario Zechner; Dex endorses it.
landing: Plan-writing guidance in ship plan §0

author: Dex
quote: these shouldn't be checked into the code
claim: Specs/plans are tactical, per-task docs stored outside the codebase (originally a symlinked repo synced like Google Docs) and archived after shipping, because keeping specs in sync with code is unmaintainable.
evidence_detail: Team practice for about a year; cites a year-old spec-kit GitHub thread complaining about sync.
landing: Challenges committing plans/evidence into docs/program and the knowledge-store design (what persists vs archives); CLAUDE.md should not carry task specs

author: Dex
quote: you're going to spend six hours a day reviewing code
claim: With AI shipping everything, human review becomes the sole bottleneck; invest 20 minutes to an hour in design and ordered breakdown into verifiable steps so review drops from six hours to about 20 minutes.
evidence_detail: Seen in 'a lot of really good teams'; six hours vs 20 minutes are illustrative, not measured.
landing: Phase sizing and ordering in the ship plan; one PR per phase with verifiable steps; owner view

author: Dex
quote: Use `diff` when the point is what changes and the surrounding shape already exists.
claim: Show change as a diff over the existing shape (component tree, file tree, call tree, pseudocode) and show the whole block only when most of it is new or order matters.
evidence_detail: Four diff examples (component, file layout, call tree, control flow).
landing: Reviewer-facing PR body and the Opus reviewer's brief: structural diff instead of file-by-file changelog

author: Dex
quote: Keep only the calls, files, props, states, and boundaries needed to answer the user's current question
claim: Place each visual next to the short text it supports and include only the elements needed for the current question; do not use every view type.
evidence_detail: Guidance paragraph.
landing: Owner view / closing message length discipline

author: Dex
quote: allow_implicit_invocation: false
claim: show-me is invoked only on explicit user request (disable-model-invocation: true in frontmatter, allow_implicit_invocation false for Codex), so skill descriptions do not compete for the model's attention or fire unasked.
evidence_detail: Config values only; visual-pr uses the same pattern with description 'Only use when the user explicitly invokes this skill by name'.
landing: Frontmatter policy for the skills being added under .claude/skills/: mark owner-only or heavy skills as manual-invocation

source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
author: Dex
quote: tanish even wrote a tool to compute them straight from the AST
claim: Call stacks can be computed deterministically from the AST by a tool rather than written by the model; Dex points to this as a way to produce the call-stack view.
evidence_detail: Links a third-party tool (Tanishq) with no evaluation. Re-opens the call-graph tooling the harness review skipped.
landing: call-graph tooling (previously skipped by the harness review); would feed program-design and review steps

source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
author: Dex
quote: we like state diagrams and sequence diagrams the most
claim: Inline mermaid state and sequence diagrams help when the chat UI renders them, though they are sometimes still slop.
evidence_detail: Preference stated; he admits they are 'usually better than reading words' but not always good.
landing: job lifecycle state machine and outbox flows in docs; plan PR body

source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
author: Dex
quote: HTML has replaced figma for a lot of our prototyping work.
claim: HumanLayer uses agent-generated HTML for mockups and explainers (and lets the agent embed HTML in replies) instead of design tools; show-me is billed as lighter and faster than HTML for most dev problems.
evidence_detail: Team practice; no numbers.
landing: owner view as an HTML explainer rather than markdown

source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
author: Dex
quote: npx skills add humanlayer/skills --skill show-me
claim: Skills are distributed as installable packages from a shared skills repo (npx skills add), and invoked as /show-me or by asking; user can say 'this is too much content. show me.'
evidence_detail: Install and usage instructions; asks users to tweet results.
landing: skill distribution: .claude/skills/ checked in; a reusable workflow library

source_title: /show-me: compact visual representations for coding agents (X article)
author: Dex
quote: the thing people used to love about claude - its voice, it's personality, its "soul" has been flushed out in the RL dungeon
claim: Dex asserts that RL post-training stripped the model's voice and personality, making agent output harder to read.
evidence_detail: Opinion; the blog version has the same sentence. The X article also says the built-in HumanLayer version has inline HTML and diagrams first-class and credits a skill originally from @backnotprop.
landing: nowhere obvious

source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
author: Dex
quote: agents got more intelligent on paper, but the experience of using them got noticeably worse
claim: Current coding agents answer in walls of jargon that are hard to read, and this happens multiple times a day even with newer models.
evidence_detail: Cites tweets from Yishan, Mario Zechner and Connor from Replicas, plus his own frequent experience; no numbers.
landing: agent output style: owner-view and closing-message readability; a skill or CLAUDE.md output rule

source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
author: Dex
quote: Restate your last message. Stop using jargon and speak coherently.
claim: A tiny restate-in-plain-language skill (Dillon Mulroy's /bro) is a cheap fix for unreadable agent replies; the full text is two sentences.
evidence_detail: Skill contents quoted in full; no measurement.
landing: a small skill under .claude/skills/ for restating a message plainly

source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
author: Dex
quote: your visual cortex was trained over millions of years to process rich visual information effortlessly
claim: Design the agent's communication for the human visual system (after Coda Hale): analysing prose is exhausting, so optimise tools to fit the human mind.
evidence_detail: Principle borrowed from Coda Hale's talk on intuition vs. attention; no data.
landing: phase closing message and one-page owner view: prefer diagrams, trees, tables over prose

source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
author: Dex
quote: You should be discussing the shape of the code
claim: Program design (types, signatures, call stacks) should be discussed with the human before agents write code; it is the phase many people now skip but is essential.
evidence_detail: Stated opinion; show-me is offered as the tool for this.
landing: phase routine: a design/shape review step before the draft PR's implementation; plan PR body

source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
author: Dex
quote: explore large diffs post-hoc to understand what to dig into during review
claim: The same compact visual forms can be used after the fact to navigate a large diff and decide where a human reviewer should dig.
evidence_detail: Stated use; no example numbers.
landing: Opus reviewer per PR / owner view: a visual outline of the diff

source_title: show-me: a coding agent skill for compact visual representations
author: Dex
quote: A shallow file tree, one line of responsibility per entry.
claim: A catalogue of compact forms (component trees, call stacks, file layouts with one-line responsibilities, pseudocode, types and signatures, and +/- diff syntax over trees and call stacks) replaces prose when explaining or proposing a change.
evidence_detail: Worked examples given for each form; no measurements.
landing: a show-me-like skill; plan PR body format for backend slice changes

author: Dex+others
quote: Codex subagents now fork from the caller's context instead of starting cold
claim: Fork-mode subagents inherit the caller's context rather than starting cold, and subagents can be resumed after finishing, erroring or interruption.
evidence_detail: Changelog; 'dramatic improvement' asserted, no numbers.
landing: Subagent design: fork vs cold start for verifiers and refuters (refuters need cold; implementers may fork)

also.quote: Codex subagents now fork from the caller's context instead of starting cold

also.claim: Version 0.155.0 (2026-08-12) added automatic context compaction and /compact for Codex, resumable sub-agents after finish or error, and fork-mode Codex sub-agents that start with the caller's context.

author: Dex
quote: everyone accepts that if you let models like like run unattended, they will write slop code
claim: Unattended models always write slop, so a team must either accept it or build something against it.
evidence_detail: Dex's summary of the whole unconference; Vaibhav agrees nobody disagreed.
landing: Rationale for backpressure and per-PR review
inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

author: other
quote: they don't update their agent's memory, they don't update their prompts or their skills, they actually just go build another linter
claim: One attendee vibe-coded about 70 deterministic Rust linters and, for each recurring anti-pattern, adds a linter that feeds the error back to the agent instead of editing prompts or memory.
evidence_detail: Relayed by Dex from an unnamed attendee (Chatham House); he does not say he does this himself.
landing: Recurring defect shapes become CI lint rules / import-linter contracts rather than new CLAUDE.md lines
inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

author: other
quote: if you can just write a list of a hundred rules of like this should never happen
claim: A small cheap fast model given a list of about 100 'should never happen' rules is nearly as good as a deterministic linter, easier to maintain, at higher cost and latency.
evidence_detail: Someone cited DeepSeek V4 Flash; Dex relays it; Vaibhav adds a $5 review against $1000 per feature argument.
landing: Cheap-model rule-list reviewer as a middle tier between lint and Opus reviewer
inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

author: Dex
quote: you should not like stop reading the code until you're very confident
claim: Aim for lights-off but keep reading all code until you have merged on the order of a thousand PRs over a month or two with no feedback needed.
evidence_detail: Dex goes from 50% to 90% unreviewed merges as an example; ambitious goals are fine but confidence must be earned.
landing: Owner-review gate and criteria for loosening it
inventory_ref: (B) August 2026 - AI That Works #69 Unconference Recap

author: Kyle
quote: Read the least amount of code you need to ship reliable software.

landing: nowhere obvious; limit plan size and polish per phase

author: Dex
quote: Time I decide I was wrong about everything.
claim: He expects to revise his current views within about three months, signalling that these practices are provisional.
evidence_detail: Closing remark.
landing: nowhere obvious; supports periodic re-audit of harness rules

source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
author: Dex
quote: Fable and Sol tied on this set at **33.3%** (10/30 strict checkpoint passes)
claim: On a 6-problem, 30-checkpoint subset, Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol both reached 33.3% strict pass, ahead of Kimi K3 on Modal (26.7%) and on Baseten (23.3%).
evidence_detail: Harnesses differed: Fable on Claude Code 2.1.219, Sol on Codex CLI 0.145.0, Kimi on OpenCode 1.18.0. Tiebreak: Fable 16 isolated passes vs Sol 14. One run per provider; Dex says Kimi results are not statistically significant.
landing: Model-choice evidence: top two frontier models tie on strict pass; an open-weights model is within about 7-10 points.

source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
author: Dex
quote: even brand-new models didn't break 35% pass rate
claim: Even brand-new models stay below 35% strict pass, which Dex compares to 2024 SWE-Bench levels, so the benchmark remains unsaturated.
evidence_detail: Best results 33.3% (Fable, Sol) on 30 checkpoints; Opus 5 24% earlier on 17.
landing: Calibration of how often agents leave regressions: roughly two out of three checkpoints fail some inherited or new test.

source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
author: Dex
quote: a similarly vague inverse relationship
claim: Cost versus final defect rate shows only a vague inverse relationship: spending more did not reliably reduce final defects.
evidence_detail: Modal Kimi cost estimated at $26.93 from token counts at $3/M input, $0.30/M cache read, $15/M output.
landing: Cost is a weak predictor of outcome across models; supports not defaulting to the most expensive model for every verifier.

source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
author: Dex
quote: Fable got the highest growth in cloned lines (9x increase betwen ck1 and ck8!!)
claim: Fable had the largest growth in cloned lines (about 9x from checkpoint 1 to 8) and the largest clone share, while Sol and Kimi K3 (Modal) did best at reducing normalized cognitive complexity.
evidence_detail: Most spread-chart metrics clustered across models; Kimi had the highest single-function complexity; all four new runs ended circuit_eval with higher mean cyclomatic complexity than Opus 4.8, Opus 5 and Sonnet 5.
landing: Different models degrade in different ways (duplication vs complexity), so a single quality metric would not catch all; relevant if choosing which model writes versus reviews.

source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
author: Dex
quote: less duplication might also map onto "less consistency"
claim: Lower duplication may reflect less consistency rather than better refactoring, so duplication alone is not a safe quality target.
evidence_detail: Dex's guess about why Opus 5 had least duplication by the end of circuit_eval; he says he has not read the code samples.
landing: Warning against gating on a single deterministic metric (clone %) without reading code.

source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
author: Dex
quote: Sol left 1,318 SLOC in persistent Python test files
claim: Sol left 1,318 lines of persistent Python tests while the other agents tested with shell scripts, fixtures or temporary files that the count excludes, suggesting newer models like shell-script and black-box testing.
evidence_detail: Dex flags a possible reporting bug and says more digging is needed.
landing: Where verifier scripts live: shell-driven black-box checks are a common model behaviour; a persistent test requirement in the routine would be needed to keep them.

source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
author: Dex
claim: Slop-line share was 86% Fable 5, 95% GPT-5.6 Sol, 82% Kimi K3 (Baseten), 79% Kimi K3 (Modal), versus 98/93/89% for Opus 4.8/Opus 5/Sonnet 5, so nearly all code trips the rules for every model.
evidence_detail: Averages across final problem snapshots; Dex again says it suggests the quality measures are over-aggressive.
landing: Same calibration caution as the July report; no model is a clean baseline.

source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
author: Dex
quote: have a small model do checkpoint N+1 for EVERY checkpoint
claim: Extend the handoff oracle: a small model attempts checkpoint N+1 from every saved workspace and that result is folded into the smart model's score for checkpoint N.
evidence_detail: Proposal with a tree diagram; Dex has not made progress on it ('where does the time go').
landing: A cold-resume style trial generalised: after each phase, a cheap fresh agent attempts the next step; failure indicates the previous phase left a poor state.

source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
author: Dex
quote: incorporate either/both of 1. Deterministic linters 2. LLM-based "adversarial review" with alternating models
claim: Next experiment: add deterministic linters and LLM adversarial review with alternating models after each checkpoint and see whether strict pass rates improve or worsen.
evidence_detail: Prototype planned, no results yet in this report; the 'alternating models' detail is the new element.
landing: Reviewer/refuter design: alternate the model family between author and reviewer; the harness uses an Opus reviewer per PR, so a different-family reviewer is a candidate variation.

source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
author: Dex
quote: The frontier is getting better, but I'm still not trusting them to run around lights off
claim: Despite better models, Dex still will not let agents run unattended in his codebase because hard coding problems remain.
evidence_detail: Conclusion statement backed by the 33.3% best strict pass on 30 checkpoints.
landing: Stance supporting human-in-loop phase gates.

source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
author: Dex
quote: that result is kinda disqualified by the fact that Opus 5's version of the test suite only has 557 tests
claim: Cross-run comparisons are invalid when the test suite changed (557 tests for the Opus 5 run, 566 for the later runs), so Opus 5's 'fewest final defects' is not comparable.
evidence_detail: Test-suite sizes 557 vs 566 on the shared circuit_eval problem.
landing: Methodology warning: pin the verifier version when comparing agent configurations across time (relevant to any harness before/after measurement).

source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
author: Dex
quote: Modal did not report a cost, so I estimated its **$26.93** total
claim: Where a provider reports no cost, derive it from saved token counts at fixed per-token rates ($3/M input, $0.30/M cache read, $15/M output).
evidence_detail: Cost-estimation method for the Kimi (Modal) run.
landing: Cost accounting practice for the workflow's evidence folders: record token counts, compute dollars afterwards at pinned rates.

author: Dex
quote: you solve all the new challenges, but you break something from number three, then you fail the strict pass
claim: Grade on strict pass (current checkpoint passes and every earlier one still passes), not isolated pass, because regressions are the real failure.
evidence_detail: Benchmark design; GPT-5.4 Codex won isolated pass while Opus 4.6 won strict pass in the March run.
landing: Reviewer per-PR check: earlier phases' register ids still pass at the head SHA, not only the new one

author: Dex
quote: ninety-five percent of the code written by Saul triggered at least one slop.
claim: Slop detectors (200+ Python AST rules) are aggressive and best used to compare models, not as an absolute bad-code verdict; cyclomatic complexity and cloned-line percentage were the most informative.
evidence_detail: 95% of Sol's lines hit at least one rule; Kimi K3 had >5x cyclomatic complexity growth checkpoint 3 to 8; models otherwise clustered closely.
landing: Deterministic complexity/duplication metrics as backpressure signals in CI

author: Dex
quote: Opus Vrote thirty thousand lines of code for half as many challenges and fifteen thousand lines of tests.
claim: Models write very large volumes of code; a six-challenge run costs about $200 at API prices, and one run is not enough, a proper run would repeat five times and average.
evidence_detail: Opus 5 wrote ~30k lines plus ~15k lines of tests for half the challenges; Dex used subscriptions so cost figures are approximate; single run per model.
landing: Budgeting verifier/refuter runs; repeat-and-average before trusting a comparison

author: Dex
quote: the frontier model has to set up the code base in a way that a small model can solve the next problem.
claim: A 'super strict pass': after a frontier model finishes a checkpoint, a smaller model must ace the next checkpoint on that code base; success is evidence the code base is maintainable enough to go lights-off.
evidence_detail: Dex's proposed next benchmark variant (e.g. a small open model solving checkpoint N+1); not yet run.
landing: Cold-resume style trial: a cheaper/fresh agent must continue from repository state alone

author: Dex
quote: they apply deterministic litters as a feedback loop during the challenge.
claim: Real lights-off factories gate the model with deterministic linters (e.g. a cyclomatic-complexity cap) plus a second model's review, so a fair benchmark should include those loops.
evidence_detail: Third proposed benchmark addition; Dex is unsure whether it helps or hurts.
landing: CI gates such as complexity caps and import-boundary contracts

author: Dex
quote: It might make them worse if you say, Hey, every time Fable writes a thing we have Soul review it
claim: Cross-model review as a standing gate is unproven and could make results worse rather than better.
evidence_detail: Stated as an open question ('very curious to see'); no data.
landing: Opus reviewer per PR; refuter design

author: Dex
quote: the skills exist to give the model things that are not in the weights.
claim: Keep skills only for knowledge the model cannot have (your type system, repo layout, branch named canary); instructions the model already follows, like 'run tests after every change', should go.
evidence_detail: His team threw out an agent-browser skill and would never add a GitHub CLI skill because the model already gets them right.
landing: CLAUDE.md trim criterion and skill admission test (information, not instruction)

author: Dex
quote: You don't need that anymore because the models just do it.
claim: Lines like 'always run the tests after every change' that people put in CLAUDE.md no longer pay for themselves in current models.
evidence_detail: Illustrative example given while explaining which skills and rules to retire.
landing: CLAUDE.md trim: audit for rules current models already follow

author: Dex
quote: you're actually detuning the model and like lowering your performance by having extra instructions in there.
claim: Informational context (facts the model cannot know) carries across model generations; procedural instructions the model can work out itself can detune it, so re-review both at every model release.
evidence_detail: Information-versus-instruction distinction from a mock-up; Dex does not go as far as 'throw everything out' (the advice he attributes to Boris Cherny).
landing: Sort each CLAUDE.md line as information vs instruction; re-audit on model change

author: Dex
quote: do not invoke this skill unless the user requests it by name.
claim: New models over-invoke skills, so about 80% of his team's skill descriptions were rewritten from 'you must use this skill if X' to 'do not invoke unless asked by name'.
evidence_detail: Stated as 80% of skills changed after Sol and Fable; no measurement.
landing: Skill description wording for the skills being added now

author: Dex
quote: don't just cargo cult all your skills from model to model
claim: Re-validate skills, CLAUDE.md and prompts when a new model ships rather than carrying them over, and shared skills need evals.
evidence_detail: Responds to Boris Cherny's throw-it-all-out advice; Dex agrees with 'You need evals on that' for team-wide skills.
landing: Model-change checklist; evals for any shared skill

author: Dex
quote: software is really discovering problems as you go. but most benchmarks just give you the whole problem up front
claim: Evaluate agents on increasing requirements over a code base they inherit, measuring both whether it works today and whether it stays easy to extend.
evidence_detail: Motivation for SlopCodeBench; 'position and velocity' framing; checkpoints up to 8 deep.
landing: Phase-sequence trials where each phase inherits the previous phase's repo state

author: Dex
quote: You can tell your codex model to use the claude CLI.
claim: Automatic cross-model review can be orchestrated with a bash script, a Ralph loop, or simply telling one agent CLI to call the other.
evidence_detail: Answer to a chat question; also mentions Greptile reviewing with the other vendor's model.
landing: Reviewer or refuter step that shells out to a second model

author: Dex
quote: every single thing in the harness can inf influence this outcome.
claim: Harness choices (code-search MCP, extra skills, grep vs indexed search) all shift results and are cheap to test by customising the open harness used by the benchmark.
evidence_detail: Answer to a question on MCP/skills; notes SlopCodeBench runs Sol in Codex CLI, Fable in Claude Code, Kimi in OpenCode, so harness is confounded with model.
landing: Measure harness changes on a fixed task set before adopting them

author: other
quote: give the whole spec up front of every single problem and then I try and solve it.
claim: Compare incremental checkpoints against the full spec given at once; if the latter is much better, the edge is in predicting requirements. Dex says he will add it to the benchmark but argues best product engineers ship small and iterate.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav's hypothesis; Dex: 'I think I'm gonna incorporate that' while disagreeing on the underlying belief.
landing: nowhere obvious

author: Dex
quote: what code do you still have to read, what code can you not read
claim: The frontier question for software factories in 2026 is which code must still be read and how to maximise confidence while avoiding an unrecoverable outage.
evidence_detail: Framing statement in the closing discussion.
landing: Owner review policy and what the one-page owner view surfaces

author: Dex
quote: the best models at our time are only getting 33%
claim: Best current models reach only about 33% strict pass (Sol and Fable tied; GPT-5.5 14.8%), so multi-checkpoint work is far from solved.
evidence_detail: Six challenges, one run each, stated not statistically significant; Opus 5 23-25% in the earlier run, Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.8 about 6%.
landing: Calibration for how much unattended multi-phase work to trust

author: Dex
quote: Fable did a little bit better, two percent better, but it cost five times as much.
claim: Spending roughly 5x more bought about 2 points less defect rate; the cost-vs-defect curve flattens toward an asymptote.
evidence_detail: Aggregate cost vs defect-rate chart across six challenges; some models are not directly comparable (different challenge sets).
landing: Model/effort routing for verifiers and implementers

author: Dex
quote: those perform pretty much exactly the same.
claim: The benchmark's 'just solve' prompt and 'plan then implement' prompt scored about the same, so a plan step did not show a measurable gain.
evidence_detail: Dex says he only skimmed the results and puts 'a big asterisk' on it; relays the paper's finding.
landing: Phase routine: whether a mandatory plan step earns its cost

author: Dex
quote: planning was a way to get the model to work for longer.
claim: Plans used to work mainly by keeping the model working unattended; models are now RL'd to keep going, so that benefit of planning is gone.
evidence_detail: Dex's account of the 15-to-10-months-ago planning wave; no data.
landing: Rationale for what the ship-plan phase routine is actually buying (scope control vs endurance)

author: Dex
quote: launch a sub agent to do part one, then I'm gonna check it, then launch another sub agent
claim: What worked better than one long run was doing one plan part at a time, each in its own context, checking between parts.
evidence_detail: Stated as how practice evolved; Ralph-style per-phase fresh context.
landing: One phase per new session in the routine; per-phase sub-agent with checks between

author: Dex
quote: they have to make it as generic as possible, versus you being able to just tell it
claim: Harness-provided plan mode prompts are generic; telling the model exactly which file with which sections to write ('ask me questions until we're aligned, then write a doc like this') beats them, and the design concept in the head should be written down.
evidence_detail: Discussion of Brooks 'design concept' locked in the context window and never written to a file.
landing: Custom plan template in the phase routine rather than built-in plan mode

author: Dex
quote: the next challenge in the new context window will see the scripts and be like, we test this with scripts.
claim: Whatever pattern the first checkpoint sets (e.g. ad hoc scripts instead of unit tests) is copied by every later fresh-context checkpoint.
evidence_detail: Explains why only Sol wrote Python unit tests while the other models used scripts; offered as a theory, mechanism not verified.
landing: Early-phase exemplars and conventions (what the first phases leave in the repo steer later phases)

author: Dex+others
quote: <important if="you are using the rpi:create-research skill">
claim: The coordination repo's whole CLAUDE.md is three <important if=...> blocks, each keyed to a specific skill (repo list for any rpi skill; pull-latest check for create-research; worktree layout for setup-worktree), so each instruction loads only for its workflow.
evidence_detail: CLAUDE.md of 43 lines in total.
landing: The 390-line CLAUDE.md trim: key phase and skill rules to the skill being used, so they are inert otherwise.

author: Dex+others
quote: if not, propose pull commands to the user
claim: Before research the agent checks every involved repo has the latest from its git remote and proposes the pull commands for the user instead of running them.
evidence_detail: Example commands for origin/main and upstream/master.
landing: Cold-resume and phase start: verify the checkout is current with remote before reading it as truth.

author: Dex+others
quote: Run all your sessions from here
claim: Human setup instructions live in HUMANS.md (README) and agent instructions live separately in CLAUDE.md, so humans' onboarding text never loads into agent context; sessions start from a sibling coordination repo that lists others via additionalDirectories and holds the shared skills and CLAUDE.md.
evidence_detail: HUMANS.md and README are the same file except one note; CLAUDE.md has no setup prose.
landing: Split FixFlow's human-facing text (owner notes, onboarding) from agent-loaded files; one place for shared agent config. Note CLAUDE.md here already has doc-map prose that is for humans.

author: Dex+others
quote: the Workspaces feature obviates the need for a standalone repo
claim: The template itself says the product's Workspaces feature may replace the standalone coordination repo; only shared AGENTS.md and skills might still justify it.
evidence_detail: Warning at the top of README; product doc link, no data.
landing: nowhere obvious (multi-repo is not FixFlow's shape, single monorepo).

author: Dex+others
quote: Create commands write a new numbered artifact. Iterate commands edit an existing one in place.
claim: Each phase has a create-* and iterate-* skill pair (22 rpi: skills); creates write numbered artifacts, iterates edit in place and are not separate phases.
evidence_detail: Reference listing of 22 skills.
landing: Skills under .claude/skills/: create/iterate pairing per artifact type

author: Dex+others
quote: Outline implementation never calls `create-plan` or `implement-plan`.
claim: Each artifact owns one concern (research=findings, design=options, PRD=what/why, TDD=how, outline=phases, PR description=review summary) and implementation modes are strictly separated.
evidence_detail: Reference table.
landing: Ship plan artifacts: one-concern-per-document rule

author: Dex+others
quote: may only be edited using the explicit write and edit tools
claim: Task artifacts are reached through a symlinked directory and the agent is told to edit them only with explicit write/edit tools, not Bash sed/python, so the sync layer sees every change.
evidence_detail: Injected prompt text.
landing: Observability of compliance: route evidence writes through tools that can be logged (a partial hook substitute)

author: Dex+others
quote: Choose the shortest path that addresses the main risk
claim: Not every task needs every phase; pick the shortest workflow (Oneshot, RPI, PRD-oriented, Freeform) that covers the main risk, sized by task.
evidence_detail: Guidance; 0.183.0 also added a new-task box suggesting a workflow by task size.
landing: Ship plan: tier phases by risk so small phases skip the full routine

author: Dex+others
quote: Setup may still be running, but the agent can start working.
claim: If workspace setup steps are running, failed or skipped, the session prompt lists each with its status and stderr so the agent knows its environment state.
evidence_detail: Injected prompt text.
landing: Phase-start environment status block (what ran, what failed) in session preamble

author: Dex+others
quote: Record all current decisions in the artifact before switching sessions.
claim: At a phase boundary, record all decisions in the artifact, then either update in-session if context remains or start a fresh session with the matching iterate skill when context is nearly out.
evidence_detail: Guide step list.
landing: One phase per new chat; decisions journal as the hand-off carrier

author: Dex+others
quote: A task can contain several sessions.
claim: Research, design, implementation and review each run in their own session sharing one task whose files live in a synced task directory (10 MB text limit per file), so a fresh session loses no history.
evidence_detail: Docs description.
landing: Evidence folder / task-directory as the cross-session memory carrier

author: Dex+others
quote: Later agent work can read reviewer comments
claim: Reviewer comments on artifacts are readable by later agent work, and a review-artifact-comments skill acts on comments one at a time, so review feedback is machine-consumable.
evidence_detail: Docs; Release 0.141.0 adds sending artifact threads back to the agent.
landing: Owner view: comments on plan files fed back to the next session

author: Dex+others
quote: It does not pick a future design, so reviewers can correct facts before they become design assumptions.
claim: Research phase only describes the current system (code, tests, named sources) and never proposes a design, so facts are reviewed separately from decisions.
evidence_detail: Design principle, no data.
landing: Cold-resume trial and knowledge store: separate verified current-state facts from decisions

author: Dex+others
quote: The agent can propose a choice, but the user owns the decision.
claim: Agents must not make product or design choices; design discussions keep each choice open until the user answers clearly, and PRD/TDD need explicit approvals.
evidence_detail: Checkpoint rule list.
landing: Phase routine decisions journal and owner-view: explicit decision checkpoints

author: Dex+others
quote: Vertical slices, which connect only what one result needs.
claim: Structure outlines should split work into vertical slices each ending runnable, visible or queryable (e.g. fixed API data verified with curl first), not horizontal layers.
evidence_detail: Illustrative example only.
landing: Ship plan phase design: each of the 40 phases names one testable result and its checks

author: Dex+others
quote: Later artifacts take priority over earlier ones, but current code is the source of truth
claim: When artifacts conflict, later ones win, but live code beats any document for questions of current behavior.
evidence_detail: Precedence order: plan > outline > TDD > PRD > design > research > ticket.
landing: CLAUDE.md/doc drift rule and cold-resume trial: code over prose

author: Dex+others
quote: Feedback on a structure outline changes the outline and does not start implementation.
claim: Feedback on planning artifacts revises the document only and never triggers implementation; implementation pauses after each phase for manual review by default.
evidence_detail: Checkpoint rule.
landing: Phase routine: review gate between plan revision and implementation

author: Dex+others
quote: Auto-advance does not create a duplicate newer phase.
claim: Auto-advance covers only safe handoffs (questions to research, research to design, plan to implement, implement to PR) and never design to outline or outline to implementation; each transition turns itself off after running.
evidence_detail: Rule list; auto-advance first appears in 0.117.3 fix and 0.115.0 Linear auto-advance.
landing: Phase routine: which handoffs may be unattended vs gated on owner

author: Dex+others
quote: code search speed and cost are more important than Sonnet's added analysis
claim: Faster Research Subagents (Haiku for the three codebase research agents) is an opt-in trade of analysis depth for speed and cost.
evidence_detail: Experiment toggle; org and user must both allow.
landing: Existing Haiku fixflow-explorer; cost routing for read-only agents

source_title: OrcaBot: Do Skills Improve Coding Agent Accuracy?
author: other
quote: the public workflow skills mostly wash.
claim: Measured against a contemporaneous no-skill baseline, five public skill packs mostly produce no reliable accuracy gain on SWE-bench Pro or SlopCodeBench.
evidence_detail: Codex 5.5 high; July SWE-bench Pro (729 instances, 1 seed): OMC +1.65, Superpowers-v6 +1.51, Karpathy +0.96, GSD -0.14, Agent Skills -1.10 vs 55.56% baseline; all gaps under 2 points.
landing: Evidence to weigh before adding workflow skills under .claude/skills/: skills should be measured against a no-skill baseline on this repo's own tasks, not assumed helpful.

source_title: OrcaBot: Do Skills Improve Coding Agent Accuracy?
author: other
quote: On SlopCodeBench, no: every skill collection actively hurt.
claim: In the June run every skill pack scored below the Codex 5.5 baseline on SlopCodeBench Strict, while all beat baseline on SWE-bench Pro.
evidence_detail: June SlopCodeBench Strict (n=3, mean): baseline 12.2, GSD 11.9, OMC 11.6, Superpowers-v5 11.4, Karpathy 11.1; spreads up to +/-2.3 exceed gaps. SWE-bench Pro June: baseline 52.80%, OMC 54.99, GSD 54.45, Superpowers-v5 54.17, Karpathy 53.08 (731 problems, single run).
landing: A reason skills for greenfield or evidence-light work may cost attention; keep skills task-scoped and test them on SlopCodeBench-style long-horizon work.

source_title: OrcaBot: Do Skills Improve Coding Agent Accuracy?
author: other
quote: It solves more checkpoints outright while breaking more of what it had already built.
claim: Superpowers v6 led July SlopCodeBench Strict but had the worst Core and Partial scores, so its win is narrow and within noise.
evidence_detail: July SlopCodeBench: Superpowers-v6 Strict 14.5 +/-2.3 vs baseline 13.9 +/-0.5; Core 62.6 vs 67.1; Partial 40.7 vs 46.3; erosion 0.46 vs 0.59; $/ckpt 1.71 vs 1.26.
landing: Verifier design: score regression (erosion/Core) separately from outright solves; one headline pass rate hides breakage.

source_title: OrcaBot: Do Skills Improve Coding Agent Accuracy?
author: other
quote: The single most important number on this page is the baseline's +2.76
claim: The same model name and harness version improved by more than any skill pack's edge in one month (silent server-side drift), so one-off benchmark numbers decay and must be compared to a contemporaneous baseline.
evidence_detail: Codex CLI v0.136.0, gpt-5.5 high, June to July: baseline SWE-bench Pro 52.80 to 55.56 (+2.76); SlopCodeBench Strict 12.2 to 13.9 (+1.7); verbosity 0.311 to 0.827. Karpathy pack (unchanged commit 2c60614) moved +3.44 and +1.8, tracking baseline.
landing: Any effort-routing or verifier-config decision (including Dex's medium-vs-xhigh finding) should be re-measured periodically; pin or log model/harness versions in evidence folders.

source_title: OrcaBot: Do Skills Improve Coding Agent Accuracy?
author: other
quote: the model got materially better at solving new checkpoints and no better at all at not breaking
claim: Across both months erosion (regression of earlier checkpoints) stayed within +/-0.02 for every arm while Strict rose, and erosion looks like a property of the workflow, not the model.
evidence_detail: Erosion June to July: baseline 0.58 to 0.59, Karpathy 0.58 to 0.58, Superpowers 0.46 to 0.46, GSD 0.54 to 0.53, OMC 0.52 to 0.54; no arm separates from baseline on per-checkpoint curves (cp1 about 75-81% down to 33-50% by cp8).
landing: Supports gating on regression (pass-before/pass-after) rather than trusting prompts for discipline; a backpressure/verifier concern.

source_title: OrcaBot: Do Skills Improve Coding Agent Accuracy?
author: other
quote: Every other pack buys its edge with 1.5-2x the tokens
claim: Heavier skill packs cost 1.5-2x the tokens and dollars of baseline without a matching gain; the two most expensive arms lost to baseline in July.
evidence_detail: July SWE-bench Pro tokens/problem and $/problem: baseline 1.37M/$0.37; Karpathy 1.37M/$0.37; Superpowers-v6 1.83M/$0.46; Agent Skills 2.07M/$0.52; OMC 2.19M/$0.53; GSD 2.70M/$0.61. SlopCodeBench $/ckpt: baseline 1.26, Karpathy 1.25, Superpowers 1.71, OMC 1.87, Agent Skills 2.00, GSD 2.02.
landing: Cost-per-pass should be tracked when adding skills or routines; a short guideline pack (Karpathy) was the only one at baseline cost.

source_title: OrcaBot: Do Skills Improve Coding Agent Accuracy?
author: other
quote: On a small task, it can compete with the actual specification for attention.
claim: The authors hypothesise that skill instructions help on hard unfamiliar-repo tasks but compete with the spec on small or greenfield tasks, and that TDD-style skills presume visible tests and a reproducible bug.
evidence_detail: Explanation offered, not tested: SWE-bench Pro has existing tests and regressions to use; SlopCodeBench keeps evaluator tests hidden and has no bug to reproduce.
landing: Supports scoping skills and CLAUDE.md content by task type (load procedures only for brownfield work) and keeping per-phase context lean.

source_title: OrcaBot: Do Skills Improve Coding Agent Accuracy?
author: other
quote: Because Codex is a single agent, multi-agent frameworks were applied as a single-agent sequential pass
claim: Methodology caveat: all runs used Codex (not Claude), skills mounted read-only at pinned upstream commits, multi-agent packs flattened to one agent, SWE-bench Pro single seed with 30-minute cap, SlopCodeBench n=3.
evidence_detail: Models: gpt-5.5 effort high via Codex CLI v0.136.0 in Docker; SWE-bench Pro public split 11 repos, 731 (June)/729 (July) instances; SlopCodeBench 36 problems/196 checkpoints, serial pytest; pack commits listed (GSD de73ad92 to 4fc89497, OMC a1720433 to 41a4c0f7, Superpowers v5.1.0 to v6, Karpathy 2c60614 both).
landing: Limits how far the results transfer to Claude Code with sub-agents; note when citing against Dex's Claude-based SlopCodeBench report.

source_title: OrcaBot: Do Skills Improve Coding Agent Accuracy?
author: other
quote: Any conclusion below about a pack, as opposed to the model, has a shelf life measured in weeks
claim: Skill packs update faster than they can be evaluated: three of four moved past the tested commit within about two weeks, so a skill library needs re-measurement, not one-time vetting.
evidence_detail: Checked 2026-08-07: GSD at a731a45, Agent Skills at d2478bf, Superpowers at 44c9b2d; only OMC still at its July commit. Pack updates conflate with drift (GSD +1.2 and OMC +0.5 Strict came in under drift of about +1.75).
landing: If third-party skills are adopted, pin commits and re-run a fixed check; own saved workflows should carry a version and a re-test date.

source_title: Pragmatic Leverage in the Software Factory
author: Dex
quote: only 25-50% of the time to ship a feature was writing the code itself
claim: Writing code is 25-50% of feature delivery time; using AI only for coding cuts 2-4 hours to 10-20 minutes but leaves planning, review and verification untouched, so using AI for planning and alignment is what gets near 2-3x.
evidence_detail: Rough proportions stated without a source.
landing: Where to spend agent effort: planning/verification phases, not only implementation

source_title: Pragmatic Leverage in the Software Factory
author: Dex
quote: expected pain = P(you'll have to change it) × how painful the change is
claim: Model planning effort on expected pain (probability of change times cost of change); a yolo two-sentence prompt gives about 50% rework, a perfect hand spec about 10%, writing it all yourself 0%.
evidence_detail: Illustrative numbers explicitly blurred into one percentage; not measured.
landing: Effort-routing heuristic: spend verification/plan effort in proportion to expected pain, which supports medium over xhigh for cheap-to-fix changes

source_title: Pragmatic Leverage in the Software Factory
author: Dex
quote: eliminated 80% of the expected pain in the first 10 minutes
claim: The 80/20 rule of AI coding leverage: the first minutes of planning remove most expected pain; do not spend 6 hours planning something where 10 minutes removed 80%.
evidence_detail: Illustrative example, no data.
landing: Time-box the Plan @ sha step; a stop-planning rule

source_title: Pragmatic Leverage in the Software Factory
author: Dex
quote: zooming in from 50kft view all the way to the 10kft view
claim: Plan in zoom levels, steering a little at each phase; if product-level open questions need technical feasibility, stop and zoom down a level rather than over-answer.
evidence_detail: Process advice; he admits no perfect process.
landing: Plan sections ordered product to architecture to design with an explicit 'escalate down' rule

source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (dhorthy reply)
author: Dex
quote: slop code bench forces a model to grapple with its own garbage code
claim: Dex prefers SlopCodeBench over Cognition's Frontier Code because Frontier Code uses a model judge for quality, whereas SCB makes the model live with its own code to earn the functionality reward.
evidence_detail: Reply to a commenter who cited Frontier Code as showing medium effort is the cost/quality sweet spot.
landing: Supports executable verifiers over model-judged quality; also notes an outside claim that medium is the sweet spot (conception citing Frontier Code).

source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (dhorthy reply)
author: Dex
quote: models don’t know how to simplify because most rl/benchmarks doesn’t penalize complexity
claim: Models fail to simplify because RL and benchmarks do not penalise complexity, and prompting for readability is hard (he has found it so with prose-writing too).
evidence_detail: Replies to a commenter who uses 'run /simplify at the end' in an implement skill and another who asked about harness fixes; Dex says the next step is a more factory-shaped harness with linter and model feedback after each coding episode.
landing: Caution that a 'simplify' skill or prompt step may help only a little; deterministic feedback may matter more than instructions.

source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (dhorthy reply)
author: Dex
quote: sol is still my daily driver for most coding tasks
claim: Dex uses GPT-5.6 Sol as his daily coding model, finds Opus 5 good for general knowledge work and visual design, and would not miss it if forced back to Opus 4.8.
evidence_detail: Personal usage statement in a reply; no measurements.
landing: Model-routing anecdote: different models for coding vs knowledge/design work.

source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (dhorthy reply)
author: Dex
quote: i think the implication is that low quality code is harder to change in the future
claim: Dex's answer to 'does slop matter?' is that low-quality code is harder to change later, which is what the checkpoint design is meant to measure.
evidence_detail: Reply to adamtaylor_13; commenters supplied two outside papers (arXiv 2605.20049 on cleanliness affecting agents; 2601.02200 on code health and AI-friendliness) which are not Dex's.
landing: Justification for investing in cleanup phases; no direct harness change.

source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (dhorthy reply)
author: Dex
quote: someone will have to re-run this bench on various effort levels. unfortunately it is not cheap
claim: Asked whether medium effort beats higher effort, Dex said the benchmark would need re-running at various effort levels (which he later did in October).
evidence_detail: A commenter (sothatsit) reported replacing Opus 4.8 xhigh with Opus 5 medium for fewer tokens and faster work; another said Medium or Low prevents Opus 5 overthinking (citing a third-party tweet).
landing: Provenance of the October xhigh finding; community anecdote pointing the same way before data existed.

source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (dhorthy reply)
author: Dex
quote: so wait is the finding that most of those skills reduce pass rates against SCB? wild
claim: A third-party SCB-based study (reported by robbomacrae, not Dex) found most popular agent skill packs reduce pass rates, and Dex reacted with surprise.
evidence_detail: Dex only asks the question; robbomacrae confirms 'Yep' and explains skills use context and target brownfield investigation that is wasted on greenfield; gck1 says dropping static skill workflows because models pick better ad-hoc workflows.
landing: Evidence relevant to adding skills: a skill can cost context and lower pass rate on tasks it was not designed for; skills should be measured, not assumed beneficial. Third-party finding only.

author: other
quote: did not include error bars on the cost and quality results
claim: Critique of the underlying paper: no explicit error bars, and if the +/- values are one standard deviation the models' outcomes are statistically indistinguishable; Dex's runs are likewise single runs.
evidence_detail: Commenter's statistical reading of the SlopCodeBench paper tables; Dex's own reports also run each setting once and caveat significance.
landing: Applies to Dex's effort-routing numbers too (one run per setting): treat 1-4 strict-pass differences as noise unless repeated.

author: other
quote: most models will miss the `database_migration` Checkpoint 2 test
claim: Critique: some checkpoint failures may come from spec ambiguity (a default_value readable as a JSON literal or SQL expression) rather than model quality, so checkpoint order and difficulty confound the results; reordering checkpoints is proposed.
evidence_detail: Commenter suspicion with no data; Dex replied he likes the idea of flipping checkpoint order and would look at releasing raw results.
landing: Reminder that ambiguous specs produce verifier failures that look like model failures; relevant to how fail-before/pass-after is interpreted.

author: other
quote: The benchmark leaves tests hidden with no fail-to-pass feedback
claim: Critique of method: hidden tests give the agent no fail-to-pass feedback, which may be why degradation is monotonic; the paper's plan_first prompt variant found no end-of-benchmark pass-rate effect.
evidence_detail: Commenter cites the original paper's plan_first variant; says agents refactor mainly when told to fix bugs, not when building features.
landing: Suggests the benchmark understates what agents can do with visible tests; in the harness, test feedback inside the loop is the difference.

source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (delbertty and others)
author: other
quote: Slop accumulates when the agent can touch anything
claim: Critique of the 'models can't be trusted' framing: it is mostly a harness problem, and constraining the agent to one seam and having it add alongside rather than edit in place helps more than model choice.
evidence_detail: Commenter experience; Dex's own reply elsewhere says he intends to test a more factory-shaped harness with linter/model feedback after each coding episode.
landing: Scope constraint per phase (one seam, add alongside) as a routine instruction; echoes slice boundaries already enforced by CI.

author: other
quote: each fix generates more feedback, which requires more fixes, i.e. slop
claim: Critique of review-then-fix loops: with Opus 5 reviewers, pedantic feedback made a simple one-table SQL migration balloon into a 200-line script, so review loops can themselves create slop.
evidence_detail: One commenter's automated review setup (skills/subagents with different specialties); they say the cause may be a prompt asking it to be pedantic.
landing: Risk for the Opus reviewer per PR and refuters: unbounded review/fix rounds can inflate code; cap rounds and require reviewers to cite a failing behaviour rather than style.

source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (willsmith72 / mellosouls)
author: other
quote: a 41% improvement is not much higher? come on that's just doomer
claim: Critique of framing: Opus 5's 24% vs Opus 4.6's 17% is a 41% relative gain that Dex calls 'not much higher', and different problem subsets make the comparison weak anyway; another commenter wants a human baseline.
evidence_detail: Dex compares his 17-checkpoint subset result to the paper's 17% on its own full set; the October post concedes subset results are not comparable with full-benchmark results.
landing: Reinforces R06-42: do not compare subset scores across runs; treat small gains as unproven.

author: Dex
quote: most interesting result to me was that it wrote twice as much code
claim: In his SlopCodeBench run Opus 5 solved more but wrote about twice as much code, almost all of it tests, so expect sloppy tests.
evidence_detail: Opus 5 23%/4 of 17 checkpoints, only three problems run; paper numbers Opus 4.6 17%, GPT-5.4 11%; unsaturated benchmark, models score 10-20%.
landing: Reviewer should check test volume and quality, not just that tests exist.

author: Dex
quote: you probably actually want a very saturated benchmark
claim: Model builders want unsaturated benchmarks, but your own evals should be saturated (target 99 percent) and are proprietary IP, because public benchmarks give weak signal on your out-of-distribution work.
evidence_detail: Dex notes SWE-bench-class benchmarks are near saturated.
landing: Build an in-repo, FixFlow-specific task set to choose reviewer/verifier model and effort rather than citing leaderboards.

author: Dex
quote: Diff the old and new outputs; only review where they disagree
claim: To qualify a new model, replay the same inputs through incumbent and candidate, diff outputs, and hand-review only the disagreements, which then enter the golden set.
evidence_detail: Guest Kevin Gregory's method which Dex adopts and restates in his outro; README example 28 of 30 agree. Paraphrased quote.
landing: Effort routing: run the same verifier task at medium and xhigh and review only where verdicts differ.

author: Dex
quote: replay the requests against the Python
claim: Prior-art migration pattern: replay sampled production requests against old and new service, progressive diff (status, then body with irrelevant fields stripped, then latency), cut over when green, with fresh traffic weekly.
evidence_detail: Dex's account of a Sprout Social Django-to-Java migration, circa 2015; he says he watched someone else build it.
landing: Cold-resume trial or prod-parity checks could use shadow replay with a normalised diff.

author: Dex
quote: anytime anyone makes a change, you'll be able to get one number
claim: Labelling about 30 cases by hand (a day or two) turns flailing prompt changes into a single regression number; evals are unit tests.
evidence_detail: Forward-deployed work with early HumanLayer customers: test cases flipped week to week with no baseline.
landing: A frozen set of ten facts (P1 cold-resume) is exactly this; extend to other routine steps.

author: Dex
quote: you should always start from vibes
claim: Grow evals gradually: one example by eye, then 10, then 100, refining each time, moving from 50 to 99 percent as confidence rises; use past disagreement cases as the first vibe check on new models.
evidence_detail: References the Enron emails eval; Kevin adds the disagreement-cases point.
landing: Pilot new verifier settings on a handful of known-hard past reviews before scaling.

author: Dex
quote: Make the accuracy score as deterministic as possible
claim: Judge free-text output by extracting booleans, enums and counts (rubric of structured outputs) rather than asking a model for a 1-10 score; compute what you can deterministically.
evidence_detail: Illustrated by the AI Tinkerers applicant scoring rubric; says one-to-ten scores do not work well. Paraphrased quote.
landing: Reviewer outputs a structured checklist per register id (pass/fail booleans) rather than prose verdicts.

author: Dex
quote: Everything in AI engineering is structured outputs
claim: No magic in AI engineering: it is structured outputs plus unneeded abstractions.
evidence_detail: Closing line of the show.
landing: Saved workflows return typed results (schema), not prose.

author: Dex
quote: Max accuracy drop allowed is zero
claim: Guest harness gates a candidate model with a relative budget (accuracy drop 0, cost at most 1.2x, p95 latency at most 1.5x), with thresholds made the easiest thing to change; Dex calls this proper engineering.
evidence_detail: Demo on 30 generated receipt cases; Sonnet 5 had perfect accuracy but about 2x latency and 1.6x cost; README: single-run evals gave wrong conclusions, missing price defaulted to 0 passed 4 of 5, run 3 repeats.
landing: Verifier model/effort gate: candidate must be no worse than the incumbent at a stated cost multiple; fail closed on unknown cost; repeat runs.

author: Dex
quote: Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Grok 4.5, Kimi K3, GPT-5.6, Gemini 3.6
claim: Model deprecation is an advance-notice outage; build the harness so a swap is a Tuesday, not a P0 (README claim, Kevin's framing; Dex hosts).
evidence_detail: Episode blurb and README.
landing: Pin model ids in the harness config in one place so a swap is a one-line change.

author: Dex
quote: Dex: with a few open-source models the deprecation problem is solved
claim: Dex raises self-hosted open-source models as the answer to deprecation; Kevin's team is moving to it.
evidence_detail: Guest says his company is switching to self-hosting for this reason.
landing: nowhere obvious (FixFlow does not run its own models)

author: Dex
quote: today's models can't be relied on to run lights-off without steering
claim: On an incrementally-revealed-spec benchmark, today's models cannot be trusted to build a codebase unattended, so human steering stays necessary.
evidence_detail: Opus 5 strict pass 4/17 (24%); Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 1/17 (6%) each; no model finished any of the 3 problems (9 runs) with zero defects, even the 'easy' one.
landing: CLAUDE.md / ship plan stance: one phase per session with human-reviewed gates rather than long unattended runs; supports keeping owner view and Opus reviewer per PR.

author: Dex
quote: I'm not totally sold on "linting the slop away" just yet
claim: Deterministic code-quality metrics are directionally useful but cannot yet parse maintainability, and the link between any one metric and 'easy to change' is not established.
evidence_detail: 41 deterministic metrics in six groups (size, complexity, duplication, decomposition, rule violations, dependency graph); most did not separate the models; only cc_max and cloned_pct separated them sharply.
landing: Caution against building a metrics pre-commit gate (harness skipped it); if any metric is gated, cc_max and clone % are the two that discriminated.

author: Dex
quote: its easy for a model to reward hack any of them
claim: Quality metrics can be gamed by the model, so a behavioural oracle (hidden tests over an evolving spec) is a better verifier than metrics or a model judging code cleanliness.
evidence_detail: Argument: 'pass all verifiers for an incrementally-divulged spec' beats 'does another model think this code is clean'; no experiment.
landing: Verifier design: prefer executable held-out checks over model-opinion review; relevant to refuter and reviewer prompts (evidence = test output, not judgement).

author: Dex
quote: a dumber model like sonnet 5 or gpt-5.6-terra can implement checkpoint N+1
claim: Proposed test of codebase quality: have a frontier model build the first N checkpoints, then see whether a smaller model can implement checkpoint N+1 on the result.
evidence_detail: Proposal only (illustrated with Fable 5 / Sol / Opus 5 handing to Sonnet 5 for ck8); not run in this report.
