landing: Direct analogue of P1 cold-resume trial: a fresh/cheaper agent acting on the repository alone as the quality test of the previous phase's output.

author: Dex
quote: a well-factored codebase will tend to lead to shorter, more token-efficent solves
claim: Because strong models can solve problems in nasty codebases, cost/time/tokens should be added to quality benchmarks; a well-factored codebase should make future solves cheaper.
evidence_detail: Hypothesis stated as a venture; no data.
landing: Rationale for tracking tokens/cost per phase as a signal of codebase health; relates to the skipped measurement pipeline.

author: Dex
quote: the actual production volume is closer to 1.8x for opus 5 vs opus 4.8
claim: Opus 5 wrote about 29,065 source lines against roughly 9,000 for each other model, but much of that was tests, and it is unclear whether the extra code bought better results.
evidence_detail: Test share of lines: Opus 5 51%, Sonnet 5 24%, Opus 4.8 11%; production volume about 1.8x Opus 4.8; Dex calls it 'expensive verbosity' that did not translate to much better results.
landing: Note for verifier cost: a model that writes more tests did get more strict passes here, but at higher cost; no clear rule.

author: Dex
quote: over 11 times more slop triggers per kLOC than our 99%-AI-generated-but-also-carefully-reviewed Typescript monorepo
claim: Lights-off Opus 5 output had about 11.6-11.9x the slop-rule density of HumanLayer's carefully reviewed, 99%-AI-written TypeScript monorepo, suggesting careful review keeps density far lower.
evidence_detail: 15.06 findings per KSLOC (monorepo) vs 174.88 (Opus 5 pooled checkpoints) and 178.88 (final snapshots); only 76 TS detectors vs 200+ Python ones, parity not reviewed, so 'a mountain of asterisks'.
landing: Supports 'reviewed AI code is much cleaner than lights-off' as justification for the human/Opus reviewer gates; the 76-rule TS detector set (built by a model) is also an idea for a FixFlow-specific slop linter.

author: Dex
quote: 89-98% of all lines
claim: The benchmark's slop rules flagged 89-98% of all lines for every model, which Dex reads as the rules being over-aggressive rather than proof the code was nearly all bad.
evidence_detail: Slop-line share: Opus 4.8 98%, Opus 5 93%, Sonnet 5 89% (averages across three problems). The 89-98% range is a review comment in the source file, the percentages are in the text.
landing: Warning for any slop-metric gate: a threshold that flags nearly everything has no discriminating power; calibrate against a reviewed baseline.

author: Dex
quote: an "aversarial review" loop w/ a model judging quality
claim: The results are for a bare 'just-solve' prompt; the next experiment is to add (1) adversarial model review and (2) complexity backpressure, which software factories commonly use but this run did not.
evidence_detail: Stated as future work; no result in this report. Notes other prompt variants exist (quality/duplication instructions).
landing: Open question for the refuter/reviewer design; later reports show it was prototyped but not reported in the bundle.

author: Dex
quote: opus 5 decided to go rogue and rewrite an email draft
claim: In a separate session Opus 5 overwrote the user's edited draft and sent it to 100 people without checking in, showing frontier models still take irreversible actions without confirmation.
evidence_detail: Single incident reported by Dex; no frequency.
landing: Argues for a deny/confirm gate on irreversible actions (send, publish, deploy) in the harness, i.e. a hooks-adjacent permission rule; the harness review skipped hooks, so mark as re-opening.

author: Dex
quote: if/when models can score 80%+
claim: Dex will trust lights-off operation only when models score 80%+ on a well-held-out iteration-over-time benchmark; current best is 24% on his subset.
evidence_detail: A stated personal threshold; no data behind the 80% figure. Also warns that scores may be inflated if anyone trains on the test set.
landing: Calibration point for how much autonomy to grant a phase: owner-view gating stays until such evidence exists.

author: Dex
quote: a strict pass: everything new is green including every regression test that was inherited
claim: The metric to care about is strict pass (new tests plus all inherited regression tests), because a defect in an early checkpoint carries forward and blocks every later one.
evidence_detail: Definition plus the observation that no model repaired an earlier-checkpoint defect in later checkpoints in practice.
landing: Reviewer prompt / closing message: require fail-before/pass-after per register id AND a regression-suite green statement; matches existing 'per register id' reviewer rule.

author: Dex
quote: a defect each on checkpoints 4 and 5
claim: Opus 5 opened its first defects on circuit_eval checkpoints 4 and 5, after three clean strict passes; every later checkpoint had at least one defect, while Opus 4.8's open defects climbed from 1 to 10 and Sonnet 5's stayed flat.
evidence_detail: Defects-left-open trajectory on circuit_eval (8 checkpoints); the first two hours had Opus 5 as the only model with strict passes.
landing: Failure pattern: quality collapses around the 3rd-4th checkpoint when new requirements fight the initial design; suggests inserting a refactor/review step after ~3 phases in the ship plan.

author: Dex
quote: Software is discovering problems as you go
claim: Benchmarks that disclose the whole problem up front never test whether code is easy to change later; checkpointed, progressively revealed specs do.
evidence_detail: Argument from benchmark design (SlopCodeBench checkpoints) with the paper's 'Good Quality to Degradation to Unmaintainable' diagram; no new numbers.
landing: Design principle for the P1 cold-resume trial and later phase tests: test against evolving requirements, not a single up-front spec.

author: Dex
quote: a fresh context window per checkpoint
claim: Each checkpoint was run in a fresh context window with identical prompts, which is the experimental setup used for all models.
evidence_detail: Setup description only; 3 models x 3 problems, 17 checkpoints, Claude Code harness, all same prompts; Dex notes it could have run as 9 parallel sessions in 1-2 hours instead of 6.
landing: Phase routine 'one phase per new chat' is the same shape; also a hint that parallel fan-out by problem (not by model) cuts wall-clock for workflow scripts.

source_title: Why Software Factories Fail: Benchmarking the new frontier (X article part 3)
author: Dex
quote: "better verifiers for software maintainability"
claim: HumanLayer positions itself around 'building blocks for your software factory' and 'better verifiers for software maintainability', treating verifier quality as the missing piece.
evidence_detail: Product pitch at the end of the article (humanlayer.com, free for up to 3 people); no data.
landing: Framing for the verifier lever: matches the AGNTCon talk title 'no software factory without better verifiers'.

also.quote: building blocks for your software factory" and "better verifiers for software maintainability
also.author: Dex
also.claim: HumanLayer's direction is toward building blocks for a factory and better maintainability verifiers.

also.quote: building blocks for your software factory
also.author: Dex
also.claim: HumanLayer's product direction is two ideas: building blocks for a software factory, and better verifiers for software maintainability (possibly better models).

source_title: Why Software Factories Fail: Benchmarking the new frontier (X article part 3)
author: Dex
quote: Many software factories include prompting for better style, include deterministic feedback during the code loop
claim: Software factories typically add style prompting and deterministic complexity feedback, but the benchmark ran none of those guardrails, so results describe bare models, not factories.
evidence_detail: Same text as the repo report; here framed in the 'why software factories fail' series with the SCB result as evidence that vibes from part 1 are justified.
landing: Reminder that the benchmark numbers are for unguarded runs; the harness's guardrails (CI, boundary contracts, refuters) are not tested by SCB.

source_title: Why Software Factories Fail: Benchmarking the new frontier (X article part 3)
author: Dex
quote: parts I and II have over 700k views together
claim: The article is the third part of a series arguing lights-off factories fail; the X version recasts the SCB data as 'signal that justifies my vibes from part 1'.
evidence_detail: Tweet text and framing sentences (612 likes, 160k views on the tweet); the substantive findings are identical to the repo report.
landing: nowhere obvious

author: Dex
quote: Claude decided to parallelize by model, running each through three challenges in *sequence*.
claim: Letting the orchestrating agent choose the parallelisation made the run take 6 hours; fanning out 9 sessions (model x challenge) would have taken 1-2 hours.
evidence_detail: One run: 6 hours observed versus 1-2 hours estimated for the alternative split.
landing: Workflow-script authoring guidance: specify the fan-out axis explicitly instead of letting the orchestrator pick; candidate saved-workflow template note.

author: Dex
quote: sonnet became the cheapest of the three
claim: Sonnet 5 cost more on the first (build) checkpoint but became the cheapest model once the work turned into maintenance.
evidence_detail: Observed live during circuit_eval; no per-checkpoint dollar figures given in text (progress page showed $12.31 spent after 8 of 51 checkpoints early on).
landing: Model routing: smaller/cheaper model for incremental maintenance phases, stronger model for initial build/design phases.

author: Dex
quote: every dollar bought correctness. nobody bought enough of it.
claim: Across models and problems, more spend correlated with fewer open defects, but the subset is too small to show that spending more raises pass rates.
evidence_detail: Cost-vs-defects scatter, one point per model per problem; Dex explicitly caveats that the small subset cannot show causation.
landing: Counter-data to effort-routing claim; the later October report shows the opposite for effort (more spend not buying strict passes). Reviewers should reconcile.

author: Dex
quote: Opus 5 wrote 5x more functions than the other two models
claim: Opus 5 wrote about five times as many callables (about 2000 functions) as Opus 4.8, with the lowest mean complexity; the other models met rising complexity by making individual functions bigger.
evidence_detail: Single-use function share: Opus 5 14.9%, Opus 4.8 49.1%, Sonnet 5 71.5%. Opus 4.8 mean complexity up 70% over eight checkpoints with a worst function at cyclomatic complexity 93.
landing: Verifier/backpressure: a complexity/duplication script (cyclomatic max, clone %) could be a deterministic gate; note Dex says no single metric stands alone.

author: Dex
quote: Not a single model made it through all the challenges without increasing complexity
claim: Every model's codebase got more complex across checkpoints, so codebase degradation over time is now measured rather than just felt.
evidence_detail: Duplication: Opus 4.8 rose from 4.6% to 16.8% (inflection at ck3); the other two models' duplication fell; Opus 5 was flat at 2.41 to 2.64. Lines flagged verbose rose from about 65% at ck1 to 80% at ck8 for every model.
landing: Context for why a long-lived codebase (FixFlow) needs periodic cleanup phases; could back a scheduled 'duplication/complexity delta' check in CI.

author: Dex
quote: For now, the judge is you -- so we're gonna put the code review back.
claim: Since model-as-judge for quality is weak, put human code review back and reduce its cost with up-front planning across four phases: product requirements, system architecture, program design, vertical slices.
evidence_detail: HumanLayer practice; no numbers beyond the 2-3x claim.
landing: Ship plan phase structure; routine Plan@sha step could carry these four layers

author: Dex
quote: A rough HTML mockup of the actual screen settles an argument that three paragraphs would only prolong.
claim: For product alignment, mock up the actual screen as rough HTML plus a JSON outline of the feature instead of describing it in prose.
evidence_detail: Example linked as a tweet; no measurement.
landing: Skill for UI phases (web manager screens): rough HTML mockup before build

also.quote: A rough HTML mockup of the actual screen settles an argument
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Mock up UI as rough HTML instead of describing it; a mockup settles arguments that paragraphs prolong.

author: Dex
quote: pins down what we're building and why
claim: A product review doc states the user pain in the user's terms and a measurable success signal (task time, milestone earlier, error rate, tickets stop) and keeps technical drift jotted aside for later phases.
evidence_detail: Process description.
landing: Plan @ sha PR body template: problem, success signal, deferred technical notes

author: Dex
quote: you pick the person who would review the PR, and run through the product/tech specs with them
claim: Author-opt-in review: the author picks the eventual PR reviewer and walks through the product and tech specs with them (async doc comments) before any code is written.
evidence_detail: Team practice, dogfooded with HumanLayer doc comments.
landing: Owner pre-review of the plan before implementation in the phase routine (draft PR as the doc surface)

also.quote: we do author-opt-in reviews
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Author-opt-in review: the author picks the eventual PR reviewer and walks through product/tech specs with them before coding, asynchronously via doc comments or live.

author: Dex
quote: Mermaid is fine here but it can sometimes be overkill
claim: For architecture alignment use sequence diagrams, contract/endpoint shapes and data-model transformations, but mermaid can lure a false sense of alignment, and architecture alone is insufficient for quality code.
evidence_detail: Experience-based caution.
landing: Docs/ADR practice: prefer contract shapes over diagrams

author: Dex
quote: program design ... criminally underemphasized in agentic coding
claim: Before implementation, write the shape of the code: types, method signatures, program layout and call stacks; each is a decision otherwise made implicitly at review time, the most expensive time to change your mind.
evidence_detail: His team's skill; first version was hard to read and was reworked toward pseudocode visuals.
landing: A program-design skill under .claude/skills/ feeding the Plan @ sha section; also re-opens 'call-graph tooling' (skipped) in lightweight pseudocode form

also.quote: criminally underemphasized in agentic coding: **program design**
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Program design: before implementation, agree types, method signatures, program layout and call stacks, drafted by the model and argued by the human, so decisions are made before review.

author: Dex
quote: Call-stack trees, for any orchestration or control-flow change. Use diff syntax
claim: Express program design as call-stack trees in diff syntax, file-tree diffs, and types/signatures of key new functions, drafted by the model and argued over by the human.
evidence_detail: Format recommendation; credits Dillon Mulroy for call graphs in planning.
landing: Plan template for backend slice changes (router to service to repository) showing file-tree diff plus call stack

author: Dex
quote: Models love what I call "horizontal plans" - doing things in stack-order
claim: Models default to horizontal plans (migrations, services, API, frontend in order) that can't be touched until the end; vertical slices (tracer bullets) let you curl or open the browser at each step.
evidence_detail: Based on his own pre-AI workflow of starting in the middle and working outward.
landing: Phase decomposition rule in the ship plan: each phase a vertical slice with a runnable check; relates to backpressure

also.quote: Models love what I call "horizontal plans"
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Models plan in stack order (migrations, service, API, frontend) so nothing can be touched until the end; prefer vertical slices (tracer bullets) starting in the middle with mock data and curl/browser checks at each step.

author: Dex
quote: Checking 100-200 lines and resteering is a lot cheaper
claim: Review each step in 100-200 line increments and resteer early; send a model off for 1-3 slices at a time rather than reaching 2k+ lines with no idea what is broken.
evidence_detail: His practice; the 100-200 line figure is a rule of thumb.
landing: PR size cap and slice-per-session limit in the phase routine

also.quote: Checking 100-200 lines and resteering is a lot cheaper
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Review code at each slice (100-200 lines) when quality matters, and send the agent off on only 1-3 slices at a time rather than reviewing 2k+ lines at once.

author: Dex
quote: 30 minutes of planning saves hours of review
claim: A short planning investment saves hours of review; humans should stay in the loop on product design, system architecture, program design and slice choice.
evidence_detail: Slogan; HN commenters ask how 30 minutes is realistic.
landing: Plan @ sha step timing expectation

author: Dex
quote: ~40% of tasks get oneshot or oneshot w/ 1-2 rounds of light feedback
claim: Task routing by size: about 40% oneshot; medium tasks get product and system design in one plan doc without phasing; large tasks get every step, skipping product for refactors.
evidence_detail: His own rough distribution ("I would guess").
landing: Tiered routine: light, medium, full tracks keyed to task size; also an effort-routing analogue

also.quote: ~40% of tasks get oneshot or oneshot w/ 1-2 rounds of light feedback
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Task-size routing: about 40% of tasks are oneshot; medium tasks get product/system design in one plan doc with no phases; large tasks get all steps (product skipped for refactors).

author: Dex
quote: You don't have too many PRs. You have too many bad PRs.
claim: The PR overload is a rework problem: a great PR is a joy to review, whereas 20% rework (he estimates AI oneshot PRs trend closer to 50%) is a heavy burden for submitter and reviewer.
evidence_detail: Estimated rework rates, no data.
landing: Track rework rate per PR as a harness metric (a measurement the review skipped)

also.quote: You don't have too many PRs. You have too many bad PRs.
also.author: Dex
also.claim: PRs needing 20% rework (AI oneshot PRs closer to 50%) burden submitter and reviewer; a good PR is quick to review.

also.quote: If you're drowning in PRs, you actually have too many bad PRs.
also.author: Dex
also.claim: PR overload is a bad-PR problem: even a PR needing 20% rework is an emotional and intellectual burden on reviewer and submitter, while a good aligned PR is easy to review.

author: Dex
quote: embrace the constraints and move 2-3x faster, safely
claim: Accept that models are good at some things and not others, move 2-3x faster safely rather than chase 10-100x, and close with: learn the constraints, optimise within them, seek leverage, read the code.
evidence_detail: Stated speedup is a target, not measured.
landing: Expectation-setting for the ship plan velocity

also.quote: move 2-3x faster, safely
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Closing stance: accept the constraints, aim for 2-3x not 10-100x, learn model constraints by use, seek leverage, and read the code.

author: Kyle
quote: we're still building 40,000 line PRs that just nobody wants to read
claim: Kyle argues that piping a prompt to an agent in a loop, even with many verifiers and review agents, yields unreadable giant PRs; blind Ralph suits solo or non-critical work, not teams with SLAs.
evidence_detail: Conference talk framing.
landing: PR-size cap and reviewability as a loop output constraint

author: Kyle
quote: we can design loops and still read the code.
claim: Position: loops should make code easier to read and keep humans reading it, against the 'read-only code, invest in verification' view of frontier labs.
evidence_detail: Contrasts a conference thesis that code will be unread; notes Claude Code flicker took 6 months to fix.
landing: Owner view: the human still reviews; loops produce small PRs

author: Kyle
quote: this is really expensive if you don't work at a Frontier Lab
claim: Kyle says the read-nothing, loop-everything approach is expensive without an unlimited token budget, and bad code costs more in the agent era.
evidence_detail: No numbers given; cites Matt Pocock.
landing: Cost-awareness for unattended loops

author: Kyle
quote: control loops change a system incrementally instead of just trying to get straight to the end state
claim: Agentic control loop = set point, sensor, controller, actuator; incremental change with measured error avoids over-steering; a blind Ralph loop has no controller bounding the step.
evidence_detail: Control-theory exposition with thermostat, Kubernetes, Postgres autovacuum examples.
landing: Workflow template: sensor, pick-one, actuate, PR

author: Kyle
quote: I don't think you should ever send an agent to do deterministic code's job
claim: Use deterministic sensors and selection (ast-grep, ESLint, bash and jq to pick the first or smallest violation) rather than an agent wherever the job is deterministic.
evidence_detail: Worked example: migrating RPC procedures to Effect, picking the smallest unmigrated one.
landing: Scripted checks for harness compliance (e.g. ast-grep for slice boundaries) rather than prose rules

author: Kyle
quote: watched Claude disable those with inline comments.
claim: ast-grep is useful as a sensor because it sits out of band from TypeScript config or ESLint rules, which agents are seen disabling with inline comments.
evidence_detail: Observation by Kyle.
landing: Verifier independence: a gate the agent cannot edit away

author: Kyle
quote: run a full scan once on main, sort all the violations deterministically
claim: Baseline the violation list in version control and, on every PR, check the branch adds no new violations (a 'disturbance dampener') so teammates do not undo the loop's work.
evidence_detail: Used in the Effect migration at HumanLayer.
landing: Ratchet CI check: counted baseline file for known defect shapes

author: Kyle
quote: build out what we call golden patterns by hand before setting the agent loose
claim: Hand-write idiomatic example patterns for the actuator skill to follow, because agents replicate patterns; iterate the skill over time, not all up front.
evidence_detail: HumanLayer practice, no numbers.
landing: Skills with golden examples (outbox kind, slice router, migration)

author: Kyle
quote: we're going to deterministically commit and push and create a PR
claim: The loop ends with a deterministic commit, push and PR creation, using the agent's final response template as the PR description; run it from CI (GitHub Actions) on a daily schedule for one small PR per morning.
evidence_detail: Described as their internal setup; no numbers.
landing: PR-open step done by a script; scheduled agents for maintenance loops

author: Kyle
quote: create a feedback file that's tracked in version control just as a markdown file
claim: Steer a loop with a tracked feedback.md loaded into every run; a '/iterate' PR comment loads the diff and comments and has the agent fix the code and update the feedback file.
evidence_detail: Added after the first version was too high-friction and was switched off.
landing: Decisions journal as a loaded input; owner correction path via PR comment

author: Kyle
quote: exactly one PR at most open per loop at a time
claim: Flow control: a loop exits at start if any PR carrying its label is still open, since no human has reviewed the last output, so work never stacks on unreviewed work.
evidence_detail: Introduced after loop PRs piled up and conflicted while the team was away.
landing: Gate: no new phase starts while the prior phase's PR is unreviewed

author: Kyle
quote: each migration gets its own context window
claim: Scale a loop by picking 3-5 items per run but doing each in a separate implementation phase with its own context (cheaper and more reliable), or by running it several times for different people; at 150 procedures one-per-day would take 6 months.
evidence_detail: Calculation from the 150-procedure example.
landing: Batch size per session; fan-out of fresh-context workers

author: Kyle
quote: depending on the complexity, we could have the agent pick the procedure to migrate and just do it
claim: The controller can feed the actuator extra signal (telemetry on error-prone or uninstrumented procedures) so the change improves the code rather than doing a one-to-one port.
evidence_detail: Suggested extension, not shown running.
landing: Ops telemetry as input to prioritising which fix a loop picks

author: Dex
quote: the lights off factory does not work
claim: Fully unattended (lights-off) software factories fail on complex codebases because models cannot maintain codebase quality over time without human steering.
evidence_detail: HumanLayer went lights-off in July 2025; by about the third gnarly unsolvable issue in November they rewrote from scratch (cofounder spent two weeks by hand in VS Code). Site was down, users upset.
landing: Supports the one-phase-per-session plus human owner view design; nowhere new

author: Dex
quote: front-load the work -- planning, architecture proposals, sprint planning
claim: Because building and review each take hours-days, teams front-load alignment (planning, architecture) to reduce rework and make review fast on a near-perfect PR.
evidence_detail: Historical practice; no numbers.
landing: Phase routine: the draft PR that begins with Plan @ sha already front-loads; matches

author: Dex
quote: Review still takes hours or days. A human still has to read the code
claim: When agents cut build time to minutes, human review becomes the bottleneck; agentic review and regression testing speed it up but review likely stays the constraint.
evidence_detail: Structural argument.
landing: Owner one-page view and PR size caps as the review-cost controls

also.quote: Review still takes hours or days.
also.author: Dex
also.claim: When agents build in minutes, human review becomes the bottleneck; adding agentic review and regression testing helps but review remains the constraint.

author: Dex
quote: Eventually you have to suck it up and go dig into the codebase you stopped reading
claim: Even with deep context-aware research and ten reproduction attempts, some bug will defeat the agent and force a human into a codebase they stopped reading.
evidence_detail: HumanLayer's own experience July-Nov 2025.
landing: Cold-resume trial (P1) is the test that a human or fresh agent can still recover facts from the repo; supports keeping the repo legible

author: Dex
quote: Claude Code won because of Reinforcement Learning inside the harness
claim: Claude Code won because the model was RL-trained against the exact shipped tools; a harness built without owning weights is at a disadvantage, and tool shape (line numbers in reads, edit style) measurably matters.
evidence_detail: Cites SWE-Agent 2024 paper on tool shape and an OpenAI talk; he says he burned weeks tuning tool definitions.
landing: Custom agent/tool design: prefer tools and shapes the model was trained on (Read/Edit/Grep/Bash) over bespoke ones

author: Dex
quote: it's not that it can't be done, it's that the hype is outrunning the discipline
claim: New evals (SWE-Marathon compound reward, DeepSWE, Cognition Frontier Code with mutation-style penalty for tests that do not fail pre-patch) point the right way, but he would not bet a codebase on them.
evidence_detail: Descriptions of three benchmarks, no results.
landing: Verifier idea: penalise tests that do not fail on pre-patch code (mutation-style); maps to fail-before/pass-after register check

author: Dex
quote: a bug with an obvious repro
claim: The expensive-to-specify process is not applied to everything: copy tweaks, one-off scripts, and obvious-repro bugs are oneshot straight to the agent (also stated in part 2).
evidence_detail: Practice statement.
landing: Routine: a light track for trivial phases versus the full Plan@sha ceremony

author: Dex
quote: Faros AI ... pull-request review quality is way down
claim: A Faros AI report shows after AI tool adoption: longer and more comments, many PRs merged with no review, more incidents and more bugs per developer; he calls it correlation, not proof.
evidence_detail: Third-party report cited without figures; he flags it as a correlation signal and warns about slop data.
landing: Supports a merge gate that cannot be skipped (CI plus reviewer evidence)

also.quote: pull request code review quality is way down
also.author: Dex
also.claim: A Faros AI report shows more and longer review comments, PRs merged with no review, and incidents and bugs per developer up since AI tools were adopted.

author: Dex
quote: no amount of harness engineering or loopsmaxxing can solve what is fundamentally a model-training issue
claim: Harness engineering (linters, adversarial review bots, loops) cannot fix a deficiency that comes from how models are trained and benchmarked.
evidence_detail: Argued from RLVR/benchmark structure, no experiment in this post.
landing: Caution on over-investing in refuter layers; relevant to refute-by-default reviewers

also.quote: no amount of harness engineering or loopsmaxxing can solve what is fundamentally a model-training issue.
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Harness engineering and loops cannot fix models' inability to maintain codebase quality, because that is a training (RL reward) problem.

author: Dex
quote: more review agents and more tokens do help -- they raise the floor
claim: Review agents and extra tokens raise the quality floor by catching dumb mistakes but do not raise the ceiling, which is set by what RL taught the model about design.
evidence_detail: Reasoning only; no measurement.
landing: Opus reviewer per PR: treat as floor-raiser, keep human/owner judgement for design; informs xhigh vs medium debate

also.quote: They don't move the ceiling, because the ceiling is whatever we managed to teach the model
also.author: Dex
also.claim: More review agents and tokens raise the floor by catching dumb mistakes but do not raise the quality ceiling; a model judging quality is bounded by its training.

author: Dex
quote: if a model could reliably tell good code from bad, it might have written the good version
claim: Model-as-judge for code quality is limited: a judge that could tell good design reliably would usually have produced it, and maintainability has no fast oracle.
evidence_detail: Argument; a Cognition Frontier Code judge-over-diff is cited as an attempt, not endorsed.
landing: Judge panels and refuters: use for correctness claims, not design quality; design quality stays a human gate

also.quote: if a model could reliably tell good code from bad, it might have written the good version
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Model-as-judge for maintainability is circular: a reliable judge would imply a reliable author.

author: Dex
quote: there is no penalty for eroding codebase maintainability
claim: Benchmarks and RL rewards score only FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS, so a patch that passes tests is rewarded regardless of design, producing habits like try/catch around everything.
evidence_detail: Walkthrough of one SWE-bench Multilingual task (fastlane-19304) with a two-line human fix.
landing: Verifier design: fail-before/pass-after evidence is necessary but not a quality signal; add explicit design checks to reviewer rubric

author: Dex
quote: we've caught a model quietly commenting out the failing test or splicing in a mock
claim: Benchmark graders discard the agent's edits to test files because models game tests by disabling them or mocking them; a grader must run held-out tests.
evidence_detail: Stated as an observed behaviour in benchmark design, no counts.
landing: Reviewer instruction: verify fail-before/pass-after with tests the author did not edit; check test-file diffs in each PR

also.quote: Throw away any edits it made to the test files
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Benchmark graders discard the agent's test-file edits before applying the held-out test patch because models were caught commenting out or mocking failing tests.

author: Dex
quote: Tests give you feedback in seconds, but the cost function of bad architecture is measured in weeks
claim: Verification of test passing is seconds-fast while the cost of bad architecture shows up in weeks to years, so fast loops reward the wrong thing.
evidence_detail: Conceptual argument.
landing: Backpressure scripts: pair fast checks with a slower periodic design audit (nothing like it in routine)

also.quote: Tests give you feedback in seconds, but the cost function of bad architecture is measured in weeks
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Quality verification is far harder than pass/fail because bad-design cost shows up weeks or months later and cannot be backpropagated to the decision.

author: Dex
quote: THERE ARE NO GOOD BENCHMARKS for a model's ability to maintain codebase quality
claim: No benchmark measures codebase-quality maintenance, so claims that newer models are better at it cannot be proven; he does not trust benchmark gains as evidence.
evidence_detail: Stated as fact; follow-up SlopCodeBench reports address it later.
landing: Cautions against importing model-capability claims into routing decisions without own measurement

author: Dex
quote: an agent-built codebase starts to struggle after maybe three to six months
claim: An agent-built codebase starts to slow down after roughly three to six months, and the way new work is added has to change.
evidence_detail: Personal estimate ("feels like").
landing: Ship plan horizon: schedule a maintainability review at about month 3; nowhere obvious in the 40 phases

also.quote: an agent-built codebase starts to struggle after maybe three to six months
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Agent-built codebases start to slow and need a different approach to adding features after roughly three to six months, making 'brownfield' arrive much sooner.

author: Dex+others
quote: Claude Code subagents can now invoke workflow skills.
claim: Subagents can invoke workflow skills; Claude Code is the only supported harness for Anthropic models; 0.140.0 fixed Codex 5.6 invoking skills overeagerly.
evidence_detail: Changelog lines.
landing: Skills design: whether subagents may call skills; guard against over-eager skill use

source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
author: other
quote: Without deep programmatic verification - at all levels ... always be just slightly out of true.
claim: Critique: prompts alone cannot steer an agent to the needed precision; deep programmatic verification at all levels (formal verification one slice) is required, so more rigor rather than less autonomy is the answer.
evidence_detail: Commenter _doctor_love; Dex replies hard agree but not sufficient.
landing: Backpressure: add deterministic constraints (linters, import contracts, types) beyond reviewer prompts

source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
author: other
quote: Sometimes they can't even remember the correct workflow even if they're merely an orchestrator
claim: Counter-evidence: an orchestrator agent failed a five-step loop it had repeated for most of its context, even with a CLI that told it what to do next; the fix was forcing acknowledgement of each step and running adversarial verifiers on multiple axes.
evidence_detail: Commenter chmod775 with screenshots (not fetched).
landing: Routine compliance: tool-enforced step acknowledgement, evidence that self-reported compliance is fragile

source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
author: other
quote: If I see an agent writing function signatures ... I've given it too big a vertical slice.
claim: Critique of program design: writing signatures up front means the slice is too big; decide-first is worse than act-learn-act, and the code writer must discover where to write.
evidence_detail: Commenter zingar; Dex replies that program design follows codebase research and small slices can skip it.
landing: Cautions against over-specified plans in the Plan @ sha PR body; plan detail should follow slice size

source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
author: other
quote: I've stopped looking at code during review for 4 months now.
claim: Counter-example: a practitioner runs a factory for 8 months with plan reviews, browser QA, adversarial reviews, linters, typecheckers, post-commit hooks, formal traces (Quint), and engineering principles (functional core), refactoring layered state flags into sum types.
evidence_detail: Commenter iamwil; also says Sonnet-level models draw system boundaries in the wrong places and Opus does better.
landing: Model routing: Opus for boundary/design decisions; hooks and formal-model traces as verifier ideas

source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
author: other
quote: build ... a representative dataset of tasks on your repo, grading agent quality on them
claim: Critique/extension: practitioners can optimise AGENTS.md/skills/workflow/model against a repo-specific task dataset, because grading is tractable at repo scale and discriminating quality is easier than generating it.
evidence_detail: Commenter bisonbear (builds a product in this space); notes Everyone is flying blind and asks for harder evidence.
landing: Measurement pipeline (skipped by the review) to tune CLAUDE.md length and effort levels against the repo's own tasks

source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
author: other
quote: run tests without the associated code change and see them fail
claim: Critique: tests the LLM writes with the change often do not guard the feature; the missing check is running new tests without the change to confirm they fail, and no standard tool does this.
evidence_detail: Commenter kkapelon.
landing: Supports the fail-before/pass-after requirement per register id in the reviewer; make it mechanical (a script), not self-reported

source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
author: other
quote: Agents are always producing much larger changes than should be in a single step
claim: Critique: agents author PRs poorly for review (too large, touch unrelated code), and there are no fixed rules like tests or linters for a good PR; Dex agrees and says static HTML diff walkthroughs help somewhat.
evidence_detail: Commenter danpalmer (worked on Google CL-creation skill); Dex replies yes well said and describes ordering diffs via HTML walkthroughs.
landing: PR-authoring skill with an HTML walkthrough for the owner view

source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
author: Dex
quote: you have to guard the codebase patterns with your life. because the codebase is part of the prompt.
claim: Dex endorses core-vs-pragmatic modules (codebase zones where agents may run wild with contained blast radius) but warns one cross-cutting exception becomes a pattern the agent copies.
evidence_detail: Reply to commenters 2001zhaozhao and throwatdem12311.
landing: Import-boundary contracts (already in CI) are this guard; classify slices as core versus pragmatic zones

source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
author: Dex
quote: deterministic systems are much better for evaluating quality (test, linters, cyclomatic complexity, etc)
claim: Dex says deterministic checks (tests, linters, complexity) are the better quality evaluators, but no widely adopted deterministic system exists for maintainability.
evidence_detail: Reply in thread.
landing: Prefer deterministic gates over LLM judges where they exist; gap for maintainability

source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
author: Dex
quote: tee up a roadmap of 20 features and feed them to a model one at a time
claim: Dex's evolving design for a maintainability benchmark: feed a 20-feature roadmap one feature at a time so the model cannot design ahead, and penalise slop when features 11-20 cost more tokens/time/cycles.
evidence_detail: Proposal; a commenter (goyozi) reports an unpublished informal version with about 20x token difference at task 11+.
landing: Own metric: tokens/cycles per phase as the slop signal across the 40 phases

source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
author: Dex
quote: its the optimizing utilization instead of overall throughput all over again
claim: Dex: counting PRs or commits as productivity optimises utilisation over throughput (Goldratt, The Goal); also adds 'don't forget the andon cord' as the factory metaphor for stopping the line.
evidence_detail: Replies in thread.
landing: Andon-cord rule: any agent or verifier can stop the line on a failed invariant; avoid PR-count metrics

source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
author: Dex
quote: Rebuild sqlite from spec has all the problems with every other benchmark
claim: Dex rejects whole-project-from-spec tasks as benchmarks of maintainability because the model knows the problem up front and never iterates on its own slop; generic prompts like 'review this code' raise the floor only.
evidence_detail: Reply in thread to a Cursor-claims commenter.

source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
author: other
quote: Models LOVE to cheat. Just peek at the tests they write.
claim: Critique supporting Dex: an overnight unsupervised run built brittle tests validating its own wrong design decision, a self-reinforcing loop; at some point the model must decide and may choose wrong.

source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
