source_title: HN thread: Why Software Factories Fail
author: Dex
quote: you know a bad pattern when you see it because at some point you were up at 2am debugging it
claim: Dex defines taste as hard-earned intuition about anti-patterns (from Jake Nations) and ties it to why a human must set what to ask for.
evidence_detail: Reply in thread; links a Jake Nations talk.
landing: Owner-written anti-pattern list (what blew up before) as a verifier input; relates to the 'known defect' sections of CLAUDE.md
inventory_ref: dated list, 2026-07-22/23 wsff essay entry (HN 49023019, line ~110)

author: Dex
quote: Agents really start to struggle after maybe 3 to 6 months.
claim: Codebases degrade under agents after roughly 3 to 6 months even with advanced prompting.
evidence_detail: Stated from own experience; quoted in third-party summary.
landing: Horizon for the 40-phase plan: schedule a human architecture review before month 3

author: Dex
quote: about 30 minutes of upfront planning
claim: About 30 minutes of upfront planning (product review, architecture, program design, vertical slices) can save hours of review and keeps line-by-line review feasible; model judges raise the floor, not the ceiling.
evidence_detail: No measurement; benchmark durations (15 min vs up to 400 hours) cited as context.
landing: Plan @ sha step; limits the value of model-judge panels as a quality ceiling

also.quote: 30 minutes over here in pre-planning and alignment can save you hours in review
also.author: Dex
also.claim: A staged up-front chain (product review, architecture, program design, vertical slices) cuts review time and makes reading every line feasible.

author: Dex
quote: there is no penalty for eroding codebase maintainability
claim: Coding RL rewards (FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS tests) never penalise design erosion, which explains try/catch-everywhere and lazy type casts.
evidence_detail: Worked example from SWE-bench Multilingual fastlane task; no measurement of slop rates.
landing: Reviewer checklist for design smells the model is not trained against (blanket try/catch, casts); mypy-strict and lint-imports already backstop some

author: Dex
quote: it penalizes the model for writing tests that don't fail on the pre-patch code
claim: Frontier Code's deterministic quality check: penalise tests that do not fail on pre-patch code (mutation-testing flavour), plus a judge model over the diff against quality rules.
evidence_detail: Describes Cognition's benchmark design; no results.
landing: Matches 'fail-before/pass-after per register id' reviewer rule; could be made a mechanical check

author: Dex
quote: we went full lights-off. Just read the specs and the tickets
claim: HumanLayer's own lights-off trial (July 2025) ended with an unsolvable bug, site downtime and a two-week manual rewrite of patterns by the cofounder around the third incident in November.
evidence_detail: First-person account; about two weeks digging through output, then two weeks rewrite; no metrics.
landing: Rationale for keeping human code review; a lights-off phase should be treated as a risk

author: Dex
quote: THERE ARE NO GOOD BENCHMARKS for a model's ability to maintain codebase quality
claim: Models improved at one-off problems but not clearly at keeping codebase quality over time, and no good benchmark exists to show otherwise.
evidence_detail: Explicitly unprovable; model-generation sketch chart only.
landing: Do not assume newer models relax review; measure on own repo

author: other
quote: +25% more review comments, +22.7% longer comments, +31.3% of PRs skip review entirely
claim: Dex cites the Faros AI report (as image alt text): since AI tools spread, review quality fell, 31.3% of PRs skip review, incidents per PR up 242.7%, bugs per developer up 54%; he calls it correlation, not a smoking gun.
evidence_detail: Faros figures: +25% comments, +22.7% longer, +31.3% skipped review, +242.7% incidents per PR, +57.9% monthly incidents, +54% bugs per developer; Dex flags it as correlational.
landing: Evidence for not letting PRs merge unreviewed; context for the Opus reviewer per PR

author: Dex
quote: Is a skill issue -- that if you're not getting good results
claim: Against the 'skill issue / spend more tokens / stop reading code' advice: he argues the limits are model-training limits, not user error.
evidence_detail: Rhetorical position.
landing: Resist a token-maxxing posture for verifiers (links to L1 effort routing)

author: Dex
quote: less time reviewing every line
claim: Front-load alignment: about 1 hour of up-front planning cuts rework and review from roughly 6 hours to 20 minutes (figure caption).
evidence_detail: Illustrative numbers in a diagram alt text, not measured.
landing: Justification for the plan-first phase routine; plan review before code

author: Dex
quote: a short doc that pins down *what* we're building and *why*
claim: Product review: a short doc fixing the user problem and what success looks like (a readable post-ship signal), kept in product terms; technical thoughts are jotted for later phases.
evidence_detail: Team practice with screenshots; not for copy tweaks, one-off scripts or bugs with obvious repro.
landing: A product-review skill or plan-template section (problem, success signal) for owner-facing phases

author: Dex
quote: how the services, endpoints, schemas, queues, and stores talk to each other
claim: System architecture step: sequence diagrams, contract/endpoint shapes and data models/query shapes, with the warning that Mermaid can give a false sense of alignment.
evidence_detail: Template with examples; says architecture alone is insufficient for quality.
landing: Plan template sections for new slices (contract, schema, sequence)

author: Dex
quote: **Call-stack trees**, for any orchestration or control-flow change.
claim: Use diff-syntax call-stack trees and file-tree diffs (NEW/MODIFIED) in plans so reviewers see control flow and layout changes; endorses call graphs in planning (Dillon Mulroy).
evidence_detail: Example snippets; no results.
landing: Plan template; the harness review skipped call-graph tooling, but this is a lightweight text version (marks a re-open of that skip)

author: Dex
quote: every one of them is a decision you'd otherwise be making implicitly during code review
claim: Types, signatures and call trees are cheap to produce and surface decisions that would otherwise be made at the most expensive moment, in code review.
evidence_detail: Stated.
landing: Plan-phase gate: signatures and layout agreed before code

author: Dex
quote: a bunch of potentially-bad model tics that you can head off during this phase
claim: Architecture review is high leverage because it catches known model tics early, but alone it does not give high-quality code.
evidence_detail: Stated.
landing: Known-tics list in a skill or reviewer prompt (model failure modes for this repo)

author: Dex
quote: only 25-50% of the time to ship a feature was writing the code itself
claim: Pre-AI, coding was only 25-50% of feature time (e.g. 2-4 hours of a two-day feature); AI that only writes code leaves the rest unaccelerated.
evidence_detail: Illustrative wheel diagrams; coding 2-4 h down to 10-20 min.
landing: Measure where phase time goes (plan/review/test), not only coding time
inventory_ref: Essay side quest (repo line 22, wsff line 110)

author: Dex
quote: if you use AI to help you plan and align, then you actually get closer to 2-3x faster.
claim: Using AI for planning and alignment, not just code, shrinks review and testing time too, giving roughly 2-3x.
evidence_detail: Diagram reasoning.
landing: Plan-phase AI assistance and aligned plan as the lever
inventory_ref: Essay side quest (repo line 22, wsff line 110)

author: Dex
quote: about 80% of the expected pain is gone in the first few minutes
claim: 80/20 rule: expected pain (P(rework) x cost) falls on an inverse-exponential curve; yolo prompt ~50% rework (2 min), afternoon hand-spec ~10% (5 h), all by hand ~0% (20 h); don't spend 6 hours where 10 minutes removes 80%.
evidence_detail: Three illustrative points (50%/10%/0% at 2 min/5 h/20 h), explicitly assumed, not measured.
landing: Effort routing for planning depth: cap plan time per phase; short plans first
inventory_ref: Essay side quest (repo line 22, wsff line 110)

author: Dex
quote: if you build a harness but you don't own the weights
claim: Claude Code won partly because Anthropic RL'd the model inside its harness; tool shape matters (SWE-Agent), so harness tools should match what the model was trained on.
evidence_detail: Cites SWE-Agent 2024 and OpenAI's talk; no numbers.
landing: Prefer the built-in tools and standard tool shapes over custom ones; keep custom agents/tools few and simple

author: Dex
quote: Those people are all really dang smart
claim: Counter-claim to StrongDM-style lights-off factories and OpenAI Symphony: he found no definitive outcome data from StrongDM and lists outages from agent mishaps.
evidence_detail: Cites FT outages, Mario's talk, Matt Pocock; no figures of his own.
landing: Keep human gate on merges; treat factory claims as unproven

author: Dex
quote: Twenty percent of the possible memories, but all really useful
claim: A memory system should be a lagging indicator promoted from volume (what many sessions repeat) rather than a single model decision, accepting fewer but always-useful memories.
evidence_detail: Design of 'context shards'; the feature was not yet built. Quote is Vaibhav's framing that Dex adopts.
landing: Knowledge-store design: promote entries into CLAUDE.md/skills only after repeated evidence, not on first sighting.

author: Dex
quote: Claude is now like obsessed with adding environment variables
claim: Auto-saved model memory generalises a one-off instruction into a standing pattern (one env var request led to env-var feature flags everywhere), and HumanLayer runs Claude with memory switched off.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav's story; Dex states memory is disabled when running Claude in HumanLayer.
landing: Check the harness for auto-memory pollution; memory files are curated by hand with a high bar.

author: Dex
quote: purely additive set. So the first 10 look good
claim: Memory/rule lists that only ever grow turn into an unreviewable pile; the design needs triage, dismiss-with-snooze (30 days, re-ask if still repeated), and decay of unused entries.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav raises the problem (CodeRabbit comparison); Dex answers with snooze and a decay supervisor.
landing: Gives a mechanism for CLAUDE.md trim: entries expire unless re-justified; knowledge-store staleness handling.

author: Dex
quote: Our Claude MD is things that are always true
claim: CLAUDE.md should hold only things that are always true for everyone; task-specific advice should be conditionally activated and injected as the conversation shows it is relevant.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav states it, citing Dex's AI Engineer talk; Dex agrees and adds always-on versus conditional as the second axis.
landing: CLAUDE.md trim: move task-specific invariants to skills or scoped docs loaded by path/task.

author: Dex
quote: you get memories activated based on the contents of the conversation
claim: Instead of editing the system prompt, inject context into the running conversation when a classifier decides it is relevant (done in the background in parallel).
evidence_detail: HumanLayer's described approach for shards; milestone two, not built.
landing: A hook or skill that injects the relevant invariant when a file or topic is touched; hooks were skipped by review (mark).

author: Dex
quote: post tool use hook that goes to our API
claim: A 'supervisor' is a post-tool-use hook that parses a written file's front matter, asks Haiku one question (open questions left?), and injects a nudge into the write response telling the agent the next phase.
evidence_detail: HumanLayer production mechanism: under a second, no agent loop, survives compactions.
landing: A hook on writes to the phase PR/journal that checks required sections and injects next-step reminders; re-opens the skipped hooks decision (mark).

author: Dex
quote: anyone that tells you they have a supervisor agent, that's all they have
claim: A supervisor agent is only a handful of small prompts with structured output that inject more prompts into the main loop, not a separate complex agent.
evidence_detail: Dex and Vaibhav; the HumanLayer one runs about 15 small pipelines keyed on tool calls.
landing: Cheap Haiku structured-output checks as reusable agents/scripts rather than full agent loops.

author: Dex
quote: if you give the agent exactly one job, it will do the job better
claim: Single-job agents with one prompt and one structured output beat the generic agent harness for focused tasks, which carries noise that is overkill.
evidence_detail: Context-engineering argument; no data.
landing: Narrow custom agents (locator, checker) in .claude/agents/ with one job each.

author: Dex
quote: I'm probably willing to spend around $10 for this system
claim: Budget cost and latency per loop: roughly $10 of supporting system per $100 main-loop task, and the trigger sets the mode (cron means batch where lag is free, a Slack message means instant).
evidence_detail: Vaibhav's illustration, with Dex agreeing; illustrative numbers.
landing: Effort/cost budget for verifiers relative to the build phase (about a tenth of main-loop cost).

author: Dex
quote: just burn the frickin' tokens
claim: Spend tokens freely until the cost shows up as a bottleneck, then engineer it; if it is not valuable, turn it off.
evidence_detail: Team rule of thumb stated twice.
landing: Counterweight to effort-routing economy; tune only after observed cost problem.

author: Dex
quote: view all the generations and then be like, okay, that one's good
claim: Build the eval set by viewing every generation in an internal admin view, marking good or bad, turning the bad ones into test cases, and having a model edit the prompt until all pass.
evidence_detail: Dex's stated method for experimental AI features; 'vibe-based evals' by Vaibhav.
landing: Decisions journal and phase outputs could double as a review log that feeds regression cases for the reviewer.

author: Dex
quote: just slice everything into shards
claim: Distil team knowledge with a batch job over only the user and assistant messages (not tool calls) extracting a structured 'fact + citations (who, quote, context)' array, then gate it through a human allow/deny list.
evidence_detail: Design whiteboard for context shards; not built.
landing: Knowledge-store pilot: extract candidate facts from session transcripts with citations, human approves before they enter CLAUDE.md.

author: Dex
quote: A new inbox. And I don't want a new inbox.
claim: Route approvals for agent-suggested changes to an inbox people already use (Slack) as a yes/no, rather than a new review queue.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav's product point; Dex agrees and wants memory feedback in Slack.
landing: Owner view and approvals stay in the PR; do not add a separate dashboard.

author: Dex
quote: The first person to kind of take on a problem takes on a heavy responsibility
claim: Design workflow: one owner thinks the feature through with mockups and scenarios, one or two others read the doc before a synchronous discussion, then the owner drives it to completion.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav describes it as what both teams do; Dex's session followed it and the feature changed 20-30 percent from feedback.
landing: Plan-before-code gate: reviewer reads the plan doc first, then the owner view; cheap to change before build.

author: Dex
quote: I want to see the HTML
claim: Show prototypes as HTML mockups or high-fidelity fake-data prototypes, not wireframes, to find out whether a feature is worth building before investing.
evidence_detail: References Marty Cagan product discovery levels.
landing: nowhere obvious (product practice, not harness)

author: Dex
quote: cut off like what's the first milestone
claim: For a very large feature, do a broad PRD, cut the first milestone, and drill into technical design only on that milestone, plumbing it end to end and testing with curl before anything else.
evidence_detail: Dex's workflow contrasted with Vaibhav's PRD to technical design to slices order.
landing: Phase slicing in the ship plan: first vertical slice proves the plumbing.

author: Dex
quote: I don't let it make the design choice of do you want this or not
claim: Give the agent the whole feature list rather than letting it cut scope for cost or time, because tokens are cheap; humans keep the product decisions.
evidence_detail: Said while joking about a new Fable/Sonnet-class workflow; hedged in jest.
landing: Scope cuts stay a human decision recorded in the decisions journal.

author: Dex
quote: you get way more detail in there than you can while you type
claim: Drive agents by voice; people dump more detail by speaking than typing (Whisperflow named).
evidence_detail: Aside during the stream.
landing: nowhere obvious

author: Dex
quote: The less context window you use, the better outcomes you'll get always.
claim: Less context used always gives better results; the early part of the window is the 'smart zone' and beyond it is the 'dumb zone'.
evidence_detail: Credited to Huntley's Ralph work; no numbers beyond heuristics.
landing: Phase routine: one phase per new session; add an explicit token ceiling to the routine

author: Dex
quote: I don't read the research docs.
claim: Match human attention to model weakness: research is hands-off (models are good at it), design/architecture needs a human in the loop, and plans should be vertical slices not horizontal layers.
evidence_detail: Describes his research/design/plan session split; horizontal plans (DB, service, API, UI) untestable until the end.
landing: Phase routine: where the owner reads (design only); plan template requires vertical slices with a check per slice

author: Dex
quote: I would rather read five separate little mini diffs
claim: Prefer five small manually verifiable diffs to one 2,000-line change, because a failure in a large diff cannot be localised.
evidence_detail: Judgement from building by hand; no data.
landing: Phase sizing / PR size limit in the routine

author: Dex
quote: the plans that we were building last summer were actually terrible.
claim: Retraction: the original RPI plans (every line as diff blocks) gave no leverage, got skimmed, and doubled review time because plan and PR were both read; plan reading is anti-leverage.
evidence_detail: Self-correction: they recommended reading plans, then stopped doing it themselves.
landing: Ship plan phase routine: avoid code-level plans; keep plan at design/outline level

author: Dex
quote: a very powerful lever to get agents to work for longer
claim: A plan doc mainly works as an anchor that keeps an agent working until the plan is done; summer-2025 interest in planning was really about longer agent runs.
evidence_detail: Burrito B2B SaaS example: without a plan, a homepage; with a plan, it keeps going.
landing: Plan acts as completion checklist in the draft PR body

author: Dex
quote: I throw the docs out and the next time I need research I just do it
claim: Retraction: research/plan docs are tactical, per-task artifacts to throw away; regenerate research fresh because tokens are cheap and stale docs mislead. Specs drift from code, so code stays the source of truth.
evidence_detail: Kept docs for 2-3 months then stopped; cites a year-old spec-kit GitHub issue on spec/code drift.
landing: Knowledge-store design (verified diagnoses) and prose-doc drift; argues for expiry or regeneration over evergreen docs

author: Dex
quote: I have very few opinions on like what sorts of docs
claim: He has found no one who found it worthwhile to maintain parity between documentation/specs and code; evergreen docs have a poor effort-to-value ratio even if AI could update them.
evidence_detail: Based on people he has seen try; not measured.
landing: CLAUDE.md and docs/ trim; the knowledge store must justify its upkeep

author: Dex
quote: We built a lights off software factory in July of 2025
claim: Lights-off factory (no human code review) built July 2025 was shut down by November 2025; production broke, Opus 4.1 could not find the root cause, and re-onboarding took about 3 weeks.
evidence_detail: Root cause was a primary key routed through the whole codebase needing a different type; days of digging.
landing: Justifies keeping owner view and human reading of designs; warns against fully unattended phases

author: Dex
quote: about three to six months of you shipping all the time with nobody reading
claim: After 3-6 months of shipping with nobody reading the code, the codebase is worse and easier to restart than fix; he expects the interval to shrink as models write faster.
evidence_detail: Own experience; newsletter adds that he thinks it would take under four months today.
landing: Owner review cadence for agent-written code; refactor-in-place loops

author: Dex
quote: it's still worth not reading the code for most of the time
claim: Retraction: he once judged unread code worth an occasional two-week manual fix, but no longer believes it, because code volume grew 10x-100x and the problem is getting worse.
evidence_detail: Stated as a change of mind after the incident.
landing: Supports reading designs and boundary code even when volume rises

author: Dex
quote: cost function of bad architecture and bad program design can't be evaluated
claim: Models are trained on SWE-bench-style fix-reproduction, which cannot score maintainability that bites 3-6 months later, so models are not trained to keep codebases healthy; his idea is a benchmark of 20 features in a row with unknown future requirements.
evidence_detail: Reasoned from benchmark design; also praises Cognition's Frontier-Code judge layers but calls them insufficient.
landing: Why the harness needs architecture checks (import-linter contracts) beyond tests

author: Dex
quote: 100K for smaller models, 200K for these like really beefy like Codeex and Opus
claim: Numeric training-wheel limits: stop around 100K tokens for smaller models, about 200K for strong ones; he personally goes to 250-400K by feel (newsletter: 300-400K of a 1M window).
evidence_detail: Personal heuristic, explicitly intuition-based; previously 40% of window, then first 100K after 1M windows arrived.
landing: Phase routine / closing message: context-used check; a stop-and-restart threshold

author: Dex
quote: I don't believe like the model writing the code is the same model reading
claim: Agentic code review raises the floor but cannot be trusted to judge code quality: asked 'is this good' a model says great, asked to critique a coworker's PR it finds faults, so models are sycophantic about code they or peers wrote.
evidence_detail: Personal experience of sycophancy asymmetry; no numbers.
landing: Reviewer prompt framing (refute-by-default, 'a coworker wrote this'); fresh-context refuters

author: Dex
quote: none of these things have intuition for software architecture
claim: Replacing code review with agentic testing, agentic review and feedback loops (Sentry, support tickets) leaves no one with architectural intuition, so a 3am failure may be unfixable by the agent; PR review becomes the bottleneck pushing teams to this.
evidence_detail: Tweet March 2026: 1-3 year period of 3am breakage as an existential threat; quoted by host.
landing: Keep human-readable designs and ADRs; do not substitute verifiers for owner understanding

author: Dex
quote: if you can make a problem very verifiable, you can kind of like treat it like a black box
claim: Back pressure: if a problem is verifiable (compiler, tests, linters, CI timing), let the model loop against the check; the core Ralph lesson is automating feedback into the model.
evidence_detail: Huntley's example: Sonnet around the clock, $6K over six weeks, a compiled language; his own CI-speed loop (change, push, subagent watches job, decide).
landing: Backpressure scripts per phase (a runnable check the agent loops on) before review

author: Dex
quote: run this llinter fix one thing commit and push
claim: Slow loops: a nightly cron in GitHub Actions runs a linter or anti-pattern check, fixes one thing, opens one PR; now four PRs each morning (e.g. React Doctor, optional-prop narrowing); scale scope only as confidence grows; a human reads every PR.
evidence_detail: HumanLayer's own practice; Kyle shipped a skill to build these; two dimensions: more conditions, more items per run.
landing: Scheduled routine (CI cron) for code-quality PRs; a saved reusable loop workflow

author: Dex
quote: not use loops to ship the features that users want
claim: Use loops to improve codebase quality, not to ship features, and read all the code; with a 60,000-line Ralph PR nobody can sign off.
evidence_detail: Distinction between loop uses; incremental and contained loops preferred over a redesigned agentic-first factory.
landing: Scope of any scheduled agent: cleanup only, small PRs

author: Dex
quote: build one loop at a time and you should keep them small and contained
claim: Add loops one at a time, small and contained; trigger them from non-human events (Sentry alert, support ticket, failing test, cron); everything except 'stop reading the code' is good advice.
evidence_detail: Advice to teams; no data.
landing: Workflow library: one named, saved workflow per trigger

author: Dex
quote: an hour spent over here in planning can save you four hours
claim: Seek leverage: an hour of planning/design can save four hours of implementation fixes; three options (lights off, read everything for 30-50% lift, leverage points for 2-3x faster at near hand-written quality).
evidence_detail: Numbers (30-50%, 2-3x, 99% accuracy, 1:4 hour ratio) from what he sees in teams; not a controlled measurement.
landing: Where to spend verifier effort: design and architecture first, implementation review lighter

author: Dex
quote: turn that into a one pager and make sure that's correct
claim: Zoom in layer by layer (sentence, one-pager, three-pager, ten-page outline, code), checking each level, to collapse the set of possible end states; do not sweat the docs but review along the way.
evidence_detail: Uncertainty-narrowing analogy; no measurement.
landing: Phase routine: staged elaboration of each phase with an owner check at the one-pager

author: Dex
quote: optimizing for utilization and efficiency of one node in your factory
claim: 'Token harder' (maxing subscriptions, utilisation of one node) optimises the wrong thing; 'token smarter' keeps control, taste and architecture judgement while getting AI value, and is harder to pull off.
evidence_detail: Example: a group chat member with six Claude accounts timed to every 5-hour reset; Goldratt's Theory of Constraints framing.
landing: Effort routing: spend tokens where they remove a bottleneck, not to maximise usage

author: Dex
quote: your engineering time is always the bottleneck
claim: Start with the smartest model; optimise cost only at scale (e.g. offload simple steps to a model about 1/1,000th Opus's cost) and only after proving value; engineering effort usually costs more than the tokens saved.
evidence_detail: Make it run, make it right, make it fast; 'millions of requests' threshold.
landing: Effort routing: do not hand-tune model tiers per verifier without measured cost; counterweight to cheap-model routing

author: Dex
quote: let me delete your end file and try again
claim: The tell that a session is in the dumb zone is the model escalating increasingly extreme attempts to make a test pass; at that point write state to a file and restart at 30-50K tokens.
evidence_detail: Observed behaviour at ~200-300K tokens; remedy is a fresh session with the hard task restated.
landing: Phase routine: a 'stuck on a test' rule that forces a fresh session with a handoff file

author: Dex
quote: how do I raise the floor so that every single turn
claim: Harness engineering is optimising the integration points of a coding agent (commands, MCPs, skills, codebase organisation); Fowler's inner harness (vendor tools) vs outer harness (what the user customises) is the best definition.
evidence_detail: Definition; credits LangChain and Martin Fowler.
landing: Names FixFlow's .claude/ surface (agents, skills, CLAUDE.md) as the outer harness

author: Dex
quote: you need to go down a level and think about what's everything
claim: Frameworks get you to 80%; going from 80% to 95-99% requires controlling exactly what goes in the context window and in what order; own the inputs to every LLM step.
evidence_detail: Based on ~100 conversations with AI engineers who discarded frameworks.
landing: Prefer explicit, owned workflow scripts over generic orchestration frameworks

author: Dex
quote: how can we add another checkpoint in that factory
claim: Add a human checkpoint before code (design review, planning, shared real-time review) rather than only at the PR; a rework loop after a bad PR is costly and committed direction is hard to steer, so restart rather than loop.
evidence_detail: HumanLayer product thesis ('kill the pull request'); no numbers.
landing: Phase routine: owner checkpoint at design before implementation

author: Dex
quote: Refactoring, clean code, the pragmatic programmer
claim: Classic software-design books (Refactoring, Clean Code, The Pragmatic Programmer) are more relevant now; his team spends effort on program design (interfaces, seams, dependency injection) so agents can maintain code.
evidence_detail: Closing book recommendation and earlier remarks on program design.
landing: Slice-boundary rules and import-linter contracts as the program-design guard

author: Dex
quote: we can teach somebody, I think, to be a really good AI developer in a few months
claim: Hiring: strong CS fundamentals are hard to teach in 3 months, while AI-development intuition can be built in a few months.
evidence_detail: Hiring heuristic.
landing: nowhere obvious

author: Dex
quote: frontier LLMs can follow about 150 to 250 instructions before it starts to drop off
claim: Models follow roughly 150-250 instructions before adherence drops (a 2025 study, older models; newer ones reportedly better), so instruction budget matters as much as information budget.
evidence_detail: Cites a 2025 study; says a later study (via Laurie Voss) shows improvement; he had not read the data himself.
landing: CLAUDE.md length/trim decision (instruction count, not just lines)

author: Dex
quote: too many conflicting instructions
claim: Context has an instruction budget as well as an information budget; conflicting instructions, and a changed-mind conversation, force the model to compute what to ignore and make far-back instructions half-attended.
evidence_detail: Mechanistic explanation, no experiment.
landing: CLAUDE.md: audit for conflicting or stale rules; prose docs that drift from CLAUDE.md

author: Dex
quote: you're not actually getting a like smarter model
claim: A bigger context window does not make a smarter model; intelligence is the ability to attend to the relevant tokens, so 1M windows are mostly longer conversations, not better reasoning.
evidence_detail: Also his March 2026 tweet that a 1M window for Sonnet 4 is unhinged when people struggle past 100K.
landing: Model/window choice for long verifier sessions; do not rely on 1M windows

author: Dex
quote: there's four things in your context window that matter.
claim: Four things matter in a context: size, quality of information (errors compound as fact), missing information (filled by guesses), and trajectory of prior agent actions.
evidence_detail: Framework; trajectory example: past turns of 'change, run tests, fix tests' make the next turn repeat it.
landing: Cold-resume trial design: missing-information check; handoff docs must carry verified facts only

author: Dex
quote: time to start over
claim: Phrases like 'you're absolutely right' or 'you're right to push back' signal a trajectory-poisoned session (mistake, user yells, more mistakes); start a new session instead of continuing.
evidence_detail: Autoregressive argument; example from his earlier No Vibes Allowed talk.
landing: Phase routine: restart rule when a reviewer or agent is corrected twice; journal the restart

author: Dex
quote: you would get a 10k token dock out of it
claim: Research step compresses ~100K tokens of code reading into a ~10K markdown doc, which seeds a fresh context for design and planning (frequent intentional compaction).
evidence_detail: Approximate sizes from RPI practice since Aug 2025.
landing: Phase routine: research artifact then fresh session; ties to the plan comment 'Plan @ sha'

author: Dex
quote: benchmarks cannot evaluate whether this loop will produce slop
claim: Pass/fail benchmarks measure solving a one-off ticket, not whether the codebase stays maintainable, so benchmark scores say little about long-run code quality.
evidence_detail: Argued from how SWE-bench/Terminal-Bench verifiers work; no numbers.
landing: Do not treat green tests/CI as evidence of quality; the Opus reviewer must judge maintainability separately.
inventory_ref: 2026-07 list: AI That Works #65 SOTA Coding Agent Benchmarks (and 2026-07-17 video)

author: Dex
quote: find the ways to insert yourself where you do a little bit of work
claim: The practical leverage is shaping the problem with a little human judgment so it looks to the model like the one-shot ticket it is already great at.
evidence_detail: Closing advice; ties to up-front design and slicing.
landing: Phase routine: human-owned plan/slice definition before the agent executes.

author: Dex
quote: a roadmap of twenty features to build, but it didn't know about each
claim: A proper maintainability benchmark would feed a model tickets one at a time from a hidden roadmap and score how well the codebase evolves; prompting 'plan for the future if needed' yields over-engineering.
evidence_detail: Hypothetical benchmark design; Vaibhav adds the over-engineering warning.
landing: Possible harness self-test: replay a sequence of phases and compare drift; no obvious landing.

author: Dex
quote: it's not done when it's merged, it's not done when it's deployed
claim: Measure engineering by how fast and safely changes reach users (DORA: deploy frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to recover), with inputs/outputs/outcomes distinguished by feedback-loop length.
evidence_detail: DORA four metrics explained; feedback time per layer given qualitatively (seconds, minutes, days-weeks, quarters).
landing: Ship plan exit criteria could be phrased as deployed-and-verified, not merged; measurement pipeline was skipped (mark).

author: Dex
quote: Models are getting a lot better at solve a one off problem
claim: Models improve quickly at one-off tickets but not at maintaining a codebase over time, so the gap is farther off than it feels.
evidence_detail: Closing summary; no numbers.
landing: Justifies keeping structural review gates even as models improve.

author: Dex
quote: Vaibhav: the only benchmark for a good software engineer is whether other people recommend them
claim: Instead of trusting benchmarks, rely on trusted humans' reports of which model is good for which task; Dex says that is why he follows Twitter and runs the show (Dex only partly endorses).
evidence_detail: Brief exchange; Dex jokes it is why he is on Twitter.
landing: Model routing decisions come from own measured runs, not leaderboards.

author: Dex
quote: you can't write a linter that generally finds patterns like this
claim: Slop patterns such as unnecessary try/catch wrapping or double typecasts cannot be caught by a general linter because the same code is sometimes correct, so deterministic backpressure has limits for quality.
evidence_detail: Reasoning about false positives/negatives; no data.
landing: Linters/import-linter cover specific rules only; the review step still carries the judgment load.

author: Dex
quote: you can explicitly encode your rules into a prompt or into a deterministic linter
claim: Explicit team rules can be encoded into a PR-review prompt or a deterministic linter, but that is not sufficient and there is no generic code-quality judge.
evidence_detail: Dex says asking an LLM how to improve code quality gives 'bullshit' answers.
landing: Rules go in reviewer prompt/CI contracts (import-linter), not in a generic 'is this good' judge.

author: Dex
quote: anything with good feedback is really, really like easy to train on
claim: Models improve at whatever RL can verify quickly; code-quality consequences arrive months later, so a verifier cannot be trained on them and models will not get better at maintainability on their own.
evidence_detail: Explanation of RL verifier constraints; the feedback loop for a bad pattern is weeks to months.
landing: Human/structural design input (program design, slices) stays necessary; do not wait for models to fix maintainability.

author: Dex
quote: zero out any changes the model made to the tests
claim: Frontier Code's verifier discards the agent's test edits when grading, then separately runs the agent's new tests against pre-patch code to confirm they fail, catching tests that test nothing.
evidence_detail: Description of the benchmark's mutation-style check; Dex endorses it and says meaningless tests slow both people and LLMs.
landing: Reviewer 'fail-before/pass-after per register id' already matches; consider making the verifier restore original tests before running.

author: Dex
quote: an adjudicator, I call the adjudicator model, read the written code
claim: Newer benchmarks add a judge model comparing the agent's patch to a golden patch plus a separate quality judge driven by written rules, producing graded scores rather than pass/fail.
evidence_detail: Description of Frontier Code's scoring structure.
landing: Reviewer prompt with written quality rules and a reference (the plan/register) is the analogue.

author: Dex
quote: the faster and cheaper you can make your back pressure
claim: Treat the agent as a control loop: the faster and cheaper the deterministic feedback (type checker, then linter, then unit, integration, human clicking), the less it drifts, and a stalled context needs a fresh window.
evidence_detail: Answer to an audience question, referencing the Ralph loop; ordering of check speed given.
landing: CI job ordering and phase routine: run type/lint/unit locally first; start a new session if the agent loses the goal.

author: Dex
quote: you might be in the dumb zone and need a new context window
claim: If an agent (e.g. a sub-agent poorly prompted by its parent) wanders off a deterministic goal state, the remedy is better parent prompting or a fresh context window.
evidence_detail: One sentence in Q&A.
landing: Supports one-phase-per-new-session; sub-agent briefs need an explicit check-your-work command.

author: Dex
quote: you have to prompt your parent model to prompt its sub agents better
claim: Sub-agent failures are mostly parent-prompting failures, so the parent must be told how to brief sub-agents and give them a verifiable end state.
evidence_detail: Brief aside, no data.
landing: Workflow script prompts / agent files: every brief states goal state and the check command.

author: Dex+others
quote: A local value replaces a shared value. A shared value replaces the built-in default.
claim: Workspace setup is layered: built-in defaults, committed workspace.json, uncommitted workspace.local.json; array fields append, repo entries merge by path.
evidence_detail: Docs description.
landing: Settings layering for .claude (shared vs local) and worktree-per-phase config

author: Dex+others
quote: Selecting Opus 4.8 now switches to Claude Code's safer auto mode automatically
claim: Selecting Opus 4.8 switches sessions to Claude Code's auto permission mode by default, and the research-questions skill captures user-given links and file paths verbatim in a 'Key Context Pointers' section (same release).
evidence_detail: Changelog lines.
landing: Permission mode choice per phase; research-question skill keeps owner pointers verbatim

source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
author: Dex
quote: a "lights-off" version where humans stop reading code entirely
claim: A fully lights-off factory where humans stop reading code quietly rots a codebase after three to six months.
evidence_detail: Stated in episode description; no data given on page, though it follows his year of observation.
landing: Keep human review checkpoints (owner view, Opus reviewer per PR); argues against removing them.

source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
author: Dex
quote: Every benchmark rewards one thing: did the test pass?
claim: Coding models are trained only on pass/fail tests and never punished for leaving code a smaller model or later human cannot work in, so slop is structural.
evidence_detail: Argument about training incentives; no numbers.
landing: Verifier design: add maintainability checks beyond tests (import-linter contracts, reviewer rubric); do not trust green CI alone.

source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
author: Dex
quote: why architecture planning, sprint planning, and code review still can't be skipped
claim: Because models are not penalised for slop, architecture planning, sprint planning and code review remain mandatory human/agent steps.
evidence_detail: Conclusion from training-incentive argument; no data.
landing: Ship plan phase routine: keep plan step and per-PR reviewer; argues against skipping them for speed.

source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
author: Dex
quote: you're not drowning in PRs so much as drowning in bad ones
claim: The bottleneck is PR quality, not PR volume; the fix is better PRs rather than faster review throughput.
evidence_detail: Episode blurb framing; no numbers.
landing: PR gating: quality of the draft PR body (Plan @ sha, decisions journal) as a filter before review.

source_title: Mastra Agents Hour: The Software Factory
author: Dex
quote: a longer-horizon benchmark that actually catches slop
claim: A benchmark that measures code across many successive changes (longer horizon) is needed to catch slop that single-task benchmarks miss.
evidence_detail: Discussed as a wished-for benchmark; no specifics on page.
landing: Measurement idea: evaluate harness changes on multi-phase runs, not single phases (touches the skipped measurement pipeline).

author: Dex
quote: anything that you can't trust the LLM to get right 99% of the time
claim: Align at the technical-design-doc level on anything the LLM cannot be trusted to get right 99% of the time; 5-10 minutes there saves hours at code review and avoids code that looks fine but hurts maintainability within about four weeks.
evidence_detail: Dex's ten years in large codebases; no measurement.
landing: Phase routine: tech design doc trigger rule
inventory_ref: AI That Works #64 Agent Observability (2026-07 line)

author: Dex
quote: even with system architecture defined and aligned... you can still end up with really bad code
claim: Mermaid/sequence diagrams are not enough: even with aligned architecture models produce overlapping objects and bad interfaces, so review type signatures and object shapes before code.
evidence_detail: Stated as common experience ('a lot of people are finding').
landing: Outline step: signatures and objects, not just diagrams

author: Dex
quote: a skill called application reliability engineering
claim: HumanLayer's reliability skill makes the parent agent use only sub-agents (same model, 'RLM mode') to fetch logs, Sentry and traces so parent context stays sparse, then reads only summaries and writes an incident report.
evidence_detail: Describes HumanLayer's live practice; no numbers.
landing: Skill + workflow: sub-agent fetch, parent reads summaries only

author: Dex
quote: just tell me what happened. Don't don't tell me what's wrong
claim: To stop the model jumping to false conclusions, ask it to report what happened and list candidate causes, expecting the last several to be filler.
evidence_detail: Dex notes Claude gets excited and states false conclusions.
landing: Refuter/diagnosis prompts: separate observation from cause

author: Dex
quote: an HTML file per folder that explains the changes in that folder at a high level
claim: A review pattern he cites: the agent generates a per-folder HTML summary so 2000 changed lines can be digested in a minute with drill-down on demand; he links it to productising code understanding.
evidence_detail: Secondhand from something he saw the prior week; HumanLayer also added a PR walkthrough feature.
landing: Owner view / reviewer output format

author: Dex+others
quote: show me the call stack
claim: Trace during planning: ask the agent to show the call stack, type signatures and object relations before approving a plan, then feed the execution trace back and ask what the design missed.
evidence_detail: Dylan's workflow described by Vaibhav; Dex presents it as part of planning.
landing: Call-graph tooling (skipped by harness review) and plan review step

author: other
quote: Observability is useful in hindsight.
claim: Instrumentation must exist before a bug occurs because it only pays off after the fact; trace everything by default, redact risky fields, and make traces queryable and typed so an agent can query them.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav's thesis; Dex adds the history and agrees; includes OTel JSON-string blow-up claim (100 bytes to ~800) as an estimate.
landing: Telemetry for routine compliance (was the store consulted); measurement pipeline (previously skipped); hooks

author: Dex
quote: Look at your damn data, as Hamel Hussein would say.
claim: Inspect the actual traces and data rather than trusting summaries or vibes; Dex also ties this to doing vibe evals.
evidence_detail: Aside at the close; attributes the phrase to Hamel Husain.
landing: Evidence folders with sha256 manifests; review of real transcripts

author: Dex
quote: 2026 is gonna be the year of no more slop
claim: Industry reaction to slop at the conference ranged from more review agents and linting to new languages; Dex names no-slop as 2026's focus and notes 70% of attendees are early in their AI journey.
evidence_detail: Conference impressions, 70/30 split is secondhand and anecdotal.
landing: none specific; context for review/verifier priority

author: Dex
quote: you can't YOLO it
claim: If the agent's work cannot be seen (via design visualizations, traces or per-folder summaries) you cannot trust it; understanding must be cheap enough to maintain without reading every line.
evidence_detail: Brief closing statement.
landing: Owner view and reviewer artifacts

author: Dex+others
quote: the session keeps going on the backup model
claim: A model refusal that triggered a fallback (Fable 5 to Opus 4.8) used to kill the session and lose the conversation; fallback is now surfaced inline and persists.
evidence_detail: Bug fix description.
landing: Workflow scripts: explicit fallback model on refusal, not session loss

source_title: AIEWF Daily Dispatch: The great loops debate (Latent Space)
author: other
quote: bottlenecked on reviews
claim: Even Anthropic's most delegated internal use (Krieger on Claude Tag) reports the human review and ability to conceptualise the work as the bottleneck, consistent with Dex's review-gate argument but a measured counter to 'just add agents'.
evidence_detail: Single remark in a Krieger interview as reported; 59% of Amplify survey respondents fear AI code creates long-term liabilities.
landing: Review-gate capacity planning for the owner view: one-page summary per PR.
inventory_ref: (C) Follow-ons and coverage by others (NOT Dex's work)

source_title: AIEWF Daily Dispatch: The great loops debate (Latent Space)
author: other
quote: It's inevitable, it's here to stay
claim: Pro-loop debaters (Huntley, Livingstone) counter Dex's caution: loops are already here, and verifiability, achievable for any code however produced, is what matters rather than stepping down an abstraction level.
evidence_detail: Debate remarks relayed second-hand; no data. Huntley himself concedes software factories are 'frontier thinking' and not yet solved.
landing: Nowhere obvious; framing for how far Workflow-script autonomy is allowed to run unattended.
inventory_ref: (C) Follow-ons and coverage by others (NOT Dex's work)

source_title: AIEWF Daily Dispatch: The great loops debate (Latent Space)
author: other
quote: orchestrate your problems away by buying more tokens
claim: Co-skeptic Pstrucha argues agentic loops are economically unsustainable: more tokens do not substitute for orchestration discipline.
evidence_detail: One paraphrased remark; the same piece cites an Amplify survey: 40% say AI cost regularly limits ambition and token usage is the second most monitored production metric.
landing: Cost tracking per phase/workflow; supports effort routing.
inventory_ref: (C) Follow-ons and coverage by others (NOT Dex's work)

author: Dex
quote: Kubernetes is actually built on control loops, but they're deterministic loops.
claim: The real value in loops is small, isolated tasks with a defined desired end state: feed in current state and let an agent or deterministic system progress toward it.
evidence_detail: Analogy to Kubernetes controllers; no data.
landing: Workflow-library design: reusable workflows should be small desired-state loops with a deterministic stop test.

author: Dex
quote: the hype is outrunning the discipline
claim: Review bots and layering abstraction have not been shown to work; he thinks the answer is to step down an abstraction level, not up, and that magic-answer loops need much more care.
evidence_detail: Says he has seen no public or private proof that review bots solve slop PRs.
landing: Treat refuter/reviewer agents as unproven for quality; keep deterministic checks and owner reading alongside.

author: Dex
quote: keep most of your work in what we call the smart zone of the context window
claim: Ralph's fresh-context restart (restate desired state, inspect code, do one next step, clear) kept work in the smart zone and let it run overnight, at some token inefficiency.
evidence_detail: Explains Ralph's motivation; no measurements.
landing: Supports one-phase-per-new-session with state held in the repo (decisions journal), not in conversation.

author: Dex
quote: The dumb zone is really ... more like training wheels.
claim: Concession/update: the smart/dumb zone is a guideline for newcomers; budget about 100k tokens, perhaps 200k with million windows, under 60k for his hardest problems, and sometimes over 300k when casually riffing.
evidence_detail: Personal practice numbers, offered as intuition, not measured limits; also says 1M windows lift the old 100k rule.
landing: Context budget in the phase routine: replace a hard 'new chat per phase' number with these guideline figures; hard phases under ~60k.

author: Dex
quote: it's flailing trying to make something happen
claim: Telltale dumb-zone sign: ~200k tokens in, the agent hacks to pass a failing test and thinking traces claim the failure is preexisting or from something else; that is the moment to reset.
evidence_detail: Personal heuristic, no data.
landing: Add 'claims a failing test is preexisting' as a stop-and-restart trigger in the routine or a skill.

author: Dex
quote: if you can automate that process, that's great
claim: With larger windows, the loop value is piping more feedback in: deterministic code watches for PR comments and builds small prompts for the agent, so humans need not remember to ask again.
evidence_detail: Example of PR-comment automation; no results given.
landing: Candidate saved workflow or hook: deterministic PR-comment/CI-state poller that builds a prompt for a fresh agent.

author: Dex
quote: the way to not loop slop together and make more slop is to like read
claim: There is no loop-engineering fix for loop slop: the answer is to read what comes out the other end; the labs have not cracked it either.
evidence_detail: Position in answer to the convergence-engineering question.
landing: Same as R13-18: owner read as non-negotiable gate; do not rely on convergence loops for quality.

author: Dex
quote: like Loom is awesome. Like go experiment, try to push the frontier
claim: Concession/endorsement: frontier experiments like Geoff's Loom are valuable for learning limits, but an unfinished one (and the PostHog-data UI loop) is an example of hype outrunning discipline.
evidence_detail: Recounts Geoff saying Loom would not work until better languages or models; Loom stalled six months.
landing: Run experiments in a sandboxed side track, never in the ship-plan phases.

author: Dex
quote: you never put it in anybody's hands. It's just like any product.
claim: Anti-pattern: disappearing for three months to build the definitive software factory from blog posts; build it as a product for teammates, start small, iterate.
evidence_detail: General product-development argument.
landing: Grow the skill/agent/workflow library from workflows actually reused in phases, not designed up front.

author: Dex
quote: build these small incremental loops throughout your system
claim: Aim for 2 to 3x speedup with small incremental loops while reading the code and owning architecture; chasing 100x blows things up.
evidence_detail: Based on his tweet that most engineers see 2-3x; no study cited.
landing: Target setting for the ship plan; prefer many small saved loops over one grand orchestrator.

author: Dex
quote: try a bunch of stuff that probably won't work, but you should acknowledge that
claim: Build intuition by trying things that may not work, and don't discard decades of software-engineering practice because something worked on Twitter.
evidence_detail: Advice in the future-of-loops segment.
landing: Treat the P1 cold-resume trial as an experiment with a recorded result either way.

author: Dex
quote: I think this is actually a problem we can only solve at the model level
claim: Final position: an unread software factory is a model-level problem the harness cannot fix; meanwhile use bounded loops that help.
evidence_detail: Refers to his Tuesday keynote; no new evidence.
landing: Same as R13-1; sets expectations that harness work lifts the floor only.

author: other
quote: I heavily exploit pre-commit hooks, folks.
claim: Geoff Huntley uses pre-commit hooks as backpressure so the agent cannot finish until rules (e.g. a boundary must not depend on another) are met; Dex does not rebut it and calls deterministic checks the part of loops that works.
evidence_detail: Geoff's practice; Dex endorses only generally (card is Geoff's idea, adopted loosely by Dex).
landing: Re-opens the skipped hooks / pre-commit gate decision: import-linter and ESLint boundaries as hook-level backpressure.

author: Kyle
quote: Set point** — the desired end state for some property of the codebase.
claim: Frame recurring agent work as a control loop: set point, sensor (measures the gap), controller (picks the next small change), actuator (coding agent opens a PR), under disturbances (teammates, dependency bumps, generated code), with a human on the loop.
evidence_detail: Conceptual model; one worked example (React Doctor) in a production monorepo, no outcome numbers.
landing: Reusable workflow library: a saved sense-control-act workflow shape for repeated audit/fix tasks (e.g. code-quality sweeps)
inventory_ref: (B) June 2026 — design-control-loop skill added 2026-06-30 by Kyle

author: Kyle
quote: Read the repo before you ask
claim: The designing agent reads CI, package files, validation scripts and existing skills/loops first and comes to the interview with proposals rather than a blank form.
evidence_detail: Phase A instruction.
landing: Skill-authoring convention: explore-then-propose before asking the owner questions

author: Kyle
quote: Make each component runnable locally and standalone before wiring it into CI
claim: Land the sensor and controller as version-controlled scripts the user can run by hand, run the actuator locally via its headless CLI, and only then wire CI, so the workflow is a thin orchestrator of pieces already proven.
evidence_detail: Phase D with completion criterion; also Phase H dry-run via a temporary push trigger.
landing: Workflow library convention: every script step runnable standalone; supports saving workflows (W5) and debugging

author: Kyle
quote: whether it can be silently disabled
claim: When choosing a sensor, weigh stability, cost and repeatability and whether the measurement can be silently disabled (e.g. by an inline lint-disable comment); the worked example put the sensor config outside the lint config for this reason.
evidence_detail: React Doctor example: chosen because 'a stray inline comment can't quietly switch it off'.
landing: Verifier/compliance design: a check an agent cannot quietly skip or disable; relevant to 'store never consulted looks like routine skipped'

author: Kyle
quote: This is the part you **tune over time** from loop output
claim: The controller (what to do now vs defer; which target, how many, in what order) ranges from deterministic script to fully agentic and is the component to tune from loop output; start simple.
evidence_detail: Taxonomy text.
landing: Phase selection / work-queue picker as a tunable script; model routing as the controller's tuning knob

author: Kyle
quote: don't manufacture separation that isn't there
claim: Components may be fused (sensor+controller, controller+actuator); do not split a loop into discrete steps the design does not have.
evidence_detail: Example collapses all three into one agent step.
landing: Workflow-script design guidance (avoid over-structured multi-agent scripts)

author: Kyle
quote: stop scheduled runs when an open PR for this loop already exists
claim: Flow control: bound work-in-progress to one open PR per loop (label-gated, scheduled runs no-op, manual dispatch bypasses) so the agent never produces PRs faster than review.
evidence_detail: Rationale: without it a daily agent could stack 5+ unreviewed PRs a week (from build-iterated-agentic-loop).
landing: Phase routine: one open draft PR per phase; owner-review backlog cap before starting next phase

also.quote: Recommended: Yes, bound to 1 open PR per agent loop.
also.author: Kyle
also.claim: Scheduled agent loops no-op when an open PR carrying the loop's label already exists, so agent output cannot pile up faster than humans review it; manual dispatch bypasses the bound; a memory file carries standing feedback between runs.

author: Kyle
quote: a check (often on PRs / pushes to main) that compares the sensor's output against a baseline
claim: Dampener: a regression gate comparing sensor output to a baseline so the measured problem cannot get worse while the loop improves it; advisory by default, graduating to blocking once trusted.
evidence_detail: React Doctor example: advisory by default, comments only on newly introduced issues, documented path to blocking.
landing: CI: ratchet checks (e.g. import-boundary or lint-count baselines) that only fail on new violations; pre-commit gate re-open

author: Kyle
quote: Scope gate** — restrict the actuator to safe directories
claim: Restrict the actuator to safe directories, exclude generated/vendored/high-risk packages, and cap each run by finding/file/package count to keep diffs reviewable.
evidence_detail: Scope gate and batch size listed as extra loop parts; prompt template says 'inspect secondary path only when necessary'.
landing: Per-phase file allow-list in the plan; batch-size caps in workflow scripts; interacts with import-linter contracts

author: Kyle
quote: Keep durable guidance only — not one-off instructions or single-run logs.
claim: A version-controlled memory file of standing feedback (scope exclusions, false positives, reviewer preferences) is loaded deterministically into the actuator on every run, after the controller; good entries are durable, and the test is whether deleting it would lose useful future-run context.
evidence_detail: Memory template; build-iterated-agentic-loop adds 'Completion criterion: deleting the memory file would lose useful future-run context, not just history'. Narrow-props memory example is one line.
landing: Knowledge-store design: separate durable standing guidance from run logs; a short deterministic-load memory file as a cheaper alternative or companion

author: Kyle
quote: Label each loop's PRs and embed a hidden marker
claim: /iterate: a maintainer comments /iterate on the loop's PR; a hidden marker in the PR body routes the comment to the workflow that created it, which loads the diff, comments and feedback and updates both the PR and the memory file; the marker is checked before checkout so non-matching workflows no-op cheaply.
evidence_detail: Implemented in workflow-template.yml gate step and agent-iteration.ts (footer and prompt modes); restricted to OWNER/MEMBER/COLLABORATOR comments.
landing: Owner feedback path on a phase PR that updates durable memory, not only the PR; marker-in-PR-body routing as machine-readable provenance

author: Kyle
quote: Put ordered behavior in `SKILL.md` as steps with checkable completion criteria
claim: Write skills as ordered steps each with a checkable completion criterion, push long templates and examples into sibling reference files, and keep one source of truth per rule across skill, prompt and memory.
evidence_detail: Skill-writing rules repeated in design-control-loop and build-iterated-agentic-loop; every phase ends with a 'Completion criterion'.
landing: Skill authoring template for new skills and the phase routine steps: each routine step ends with an observable completion criterion

author: Kyle
quote: Each phase above names the references relevant to it — read each one when you reach that phase.
claim: Progressive disclosure inside a skill: each phase of SKILL.md names exactly which reference files to read at that phase, rather than loading all references up front.
evidence_detail: Every phase begins with 'Read the following references:'. Contrasts with the improve-claude-md advice against sharding CLAUDE.md.
landing: Skill structure and phase routine: per-step reads list; limits context loaded per phase

author: Kyle
quote: the `name` in the skill's frontmatter must match its directory slug
claim: A skill's frontmatter name must equal its directory slug (.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md) or it will not resolve.
evidence_detail: Bolded IMPORTANT in both skills.
landing: Checklist for the skills being added; a trivial CI check could enforce it

author: Kyle
quote: You are running in a sandbox or CI runner environment. Do not stop and ask for feedback
claim: Unattended-agent prompt shape: Context (begin with the named skill), Scope (primary path, secondary only if needed), numbered Instructions (one small reviewable increment, no adjacent cleanup), Validation commands, Important Rules, Finishing Up, and a fixed Output Format that becomes the PR body.
evidence_detail: Template with placeholders; repo-specific targeting lives in the prompt, generic judgement in the skill.
landing: Workflow library: a saved prompt skeleton for headless phase agents; split of repo-specific vs generic content between prompt and skill

author: Kyle
quote: Lead with summary stats - Reviewers should know scope immediately
claim: The agent's final response is a defined template: lead with summary counts, group by resolution (fixed/ignored/skipped), highlight risk levels, give manual verification steps for medium/high risk, keep it scannable.
evidence_detail: Three example templates (fix/migration, generation, refactor). Each issue gets an explicit FIXED, IGNORED (with reason) or SKIPPED (needs human) outcome.
landing: Six-question closing message and per-register-id outcome list; an explicit 'skipped, needs human' outcome makes silent skipping visible

author: Kyle
quote: three honest options — **fix**, **ignore**
claim: Give the actuator three honest options per finding (fix, ignore with a recorded reason in config, or skip for a human) and validate and commit each change separately.
evidence_detail: React Doctor loop: validates with typecheck, quality, and the sensor on staged files; one commit per issue.
landing: Phase agent and reviewer verdict vocabulary; per-item commits make fail-before/pass-after attributable per register id

author: Kyle
quote: Use `--max-turns` or `--max-budget-usd` when the repo needs spend guards.
claim: Headless Claude Code runs (claude -p) can be bounded with --max-turns or --max-budget-usd; the final assistant message is extracted from stream-json output with jq and used as the PR body; tee all output to a file for debugging.
evidence_detail: Command templates for Claude Code, Codex (--output-last-message), OpenCode, CodeLayer; also states broad permission modes are for trusted isolated runners only.
landing: Headless runs for scheduled audits; saved raw transcript (agent-output) as evidence that a routine step ran

author: Kyle
quote: Check iterate marker to bound work-in-progress
claim: A scheduled agent workflow skeleton with discrete sensor, controller, actuator and extract-PR-body steps, a concurrency group, an actor-authorisation gate on comment triggers, a no-commit-no-PR guard, and an upload of the raw agent output as an artifact.
evidence_detail: Template YAML; model defaults shown are Opus with thinking high for fresh runs and Sonnet for the /iterate path.
landing: Saved workflow/CI template; shows a split of effort by task (full cycle on the stronger model, feedback iteration on the cheaper one) as a small model-routing example

author: Kyle
quote: Golden patterns first. Before automating, establish what a good change looks like
claim: Before automating a migration or cleanup, find the golden patterns in the existing code with the user and encode them in the actuator skill so the agent follows established conventions.
evidence_detail: Phase B4 instruction.
landing: Skill content for migrations/refactors: exemplar file paths named in the skill

author: Kyle
quote: increase the schedule frequency; widen the controller's batch
claim: Once a loop is tuned and producing consistent output, speed it up by raising frequency, widening batch size, running the cycle N times per run, or running it several times with one PR per teammate.

claim: Split content by stability: the skill holds reusable judgement; the workflow prompt holds repo-specific scope, validation commands and memory interpolation; no rule should be repeated in skill, prompt and memory.
