landing: Where phase-specific facts live (plan vs skill vs CLAUDE.md); single-source-of-truth rule

author: Kyle
quote: Temporarily add a `push` trigger for the current branch
claim: Dry-run a new scheduled workflow by temporarily adding a push trigger on the branch, watching it run, then removing the trigger; review the PR it opens before trusting it.
evidence_detail: Step 9; reason is workflow_dispatch is unavailable until a first run. Also: validate YAML parses and every referenced path exists.
landing: P1 cold-resume trial analogue: first run of a routine is a deliberate dry run reviewed by a human before it is trusted

author: Kyle
quote: Treat live code paths as the source of truth for the prop contract.
claim: Derive the type contract from non-test, non-Storybook call sites; support code (tests, stories, mocks) is evidence of widening only, and must adapt to the strict contract rather than weaken it.
evidence_detail: Worked actuator skill with 11 steps and a review checklist.
landing: Reasoning model for tests vs production code; parallels CLAUDE.md rule that the web app reads the live API, not mock seeds

author: Kyle
quote: Types should be as strict as possible so code can be as simple as possible.
claim: Every optional prop is another state to handle, test and keep correct; make types strict (required nullable over optional, derive types from live APIs) so defensive fallbacks (?? [], optional-call handlers) can be deleted.
evidence_detail: Anti-patterns list: optional callbacks for stories, default* props for Storybook, accepting multiple API shapes.
landing: Mobile TypeScript strict-typing cleanup loop; example candidate for a saved scheduled workflow

author: Kyle
quote: Focus only on `apps/riptide-ui`; do not make changes in `apps/riptide-cloud`.
claim: The whole standing memory for a working loop is one scope-exclusion line; memory stays minimal and scope-oriented.
evidence_detail: The example memory file contains a single guidance bullet; skill also ends with a Review Checklist of verifiable properties of the diff (types derived from live sites, no inert menu items, shared variants compile).
landing: Calibration for the knowledge-store pilot: a working loop needed one line of standing memory; also a skill-end review checklist as the reviewer's rubric

source_title: AI for code is a deeply technical engineering craft
author: Dex
quote: more tokens wont save you, more thinking + skill + llm intuition will
claim: Using AI for coding is a technical craft, and spending more tokens does not substitute for skill and judgment.
evidence_detail: Opinion, says he has said it for about 9 months; 646 likes, no data.
landing: Supports routing effort by task rather than defaulting verifiers to maximum effort.

author: Dex
quote: people are going way too far on the, like throw more tokens at the problem
claim: Throwing more tokens at a problem works only when the problem is verifiable; it is over-applied to problems that are not.
evidence_detail: Argument from the Ralph/compiler example; no numbers.
landing: Effort routing and verifier design: spend tokens only where a deterministic check exists

author: Dex
quote: you start with three prompts and then you wake up the next day and suddenly you have a hundred
claim: Engineers glue agent systems together and prompts sprawl until only the author can use them (people reinventing Gastown).
evidence_detail: Observation of many practitioners.
landing: Warning about uncurated skill/prompt sprawl as skills are added

author: Dex
quote: Nobody owes you cheap inference.
claim: Serious enterprise customers pay per token anyway; do not plan around subsidized flat-rate inference.
evidence_detail: Stated from enterprise customer experience.
landing: Cost-aware effort routing (verifier effort level, model choice)

author: Dex
quote: most of the vertical AI shipped to enterprise is ignoring the bitter lesson
claim: Teams actually delivering vertical AI results build specific prompts, pipelines and workflows for today's models rather than waiting for the models to improve; there will always be a jagged frontier.
evidence_detail: Paraphrased from transcript ("They're all ignoring the bidder lesson"); no data.
landing: Supports investing in a reusable workflow library despite model churn

author: Dex
quote: if you can create good deterministic back pressure
claim: More tokens help when you can build good deterministic backpressure; a programming language is infinitely verifiable (compile, run, fix), so the model can check its own work.
evidence_detail: Ralph Wiggum language-building example; no numbers.
landing: CI gates and verification scripts as backpressure; phase routine should name the deterministic check per task

author: Dex
quote: I think one of my predictions is by the end of 2026, most agents are gonna remove the Bash tool
claim: Prediction: by end of 2026 most agents will drop the general Bash tool for narrower scoped tools or a minimal bash-like thing, for safety, security and reliability.
evidence_detail: Prediction; he notes the MCP context-clutter complaint holds only if a Bash tool exists.
landing: Tool permissions / allowlists in .claude settings; narrow scoped tools or agents

author: Dex
quote: we tried the, like don't read the code thing for about six months
claim: His team tried not reading code for about six months, then ran from it and threw out the whole codebase (frontend and backend tangled) to restart greenfield.
evidence_detail: Own team experience; codebase discarded.
landing: Owner/reviewer reading of code in the phase routine; argues against fully hands-off phases

author: Dex
quote: I have a little journal of things that AI is not good at solving
claim: Keep a personal journal of problems AI failed at and re-run them as evals on each new model or workflow.
evidence_detail: Example: a cross-component race condition he tests every new model against for about six months.
landing: A standing set of hard-case evals to re-run when changing model or effort level; decisions journal

author: Dex
quote: you improve the factory 10%, well, you get, you know, 20% of your time back
claim: Investing in the software factory (sandboxes, CI/CD, automated testing) gives compounding returns, a point past which you leave others behind.
evidence_detail: Illustrative numbers from experience, no measurement.
landing: Justifies saving workflows and agents as reusable factory assets

author: Dex
quote: if you put a human in here, it is high leverage for a human to read it
claim: Build workflows that put humans at high-leverage points, e.g. reviewing a 200-line markdown summary of a change at the 25,000-foot level before 1000-2000 lines of code are written.
evidence_detail: Stated as principle; the same ratio appears in the Qodo episode.
landing: Plan @ sha PR body and owner one-page view as the human review point

author: Dex
quote: the quadratic nature of a attention and the like increasing cost and decreasing quality
claim: The durable, model-independent skill is understanding attention: quality falls and cost rises as the context window fills, so context management stays relevant across model generations.
evidence_detail: Conceptual argument; no numbers.
landing: Basis for one-phase-per-session and for trimming always-loaded CLAUDE.md

author: Dex
quote: learn how to push those models 10 to 15% further on specific tasks
claim: Harness and workflow customisation gets 10-15% (maybe 50%) better results on a specific task and the skill carries across models even when custom code is obsoleted by the next model.
evidence_detail: Estimated range, not measured; framed against the bitter lesson.
landing: Argues that per-task workflow scripts are disposable but the understanding is kept; relevant to what to save

author: Dex
quote: Agents are code rotators.
claim: A coding agent rotates a mash-up of your code and its SWE-bench-shaped weights into new code according to the prompt, so the right mental model is not a junior engineer.
evidence_detail: Mental-model metaphor, no test.
landing: Framing for CLAUDE.md content: the code and prompt dominate, so context in the repo matters more than persona text.

author: Dex
quote: they will make a big mess
claim: Models are good at some things but not codebase architecture; left unattended they make a mess, and the industry cycles from 'stop reading code' back to reading it about every five months.
evidence_detail: His team: stopped reading code in August, reverted around Nov/Dec after about 5 months, rebuilt most of the product.
landing: Human architecture review gate in phase routine; do not drop code reading

author: Dex
quote: you can't ask a model on a scale of one to 100, how good is this PR?
claim: Use models for binary classifications (has unit tests? do they cover the thing that matters?) and compute the score deterministically yourself; never ask for a holistic score.
evidence_detail: Design principle for code review bots; no numbers.
landing: Reviewer prompt design: per-register-id yes/no questions with a deterministic roll-up instead of an Opus holistic verdict

author: Dex
quote: you can't leak the understanding of what is good or bad into the model
claim: Do not leak what you want to hear into the reviewing model, because it will tell you what you want to hear; keep the reviewer independent of the desired answer.
evidence_detail: Reasoning about sycophancy; the hosts agree models follow instructions.
landing: Refuter prompts that avoid stating the author's expected conclusion; supports refuted-by-default, fresh context

author: Dex
quote: it's very easy to accidentally, like, have AI for code review be kind of useless
claim: Naive AI code review is useless: asked to find problems it lists about 30 issues, asked if the PR is good it approves; the models are too easily oversteered.
evidence_detail: Experience, no measurement.
landing: Opus reviewer per PR; guard against prompt framing that determines the verdict

author: Dex
quote: reading 100 or 200 lines of Markdown, and that at least grounds me
claim: A good review bot explains the PR by compressing thousands of lines into 100-200 lines of markdown so the human knows which parts to check.
evidence_detail: Seen in review bots; no numbers.
landing: Owner one-page view and PR body summary

author: Dex
quote: you actually don't have too many PRs. What you have is too many bad PRs.
claim: The review bottleneck is bad PRs, not PR volume; AI-era PRs usually need 50% or more rework, and perfect PRs are a joy to review.
evidence_detail: Says rework is 'usually more like 50% or more' without data.
landing: Put quality upstream of review (plan/design) rather than adding review volume

author: Dex
quote: most of the PRs that come through need less than 5% rework
claim: Upstream alignment on a roughly 200-line markdown design doc (after research, before plan) for a 2,000-line change brings PR rework under 5%, versus 50% typical.
evidence_detail: Team of three; rework figures are stated, not measured; show notes say 50% to under 5%.
landing: Design-doc step between research and plan in the phase routine; Plan @ sha PR

author: Dex
quote: you're just shifting the bottleneck to some other place
claim: A Linear-ticket software factory with research/plan review stages just converted 40 to-do tickets into 40 tickets in research and review; the bottleneck moved rather than disappeared.
evidence_detail: Internal experiment from about September; no timings.
landing: Owner review capacity as the limiting resource; limit the number of concurrent phases

author: Dex
quote: Any specification that takes the same amount to read as the code itself, just read the code.
claim: A spec only has leverage at roughly 20% compression of the code; a 1,000-line line-by-line plan drifted about 20% from the final code, so it was not worth reviewing.
evidence_detail: Plan files of about 1000 lines; end code differed about 20% from plan.
landing: Keep plan documents short and decision-level; avoid line-by-line plans in the phase routine

author: Dex
quote: I hate the word spec
claim: He avoids the word 'spec' because it is semantically diffuse (PRD, detailed PRD, code in English); name the artifact by its level of detail.
evidence_detail: Terminology argument.
landing: Precise artifact names in CLAUDE.md and phase routine (plan, design doc, register)

author: Dex
quote: the smaller you can make those tool cycles, the more you can break down
claim: Split a broad agent into a classifier handing off to specialised agents with about 30 tools each; this is more brittle but solves the specific tasks better, a trade-off.
evidence_detail: Illustrative numbers (20 agents, 30 tools).
landing: Narrow custom agents and sub-agents beside the Haiku locator

author: Dex
quote: every token in is the only thing that influences
claim: Context engineering means deciding deterministically what goes into each single LLM call; the tokens in are the only control over the quality of tokens out, including at turn 50.
evidence_detail: Definition.
landing: Basis for trimming CLAUDE.md and deciding what loads per phase

author: Dex
quote: the model who is doing the conversation has no way to modify its own memory
claim: Good memory systems are deterministic: a separate model in a separate context compacts conversations into decaying-resolution summaries (14 days, weekly, monthly) that are injected without the working model editing them.
evidence_detail: Describes implementations he has seen.
landing: Knowledge-store design: a separate writer step and deterministic injection, not agent-chosen recall

author: Dex
quote: you're going to end up building it yourself
claim: Off-the-shelf memory systems or agent harnesses get you to 80% quickly; at the wall you reverse engineer them and end up building your own, and high-quality products engineer every token.
evidence_detail: Opinion from observed products.
landing: Knowledge-store pilot: build the primitives in-house rather than adopt a memory product

author: Dex
quote: split your workflow up into smaller sessions to get better results
claim: Splitting the workflow into smaller sessions raises the ceiling on the hardest solvable problem, and the RPI system had to be adapted from power users to average users.
evidence_detail: Rolled RPI out to companies from startups to Fortune 500 over 2-4 months.
landing: Supports one phase per new session; note that a routine must survive average-user use

author: Dex
quote: I would rather have him tear apart a 200-line Markdown doc
claim: Seek review of the design doc before the code is written, because changes are cheap before the author is attached to polished, test-passing code.
evidence_detail: His practice with CTO Kyle; design review optional in a three-person team.
landing: Plan @ sha draft PR reviewed before implementation begins

author: Dex
quote: a benchmark for, like, a long-term code maintainability
claim: Planned benchmark: a model implements 20 features without seeing the roadmap, then a smaller model implements the 21st, to measure whether code gets worse over time (not one-off PR reproduction).
evidence_detail: Work in progress; no results given (later report is SlopCodeBench).
landing: Possible measure of architecture quality across phases; precursor of SlopCodeBench

author: Dex
quote: hard to, like, evaluate deterministically in a, like, reinforcement learning gym
claim: Models cannot be RL-trained on architecture because 'is it well designed' has no deterministic check beyond asking another model; he sees no path to models being good at architecture, so bake opinions into skills.
evidence_detail: Reasoned claim.
landing: Keep human architecture review; encode architecture opinions as skills and import-linter contracts

author: Dex
quote: Generating low-quality code is nearly free; defending against it is expensive
claim: The war on slop is asymmetric: producing bad code is free while defending against it costs far more (OpenCode and Pydantic drowning in bot PRs).
evidence_detail: Attributed to a Swyx talk framing; examples are projects drowning in PRs.
landing: Argues review capacity rather than generation is the constraint; cap outputs

author: Dex
quote: your job is now to wear the senior engineering hat
claim: In the AI era the junior's job is to make the system safer (guardrails) so the model just goes; accumulated senior taste should be captured and applied at design time, which is worth more than at review.
evidence_detail: Opinion; cites Mario Zechner on embracing friction.
landing: Encode owner taste as skills, rules and contracts used at design time

author: Dex
quote: Shipping is, like, getting it deployed, testing it, monitoring it in production
claim: Shipping differs from coding; feedback loops wiring support queue, Sentry and Datadog back to a model can be automated but architecture still needs a human.
evidence_detail: Credits Guillermo Rauch for the framing.
landing: Production feedback loop (Sentry) as a verifier input for post-deploy phases

author: Dex
quote: Opus 4.5, I actually think, is not as smart a model as Opus 4.1
claim: His view that Opus 4.5 was less smart than Opus 4.1 but faster, cheaper and better for people who did not know what they were doing.
evidence_detail: Personal opinion; no benchmark.
landing: Model-choice per task: capability is not monotonic with version number; test before assuming

author: Dex
quote: things that agents are good at are things with back pressure
claim: Agents do well where the loop gives automatic, deterministic feedback (compile, run, inspect), and badly where the outcome is not machine-checkable.
evidence_detail: Illustrated with a Ralph-Wiggum compiler build loop (spec, write program, compile, run); no numbers.
landing: CLAUDE.md or ship plan: prefer phases whose success is checkable by a script; flag phases lacking a check

author: Dex
quote: Short and sweet
claim: The deploy/PR-to-production gap is the bottleneck of agent-speed shipping; manual review after the PR is the slow stage, which a prod-data experiment step in CI could shorten.
evidence_detail: Dex restates Vaibhav's whiteboard (write/test loop is hot, PR to deploy is slow); Dex endorses it in the outro.
landing: CI: a job running checks on prod-shaped data; phase routine's reviewer step

author: Dex
quote: we're only allowed to have like 10 live experiments at a time
claim: Cap the number of concurrently live experiments Kanban-style so new ones must displace old ones (Vaibhav's proposal, Dex frames it as a work-in-progress limit).
evidence_detail: Framing of Vaibhav's idea of reserving a traffic slice for experiments; speculative runtime semantics.
landing: WIP limit on open draft PRs or live default-OFF features; nowhere obvious

author: Dex
quote: it's not good at assessing visual things
claim: Screenshot-based self-checking is weak backpressure for UI because model vision cannot get things pixel perfect, even with a browser feedback loop.
evidence_detail: His own motion-graphics attempt the day before: overlaps and gaps in lines the agent could not fix.
landing: Web manager UI phases: do not accept agent screenshot review as a verifier; require owner look or measured signal

author: Dex
quote: basically doing a taste approximation it can go and pull the data
claim: Replace agent taste judgement with production metrics: ship several variants behind flags and let the agent read conversion data as its own backpressure.
evidence_detail: Hypothetical conversion rates of 3%, 7%, 5% across three variants; no real experiment.
landing: nowhere obvious (single-tenant shop app, little traffic); maybe ops console metrics

author: Dex
quote: turn it on at 0.01%, make sure nothing's broken
claim: Agents may merge to production but a gradual ramp (tiny percentage, then widening over hours or days) with an agent reviewing metrics at each step should switch features on.
evidence_detail: Stated as the 'real magic' in discussion; no case study.
landing: Deploy path (manual railway up, mobile EAS builds): staged rollout of mobile builds; settings-gated features already like dispatcher default OFF

author: Dex
quote: two dimensions of how you activate your feature flags
claim: A flag can be activated along population (percentage or cohort) and along duration, and what matters is what you do with the outputs of that activation.
evidence_detail: Whiteboard discussion, endorsing Vaibhav's framing.
landing: shop_setting registry / enable_dispatcher gating: time-boxed enablement as a pattern

author: Dex
quote: they spend a lot of their time running around cleaning up feature flags
claim: Staff engineers at large teams spend much time cleaning stale flags; abandoned experiments leave dead code paths and lost context, so every flag needs an owner and an exit.
evidence_detail: From HumanLayer's work with staff engineers on teams of hundreds or thousands; no counts.
landing: Ship plan: any default-OFF flag (dispatcher, advances) gets a removal/decision date in the decisions journal

author: Dex
quote: take twice as long and you go clean up the parts of the code base
claim: Pay down mess incrementally by cleaning the code you touch on each feature (Ron Jeffries style) instead of scheduling big refactors.
evidence_detail: Cites a Ron Jeffries refactoring post; Vaibhav says his team does this plus occasional rewrites.
landing: Phase routine: a 'leave touched code cleaner' line; or nowhere obvious

author: Dex
quote: every deployment in a large distributed system is an experiment
claim: Every deploy is a rollout, so schema and API changes must support old and new versions side by side (new table or endpoint, old path kept).
evidence_detail: Prompted by a viewer question on DB schema changes behind flags; SaaS has two live versions vs shipped software with many.
landing: Alembic migration rules in CLAUDE.md (NOT VALID then VALIDATE, deploy ordering); mobile APKs in the field already create a multi-version fleet

author: Dex
quote: don't try to do that from day one because you're going to spend three months
claim: Build backpressure automation incrementally: start with a CLI or MCP that queries the metrics and a manual agent session, automate the loop only later, to avoid building a software factory before learning.
evidence_detail: Experience-based failure case he says he sees ('people try to over automate this on day one'); no numbers.
landing: Ship plan sequencing: manual-first before saving workflows or building verifier pipelines

source_title: Context Forking to Save Time, Tokens and Trouble
author: Kyle
quote: the context window only lets you push or pop from the newest end
claim: Model the context window as a downward-growing stack: you can pop whole user-message turns but not edit the middle, because random access causes cache misses, mangles context and breaks the harness's read-before-edit state.
evidence_detail: Conceptual model with three stated reasons; no measurement.
landing: compaction and context budget: why editing history is not an option; rewind instead

source_title: Context Forking to Save Time, Tokens and Trouble
author: Kyle
quote: I'll fork the conversation to explore different design & architectural paths.
claim: Build high-quality codebase context once, then fork the session several times to explore alternative designs, review the results and pick one or decide more research is needed.
evidence_detail: Author's own habit in the design phase.
landing: phase routine: fork from a warmed research session for alternative plans; judge-panel inputs

source_title: Context Forking to Save Time, Tokens and Trouble
author: Kyle
quote: reads all 40,000 tokens one chunk at a time
claim: When the agent floods context with a huge file or command output (the 40,000-token example), rewind to before it rather than continuing in a polluted window; harnesses often guard this by writing output to a file and showing the path.
evidence_detail: One example number (40,000 tokens); no experiment.
landing: output backpressure: output-to-file guards; rewind instead of compaction after a context blow-up

source_title: Context Forking to Save Time, Tokens and Trouble
author: Kyle
quote: Rewinding to course-correct an agent
claim: If the agent missed something mid-implementation, rewind to the turn boundary before it and re-steer rather than appending a correction to a long history.
evidence_detail: Listed use case with a diagram; no data.
landing: phase routine: course-correct by rewinding rather than piling on corrections

author: Dex
quote: It runs a real `claude` session inside tmux, sends a prompt, and emits stream JSON.
claim: Shannon lifecycles a real interactive Claude Code session in tmux and tails its on-disk transcript JSONL, giving a headless claude -p style SDK without ever using claude -p or calling the API directly.
evidence_detail: README architecture diagram; no measurements of why interactive differs from -p.
landing: Workflow orchestration: drive interactive sessions headlessly, and read the transcript JSONL as an audit trail of whether the routine/store was used (W2)

author: Dex
quote: `@dexh/shannon-agent-sdk` is a Claude Agent SDK-compatible facade
claim: A Claude Agent SDK-compatible facade lets code written against the SDK run on a subscription-backed interactive session instead, with parity still in progress.
evidence_detail: README; parity tracked in GOAL_PROGRESS.md (not in bundle).
landing: Workflow library: SDK-compatible drivers for saved workflows; cost routing

author: Dex
quote: the model itself actually is still obsessed with like cleaning up the output before it sees it
claim: Dex says agents pipe test output through head/tail/grep, miss the failing test, and re-run a five-minute suite repeatedly, burning time and context.
evidence_detail: Example: bun run test into head -n40 then re-run into grep error; he says auto-offloading long output to a file helps but the model's habit persists.
landing: Output backpressure: a wrapper script that runs the suite once, writes full output to a file, and prints only a capped summary plus path.

author: Dex
quote: if it accidentally doesn't do that, then you just ate 5,000 tokens of extra context
claim: Dex argues that relying on the model to remember to filter tool output (jq on gh pr create) is fragile, and that code mode makes output shaping deterministic by logging only the needed field.
evidence_detail: gh pr create example; 5,000-token figure is illustrative. Rhys notes it shows up in code mode as console.log(result.url).
landing: Enforce output limits in scripts rather than in prompt instructions; cap tool output by construction.

author: Dex+others
quote: hides a bunch of the intermediate stuff.
claim: Dex endorses chaining tool calls inside one code block so intermediate results never enter context (fetch from A, insert into B, log only the final field), instead of one tool call per hop or a bespoke tool per source/destination pair.
evidence_detail: Dex's walk-through; Vaibhav adds that hops become upper-bounded at two model calls instead of N.
landing: Saved workflow scripts that do multi-step gathering (register lookups, CI status, diff stats) and return a short result rather than many tool calls in the main context.

author: Dex
quote: I think bash is going to be considered harmful by the end of 2026.
claim: Dex predicts people will move away from raw bash as the agent execution environment toward code-based execution.
evidence_detail: Prediction made in passing alongside Rhys's list of bash problems (global CLI state, no read-only vs destructive signal, not shareable).
landing: Watch item: shell-script hooks and gates may later be better as typed scripts; no immediate change.

author: Dex
quote: build these as first class tools... then you pull that in and make it first class
claim: Dex's rule of thumb is to build the very common tools as first-class tools, let users bring MCPs for the long tail, and promote a long-tail tool to first class when it becomes popular so you can context-engineer it.
evidence_detail: Recalled from an earlier whiteboard on MCP versus bash; example is everyone adopting Notion.
landing: Promotion rule for skills/agents/scripts: repeated manual steps become a first-class skill or script once they recur.

author: Dex
quote: you are gonna have to start your context window with 50,000 tokens
claim: Dex notes that listing tools only at the start of a context window makes MCP tool sets static per context and that large tool lists eat context, which tool search tries to offload.
evidence_detail: Paraphrase of his exchange with Vaibhav and Rhys (MCP list-tools at context start; Claude offloads tools to search when there are too many). The 50k figure itself is carded at R29-5.
landing: Keep always-loaded context (CLAUDE.md, skill descriptions, MCP tool lists) small; load detail on demand.

author: Dex
quote: evaling a CLI for agent friendliness is a really interesting story
claim: Dex flags evaluating a CLI for agent-friendliness as a topic worth an episode, after Vaibhav says BAML measured theirs with a benchmark harness.
evidence_detail: Interest only; no result or number given in this episode.
landing: Idea: measure agent-facing scripts/CLIs (do agents use them correctly first time) before relying on them as backpressure.

author: other
quote: you have to look at the primitives, not the implementation of the primitives
claim: Guest Rhys Sullivan argues for managing a tool catalog (name, input, output) and a good OpenAPI spec rather than betting on bash or code mode, since the format will change; Dex responds 'I like it' and summarises it in his outro.
evidence_detail: Guest's closing takeaways; Dex adopts them in the recap ('schemas and input types').
landing: Keep FixFlow checks and workflows as format-independent scripts with typed inputs and outputs, so they can be re-hosted as skills, hooks or workflows later.

author: Dex
quote: you can basically say like, only give me two levels of depth and everything else, just leave the reference
claim: Dex endorses depth-limited type/schema disclosure, showing two levels and leaving references to fetch on demand, as a token-efficient way to describe tools.
evidence_detail: Dex restating Rhys's implementation; a progressive-disclosure example.
landing: Progressive disclosure for CLAUDE.md: summary at the top, detail behind references loaded only on demand.

source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
author: Dex
quote: you can context engineer the models faster than the labs can release a new model every six months
claim: Dex argues that building your own context engineering and harness on top of a model beats waiting for the lab, because labs ship new models only every few months.
evidence_detail: Stated as an argument against the 'bitter lessoned away' claim; no numbers, a reasoning-trace example (small models with thinking off).
landing: Justifies keeping a custom FixFlow outer harness (phase routine, workflows) rather than waiting for lab features.

source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
author: Dex
quote: Claude is nice for human readable plans... short and high level.
claim: Dex uses Claude for plans a human will read and interact with (short, high level, human-sounding) and GPT on high/xhigh when he does not want to spend time making the model build code-base understanding first.
evidence_detail: Personal model-by-task preference stated at end of episode.
landing: Model-per-task routing: plan and owner-view writing on one model, deep codebase understanding on another.

source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
author: Dex
quote: It's the velocity, not the position.
claim: Dex endorses the view that durable skill is rebuilding on each new model/harness release, not mastering any one loop, so test each new model against your own case.
evidence_detail: Closing exchange; Vaibhav: 'Your job is to always build the next while loop' and A/B-test each new model for customer value.
landing: Argues for periodic re-evaluation of the harness (model, effort, verifier choices) rather than freezing the phase routine.

source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
author: Dex
quote: for every one good article, there's like 10... half AI written slop of people just engagement farming
claim: Dex says most harness engineering articles are AI-written engagement farming and that his job is to cut through hype and jargon, warning against copying them uncritically.
evidence_detail: Opening framing, tied to an OpenAI engineer's apology for 'harness engineering hype'.
landing: Source-quality caution for the review; nowhere obvious in the harness.

source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
author: Dex
quote: Can dumb model with good harness beat the good model with bad harness?
claim: Dex treats lab-trained tool shapes as mattering mostly for tool-calling reliability: swapping to a differently trained model in the same harness degrades results, and he describes a proxy that can divert one harness's traffic to another model.
evidence_detail: Claims GPT-5 in the Claude Code harness gets 'terrible' performance (Vaibhav corrects to 'slightly different'); no measurement.
landing: Caution on running the same agent files or skills under a different model for verifiers: tool and prompt shapes tuned for one model may degrade on another.

source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
author: Dex
quote: you have like the model... and then what we might call the inner harness
claim: Dex splits a coding agent into the model, an inner harness (tool definitions, implementations, what tools return, such as offloading long bash output and rejecting long reads) and an outer harness (orchestration around it).
evidence_detail: Examples given: edit returns file info, long bash output auto-offloaded to a file, long reads rejected in favour of limit/offset.
landing: Vocabulary for the review: FixFlow only controls the outer harness (CLAUDE.md, routine, workflows); tool-output shaping sits in the inner harness.

source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
author: Dex+others
quote: If you've got a while loop that has more information than the one inside of it does, you can do better.
claim: Dex endorses Vaibhav's framing that alpha comes from stacking outer loops that carry more information about the process (RPI is such a loop around the inner agent loop).
evidence_detail: Vaibhav's drawing; Dex agrees ('this is a really good picture'), cites Codex goal mode / Ralph-style orchestrators as another stacked loop. Vaibhav said RPI boosted him more than any model or harness choice.
landing: Supports the phase routine and saved workflows as outer loops that carry process knowledge (phase, PR, register ids) the inner agent lacks.

source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
author: Dex
quote: I don't think there's a moat in it.
claim: Dex says a new orchestrator layer (e.g. a goal-generating loop that fans out to goal-completing loops) is probably about a hundred lines of Python or TypeScript, so he treats such stacking as hype with no moat.
evidence_detail: Reaction to a posted orchestrator built on Codex goal mode.
landing: Caution against heavy investment in a bespoke multi-agent orchestration library; a saved workflow script is cheap and replaceable.

source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
author: Dex
quote: you start your context window at 50,000 tokens because there's 32,000 tokens of tools
claim: Dex says Opus 4.7 in Claude Code with no customisation starts at about 50k tokens (32k tools plus 10k system prompt) before any user content.
evidence_detail: Stated from memory in answer to a chat question about why Claude Code is a poor harness for 4.7; no measurement shown.
landing: Context budget accounting: baseline load of tools/system prompt plus CLAUDE.md (390 lines) counts against the working window each phase.

source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
author: Dex+others
quote: if you're doing a hundred turn operation, reducing your accuracy by 1% actually has like a 25% impact
claim: Dex cites the compounding chart: a small per-call accuracy loss over a hundred-plus tool calls drops end-to-end success sharply, so tool shape matters in long agent runs.
evidence_detail: Dex recalls Vaibhav's chart (1% per-step loss gives roughly 25% or more at 100 steps); Vaibhav adds 'real fast' at 500 calls. Arithmetic, not an experiment.
landing: Argues for fewer steps and fewer unverified handoffs per phase; informs per-phase step budgets and verifier placement.

source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
author: Dex
quote: reasonably, the tools are damn simple. There is no nested object
claim: Dex says Claude Code works because its core tools (read, write, edit, bash) are simple with no nested objects, so the model has a good chance of calling them correctly.
evidence_detail: Dex's synthesis after the recursive-types/discriminated-unions discussion; also notes the Anthropic API did not support discriminated unions.
landing: Design rule for any custom agent, skill or script interface FixFlow adds: flat, simple tool/argument shapes.

source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
author: Dex
quote: The worst harness in the world is just YOLO prompting a model.
claim: Dex says a dumb model with a narrowly scoped, optimised harness can beat a strong model with a bad harness, and the spectrum runs from YOLO prompting to fully programmatic control.
evidence_detail: Answer to a chat question; ties to the context engineering argument, no numbers. Vaibhav: 'depends on the delta'.
landing: Supports effort/model routing: narrow, well-scoped steps let cheaper models or lower effort work; the harness does the heavy lifting.

source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
author: Dex
quote: been experimenting a lot with 5.5 on low mode.
claim: Dex reports using GPT-5.5 on low reasoning effort for already-planned work, and warns that extra-high effort can produce absurd over-testing (a thousand unit tests for a button colour change).
evidence_detail: Personal usage; the over-testing story is second-hand from Ben Davis and others. He says he has not yet formed a feel for higher effort levels.
landing: Effort routing: default low effort for execution of a settled plan; cap effort for verifiers to avoid over-elaboration.

author: Dex
quote: falls back to seeded fixture data so the UI still renders
claim: The app falls back to seeded fixture data when the live data source has no match, and the seed script uploads only git ls-files entries so .env and ignored files stay local.
evidence_detail: Ordinary setup README; no harness ideas beyond that.
landing: nowhere obvious

source_title: Designing AI systems for human leverage and why models cannot architect
author: Dex
quote: NEED HUMAN TO DESIGN THE ARCHITECTURE
claim: The AI can read huge codebases, propose design options, outline plans and rip out the changes, but a human must design the architecture.
evidence_detail: Opinion list of what AI can and cannot do; no experiment cited in this tweet.
landing: Phase routine: keep an explicit human-owned architecture step before the plan, and let agent steps run unattended after it.

source_title: Designing AI systems for human leverage and why models cannot architect
author: Dex
quote: might need human to fiddle with the order to make it hands-on testable during the build
claim: Ordering a plan into milestones that are incrementally testable is a second human-needed step, because coding RL such as SWE-bench-multilingual does not teach it.
evidence_detail: Claim about training signal; no data given.
landing: Ship plan phase design: a human or owner check on milestone order and testability before a phase starts.

source_title: Designing AI systems for human leverage and why models cannot architect
author: Dex
quote: you're splicing A and B into every other step
claim: Yolo back-and-forth with the agent splices human design and ordering work into every step; better to let the AI run and plug the human in only where needed.
evidence_detail: Workflow argument, anecdotal.
landing: One-phase-per-session routine: batch human decisions at the start (plan) rather than interleaving them.

source_title: Designing AI systems for human leverage and why models cannot architect
author: Dex
quote: we need to get clever with new evals and benchmarks
claim: Making models good at architecture and incremental testability needs new evals; he follows SlopCodeBench for this.
evidence_detail: Pointer to SlopCodeBench; no numbers in the tweet.
landing: Evidence base for effort-routing and verifier choices (links to his SlopCodeBench reports).

source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
author: Dex
quote: exhaust all the avenues in the single-while-loop stack
claim: Exhaust the single agent loop before adding a second loop, and fix the instruction set with your team rather than throwing more compute at it (speaker not individually attributed in the README).
evidence_detail: README highlight quote; README only.
landing: Workflow-tool orchestration: justify each added agent layer

source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
author: Dex
quote: Look at the damn data.
claim: Inspect what comes back instead of telling the model to figure it out; people never look at the returned data (speaker not individually attributed).
evidence_detail: README highlight quote; README only.
landing: Evidence folders: reviewers read raw outputs, not summaries

source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
author: Dex
quote: The evals are what survive.
claim: Code written around a model release may go stale, but a production-grounded eval set outlives models and harnesses; beware overfitting if the generated prompt looks like 60 if-else cases (speaker not individually attributed).
evidence_detail: README highlight and takeaway; README only.
landing: Knowledge-store pilot: cold-resume trial as a durable eval

source_title: AI That Works #54 Harness Engineering Without the Hype
author: Dex
quote: Only build your own harness if you're going to RL a model
claim: Building your own harness only pays when training a model on your tools; otherwise you compete with a 40-50 person team improving the stock harness (speaker not individually attributed).
evidence_detail: README takeaway; README only.
landing: Reinforces using Claude Code's built-in hooks, skills and agents rather than a custom harness

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: you have an instruction budget
claim: Every prompt, CLAUDE.md, system prompt, tool set and MCP draws on one limited budget of instructions the model can follow.
evidence_detail: Cites Kyle's CLAUDE.md post: frontier models follow about 150-200 instructions before half-attending to all; number inflated a year on but a budget still exists.
landing: CLAUDE.md length trim (W1); count instructions across CLAUDE.md plus skills plus phase routine

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: what's the right speed you can go
claim: Agent swarms and maximal token spend are the wrong bottleneck; the question is a sustainable speed, since 10x output thrown away in six months is burned time and money.
evidence_detail: Contrasts last year's 'spend as many tokens as possible' with this year's rate question; says he is iffy on agent swarms.
landing: Ship plan pacing; effort routing (token smarter, not harder)

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: anyone here the rag pipeline?
claim: Context engineering has two reads: put better information in the window, and put better instructions in it; the second is the one people neglect.
evidence_detail: Framing remark before the instruction-budget argument.
landing: CLAUDE.md and knowledge-store design: audit instructions, not only facts

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: over about 100,000 tokens
claim: The dumb zone begins around 100,000 tokens for a Claude model (the GPT figure differs), so more context past that degrades results.
evidence_detail: Number quoted from memory, attributed to the earlier dumb-zone talk; he flags the GPT threshold as different.
landing: One-phase-per-session rule; compaction trigger around 100k tokens

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: same amount of attention spread out over more instructions is not going to fix this
claim: A bigger context window does not fix instruction overload; attention is spread thinner over more instructions.
evidence_detail: Response to the idea that more context capacity removes the budget.
landing: CLAUDE.md trim rationale

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: difference between 99% and 97% is a 27% gap
claim: In long-horizon agentic tasks small per-step reliability gains compound, so by turn 20 a 99% versus 97% step reliability is a 27% gap.
evidence_detail: Arithmetic of compounding over 20 turns, used to justify context engineering past the naive-prompting frontier.
landing: Why per-step verification and short sessions matter

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: won't this just get bitter lessened?
claim: Context engineering will be partly obsoleted by each new model but keeps you 1-10% ahead of naive prompting; it can let a small cheap model do a bigger model's work.
evidence_detail: Cites Dan Shipper's 'surfing the models' and Swix's view that the bitter lesson will win eventually; example: get GPT-OSS to do GPT-5-high work.
landing: Decision to invest in saved workflows versus waiting for models; cheaper model routing

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: Design is where we're going. Structure is how we get there.
claim: Planning is split into a design discussion (current state, desired end state, patterns to follow, open questions; about 200 lines) and a structure outline (phases and checkpoints), mapping to design review and sprint planning.
evidence_detail: Used internally and with customers; QRSPI = questions, research, design, structure outline, plan, worktree, implement, pull request.
landing: Phase routine and draft-PR 'Plan @ sha' body: add a short design/outline artifact before the plan

also.source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
also.quote: Here's the current state, the desired end state. It has the patterns to follow.
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Step D (design discussion, ~200 lines): current state, desired end state, patterns to follow, resolved decisions and open questions in one editable markdown artifact.

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: brain surgery on the agent before it actually goes and slops out
claim: The design doc is the cheap place to steer the agent: have it brain-dump its understanding and the patterns it found, and correct bad-pattern choices before any code exists.
evidence_detail: Legacy codebases have six ways to do everything; the human picks the right one at the design step.
landing: Decisions journal in the draft PR; owner checkpoint after design

also.quote: do brain surgery on the model and update the patterns it's going to follow
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Reviewing the design doc before planning lets you correct the model's understanding cheaply, instead of re-steering after code exists.

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: you can't RL a model on architecture
claim: Humans must stay in the loop at design because bad architecture has a cost measured in months and years, so it cannot be trained against five-minute test cycles.
evidence_detail: Reason given for keeping the human at the design step; cites the Brooks 'design concept' idea via Matt Pocock.
landing: Which phases require an owner decision versus verifier approval

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: models just absolutely freaking love these horizontal plans
claim: Models plan by layer (database, services, API, front end) producing 1200 lines before anything is checked; the outline step should force vertical slices with a check after each small increment.
evidence_detail: Large debug surface when something breaks; remedy is a human re-steer at the structure outline ('build it the way you would have as an engineer').
landing: Phase sizing and per-slice fail-before/pass-after checks in the reviewer routine

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: 85 instructions plus your cloudmd plus your system prompt plus your tools
claim: A single mega-prompt of 85 instructions on top of CLAUDE.md, system prompt, tools and MCP is very unlikely to get adherence, and the plan step was skipped about half the time.
evidence_detail: Customer onboarding: experts got great results, teammates did not; without the 'magic words' the model skipped the Q&A step roughly 50% of the time.
landing: Phase routine in ship plan section 0: check how many instructions it carries and whether any step can silently be skipped

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: you just bot check it
claim: The line-by-line plan is for the agent, not for humans; reviewers read the high-level documents and the code, and only spot-check the plan.
evidence_detail: Higher-order documents give more leverage: the human reads less and the model uses fewer tokens.
landing: Owner one-page view built from design/outline, not the full plan

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: if you don't trust what the model's going to do
claim: The high-level documents can be expanded on demand: if the outline is not trusted, ask the model to add detail.
evidence_detail: Docs start high level and are plain markdown.
landing: Progressive-disclosure plan artifacts in the draft PR

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: Brooks had this idea of this thing that is never written down
claim: Writing the shared understanding of the design into a 200-line markdown artifact gives alignment with the agent and with teammates, and shortens code review.
evidence_detail: Alignment work not worth doing by hand in a Google doc becomes worth it when AI drafts it; compresses code-review cycles; two-hour coding tasks used to take two days because of alignment.
landing: Knowledge store and decisions journal: externalise the design concept

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: you're not going to go 2x faster
claim: Using AI only for coding speeds you up modestly; the larger gain comes from using it for planning and team alignment, which cuts rework and review time.
evidence_detail: Large-org experience (hundreds of engineers); no numbers.
landing: Where the harness spends agent effort: plan and review rather than only implementation

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: Raise your hand if you use this prompt.
claim: A methodology that works for an expert often fails when handed to a team, so rollout needs time spent watching real users struggle with it.
evidence_detail: Thousands of engineers and companies of all sizes since October; 'hundreds of hours' watching users; RPI use claimed at Uber and Block.
landing: P1 cold-resume trial design: test the routine with an agent other than the author

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: There is no magic prompt.
claim: The QRSPI prompts are deliberately unpublished; the point is to learn instruction budgeting, and if results are poor, break the three prompts into about eight smaller workflows.
evidence_detail: Derivation left as an exercise; open-source HumanLayer prompts are the starting point.
landing: Skill and workflow library: many small prompts, each owned and tested

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: how do we evaluate that?
claim: Teams adopting a prompting system need to know what is working and why, and how to evaluate changes to the prompts; he offers no answer in this talk and points to a separate adoption talk (process, defensible metric, one person shipping non-slop).
evidence_detail: Open problem stated; also says he has no answer yet on testing and verification.
landing: Measurement pipeline (skipped by the harness review): mark as re-opening

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: Repeat the most important instruction at the very end of the prompt
claim: A standard prompting rule: repeat the most important instruction at both the start and the end of the prompt.
evidence_detail: Cited as what the 'magic words' implement; not claimed as a fix.
landing: CLAUDE.md structure: place critical invariants at top and end

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: what is PR slop, where does it come from, and how to combat it
claim: The talk abstract promises a view on what PR slop is, where it comes from and how to combat it, but the delivered keynote does not cover it.
evidence_detail: Event-page abstract only; absent from the transcript read.
landing: nowhere obvious; check later talks or posts for the PR-slop argument

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: if you build a tool that requires hours of training, like go fix the tool
claim: If a workflow only works when the user says magic words, the tool is at fault, not the user.
evidence_detail: Seven hours of training for three steps; some users got bad plans for lack of one repeated sentence.
landing: Phase routine should not depend on the agent being told a particular phrase; cold-resume trial P1

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: don't use prompts for control flow if you can use control flow for control flow
claim: Sequencing, branching and step selection belong in code (switch and if statements) around small prompts, not in one prompt that describes the workflow.
evidence_detail: Stated as the lesson after splitting create_plan; also a classify-then-smaller-instruction-module example from customer support bots; says a smaller, dumber model may then suffice.
landing: Workflow scripts (W5) and a phase driver instead of prose in ship plan section 0

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: now they're all under 40 instructions
claim: The 85-instruction create_plan prompt was split into design, structure and plan prompts, each under 40 instructions.
evidence_detail: Before/after instruction counts only; no adherence rate given.
landing: Skills split: keep each skill or agent prompt under about 40 instructions

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: hide the ticket from the researcher programmatically
claim: Research stays objective if one context turns the ticket into questions and a second context, never shown the ticket, answers only the questions.
evidence_detail: Bad research (given the ticket) carries opinions steered toward the model's first-picked solution; can be done with plain prompting and a workflow, same as deep-research systems.
landing: Cold-resume trial and verifier design: refuters/researchers get questions, not the proposed answer; Workflow script step

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: a good research is mostly facts, but a bad research will have opinions
claim: Research output should be a compressed, objective snapshot of how the code works today, with no opinions or implementation planning.
evidence_detail: Lazy 'research, I have to do this' prompts versus ticket-derived questions such as how endpoints are registered.
landing: Knowledge-store entries for verified diagnoses: facts only, separate from proposals

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: Don't read the plans, just read the code.
claim: Reading a long plan is not leverage because a thousand-line plan costs about as much reading as the thousand lines of code, and the code must be read anyway; review the code, not the plan.
evidence_detail: Reverses his November 2025 'you have to read the plan' advice; order-of-magnitude equivalence of plan and code length.
landing: Owner review of draft PR bodies and plan docs: where human reading effort goes

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: Please read the code.
claim: Not reading the code (lights-off software factory) failed over about six months and forced ripping out large parts of the system; he advises reading every line and aiming for 2-3x rather than 10x.
evidence_detail: Own six-month experience; warns of three weeks of re-onboarding downtime if nobody has read the code for three months.
landing: Owner view and reviewer role: keep a human code-read step on the critical paths (money, outbox, lifecycle)

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: you find out your unknowns during planning instead of during implementation
claim: Extend learning tests to UX unknowns: build throwaway pure components in Storybook before the plan, because a plan document cannot tell you whether a UI will look good.
evidence_detail: Describes HumanLayer's own practice; the tips-to-modals feature had plan docs he could not judge visually.
landing: Phase routine pre-plan step: a cheap proof script or stub that resolves an unknown before the plan is written

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: This is why we do plan mode.
claim: Reading the plan catches stale-knowledge errors: the default plan picked Storybook 8 and he knew 10 was current; Crispy would have web-searched the latest version.
evidence_detail: Observed live in Vaibhav's repo; same issue with an old Rust crate version in the plan.
landing: Plan/research step: check dependency versions against the web, not the model's memory

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: Always read, you have to read the plans. You should read something.
claim: A human must read the plan even when little else is read.
evidence_detail: Said while reviewing Vaibhav's plan.
landing: Phase routine: owner view/plan review checkpoint

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: you could do it incrementally
claim: Migrate a brownfield repo to a new pattern one component at a time with a small scoped prompt, not an all-at-once migration.
evidence_detail: Advice during a live migration; the prompt asked for a single, already-pure component.
landing: Phase sizing: one small slice per phase, bootstrap then add one

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: find a way to move things out of Figma earlier and earlier
claim: Agents are good at code in distribution and poor at WYSIWYG tools or MCP into them, so make mockups be the real components and drop the translation step.
evidence_detail: Teams moving fastest do this; his designer 'hates Figma now'; no numbers.
landing: nowhere obvious (design handoff for the web manager)

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: if you're not willing to migrate to a monorepo
claim: Second-hand claim: agent-tool vendors refuse enterprise clients unwilling to move to a monorepo because agent results are much better there.
evidence_detail: Reported from unnamed people who build coding agent tools.
landing: nowhere obvious (FixFlow is already a single monorepo)

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: it's only as good as the data set that you create
claim: Snapshot tests are brittle and only as good as the cases captured, so every production failure should be turned into a new snapshot case; he prefers visual checking for now.
evidence_detail: Answer to an audience question.
landing: CI/regression policy: each production bug adds a fixture or regression test

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: Kyle wanted to integrate this charting library
claim: Get a new library working in isolation first (in Storybook) before wiring it, as a learning test.
evidence_detail: Kyle's charting library for dashboards; 'once baked, it just works everywhere'.
landing: Phase routine: spike new dependencies in isolation before the plan

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: we will as a team review just the storybook stuff
claim: Review the design artifact on its own in PR review: pull down and look at only the components.
evidence_detail: Team practice at HumanLayer.
landing: Reviewer step for UI PRs: inspect the rendered artifact, not only the diff

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: you can freeform and jump straight to structure outline skill
claim: Use a lighter path for small tasks: freeform, then a structure-outline skill as a mini plan, rather than the full Crispy flow, which takes 15 to 20 minutes.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav says full Crispy plan mode takes 15-20 minutes; Dex suggests the mini plan.
landing: Phase routine: a tiered path (full plan versus mini outline) by task size

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: your options are either get your AI to write Stitch or Figma or Canva
claim: Prefer working where the model is in distribution (React code on disk) over tools reached through MCP.
evidence_detail: Argument for Storybook over Figma MCP.
landing: nowhere obvious

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: you can't read the plan and know whether it's going to look good
claim: Frontend work needs a different workflow from backend: for backend, reading the plan is enough to judge it, for frontend you have to see it, so heavy up-front markdown planning is a poor fit.
evidence_detail: Stated as the motivation for the episode; no measurements.
landing: Phase routine: declare which phases need a visible artifact before plan approval (web manager UI phases)

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: you don't need a plan to build one pure component
claim: Do not plan small, visually judged pieces: build the pure component family from an outline, riff on its states, and only then write the plan for the multi-system wiring.
evidence_detail: His own workflow; plan only for work spanning four systems across two repos.
landing: Phase routine: a lighter path for small UI phases versus the full plan-first path

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: unit testing for visual stuff
claim: Storybook is unit testing for UI: reproduce a bad state by setting props rather than clicking through a running app to recreate it.
evidence_detail: Example: a to-do card wrong in 'deleting' state fixed by editing props in a story; 'every bug adds a story' is how their Storybook grew.
landing: Web manager (src/): Storybook or a props-driven state gallery as a fast verifier for UI bugs

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: you have pure components that just take props and render
claim: Split pure render-only components from wired components that fetch and hold state; only pure ones go in Storybook and the agent reasons about one thing at a time.
evidence_detail: Architecture rule; HumanLayer keeps pure ones in packages/ui shared by apps; Riptide has a story per coding-agent output type.
landing: CLAUDE.md or src/ conventions: pure vs wired component rule; smaller per-task context

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: make sure it's actually importing your shared components
claim: Failure mode: Claude draws a duplicate component inside Storybook instead of importing the real one, so the story never exercises the app; check the story imports the shared component.
evidence_detail: Seen repeatedly by him; he checked the generated stories file during the demo.
landing: Reviewer checklist item: verify the test or story imports the production code under test, not a copy

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: Claude understands this concept of pure versus wired. It's not super baked in the training set
claim: The model does not know the pure/wired pattern by default, so it must be stated in the prompt or instructions.
evidence_detail: His experience; 'if you prompt it properly, you can get there'.
landing: CLAUDE.md / skill: a short pattern rule for the web app

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: I just use agent browser basically
claim: Close the visual loop with a browser-agent skill that screenshots the story and feeds the PNG back to the model; no human for pure visual changes.
evidence_detail: Uses Vercel's agent-browser skill; fell back to the browser agent shipped in gstack.
landing: .claude/skills/: a screenshot/browser verification skill for the web manager

source_title: AI That Works #53 Agentic Coding for Frontend Apps
author: Dex
quote: maybe we need a skill for like setting up storybook and extracting styles
claim: Bootstrap friction (styles, theming) is a candidate for a reusable skill; he bootstrapped faster by pointing the agent at an existing Storybook as a starter template.
evidence_detail: Five components in about five minutes by copying another repo's Storybook.

author: Dex
quote: What about the system allowed them to break something
claim: When a change breaks something with no failing test, ask why a contract, type or pre-merge check did not enforce the dependency; fix the system, not the person.
evidence_detail: Said in reply to a question on code breaking dependents; no example.

author: Dex
quote: unidirectional data flow where all writes go to an API server
claim: Riptide uses one-way data flow: all writes go to the API and the database, and database changes stream to subscribed clients; cancellation propagates down to the source request.
evidence_detail: Brief description of Riptide architecture.
landing: nowhere obvious

author: Dex
quote: It only streams when the JSON block is finished.

evidence_detail: Observed behaviour discussed during the whiteboard section.

author: Dex

source_title: Alex Lavaee: From RPI to QRSPI
author: other
quote: The framework grew from 3 steps to 8. That's added complexity
claim: Critique: QRSPI adds ceremony, and if the workflow needs too much ceremony engineers will skip steps and return to the original problems.
evidence_detail: Reports community pushback; no data. Also states eight stages while Dex's talk and interview say seven.
