author: other
quote: Question, Research, Spec, Plan, Implement
claim: Critique of fidelity: the wiki expands the acronym differently (Spec for Design, five steps, drops Structure and Worktree), showing the framework is easily misreported secondhand.
evidence_detail: Compare talk: Questions, Research, Design, Structure, Plan, Worktree, Implement, PR.
landing: Use the primary talk only; do not rely on secondary summaries when copying QRSPI

author: Dex
quote: Do not outsource the thinking. If you let the model make decisions
claim: Dex's rule: do not outsource the thinking; ask the model for options and decide yourself, because a model told to do a thing follows its first tokens down one path while one asked to choose reads what you want.
evidence_detail: Explained during Vaibhav's live design session; Vaibhav adds that models are sycophantic and a suggestion must be marked as a suggestion.
landing: Phase routine: design/decision step should present options for the owner rather than direct instructions; wording rule for prompts that suggest.

author: Dex
quote: so that you can do brain surgery on it before
claim: Dex says the markdown docs (research, design) exist so the model dumps its thinking and patterns for you to re-steer at a high level before dropping to code.
evidence_detail: Describes RPI use in Riptide; no numbers.
landing: Decisions journal in the draft PR: surface the model's plan in readable form before implementation.

author: Dex
quote: I always want to be able to resume from the document.
claim: Dex keeps every decision tracked in a document outside the context window (unidirectional: read doc, tell Claude, Claude updates doc) so a session can die or drift and be resumed from the doc.
evidence_detail: Contrasted with Vaibhav, who keeps long context and writes to disk only at checkpoints, saying per-decision writes halve his speed.
landing: Directly the P1 cold-resume trial and one-phase-per-session; also the knowledge store: state lives in repo files not chat.

author: Dex
quote: I usually try to recontinue it at over like a hundred K tokens.
claim: Dex's own habit is to restart a session once past about 100K tokens, though he says the dumb-zone figure is a rule of thumb for people without intuition and some reasoning-heavy tasks should stay under 50K while others tolerate 800K.
evidence_detail: Numbers 100K, 50K and 800K are practitioner habits, not measurements; Vaibhav reports 3-4 features at up to 800K with good outcomes.
landing: Context budget rule for phase sessions: a numeric trigger (about 100K) for ending a session and resuming from the PR/decisions journal.

author: Dex
quote: you're totally fine at 120 or 220 or 320k tokens
claim: Dex passes on Chris's distinction that long context is fine for reading and summarising documents but multi-turn tool-calling loops (run test, fix, rerun) are where the model spins out.
evidence_detail: Second-hand from a Twitter post; no numbers beyond the quoted token counts.
landing: Verifier/implementer sessions with test loops should be kept short; reading/research sessions can run longer.

author: Dex
quote: might be going back to Opus 4-5 for certain things
claim: Dex says HumanLayer published early findings on 1M-context models and may go back to Opus 4.5 for some work, and that a 1M window is the same model stretched with techniques like YaRN rather than added intelligence.
evidence_detail: Brief remark; refers to a Kyle blog post and defers the discussion; the YaRN claim is stated as fact without evidence.
landing: Model routing: evidence that a newer or larger-context model is not automatically better for all phases.

author: Dex
quote: get the foundation there, make it work end to end
claim: Dex endorses building the most foundational layer first and making it work end to end (vertical slices, tracer bullets) instead of making the model design everything up front.
evidence_detail: Aside in the BAML design session.
landing: Phase ordering in the 40-phase plan: thin end-to-end slice before breadth.

author: Dex
quote: remove that section, and then it'll come up in the design discussion
claim: Dex's tip: delete sections of a ticket you are unsure about so they do not enter as pre-banked decisions; the model then researches code patterns and raises them in the design discussion.
evidence_detail: His own habit; Vaibhav replies his case is novel so no patterns exist.
landing: Plan authoring: mark unknowns as open questions for the design step rather than writing guesses into the plan.

author: Dex
quote: 200 lines of spec that's gonna turn into thousands of lines of code
claim: Dex stresses that one wrong line in a 200-line spec multiplies into thousands of lines of code, which is why hours go into reading the ticket and design before any implementation.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav adds a 12-minute ticket read and about 2.5 hours design plus 5 hours ticket-2 work, then a 16,000-line closures PR done in about 36 hours with sleep; single-developer anecdote.
landing: Owner review of plan before implementation; supports review budget placed on the spec rather than the diff.

author: Dex
quote: But if it's 30 % wrong, then I know it's easy to just start over
claim: Dex's rule: if an implementation is about 5% wrong, steer it; if about 30% wrong, drop the ticket in again and restart, because tokens are cheap compared to the effort of re-steering a model that has gone down a bad path.
evidence_detail: Endorses Vaibhav's habit of nuking the branch, fixing the ticket and rerunning; percentages are intuition.
landing: Phase routine: an explicit restart rule (discard branch, amend plan, re-run) instead of long repair chains in one session.

author: Dex
quote: it will find a bunch of like bad patterns or bad architecture
claim: Dex says models are sycophantic judges: asked whether code is good they say yes, asked what is wrong they find problems, so a free-form model verdict cannot deterministically evaluate quality.
evidence_detail: Observation from his own posting; no measurement in this episode.
landing: Refuter design: refute-by-default framing is the deliberate counter; also a caution on any verifier that returns an open-ended opinion.

author: Dex
quote: you do a bunch of Boolean classifiers on the thing you're evaluating
claim: Dex's fix for unreliable model grading is to have the model answer many yes/no questions (is it X, does it do Y) and compute the score from those flags in deterministic code.
evidence_detail: Refers to a JP Morgan emails episode from months earlier; no numbers.
landing: Verifier output format: per-register-id boolean checks (fail-before/pass-after) tallied by a script rather than a prose verdict.

author: Dex+others
quote: you're adding slop at the final layer
claim: Dex and Vaibhav agree that an auto-reviewer (CodeRabbit, 50 comments on a 25,000-line change) adds slop at the final layer because a model always finds something to say; read it and choose, do not pass it all back.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav's wording; Dex adds the model's incentive to generate more tokens; Vaibhav has Claude summarise the comments.
landing: Reviewer scope: cap reviewer findings and require the owner to triage; supports capped outputs and against automatic apply of all review comments.

author: Dex
quote: you can paralyze two hard tasks at a time.
claim: Dex limits himself to one primary task plus one or two secondary tasks, always returning to the primary when unblocked, to minimise cycle time per task rather than spreading attention.
evidence_detail: Personal practice; grounded in factory flow theory, no measurement.
landing: Owner workflow: one phase in flight with at most a secondary phase, matches one-phase-per-session.

author: Dex
quote: optimize a station that is not the bottleneck, the less efficient the overall system becomes
claim: Dex (citing The Goal) argues that optimising non-bottleneck steps adds work in progress and lowers throughput; finish work nearest done first and optimise the slowest step of the pipeline.
evidence_detail: Book summary and a story from an early-career manager; no software data.
landing: Where to spend effort in the harness: find the real bottleneck (owner review? verifier cost?) before tuning a step; relevant to the xhigh-everywhere verifier question.

author: Dex
quote: be very explicit about when is this, you know, relevant to your task
claim: Dex wraps CLAUDE.md rules in an XML 'important: if you are doing X' block stating exactly when they apply, because the system message tells Claude to ignore context unless highly relevant; his CLAUDE.md is a repo map plus exact commands like the DB query.
evidence_detail: Shows the snippet and a multi-repo template (git pull the branch before research); no adherence numbers.
landing: CLAUDE.md trim and rewrite: make each retained rule conditional on a named situation; map-of-repo style; a pre-research sync step as a routine item.

author: Dex
quote: this is a deep link into the Riptide app
claim: HumanLayer's PRs carry a link to the artifacts list and a deep link to the task that produced them, so a reviewer can open the agent sessions behind the change.
evidence_detail: Shown on screen with a Closures PR; Dex says no one will read every session.
landing: Draft PR body 'Plan @ sha' plus evidence folder: a link from PR to the session transcript/evidence gives an outside check on whether the routine ran.

author: Dex
quote: you have to unlock it by doing 100 sessions or something.
claim: Dex says HumanLayer considered letting experienced users auto-advance past the design discussion but gated it behind many sessions; for now the design step needs human reading, as Vaibhav insists he must know it is correct.
evidence_detail: Half-joking product idea; the human-read design gate is Vaibhav's stated practice.
landing: Phase routine: keep the human checkpoint on design/plan, auto-advance the rest; earn automation by track record.

author: Dex
quote: the benefit is that you get research without opinions.
claim: Dex defends the RPI research step as a separate pass with a context window that stays objective (research questions first, then research), accepting multiple passes over the same code and slower research.
evidence_detail: Brief comment while research ran 15+ minutes; he adds fast code-search models and LSP/call-graph tools as ways to speed it up.
landing: Call-graph/LSP tooling (a skipped item) and research-first agent design: re-opens call-graph tooling.

author: Dex
quote: auto research doesn't work well unless you have a good way to collect metrics
claim: Dex says auto-research style loops (an agent tuning prompts, models and sub-agents) need a good metric signal, and HumanLayer is building evals on coding agents, e.g. to make the research step faster.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav suggests a latency metric over scenarios of long/short tickets and different codebases; nothing built or measured yet.
landing: Measurement pipeline (explicitly skipped by harness review): marks a re-opening; a metric is the precondition for tuning effort levels.

author: Dex
quote: automate the process of building confidence that something is stable enough to ship
claim: Dex defines the purpose of testing as automating confidence that a change is stable enough to ship and better than what existed, and with non-deterministic systems wants many sliceable dimensions per test case to see which category moved.
evidence_detail: Restatement of Vaibhav's scenario/metric design (80% scenario thresholds, quorum runners); no data.
landing: Acceptance gate design: scenario-sliced pass rates rather than a single boolean for model-involved behaviour.

author: Dex
quote: distill them out into another like high level, almost like PRD style.
claim: After a long design discussion, Dex and Vaibhav have the model rewrite the decisions into a fresh clean ticket as if known on day one, then rerun the pipeline; the second design pass is so clean it needs little thought.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav reports about 2.5 hours design plus 5 hours on ticket 2, then auto-advanced implementation; Dex describes the step.
landing: Phase routine: at a session boundary, regenerate the plan from decisions journal so the next session starts from a single clean source.

author: Dex
quote: shifting away from "token harder" to "token smarter"
claim: The AI coding meta is moving from maximizing token spend to spending tokens more smartly.
evidence_detail: Observation across circles, naming Ralph wiggum, RPI, conductor, cmux as the August 'token harder' wave.
landing: Effort routing: do not default verifiers to xhigh

author: Dex
quote: rarely hit 50% of claude max quota
claim: His team went from 3k per engineer raw token spend to rarely using 50% of a Claude Max quota because they care about avoiding slop architecture.
evidence_detail: Self-reported, with footnote 'probably still moving faster than you'; no measurement.
landing: Cost/effort routing in Workflow scripts

author: Dex
quote: you are being held back by your inability to spend tokens
claim: The August 2025 mandate was to spend many tokens via Ralph wiggum loops, RPI, and parallel worktree tools, which he now treats as the wrong emphasis.
evidence_detail: Retrospective characterisation.
landing: Workflow orchestration: parallel fan-out only where it earns its cost

source_title: The Humans in the Loop Deep Dive reprint
author: Dex

claim: RPI had no magic; the value was context engineering, and the team is productizing collaboration features around coding agents.
evidence_detail: Product framing (Google Docs/Figma-like collaboration); reprint of Heavybit text with no new material.
landing: nowhere obvious

author: Dex+others
quote: MCP does not cause context rot.
claim: Dex relays Kyle's point that the protocol is not what rots context; the design of the tools (tokens used, inefficient prompts) is, and the same tools as CLIs would rot it equally.
evidence_detail: Attributed to his co-founder Kyle; no measurement given in this episode.
landing: Skills/tools authoring: judge each tool or skill by the tokens and instructions it adds, not by its transport.

author: Dex
quote: MCP is not for a different way to call APIs.
claim: Dex argues MCP is a plugin system for letting users bring tools you did not anticipate; if you know the functionality you need, write against the SDK instead.
evidence_detail: Argument, with Claude Code extensibility as example.
landing: Skill/agent design: build first-class, in-repo scripts for known needs; reserve external plugins for the long tail.

author: Dex
quote: you have an instruction budget for every model
claim: Dex states every model has an instruction budget: the more instructions (including every function definition in an MCP server), the worse it adheres to any one, including the latest user message.
evidence_detail: Stated as established; Vaibhav cites GitHub MCP at ~50-60k tokens added per call.
landing: CLAUDE.md trim (W1): supports treating each rule line as spending a finite budget; also skill descriptions loaded every session.

author: Dex
quote: Migrate it and build a first-class integration.
claim: Dex's rule: do context engineering and token pinching on the high-use paths, let the long tail run through generic lower-quality mechanisms, and promote a long-tail item when usage shows it is popular.
evidence_detail: Compares to the earlier reasoning episode: make it work on a beefy reasoning model, then optimise the frequent case for a small model.
landing: Workflow library (W5) and effort routing (L1): save and tune only the workflows that recur; run rare ones generically at high effort.

author: Dex
quote: give people ways to visualize it
claim: Dex praises Claude Code's /context command and says a harness should show users how many tokens MCPs and skills consume, then give tools to prune them (and tell users when an MCP has gone unused).
evidence_detail: Refers to the Claude Code /context command; the unused-MCP warning is Vaibhav's idea that Dex likes.
landing: Context-budget measurement: run /context at session start to record what CLAUDE.md, skills and agents cost; supports the W1 trim decision with a number.

author: Dex
quote: Just remove the directory as a parameter
claim: Dex says parameters the deterministic side already knows (e.g. the working directory) should be injected by a closure and removed from the tool schema so the model never has to pass them, and the tool schema should shrink to what the user has connected.
evidence_detail: Code sketch of a ticket-fetch tool with zero/one/many sources; Vaibhav adds auditing highly frequent tools' parameters.
landing: Custom agents/skills: scripts that take fewer arguments because the harness fills ids (shop, phase, SHA) itself.

author: Dex
quote: the things that are super, super common should be here
claim: Dex criticises Claude Code's tool-search design: the commonly used tools (read, edit, bash, fetch) should stay in the main context and only the rare ones be offloaded behind search, because making the agent search for the right tool adds turns.
evidence_detail: Says he has seen the agent search to find a tool and the skill tool; Vaibhav agrees but states he could not share Codex details.
landing: Skill loading: keep the few always-needed skills/rules always loaded, put rarely used material behind on-demand lookup.

author: Dex
quote: If you are willing to put in the time and do this context engineering.
claim: Dex argues models have a jagged frontier and that hand context engineering on your specific tasks extends your frontier beyond the default, so it is not simply thrown away when a model improves.
evidence_detail: Whiteboard in radial coordinates with illustrative 90%/40%/50% figures, not measured.
landing: Justifies investing in harness tuning even though models improve; counterweight to 'bitter lesson' objections.

author: Dex
quote: when it wants to send money, that's a permission escalation
claim: Dex says a human-in-the-loop approval of an agent action is not deterministic (the agent could click or fill differently) and proposes per-action signed tokens (Rich Authorization Requests style) that bind exactly the approved action with a short expiry, with read access granted separately from write.
evidence_detail: Design proposal using JWT/passkey signing; no implementation shown.
landing: Closes the gap between 'approved' and 'done': a machine-checkable binding between what the owner approved and what ran; loosely relevant to phase routine compliance checks.

author: Dex
quote: skills only work if you have a bash tool.
claim: Dex notes skills offload auth and execution to CLIs/curl and so need a bash tool; in locked-down enterprise settings without bash they degrade to prompt modules, and bash trades determinism for flexibility and context efficiency.
evidence_detail: Reasoned trade-off, no measurements.
landing: Skills design: each skill should wrap a repo script or CLI (deterministic part) with a prompt shell, not carry logic only in prose.

author: Kyle
quote: instruction adherence was dramatically degraded, and not just at longer context lengths
claim: After a couple of weeks with Opus 4.6 (1M context) HumanLayer saw worse instruction adherence even within the 200k range (ignoring design docs, trivial mistakes, disobeying) and switched back to Opus 4.5.
evidence_detail: Weeks of team use; no benchmark numbers.
landing: model/effort routing: do not assume a bigger-window model follows instructions better; pin verifier model by evidence

author: Kyle
quote: how many instructions they can follow reasonably well before instruction adherence drops off
claim: There is a measurable per-model 'instruction budget' that correlates with model size, and extended-context variants (YaRN-style) get a bigger window but the same budget.
evidence_detail: Refers to an earlier study (chart not visible); the YaRN claim is stated as 'likely'.
landing: CLAUDE.md length target; phase routine: cap instructions loaded per phase

author: Kyle
quote: digging us deeper into the dumb zone
claim: Treat the context window as a haystack in which every CLAUDE.md line, tool description, tool result and message competes; a bigger haystack with the same needle makes finding the relevant instruction harder.
evidence_detail: Analogy, no numbers.
landing: CLAUDE.md trim; one phase per new session

author: Kyle
quote: All non-trivial operations should be delegated to sub-agents.
claim: A 'subagent-orchestrator' skill tells the parent to delegate research, codebase understanding and verbose bash/gh/aws investigation to sub-agents, use one sub-agent per distinct task, and not split overlapping tasks; it kept Opus coherent at longer context.
evidence_detail: Skill text printed in full; reports it helped 'in combination with our existing workflow skills'; no numbers.
landing: an orchestrator skill in .claude/skills/; sub-agent delegation for log/CI digging

author: Kyle
quote: trigger at the 100k token mark instead of 40% of the usable context
claim: HumanLayer's context-high warning was moved from ~40% of Sonnet's 168k usable window (~100k tokens) to a flat 100k tokens for long-context models, which is only 10% of Opus 1M.
evidence_detail: Concrete thresholds: 168k = 200k minus 32k output reserve; 40% about 100k; 10% of 1M.
landing: phase routine: a ~100k-token wrap-up trigger inside a phase; context budget check (the harness review skipped a context system)

author: Kyle
quote: Context isolation beats context expansion.
claim: Keep each window small and focused via sub-agents, progressive disclosure and context-efficient backpressure rather than a larger window; long-context models degrade at all lengths, not just long ones.
evidence_detail: TL;DR of the post; supported only by the team's experience.
landing: validates one-phase-per-new-session; sub-agent use inside phases

also.author: Dex

author: Dex
quote: Do not shard into separate files that require the agent to make tool calls to discover
claim: Avoid progressive disclosure into separate files unless the content is very verbose; conditional inline blocks keep everything visible while weighting what matches, so sharding is a last resort.
evidence_detail: Argued as the point of <important if>; contrasts with sharding into docs the agent must go and read.

also.quote: Do not shard into separate files that require the agent to make tool calls to discover
also.author: Dex

author: Dex
quote: claude plugin marketplace add dexhorthy/slopfiles
claim: Skills are distributed as plugins through a git-hosted marketplace installed with two commands, making configuration shareable and versionable.
evidence_detail: Install instructions.

author: Dex
quote: Pause, reset, and change approach rather than continuing to thrash.

source_title: Getting Claude to Actually Read Your CLAUDE.md
author: Dex
quote: explicitly tells the model the contents "may or may not be relevant."
claim: Claude Code wraps CLAUDE.md in a system-reminder saying the contents may not be relevant, so the longer the file, the more sections the model treats as optional.
evidence_detail: Stated as observed behaviour of the harness; no measurement.

source_title: Getting Claude to Actually Read Your CLAUDE.md
author: Dex
quote: <important if="you are writing or modifying tests">

source_title: Getting Claude to Actually Read Your CLAUDE.md
author: Dex

claim: Do not wrap everything: project identity, directory structure and tech stack stay unconditional, and each condition must be narrow ('you are writing code' matches almost everything and defeats the purpose).
evidence_detail: Rules of thumb from his own use.
landing: CLAUDE.md trim: keep stack table unconditional, conditionalise the invariants by task type

source_title: Getting Claude to Actually Read Your CLAUDE.md
author: Dex
quote: stale code snippets, style rules that should be in a linter, vague instructions
claim: An improve-claude-md skill automates restructuring a CLAUDE.md: extracts foundational content, wraps the rest in conditions, and removes stale snippets, linter-able style rules and vague instructions; output should still be reviewed.
evidence_detail: Skill description; he says 'it's not perfect'.
landing: the CLAUDE.md trim: run or copy this skill as a first pass (gated behind the knowledge-store pilot)

author: Dex
quote: the word "spec" is broken anyway

evidence_detail: Terminology claim.

author: Dex
quote: i own the execution, and give little things to the agent
claim: The conservative option is to own execution yourself and delegate small pieces to the agent while checking along the way.
evidence_detail: Described as the 'decel' default.
landing: Phase sizing: small delegated units with checks
inventory_ref: (B) March 2026 — Spec is the new code is not enough

author: Dex
quote: here have some alpha on what we've been working on the last few months
claim: HumanLayer has a QRSPI method (linked hlyr.dev/qrspi-mlops) as the successor to RPI, held back for AI Engineer Miami.
evidence_detail: Link only; the target page was not read in this task.
landing: Phase routine design: check linked QRSPI material for question/design/structure stages

author: Dex
quote: roughly the same length and detail as the code itself
claim: A spec detailed enough to reliably generate quality code is about as long and detailed as the code, so reviewing it adds little over reviewing the code.
evidence_detail: Endorses Gabriella Gonzalez's blog post; no numbers.
landing: Ship plan: plans/specs should not be reviewed as a substitute for code; keep plan short and review code
inventory_ref: (B) March 2026 — Spec is the new code is not enough

author: Dex
quote: you ABSOLUTELY SHOULD care about the code at that level of abstraction
claim: Except for prototypes and side projects, engineers should still read and care about code, even for zero-to-one software.
evidence_detail: Stated position.
landing: Owner view and reviewer expectations; human code reading stays in loop
inventory_ref: (B) March 2026 — Spec is the new code is not enough

author: Dex
quote: lets you resteer the model *before* it slops out N-thousand LOC
claim: The safe way to gain leverage over coding agents is a mechanism that lets you resteer before large code is generated, not a spec and not AskUserQuestion rounds.
evidence_detail: Points to unnamed mechanism; teased QRSPI work.
landing: Phase routine: early checkpoint (draft PR with 'Plan @ sha' and decisions journal) before implementation
inventory_ref: (B) March 2026 — Spec is the new code is not enough

source_title: What's Missing to Make AI Agents Mainstream?
author: Dex
quote: our implementer agent uses faster, smaller models for writing the code and running the tests
claim: Implementer sub-agent uses a small fast model to write code and run tests while a larger model spot-checks, keeping the parent context low for re-steering.
evidence_detail: Described HumanLayer practice; no cost numbers.
landing: Model routing per agent file (cheap implementer, strong spot-checker); effort routing

source_title: What's Missing to Make AI Agents Mainstream?
author: Dex
quote: you always get better results if you use less of them
claim: No matter how large context windows get, using less context gives better results, and deciding how to use less is the engineer's job.
evidence_detail: Repeated principle; refers to his testing-feedback blog on deterministic failure signals instead of full test dumps.
landing: Backpressure scripts that return only failures; capped outputs

source_title: What's Missing to Make AI Agents Mainstream?
author: Dex
quote: I don't know if I actually recommend that people should use Ralph to write production software.
claim: Ralph loops are valuable for the context-engineering lessons, not as a production technique; techniques will not last six months.
evidence_detail: Interview opinion.
landing: Do not adopt loop-until-done automation for production phases; keep fresh-session discipline

source_title: What's Missing to Make AI Agents Mainstream?
author: Dex
quote: Match the format of this code we found in the codebase in this other file
claim: LLMs excel at finding and following patterns, so surface all applicable codebase patterns and let humans choose old versus new before coding.
evidence_detail: Interview reasoning for the design step.
landing: Pattern catalogue as retrievable knowledge-store items instead of CLAUDE.md prose

source_title: What's Missing to Make AI Agents Mainstream?
author: Dex
quote: once you get to know what the input space would be, you can give people a happy path
claim: Decompose a workflow into a reliable happy path once the input space is known, with an escape hatch to a free-running LLM for the unexpected; choose your place on the autonomy slider.
evidence_detail: Interview opinion.
landing: Saved workflows for recurring phase types with an explicit eject-to-human path

author: Dex
quote: We could have run cursor in a network sandbox
claim: Dex frames prompt-injection risk as Simon Willison's lethal trifecta (untrusted content, private data, external communication) and says removing any one leg (cut prod DB access, network-sandbox to the inference API only, or put a guardrail) fixes it.
evidence_detail: Walks through a disclosed Zendesk-to-Cursor-MCP exfiltration to a Supabase prod DB; no numbers.
landing: Agent permission model for fixflow: no single agent session should hold untrusted input (customer text), prod DB credentials and outbound network together; relevant to WhatsApp dispatcher and any prod-DB-reading agent.

author: Dex
quote: the best way to really learn how to do this stuff
claim: Dex says the best way to learn these systems is to play with the models directly and watch the whole context window, as in the live prompt-injection iteration.
evidence_detail: Aside during the demo.
landing: Phase routine: hands-on trial runs (P1 cold-resume) are the way to learn what the routine does, not reading about it.

author: Dex
quote: every issue gets reviewed by a human before it's allowed to be seen
claim: HumanLayer puts a human triage queue between public GitHub issues and the Linear tickets its background agent can read, so outsiders cannot prompt-inject the agent or steer product work.
evidence_detail: Describes HumanLayer's own practice; no incident or numbers.
landing: Phase routine / ship plan: a human-gated intake before any agent reads externally authored text (issues, customer messages, scraped docs).

author: Dex
quote: if the output contains any strings that were in the system message, block it
claim: Dex names three guardrail tiers (deterministic rules on output, inference on the input before the main call, background inference) and says the cheap deterministic tier should go first, including substring-matching the system prompt in outputs.
evidence_detail: Conceptual; ties to the earlier evals episode's deterministic tier.
landing: Output backpressure: deterministic checks (grep/regex/CI contracts) before any LLM verifier; supports capped outputs and cheap scripts running before refuters.

author: Dex
quote: you like kick off a background task, right?
claim: Dex restates Vaibhav's design of a background guardrail agent that is launched on every new message added to the context and cancels the main stream if it flags a problem, rather than blocking in a linear pipeline.
evidence_detail: Design sketch on whiteboard; Dex links it to an earlier voice-agent supervisor episode; Vaibhav adds a distilled sub-10ms classifier (OpenAI paper claimed, not shown).
landing: A background supervisor/checker running alongside a phase session (e.g. watching for routine steps skipped) rather than a closing-message self-report; hooks-adjacent, re-opens skipped 'hooks' idea.

author: Dex
quote: layers of defense in depth so that even if someone pops one of them
claim: Dex argues a single guardrail is never enough: stack string-contains, regex, structured-output validation, a light classifier and slower background classifiers, like infrastructure security layers.
evidence_detail: Analogy to firewall/2FA/SSO/air-gap; no measurements.
landing: Verifier design: layered cheap-to-expensive checks (lint, import-linter, tests, then Opus reviewer) with each layer having a named purpose.

author: Dex
quote: you have to be careful on the autonomy versus safety pipeline
claim: Dex warns that each guardrail narrows what the agent can do (a guardrail that only allows event content makes everything about events) and that safety, speed and correctness must be balanced without hampering the agent.
evidence_detail: Concerns false positives and latency; Vaibhav notes Claude Code/Codex default to broad permissions for this reason.
landing: Guardrail/verifier tuning: refute-by-default verifiers have a false-positive cost; consider where strictness stops paying.

author: Dex
quote: Never run the client of your inference on someone else's workstation.
claim: Dex says anything running inference on the user's machine can be sniffed, so the system prompt is not a secret there; keep valuable prompts behind a cloud API.
evidence_detail: Cites how Claude Code's system prompt was obtained via proxy; no numbers.
landing: Nowhere obvious; FixFlow prompts are not IP. Possible relevance to what goes into the mobile app vs backend.

author: Dex
quote: the instruction following for the system message will be stronger
claim: Dex observes that instruction following for the system message is stronger than between user messages, which is why developer rules belong in the system role.
evidence_detail: Observed in a live demo where a secret leaked from a user-role message but not a system-role one.
landing: CLAUDE.md placement: always-loaded system-level rules carry more weight than rules buried in chat or files read later.

author: Dex
quote: AI engineering is 90 % software engineering.
claim: Dex endorses the view (via swyx) that AI engineering is mostly ordinary software engineering, so layering, caching and defence-in-depth patterns carry over directly.
evidence_detail: Passing remark about a Twitter conversation.
landing: Nowhere obvious; framing for treating the harness as ordinary engineering with tests and gates.

source_title: Why review agents do not solve slop
author: Dex
quote: too easy to oversteer with "is this code good" or "is this code bad"
claim: Code review agents are unreliable because a binary good/bad prompt is easily oversteered, so they do not solve the too-much-AI-code problem.
evidence_detail: Argued from the sycophancy/flip-flop quoted post (60% flip rate cited by quoted author, not Dex).
landing: Reviewer prompt design: Opus reviewer is refute-by-default with per-register-id fail-before/pass-after, which is rule-grounded rather than 'is this good'
inventory_ref: (B) March 2026 — Why review agents do not solve slop

source_title: Why review agents do not solve slop
author: Dex
quote: why weren't those rules / guidelines grounded in your original plan?
claim: Objective review rules should already be grounded in the original plan rather than invented at review time.
evidence_detail: Rhetorical question, no data.
landing: Ship-plan phase routine: put acceptance rules in the plan at 'Plan @ sha' so the reviewer checks against them
inventory_ref: (B) March 2026 — Why review agents do not solve slop

source_title: Why review agents do not solve slop
author: Dex
quote: There is something to be said for "throw more tokens at the problem"
claim: Throwing more tokens at verification can work, but only if done thoughtfully.
evidence_detail: Qualified statement, no data.
landing: Verifier effort routing (xhigh vs medium) and refuter panels
