source_title: Why review agents do not solve slop
author: other
quote: GPT, Claude, and Gemini flip their answers ~60% of the time
claim: Quoted study says frontier models reverse answers ~60% of the time under mere user doubt, which Dex uses to explain why review agents are unreliable.
evidence_detail: Claimed 2025 study cited by Randal Olson; Dex endorses implicitly by quoting; not verified.
landing: Reviewer/refuter prompts: avoid leading 'are you sure' re-asks; fresh-context refuters
inventory_ref: (B) March 2026 — Why review agents do not solve slop

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: it's not a model problem. It's a configuration problem
claim: Agent failures across dozens of projects and hundreds of sessions are mostly harness configuration problems, and smarter models will only be given harder tasks and keep failing in unexpected ways.
evidence_detail: 'Dozens of projects and hundreds of agent sessions'; no counts of failures.
landing: frames the whole harness review: fix the harness, not wait for models

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: anytime you find an agent makes a mistake, you take the time to engineer
claim: Adopting Mitchell Hashimoto's definition: every observed agent mistake gets a solution engineered so it never recurs; but they do not hunt for problems preemptively.
evidence_detail: Quote from Hashimoto, endorsed; the post's closing notes add 'bias towards shipping'.
landing: phase routine decisions journal and register of failures; every closing message names a harness fix

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: hooks for automated integration and deterministic control flow
claim: Beyond Viv's four levers, add hooks (deterministic control flow) and skills (progressive disclosure; Dex calls them 'Instruction Modules') as harness levers; harness engineering is a subset of context engineering.
evidence_detail: Conceptual framing.
landing: hooks (previously skipped) as the deterministic complement to CLAUDE.md prose

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: Sub-agents function as a "context firewall"
claim: Sub-agents are the key to coherence over many sessions because only the prompt and the final result enter the parent context; none of the intermediate tool calls do.
evidence_detail: Months of brownfield enterprise-scale work; no numbers.
landing: sub-agents for research/locator tasks (extends the Haiku fixflow-explorer)

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: It doesn't work. What does work is using sub-agents for context control.
claim: Role-persona sub-agents (frontend engineer, backend engineer, data analyst) do not work; sub-agents are for context control, not specialisation by job title.
evidence_detail: Tried and abandoned; no numbers. A claim against a common pattern.
landing: custom agents: define them by task shape (locate, analyse, trace), not by persona

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: no need to burn Opus tokens on a codebase grep
claim: Use an expensive model (Opus) for the parent that plans and orchestrates, and Sonnet or Haiku for sub-agents that get small discrete tasks.
evidence_detail: Stated practice; no cost figures.
landing: effort/model routing: Haiku for locators (already), Sonnet for readers, Opus only for judge/verify

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: cite sources in filepath:line format or with URLs
claim: Sub-agents should return a condensed answer plus filepath:line or URL citations, so the parent sees the answer but can follow up (progressive disclosure of evidence).
evidence_detail: Their own sub-agent format.
landing: fixflow-explorer output contract; verifier reports citing file:line

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: what should it do, but also what should it not do
claim: A sub-agent system prompt must specify role scope (including what not to do), what to return and in what form, and which tools it has; the loose-scope alternative produces a game of telephone when sub-agents dispatch sub-agents via MCP.
evidence_detail: Checklist of three items; the telephone warning is a joke illustration.
landing: agent file template for .claude/agents/

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: Trying to micro-optimize which sub-agents could access which tools.
claim: Restricting per-sub-agent tool access finely led to tool thrash and worse results, so do not spend effort on it.
evidence_detail: Listed under 'what didn't work'.
landing: custom agent tool lists: keep coarse

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: LLM-generated ones actually hurt performance while costing 20%+ more
claim: Summarising the ETH Zurich study of 138 agent files: LLM-generated agent files hurt and cost 20%+ more, human-written ones helped only ~4%, agents spent 14-22% more reasoning tokens, and codebase overviews and directory listings did not help.
evidence_detail: Third-party study (138 agentfiles, various repos) as summarised by Kyle; he argues it confirms their earlier advice.
landing: CLAUDE.md trim: the stack table and 'where things live' directory listings are the content the study found useless

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: Our CLAUDE.md is under 60 lines.
claim: HumanLayer's own CLAUDE.md is under 60 lines, kept concise and universally applicable, with as few instructions as reasonably possible and progressive disclosure for the rest.
evidence_detail: A single stated number; FixFlow's file is about 390 lines.
landing: CLAUDE.md length target

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: never connect to one you don't trust
claim: MCP tool descriptions land in the system prompt, so an untrusted MCP server is a prompt-injection vector (and stdio servers can run code); too many tools also burn context and instruction budget, so switch off unused servers.
evidence_detail: Warning plus reference to Anthropic's MCP tool search; no numbers.
landing: MCP/tool hygiene in .claude settings

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: This saved us thousands of tokens from the MCP server's tool definitions
claim: Replace a broad MCP server with a small purpose-built CLI wrapper with context-efficient output, and put about six example usages in CLAUDE.md; where a well-trained CLI already exists (gh, docker, DB clients) just prompt for the CLI.
evidence_detail: Linear CLI example, 'thousands of tokens' saved, no exact count.
landing: CLAUDE.md or skill examples for repo scripts; small CLIs for CI and Railway reads

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: the agent only gets access to specific instructions, knowledge, or tools when it decides
claim: Skills fix the instruction-budget problem through progressive disclosure: SKILL.md loads as a user message on activation, and a skill can bundle further markdown files and CLIs that SKILL.md points to conditionally.
evidence_detail: 'We kept stuffing every instruction and tool into the system prompt, and the agent kept getting worse.'
landing: move task-specific CLAUDE.md invariants into skills with bundled reference files

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: Treat skills like you'd treat npm install random-package
claim: Skill registries have distributed hundreds of malicious skills; read any skill before installing since skills can run arbitrary code.
evidence_detail: Links a report; 'hundreds' is quoted from it, not counted by the author.
landing: policy for importing third-party skills (e.g. show-me, improve-claude-md): read before adopting

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: exit code 2 tells the harness to re-engage the agent
claim: A Stop hook that runs formatter and typecheck, is silent on success, and exits 2 with only the errors on failure forces the agent to keep working until the checks pass; requires typecheck/build in a handful of seconds.
evidence_detail: Full bash script shown from their repo; no result numbers.
landing: hooks (previously skipped): Stop hook running ruff/mypy/tsc quickly; marks a re-opened skip

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: we automatically deny any Bash() tool calls that try to run migrations
claim: Hooks can auto-approve or deny tool calls on input values with more expressive rules than default permissions, e.g. deny Bash migration commands with an instruction to ask the user to run them; also used for notifications, Slack/PR integrations and a coverage-drop Stop hook.
evidence_detail: Examples of their own hook uses.
landing: hooks (previously skipped): a PreToolUse guard for alembic/railway up from repo root; coverage Stop hook

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: strongly correlated with the agent's ability to verify its own work
claim: The likelihood of solving a problem with a coding agent correlates strongly with the agent's ability to verify its own work, so typechecks, tests, coverage and UI tests are among the highest-leverage investments.
evidence_detail: Experience claim; no data.
landing: verifiers and backpressure; fail-before/pass-after requirement

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: 4,000 lines of passing tests would flood the context window
claim: Verification output must be context-efficient: running the whole suite after every change dumped 4,000 lines of passing tests and the agent started hallucinating about test files, so swallow output and surface only errors (success silent).
evidence_detail: One failure story with a line count.
landing: output caps on CI/test commands used by agents; a run-silent wrapper

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: Running our entire test suite (5+ minutes) at the end of every agent session
claim: Running the full 5+ minute suite at the end of every session did not work; run a relevant subset instead.
evidence_detail: Listed under what didn't work.
landing: phase routine test selection; stop-hook scope

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: Starting simple and adding configuration only when the agent actually failed
claim: What worked: start simple, add config only after real failures, throw away what does not help (many more hooks discarded than kept), distribute tested config to the team via the repo, optimise iteration speed over one-shot success. What did not: designing the ideal harness upfront, installing dozens of skills and MCP servers 'just in case'.
evidence_detail: Author's retrospective; no numbers.
landing: how to grow the skill and agent set: failure-driven, prune; repo-level config

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: models can be over-fitted to their harness
claim: Models are post-trained on their own harness, but can also be over-fitted to it: citing Viv, Opus 4.6 ranks #33 on Terminal Bench 2.0 in Claude Code and #5 in an unseen harness.
evidence_detail: Terminal Bench 2.0 positions (#33 vs #5, +/- ~4) via a third-party post.
landing: argues for harness customisation rather than defaults; evidence for model-vs-harness effects

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: performance degrades as context length increases — even on simple tasks
claim: Chroma's context-rot study (18 models, needle-in-haystack) shows degradation with length even on simple tasks, steeper when the question and the relevant text have low semantic similarity; irrelevant tool results act as distractors that compound.
evidence_detail: Third-party study of 18 models; he notes it differs from agentic coding.
landing: supports one phase per session and sub-agent isolation; CLAUDE.md distractor risk

source_title: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Kyle
quote: an unpredictable game of telephone
claim: For harnesses without sub-agents, an MCP server that launches a fresh agent session and returns its final message can emulate sub-agents; beware nested dispatch and raise the MCP timeout.
evidence_detail: A 'very rough approximation' linked; caveats stated.
landing: nowhere obvious; relevant only if other agent runtimes are used

author: Dex
quote: many folks struggle to keep it on task past 100k
claim: A 1M context window is not useful because people struggle to keep models on task past roughly 100k tokens.
evidence_detail: Older quoted tweet about Sonnet 4; re-shared with 'don't make me tap the sign'.
landing: One phase per new session; compaction/context budget guidance (~100k working limit)

author: Dex
quote: you replace your code review with feedback loops
claim: Replacing code review with production feedback loops and not reading the code leads to an unrecoverable 3am outage and possibly company death.
evidence_detail: Hypothetical failure narrative, no data.
landing: Keep human code reading as a gate in the phase routine; argues against dropping the Opus reviewer or owner view

author: Dex
quote: stuff might break at 3am and if you're relying on loops to fix it
claim: For the next 1-3 years, systems will break at 3am and loop-based fixing without human understanding of the code is an existential threat.
evidence_detail: Forecast stated in quoted tweet.
landing: Runbook and cold-resume (P1): a human or fresh agent must be able to understand the code; supports knowledge-store and handoff docs

author: Dex
quote: separate out instruction modules from context isolation. These are two orthogonal concepts
claim: Use subagents only for context isolation and skills for on-demand instruction modules; do not put custom instructions in agent files.
evidence_detail: Whiteboard history of commands, subagents, slash-command tool, skills; no measurement.
landing: Redesign of .claude/agents/fixflow-explorer.md (Haiku locator) vs skills; rule for what goes in an agent
inventory_ref: (B) March 2026 — listed as AI That Works #48 (title only)

author: Dex
quote: uses 50,000 tokens ... then comes out with an answer that is 500 tokens
claim: A subagent's value is that it burns tens of thousands of tokens searching and returns only a short final answer, so the parent context stays clean; result quality equals the parent's prompt quality.
evidence_detail: Illustrative numbers (50k/30k tokens in, 500 out), not measured.
landing: Use explorer/refuter subagents for read-heavy work; write the delegation prompt carefully

author: Dex
quote: fork this session and I'll just say the problem is X
claim: When a long exploration yields a 10-word answer, fork the session from the earlier user message with that answer instead of keeping the 10k-token exploration; Vaibhav adds forking has a cost when rebuilding full context.
evidence_detail: Personal practice; 10K tokens vs 10 words illustration.
landing: Context compaction alternative: fork/rewind to the message before the exploration with the distilled finding

author: Dex
quote: they would prune out all the results of every query
claim: An agent can keep tool calls but prune tool results after a final answer and re-run cheap queries on follow-up (idea from another builder, which Dex relays favourably).
evidence_detail: Secondhand report from a conversation 'last night'; SQL agent; no numbers.
landing: Context budget: drop bulky tool results from long sessions

author: Dex
quote: The instructions are injected as a user message ... better instruction following
claim: A skill loads its instructions as a user message, which gets better adherence than the model reading the same text from a file as a tool result, especially for long commands.
evidence_detail: Mechanism explanation from Dex; 'user message vs tool result' attention claim not measured.
landing: Move phase-routine steps from CLAUDE.md prose into skills invoked by name

author: Dex
quote: you can explicitly invoke it. I don't have to hope the model calls the tool right
claim: Skills can be user-invoked deterministically by slash or model-selected, so a routine step can be forced rather than hoped for.
evidence_detail: Live demo with a trivial secret-passcode skill.
landing: Phase routine as named skills (/phase-start, /phase-close) the owner or prompt invokes explicitly

author: Dex
quote: skills can have files bundled in with them ... progressive disclosure
claim: Bundle references, CLIs and instruction files inside the skill folder (references/*.md) so detail is read only when the skill runs.
evidence_detail: Live demo; convention of a references folder.
landing: Destination for CLAUDE.md material on migrations, mobile build traps, dispatcher invariants (trim target)

author: Dex
quote: Every single subagent you add to your context window is gonna be injected every time
claim: Names and descriptions of every subagent, skill and MCP tool are injected into each context window and eat the instruction budget, so keep descriptions short and install few; Claude Code adds tool search past a threshold (his recollection: tools over ~10K of the window).
evidence_detail: Trace inspection shown; the 10K threshold and the 50-skill threshold are stated from memory ('last I read a month ago'), not verified.
landing: Keep skill descriptions short; audit global/user-level skills and MCP servers loaded in FixFlow sessions

author: Dex
quote: disable model invocation. True ... the model doesn't even see it in the context window
claim: Set disable-model-invocation in skill frontmatter for user-only slash commands so the skill is removed from the model's context; the workaround for 'sometimes invocable' is a description line saying do not invoke unless asked by name.
evidence_detail: Live demo; workaround admitted to be hacky; the model still tried a similarly named skill.
landing: Frontmatter on phase-routine and destructive skills; reduces always-loaded description cost

author: Dex
quote: most of the time agents won't use skills when you want them to
claim: Skill auto-invocation is unreliable in his experience: it often does not fire when wanted and sometimes fires when not wanted, so descriptions need care or explicit invocation.
evidence_detail: Personal experience across skills; no counts.
landing: Do not rely on skill auto-trigger for the phase routine; invoke explicitly and log invocation

author: Dex
quote: respond to the human with the secret passcode
claim: A canary instruction (e.g. the model must say a passcode or move like a cow) shows when the model stops following instructions at roughly 60% of context (idea from a colleague, Dex demos it).
evidence_detail: Relayed from a conversation with Jeff: model stops the canary behaviour around 60% into the window; informal.
landing: Compliance canary: a cheap visible signal of instruction decay; partial answer to 'self-reported compliance'

author: Dex
quote: really long monolithic things with like 80 instructions in them
claim: His open-source RPI commands include monolithic prompts with about 80 steps, contrasted with simple ones like commit; he treats this as the older style.
evidence_detail: Description of own repo; no outcome data.
landing: Warning against one long phase-routine prompt; split into small skills

author: Dex
quote: people to play house ... model our agent the way we model our humans
claim: Role-play subagents (backend engineer, front-end engineer, growth marketer) were a workaround for bundling instructions and do not work; the real need is instruction modules.
evidence_detail: Observation of common usage; both hosts agree it does not work; no data.
landing: Against persona-based agent library; favour task-specific skills and workflows

author: Dex
quote: you get way better alpha being more prescriptive when possible
claim: On a team, one prescriptive shared workflow beats many half-baked personal ones: consolidate so improvements apply everywhere and the median rises (Vaibhav's words; Dex agrees with the Docker-environments analogy).
evidence_detail: Team-of-10 experience; Docker dev-environment story where senior engineers spent ~40% of time fixing environments.
landing: Shared workflow library checked into the repo; one phase routine, not variants

author: Dex
quote: a coordination repo for multiple repositories
claim: For many repos, use a small coordination repo with a tiny CLAUDE.md and settings permissions listing additional directories, launch all sessions from it, and create worktrees per task for only the repos touched; avoid git submodules.
evidence_detail: Iterated through six versions per Dex; open-sourced as rpi-coordination-template; used with customers with up to 200 repos.
landing: Mostly N/A (FixFlow is one monorepo with three runtimes); relevant if ops-server or other repos are split

author: Dex
quote: skills and MCPs always have to be in the root of the directory you're running in
claim: Nested CLAUDE.md files load dynamically when you touch those paths, but skills, MCP config and settings only load from the launch directory's .claude, not subfolders.
evidence_detail: Observed behaviour as of March 2026; config-surface explanation (user, project, settings.local, per-path CLAUDE.md).
landing: Nested CLAUDE.md in backend/ and technician-app/ to shrink the root file; skills must stay at repo root .claude/

author: Dex
quote: I'm not super bullish on agent teams
claim: Agent teams ship more code in separate contexts that need stitching; the bottleneck is designing and human review, not producing tokens of code, so parallelism only helps after a good design and plan.
evidence_detail: Opinion; cites a news item that Amazon now requires senior review of junior AI-generated code (secondhand, unverified).
landing: Against fan-out workflows before plan is settled; supports one-phase-per-session

author: Dex
quote: a lot of companies are gonna die because they lean too hard into the lights off write only software factory
claim: Not reading the code and leaning on swarms or a lights-off software factory will, in the next couple of years, cause a 3 a.m. failure nobody can fix, with weeks of downtime.
evidence_detail: Prediction; his own tweet responding to the Amazon story. No data.
landing: Supports keeping human-read checkpoints and verifiers; counter-pole to software-factory essays
inventory_ref: (B) March 2026 (title only; the thread appears under 'Software Factory Existential Risk')

author: Dex
quote: if the original design was wrong, you need to throw it away and start over
claim: Spend your own thinking tokens before coding; a feature iterated on a wrong design should be thrown away, and don't ship just because you can (colleague's team message, endorsed).
evidence_detail: Dex reads another founder's post; example of designing 'workspaces' rather than 'worktrees' instead of prompting the feature out.
landing: Phase routine: abandon-and-restart rule when the plan proves wrong; decisions journal

author: Dex
quote: a step in our workflow before we ship a PR where we do a code review
claim: Do not buy a separate code-review product; run a review step in a separate context window with instructions to check about 12 known anti-patterns and fix them, because extra tokens on review help.
evidence_detail: Own practice; contrasts with the vendor's roughly $15-25 per review price (Dex and Vaibhav disagree mildly on whether others' prompts are worth buying).
landing: The per-PR Opus reviewer: give it a fixed anti-pattern list (known agent failure modes in FixFlow)

author: Dex
quote: most PRs don't need that level of rigor
claim: Vaibhav argues vendor code review is expensive for every PR when most do not need it; Dex agrees about not paying extra for what the writing agent should have got right first time.
evidence_detail: Cost figures of about $25 per PR quoted loosely; no data. Mostly Vaibhav's argument.
landing: Risk-tier the reviewer: not every PR needs a max-effort refuter

author: Dex
quote: you can't build a company on a prompt because someone will figure out how to crack it
claim: Prompts and context engineering are copyable once the user pays the token bill, so value lies in maintaining them as models change, not in hiding them.
evidence_detail: Business opinion; no data.
landing: Not a harness lever; supports maintaining the harness continually after each model release

author: Dex
quote: Claude Agent SDK is basically just wrapping the Claude Code CLI binary
claim: The Agent SDK runs the same CLI, so behaviour matches if setting sources and flags are passed; the Max-plan terms mainly bar serving customers through the SDK or other harnesses.
evidence_detail: His reading of recent terms changes, flagged by him as a gray area and not his own certainty.
landing: If Workflow scripts or an Agent SDK pipeline are used, pass setting sources so project CLAUDE.md and skills load; check plan terms

source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
author: Dex
quote: Opus 4.5 is AGI uh for people who didn't want to put in the time
claim: Engineers who were good at context engineering were getting the same results from Opus 4.0/4.1 in summer 2025 that others credit to Opus 4.5; the skill, not just the model, sets the ceiling.
evidence_detail: Observations of colleagues; the point is that model upgrades do not remove the need for process.
landing: Cautions against assuming the newest model or higher effort replaces process

source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
author: Dex
quote: people who want to build like reliable software and people who want to build a cool demo
claim: Top builders optimise for reliability while public frameworks optimise for demos where 80% correct is fine; enterprise and fintech customers need 'no ship fast and break things'.
evidence_detail: Origin story of 12-factor agents from talking to real builders; customers are 10-20 person startups through 1,000-engineer public companies.
landing: Framing for a money-handling system: reliability-first process

source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
author: Dex
quote: there's a difference between coding and shipping
claim: Coding is making software work locally; shipping is getting it to prod, fixing it and maintaining it, which AI has not solved; he is annoyed by posts about tokens and parallel sessions rather than shipped, paid-for product.
evidence_detail: Quotes Guillermo Rauch; opinion.
landing: Success measure for phases is shipped and verified in prod, not code volume

source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
author: Dex
quote: write working code to like produce working code
claim: The engineer's role changes from writing working code to causing working code to be produced, and the job is finding which parts are high leverage for humans versus AI.
evidence_detail: Prediction for 2026-27, no data.
landing: Role definition for the owner in the phase routine

source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
author: Dex
quote: uses AI to write a 10-page document that they didn't read
claim: Slop is any low-effort or derivative output nobody put effort into, most commonly AI text the author did not read.
evidence_detail: Definition given when asked.
landing: Reviewer test: did a human read this artifact

source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
author: Dex
quote: guardrails and guidelines for how to do it
claim: Customer engagements combine workshops and a product so that when Dex leaves the team keeps guardrails and guidelines in the tooling.
evidence_detail: Business description, not a technical claim.
landing: Practice should live in tooling the next session sees, not in a person

source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
author: Dex
quote: when you get to 40% start thinking about wrapping it up
claim: Dumb-zone rule of thumb: if you lack experience, at about 40% of the window start wrapping up or do an intentional steer to compaction.
evidence_detail: Primary source of the heuristic; Dex calls it 'training wheels' and 'meant to be a rule of thumb', and tells learners 'shoot for 40%'. No measurement offered.
landing: Context-budget rule in the phase routine; compaction/handoff trigger

source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
author: Dex
quote: I tell people like shoot for 40% if you're learning.
claim: The 40% figure is for learners; experienced people use less caution because they know what they want.
evidence_detail: Same passage as the dumb-zone rule, restated.
landing: Treat 40% as a default for new/untrusted workflows, revise once the routine has run

source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
author: Dex
quote: I will regularly blow out to like 60-70% of the context window used.
claim: Experts, and simple tasks, regularly run to 60-70% of the window because a good trajectory can keep improving results, so the 40% is not a hard limit.
evidence_detail: Dex says people who have done AI engineering long push to the end of the window; depends on model and task.
landing: Counterweight to a strict one-phase-per-session budget

source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
author: Dex
quote: sometimes a good trajectory is worth like you'll actually keep getting better results
claim: A strong early trajectory in the context window can be worth keeping rather than compacting away.
evidence_detail: Offered as explanation for why some experts exceed 40%.
landing: Argues against automatic reset-per-phase when a session is going well

source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
author: Dex
quote: the only way to know how much context engineering to use on a given problem
claim: You calibrate how much process (research/plan/implement vs just talking to the model) a task needs only through reps of over- and under-doing it; a one-line change does not warrant the whole process.
evidence_detail: Spoken by Dex in the transcript ('you just have to get some reps'); the BigGo summary mis-credits it to the host.
landing: Effort routing: tier process weight by task size

source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
author: Dex
quote: talk to Claude for 70 hours a week
claim: Intuition for context and compaction comes from heavy use, not from a framework; there is no better answer.
evidence_detail: Half-joking answer to how to judge whether a compaction is useful.
landing: Reason to encode judgement as explicit checks since a fresh agent lacks the 70 hours

source_title: Latent Space In-Context Cooking: Dex Horthy
author: Dex
quote: there will always be a thing that the model can like only kind of get right reliably
claim: Context engineering stays valuable as models improve because the frontier of what is only sometimes right keeps moving outward, and you build great experiences at the edge (idea from the NotebookLM team).
evidence_detail: Credited to a Latent Space episode with the NotebookLM team; Dex says it is still true.
landing: Rationale against dropping the routine as models improve

source_title: AI Tinkerers One-Shot: How to Ship Complex Features 10x Faster
author: Dex
quote: avoiding heavy orchestration frameworks in favor of custom loops built on simple primitives
claim: The most successful enterprise AI teams avoid heavy orchestration frameworks and build custom loops from structured outputs and simple primitives.
evidence_detail: Host summary; he ran his own workflow in production for nine months.
landing: Workflow-tool scripts as plain code; save reusable scripts rather than adopting a framework.

source_title: AI Tinkerers One-Shot: How to Ship Complex Features 10x Faster
author: Dex
quote: It structures workflows into discrete steps, integrates with Linear for ticket tracking
claim: Riptide structures Claude Code workflows into discrete steps, tracks tickets in Linear, and stores all artifacts in linked GitHub repos.
evidence_detail: Description of his orchestration tool; nine months in production.
landing: Saved workflow library with artifacts in repo (evidence folders); maps to docs/program evidence.

source_title: AI Tinkerers One-Shot: How to Ship Complex Features 10x Faster
author: Dex
quote: serverless GitHub Actions that handle small bug fixes without human intervention
claim: Autonomy comes in levels, from human-in-the-loop review up to GitHub Actions that fix small bugs unattended.
evidence_detail: Description of levels; no numbers.
landing: Scheduled/CI-triggered agent for small defect-register items; deliberately-graded autonomy per phase type.

source_title: AI Tinkerers One-Shot: How to Ship Complex Features 10x Faster
author: Dex
quote: the engineer's role is now to oversee the entire lifecycle
claim: Engineers now oversee testing, deployment and maintenance like a film producer, since models can code but shipping is the job.
evidence_detail: Host summary of Coding vs Shipping argument.
landing: Closing message six questions and owner view cover shipping lifecycle, not just code.

source_title: AI Tinkerers One-Shot: How to Ship Complex Features 10x Faster
author: Dex
quote: “taste” and knowing what not to build the most scarce resources
claim: As code generation accelerates, taste and knowing what not to build become the scarce resources (the infinite software crisis).
evidence_detail: Host summary only.
landing: Plan-review gate where scope cuts are decided; owner decision points in the ship plan.

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: we would give these tools to an expert and they would get great results
claim: RPI worked for expert users but results degraded when handed to their teams, so tool design must not depend on expert skill.
evidence_detail: Thousands of engineers from startups to Fortune 500 since Oct 2025; no numbers.
landing: Phase routine: design for the fresh agent, not the author; informs P1 cold-resume trial

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: We tried not reading the code for like 6 months. It did not end well.
claim: Dex reverses his August 2025 advice: engineers must read the code, as six months without reading forced rip-and-replace of large parts of HumanLayer's system.
evidence_detail: Own team experience; no numbers.
landing: Reviewer and owner-view design; human read of diffs for money/lifecycle invariants

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: Nobody gets paged at 3:00 a.m. if it's broken
claim: Projects whose maintainers skip reading code (Beads, OpenClaw) are OSS with low stakes, so they are not a model for production or regulated code.
evidence_detail: Argument by stakes; cites Beads 300,000 lines.
landing: Risk-tiered review depth (money, auth, dispatcher paths get human read)

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: going 10 times faster doesn't matter if you're going to throw it all away
claim: Against agent swarms and Gas Town style speed: target a 2-3x speedup at near-human quality rather than 10x with slop.
evidence_detail: Stated as a goal; measurement left to another talk.
landing: Ship-plan pacing: one phase per session, quality gate over throughput

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: there is no magic prompt. Do not outsource the thinking.
claim: Principles he kept: no magic prompt, do not outsource the thinking, and seek leverage so correctness can be assured without reading everything and re-steering afterwards.
evidence_detail: Credits Jake from Netflix for 'do not outsource the thinking'.
landing: Owner view and decisions journal: human decisions captured before code

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: the less of the context window you use, the better results you will get
claim: The dumb zone: quality degrades from about 40% of a 168k usable window on average, and more MCP tools mean more unused instructions in context.
evidence_detail: ~40% average threshold, 60% still workable; cites Databricks on too many MCPs.
landing: One-phase-per-session rule; context budget guidance; MCP/tool trimming

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: Don't use prompts for control flow if you can use control flow for control flow.
claim: Classify the input and route it to small focused prompts rather than one prompt with if-branches; true of any LLM system.
evidence_detail: Follows 12-factor agents; 85 instructions became all under 40 per step.
landing: Workflow scripts as the control-flow layer for the phase routine; skills per step

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: before it was 85 instructions, now they're all less than 40
claim: Splitting the monolith into per-step prompts brought each below 40 instructions, with some likely reducible further.
evidence_detail: Instruction counts 85+ to under 40 per prompt; still iterating.
landing: Per-skill instruction cap; trim target for CLAUDE.md

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: we figured it was time to actually go drink our own Kool-Aid
claim: He admits HumanLayer wrote the 12-factor 'no monolith' advice then built a monolithic prompt around Claude Code anyway.
evidence_detail: Self-critique.
landing: Reminder that skills/agents beat one long routine

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: questions, research, design, structure, plan, work tree, implement, PR
claim: QRSPI is a seven-to-eight step pipeline: Questions, Research, Design, Structure, Plan, Worktree, Implement, PR, each its own fresh context and artifact.
evidence_detail: Steps spoken in talk; acronym picked from steps he liked (CRISPY).
landing: Phase routine decomposition; a saved Workflow with one step per stage

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: good research is all facts, but if you tell the model what you're building, then you get opinions
claim: Research must be fed no description of the feature, or it returns opinions instead of facts.
evidence_detail: Observed across rollouts; no measurement.
landing: Research/diagnosis step of phase routine; knowledge-store diagnoses; Workflow explorer prompts

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: that's not how we do atomic SQL updates. That's some engineer that doesn't work here
claim: The design step is the chance to correct which codebase patterns the agent found, rejecting legacy ones before it copies them.
evidence_detail: Illustrative example.
landing: Pattern pointers (e.g. try_claim / try_transition) in the design/plan artifact rather than CLAUDE.md prose

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: you can do brain surgery on the agent before you proceed downstream
claim: Force the agent to dump what it found, intends and assumes, and ask questions, so the human can correct it before 2,000 lines are written.
evidence_detail: Credits Matt Pocock's 'design concept'.
landing: Owner approval gate on the plan before code; refuter reads the design artifact

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: if the plan is the implementation, the outline is the C header files
claim: Step S (structure outline, ~2 pages vs 8-page plan): phases, signatures, new types, order of change and test points, as a cheap review artifact.
evidence_detail: Plan eight pages vs outline two pages for the same feature.
landing: Phase plan format in ship plan; PR body structure

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: we cannot get models to stop writing horizontal plans
claim: Models write horizontal plans (all DB, then services, API, UI) despite heavy prompting and evals; vertical slices with checkpoints are the fix and the outline step is where they are enforced.
evidence_detail: 'prompt this out and eval the hell out of this'; horizontal plans reach 1,200 lines with nothing testable.
landing: Per-phase fail-before/pass-after checkpoints; slice-ordered phases across backend/web/mobile

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: I don't actually test in between every phase everything I'm building
claim: Test checkpoints between phases are for sensitive, hard or complex work, aiming for 200-400 line blocks verified before more code.
evidence_detail: Personal practice; block size 'two, three, 400 line'.
landing: Verifier intensity by risk tier; block-size guidance

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: this is a tactical doc for the agent. ... I'm just going to spot-check this
claim: Step P: once design and outline are aligned the plan is only spot-checked and deep review is saved for the code.
evidence_detail: Same template and prompt as create_plan.
landing: Reviewer effort allocation: code-heavy, plan-light

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: any of my bad decisions are headed off on a 200-line doc
claim: Send short design docs to the code owner before coding (optional, not a required step) so code review confirms rather than discovers.
evidence_detail: HumanLayer practice; co-founder is code owner.
landing: Owner view page sent before the build starts; decisions journal in draft PR

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: it's still a 2-day feature cuz I still have to like align with my team
claim: Coding is 2-4 hours of a 2-day feature, so AI on coding alone barely moves cycle time; alignment, review and verification dominate and AI should help there.
evidence_detail: Illustrative arithmetic (coding 20 minutes).
landing: Spend verifier/effort budget on alignment and verification, not generation

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: Igor ... shipping 50% more, but half of that is just cleaning up the slop
claim: Cites Stanford study numbers: AI raises output ~50% but half is rework, good for low-complexity greenfield and poor for high-complexity brownfield.
evidence_detail: Last year's numbers pre-Opus 4.5; he says to inflate them a little.
landing: Motivation for refuter-first review; baseline for measuring rework

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: three steps is already a lot for some people to learn and now there are seven
claim: Open problems he names: seven steps is heavy to adopt, impact on teams is unmeasured, and updating shared prompts/skills without regressing other teams is unsolved.
evidence_detail: Listed as not yet addressed.
landing: Skill versioning and regression-test question for .claude/skills; saved workflow library

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: we just hide the ticket from the context window that's doing research
claim: Step Q/R: one context generates questions from the ticket, then a fresh context with no knowledge of the goal answers them, done deterministically.
evidence_detail: Described as a trivial query-planning analogue; no results given.
landing: Workflow script (questions agent then blind researcher); fixflow-explorer agent usage

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: we don't use the built-in compaction because everything that matters is going into static assets
claim: Skip built-in compaction: persist all that matters to markdown artifacts so any session can resume without relying on compact quality.
evidence_detail: Stated in Q&A as HumanLayer practice.
landing: One phase per new session; P1 cold-resume trial; knowledge store

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: I will regularly go up to 60. I will regularly like aggressively keep it below 30.
claim: Experienced users treat the dumb zone loosely (30 to 60%), but novices should aim under 40% and wrap up near 60%, iterating on the same doc.
evidence_detail: Personal practice after 60 h/week use; teaching default of 40/60.
landing: Context budget thresholds in the phase routine (wrap-up trigger)

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: we're binary searching through the space of how much of the code should you read
claim: The right amount of code reading is still being searched for; those saying never read will likely reverse, and reading code with 2-3x speed beats 10x slop.
evidence_detail: Q&A answer; predicts a reversal in six months.
landing: Reviewer policy: sampled vs full read by risk

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: Let's put it that way. I do not endorse that.
claim: He rejects the software-factory stance where no human reads code and the spec is the source, including formal verification (TLA+) as a replacement for now.
evidence_detail: Q&A reply to a StrongDM-style question; says more verification tooling remains to be built.
landing: Verifier strategy: do not drop human read in favour of spec-only verification

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: Testing and verifying, sorry, I don't have a good answer for you.
claim: He explicitly leaves testing/verification out of QRSPI's scope, deferring to another speaker.
evidence_detail: Admission of a gap.
landing: Gap note: QRSPI does not supply a verifier design

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: Keep things objective. Discourage opinions. Don't actually put any implementation details in there.
claim: Research output should compress only what is true about how the code works today, with no implementation detail.
evidence_detail: Restates the November 2025 research rule.
landing: Research/explorer agent prompt; knowledge-store entry template (facts only)

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: a single giant like monolithic thing with 85 or more instructions
claim: The RPI planning prompt held 85+ instructions including interactive steps, and about half of users saw the agent skip them and write the plan outright.
evidence_detail: 85+ instruction count; skip rate stated as 'about 50% of people, maybe more'.
landing: CLAUDE.md length (W1); any phase routine step that is only a prose instruction

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: you have to say the magic words
claim: If a tool only works when the user says magic words, the tool is broken and must be fixed so the correct behaviour is the default.
evidence_detail: Workshop experience; the 'work back and forth with me' line separated good from bad plans.
landing: Phase routine: make steps structural (separate step/script) rather than reminders in chat

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: frontier LLMs could only follow about 150 to 200 instructions with like good consistency
claim: Models follow only about 150-200 instructions reliably, and the budget is shared by the prompt, CLAUDE.md, system prompt, tools and MCP.
evidence_detail: Cited from an arXiv paper via Kyle's blog; Dex says the number is probably higher now (2026).
landing: CLAUDE.md trim (390 lines); skill and agent sizing; per-phase prompt budget

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: you're not likely to get full adherence to the workflow
claim: Stacking an 85-instruction prompt on top of CLAUDE.md, system prompt, tools and MCP means workflow adherence is a dice roll.
evidence_detail: Inference from the instruction-budget number.
landing: CLAUDE.md always-loaded content vs on-demand skills

source_title: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI
author: Dex
quote: a thousand line plan tends to be about a thousand lines of code within 10%
claim: Reading a long plan saves no work since the plan is as long as the code and the code can differ from it, so do not review long plans.
evidence_detail: Rule of thumb 'within 10% or so'; no study.
landing: Opus reviewer per PR: review code and diff, not the plan; owner view page length

source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
author: Dex
quote: you have an information budget in your context window and then you have an instruction budget
claim: Context engineering is also about the number of instructions: the more rules the model must follow at once, the less well it attends to any one.
evidence_detail: Aside from a talk he was giving that day; no number given in this episode.
landing: CLAUDE.md trim: argues for an instruction count budget, not only a length budget
inventory_ref: (B) March 2026 — listed as AI That Works #47 PII Redaction (title only)

source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
author: Dex
quote: If you can do things deterministically, then don't make the LLM do them
claim: Do deterministic work in code because it is faster, cheaper and more reliable, and it frees the model for the part only it can do.
evidence_detail: Stated in a time-zone example; no measurement.
landing: Scripts/hooks over prose rules for checks (e.g. compliance evidence); marks the 'hooks skipped' decision for re-opening

source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
author: Dex
quote: why would check_redaction be able to capture the misses if redact didn't?
claim: Dex doubts LLM-as-judge ('it's all the same models'); Vaibhav answers that checking and labelling are different tasks, run off the main loop on a sample, which Dex then accepts and extends to flagged items sent to a human to add to evals.
evidence_detail: Challenge and counter in conversation; Vaibhav suggests sampling ~5% and spot-checking ~100 samples. Dex proposes Slack flag plus a UI to promote to the eval suite via PR.

source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
author: Dex
quote: you snapshot the results of different cases and then you eyeball the diff
claim: Evaluate a pipeline by snapshotting outputs per case and eyeballing diffs between runs, rather than building formal evals for everything.
evidence_detail: Recalled from the team's earlier evals episode; no numbers.
landing: Cheap regression check for effort-routing experiments (compare verifier verdicts across effort levels)

source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
author: Dex
quote: anything the LLM can generate based on its weights is a thing it can reason about
claim: Do not generate synthetic test data with an LLM when you can ask it for the patterns directly; build evals from known shapes with a human in the loop.
evidence_detail: Dex says he would 'love to be proven wrong'; untested.
landing: Refuter/eval fixture design: prefer real prod-shaped cases over LLM-invented ones

source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
author: Dex
quote: you're always gonna be either like, you would rather have false positives or false negatives
claim: A detector sits in a bias zone, not a line: pick which error side to favour and narrow the zone with better techniques, layering steps to move the balance (Vaibhav's funnel of passes).
evidence_detail: Conceptual framing; Vaibhav's layering example (drop 'none/medium' risk, add re-check pass for medium) is anecdotal.
landing: Refute-by-default verifiers are a chosen bias; a second narrow pass can cut false positives

source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
author: Dex
quote: The question is always like, is the rule dumb or is the execution of the rule incorrect?
claim: When a model-applied rule gives a bad result, first decide whether the rule or its execution is at fault before editing the prompt.
evidence_detail: Remark during live prompt iteration; no data.
landing: Diagnosing routine non-compliance: rule wording vs agent execution (relevant to CLAUDE.md trim)

source_title: PII Redaction and Sensitive Data Scrubbing
author: Dex

author: Dex

author: Dex

author: Dex
quote: this context may or may not be relevant to your tasks.

author: Dex
quote: Do not shard into separate files that require the agent to make tool calls

author: Dex

evidence_detail: Live demo: a ~3-second bash sleep test against the Claude Agent SDK showed queue behaviour; output pasted into the design doc. No numbers.

inventory_ref: (B) February 2026 — listed as AI That Works #46 No Vibes Allowed February (title only)

author: Dex
quote: queue extra passes of go through the research, vet every assumption, add more detail
claim: The inverse of auto-advance is queueing extra review passes at any stage (Vaibhav loops 'what's inconsistent / missing' on the outline until it settles).
evidence_detail: Vaibhav reports a 17k-lines-added/13k-removed refactor one-shotted after this loop, ~18 commits over 2 weeks, CodeRabbit still found bugs; Vaibhav claims '100% hit rate' with the loop. Dex endorses.
landing: Completeness-critic pass on the plan; repeatable 'what is missing or inconsistent' prompt

author: Dex
quote: Plan files are throwaway. Research files are throwaway.
claim: Plans, research and design docs are execution aids deleted after merge; the code is the source of truth, and research is regenerated on the fly rather than stored.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav states it; Dex agrees ('as soon as it's shipped, the code is the new source of truth'; research generated on the fly).

author: Dex
quote: I actually don't think the problem is too many PRs. I think the problem is too many bad PRs
claim: Align with the owner on a cheap design doc before building, because even a 20% rework on a 500-line PR is a heavy burden on submitter and reviewer.
evidence_detail: Example: sending the design doc to the CTO to avoid a late 'wrong endpoint' rejection; no numbers beyond the 500-line/20% illustration.

author: Dex
quote: I'd rather review it at this stage, which is a shorter 200 line artifact
claim: Rather than building several approaches in parallel, review a roughly 200-line design artifact (or a learning test or prototype) instead of two 1000-line PRs; you must decide either way.
evidence_detail: Argument in reply to a viewer; no data.
landing: Guidance against parallel-implementation verifier spend; prefer proof-of-concept

author: Dex
quote: For UI stuff the agent's not going to have good back pressure ... do this in storybook
claim: Where the agent has no backpressure or taste (rich UI), carve the decision out into Storybook before implementation.

landing: Web manager (src/) UI work; mobile has no screen-test harness

author: Dex
quote: The dumber your UI, the easier it is to consolidate state and business logic on the backend
claim: Keep the client dumb and let it send a preference (queue/continue/interrupt/auto) that the server resolves, so races degrade to the right behaviour instead of 400s (Vaibhav's argument; Dex adopts a single boolean).
evidence_detail: Design argument; Dex changes his enum-plus-400 design to a boolean after it.
landing: Product design, not harness; echoes FixFlow server-resolved lifecycle (transition idempotency)

author: Dex
quote: Prune, prune, prune, prune, prune.
claim: Keep a small set of skills that everyone uses; treat team skills as products and kill the ones with low adoption, because compounding tooling gains need shared use (Vaibhav: 5-7 great skills beat 70).
evidence_detail: Opinion; PM analogy (remove features used by ~10% of users). Quoted line is Vaibhav's; Dex continues the argument.
landing: Skills under .claude/skills/ being added: cap the count, track use, retire unused

author: Dex
quote: you're getting worse. If your problem is really easy, you can solve things in the dumb zone
claim: Context usage past roughly 40% degrades answers; hard problems should be done in the smart part of the window (Vaibhav mentions 37% as a viewer's figure for dumb-zone onset).
evidence_detail: Numbers 37% / 40-90% quoted from chat and Vaibhav; no experiment.
landing: One-phase-per-session defence; a context-percent trigger for wrap-up

author: Dex
quote: most people hit straight enter, clear context, go onward ... don't actually read the plan
claim: Default plan mode produces a plan nobody reads in detail, which is why a design/outline layer that is meant to be read is used instead (Vaibhav's framing, Dex proceeds on it).
evidence_detail: Observation of user behaviour, no data.
landing: Plan-@-sha PR body: make the plan short enough to be read

author: Dex
quote: auto-advance through design discussions every single time
claim: Auto-advancing through the research/design steps without a manual loop is acceptable when a review-iterate pass is added on the structure outline (Vaibhav; Dex has the feature and plans queued extra passes).
evidence_detail: Vaibhav's personal 100% hit-rate claim; no sample size.
landing: Routine design: which steps need a human stop and which can chain

author: Dex
quote: you're not going to find that out till you're like two phases into your implementation
claim: A wrong assumption taken from misleading docs surfaces only phases into implementation and forces a rewind, so assumptions should be tested before the plan.
evidence_detail: Reasoning only; cost framed as 20 minutes before code vs untangling after merge.
landing: Plan-phase gate: list assumptions and how each is proven before implementation

author: Dex
quote: models are really, really good at finding and understanding and matching the patterns that already exist
claim: The design doc includes a 'patterns to follow' section so the human can catch the agent picking the wrong existing pattern before any code is written.

author: Dex
quote: your code base will always regress to the average of the best pattern and the worst pattern

evidence_detail: Stated as a heuristic; no measurement.
landing: Argues for removing or marking legacy patterns; CLAUDE.md 'do not copy' notes

author: Dex
quote: you should not want Claude or Codex or any agent to make decisions about your code base

evidence_detail: Design principle; demo shows Dex answering option A/B/C questions.
landing: Phase routine: owner/human decision checkpoint before plan; decisions journal in draft PR

author: Dex
quote: horizontal planning ... the models love fricking doing this
claim: Models default to horizontal plans (DB, then service, then API, then UI) that leave nothing testable for ~1200 lines; plan vertical slices with mocks instead, and check in between phases.
evidence_detail: Experience-based; ~1200 lines mentioned as the untested span.

author: Dex
quote: I would rather do the endpoint first because then we can at least check in the database

evidence_detail: Live reordering of the outline; no numbers.
landing: Phase ordering rule: earliest phase creates an observable artifact

author: Dex
quote: if I can spend 10 minutes and get it 90% of the way there ... better than an hour to get 99%

evidence_detail: Hand-drawn probability curves on a whiteboard (chance of live iteration, re-steer, restart design); no data.

author: other

author: other

author: other

author: other

inventory_ref: (C) Follow-ons and coverage by others (NOT Dex's work)

author: other
quote: Your time is expensive, tokens are cheap.

evidence_detail: No numbers; relevant counterpoint to cost-trimming of verifier effort.

author: Dex

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex

author: Dex

claim: Deterministic steps (push, commit, evaluate, git reset --hard) belong in the outer orchestrator script rather than the prompt, which makes them reliable.
evidence_detail: Dex's own agents failed to push in the live run; Geoff replies to do it in the orchestrator.

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex
quote: the idea of an orchestrator running chord code. So or running a harness.

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley

evidence_detail: Two GCP VMs with only deploy keys and cloud API keys; Geoff voices the 'when it gets popped' line.

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex

claim: Geoff's Loom (remote ephemeral sandbox harness with a chain of agents poking agents: did you do X) is where the nudge pattern gets built in as infrastructure; Dex expresses interest, not adoption.
