landing: Chained verifier agents that poke the builder; a workflow library

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex
quote: Now these things will pull in any GitHub issues that get open.
claim: Dex feeds a 'known issues' folder and live GitHub issues into the loop as inputs next to the specs, and jokes that issues could prompt-inject the loop.
evidence_detail: Observed in the live stream when a flatten-directories bug was found.
landing: Register ids as loop inputs; also an injection risk to name

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex
quote: Human on the loop is better than human in the loop
claim: Position (Geoff voices it, Dex agrees): the human designs and steers the loop and may stop it at chosen points, while the model does not decide when and how.
evidence_detail: Stated in conversation, no data.
landing: Phase routine design: human gates at PR review, not per step

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex
quote: I do have some concerns that people will just like try the official plugin
claim: Dex criticises Anthropic's official Ralph plugin as not the real technique, since it keeps one session alive and relies on the model to emit a completion promise.
evidence_detail: Side-by-side live comparison of the plugin against a plain bash loop.
landing: Anything in-session (stop-hook loops) vs fresh-process loops

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex
quote: This is funny because it's all in one context window. It's just seeing its own context
claim: Observed: the plugin run, in one context, repeated a done-checkmark for 110 iterations, while the fresh-start bash loop re-learns and finds new work.
evidence_detail: Plugin hit iteration 110 with no completion promise; the stop hook kept firing on a finished project.
landing: Verifier design: fresh context beats a self-assessing session (matches refuter pattern)

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex
quote: compaction is the devil
claim: Geoff says, and Dex's setup follows, that auto-compaction is lossy and can drop the specs and goal, so the loop should never compact and should hold one goal per context window.
evidence_detail: Explained on the whiteboard diagram; no measurement.
landing: Context-budget policy: one phase per new session; avoid compaction

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex
quote: One context window, one activity, one goal
claim: Each loop iteration sets exactly one objective and re-allocates the same fixed context (specs, plan) deterministically.
evidence_detail: Whiteboard explanation; the prompt says 'implement the single highest priority feature'.
landing: Phase routine: one phase per chat, fixed starting read-list

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex
quote: Deliberate malicking context about your application.
claim: Reserve roughly 5,000 tokens at the head of every iteration for what is being built, as an index or README of links to specs, injecting specific files by name when the model drifts.
evidence_detail: Stated as a rough budget; the 'vibes' are admitted.
landing: CLAUDE.md as a small index to specs; trim target

source_title: Ralph Wiggum Showdown with Geoffrey Huntley
author: Dex
quote: There is a dumb zone. You should stay out of it.
claim: Leave headroom in each iteration for test failures and for committing and pushing, so the whole task, including the fix-up, fits in the smart zone.
evidence_detail: Diagram of a performance-degradation line; position not given as a number in this video.
landing: Phase sizing: size a phase so the closing steps (PR, journal) still fit

author: Dex
quote: ensure all tests and linting passes with `bun check && bun test`, then update IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md
claim: Backpressure inside the loop: one combined check command must pass before the plan file is updated and a commit is made, and the plan file is rewritten with progress each iteration.
evidence_detail: Prompt step 2 and 3; no measurements.
landing: Phase routine: single verification command gate before the decisions journal / PR update

author: Dex
quote: including anything in the out of scope / future work - that's now in scope!
claim: The prompt declares deferred and out-of-scope plan items in scope so the loop never stalls waiting for a human to promote them.
evidence_detail: One line in the prompt; plan shows a 'Deferred Features (COMPLETE)' phase consumed this way.
landing: Ship plan: how deferred register items are picked up (counter-example to FixFlow's gated phases)

author: Dex
quote: list open issues and compare with known-issues/
claim: Each iteration begins by syncing GitHub issues into a local known-issues/ folder (as markdown) and folding new ones into the implementation plan, making human feedback an input to the loop.
evidence_detail: Curl/jq commands in the prompt; the plugin variant stores issues as JSON instead.
landing: Phase routine step 0: pull the owner's field defects into the plan before choosing the next item

author: Dex
quote: do not include any claude attribution
claim: The loop commits with git add -A and a plain commit message, explicitly without Claude attribution; the plugin variant also pushes to main each iteration.
evidence_detail: Prompt lines 3 and 4 (push only in the plugin repo).
landing: nowhere obvious; contrast with FixFlow's branch-never-main and attribution rules

author: Dex
quote: parallel processing of files to significantly speed up builds
claim: The Ralph-built repo produced a very large amount of agent-written documentation (IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md about 343 KB, README about 144 KB, many GIT_* research files), showing the loop's output sprawl when no one prunes it.
evidence_detail: File sizes observed locally (343,275 and 143,883 bytes); Dex does not comment on it.
landing: Phase routine: a size cap or prune step on plan/journal files so cold-resume reads stay small

author: Dex
quote: implement the single highest priority feature using up to 5 subagents
claim: The Ralph prompt shape: each fresh iteration reads the specs, the code and an IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md, implements exactly one top-priority item, with a cap on subagents.
evidence_detail: The prompt file itself; the repo it produced is the evidence (322+ tests, all milestones complete per the plan), no cost or failure rate given.
landing: Phase routine in ship plan §0: one item per fresh context, plan file as the state carrier

author: Dex
quote: PLEASE READ AT LEAST 1500 LINES AT A TIME DONT DO PARTIAL READS
claim: His global rule forces whole-file reads (minimum 1500 lines) because partial reads make the model add duplicate functions that already exist deeper in the file.
evidence_detail: Stated as a rule with a failure story, no numbers.
landing: A short always-loaded read-whole-file rule in CLAUDE.md or the explorer agent prompt; counters the repo's habit of limit/offset reads.

author: Dex
quote: AFTER FETCHING THE TICKET - PAUSE and ask the user how you want to proceed.
claim: A fetch step (Linear ticket into thoughts/shared/tickets) is followed by a mandatory pause with a scripted menu (research, plan, or other) rather than auto-proceeding.
evidence_detail: Scripted response template.
landing: An explicit checkpoint at phase entry in the routine: ingest, then ask which mode.

author: Dex
quote: If you are writing a one-off script for python, you must use uv scripts
claim: One-off Python scripts must be self-contained uv scripts with dependencies declared in a header comment, so they run with no environment setup.
evidence_detail: Rule with template; note CLAUDE.md here says no python on PATH in the user's setup is a separate concern.
landing: A convention for saved verifier/audit scripts (self-describing, dependency-declared) in a workflow library.

author: Dex
quote: ENV files (.env/.env.local) contain secrets - NEVER modify them
claim: Hard rule that env files are never modified by the agent.
evidence_detail: One line; no enforcement mechanism (no hook or deny rule in settings.json).
landing: Prose-only guard; the contrast with a settings deny rule is the point (his settings.json has no deny list).

author: Dex
quote: use Linear branch names when available (from gitBranchName field)
claim: Branch and worktree names derive from the ticket system field; if only a number is known, infer the team prefix from branch name or $PWD.
evidence_detail: Naming rule.
landing: A branch-naming rule tying each phase PR to its plan register id.

author: Dex
quote: "MAX_THINKING_TOKENS": "32000"
claim: His personal setup sets a 32000 thinking-token budget, while the claudelayer project config sets only 4000 with alwaysThinkingEnabled false.
evidence_detail: Two config values in two repos; no stated reason or comparison.
landing: A thinking-budget knob per agent/role (verifiers vs explorers); his own repos differ by 8x.

author: Dex
quote: DELETE 10% minimum from every file you touch
claim: He mandates deleting at least 10% of every touched file and 'ALWAYS REDUCE AND DELETE AS MUCH CODE AS POSSIBLE' as a standing agent rule.
evidence_detail: Imperative rule, no measurement; also appears as a verification checklist item.
landing: A deletion-bias line in a phase checklist or reviewer prompt; conflicts with FixFlow's money/ledger code where deletion is risky.

author: Dex
quote: Each file change should include a test change or new test
claim: Rule that every changed file is paired with a test change, plus run linters immediately and run tests after each change.
evidence_detail: One line in a rules list.
landing: A reviewer check that each changed source file has a matching test diff, citable per register id.

author: Dex
quote: model: sonnet
claim: The implementer is a custom agent on Sonnet with Read, Edit, Write, Grep, Glob, Bash, TodoWrite, Task tools whose body is the implement_plan command, so one text serves as slash command and agent.
evidence_detail: Frontmatter plus body identical to the command.
landing: Turning a phase routine into an agent file with a pinned model and tool list rather than relying on session defaults.

author: Dex
quote: Basically a "Super Grep/Glob/LS tool" — Use it if you find yourself desiring one of these tools more than once.
claim: The locator has tools Grep, Glob, LS only (no Read), is told not to read file contents, and its description tells the parent to use it whenever it would run grep/glob more than once; model is inherit, not a small model.
evidence_detail: Frontmatter and 'Don't read file contents' guideline.
landing: Compare with FixFlow's Haiku locator: tool-restriction to enforce locate-only, and the delegation trigger written into the description.

author: Dex
quote: Always include file:line references for claims
claim: The analyzer returns a fixed format (Overview, Entry Points, Core Implementation, Data Flow, Key Patterns, Configuration, Error Handling) with file:line for every claim and 'Don't guess about implementation'.
evidence_detail: Output-format spec; the model is inherit and the prompt says 'ultrathink'.
landing: A fixed output schema with mandatory file:line for sub-agent returns, making claims checkable by a refuter.

author: Dex
quote: You are a pattern librarian, cataloging what exists without editorial commentary.
claim: The pattern-finder returns concrete code snippets with file:line plus the existing test pattern for similar features, forbidding any ranking of patterns, which gives planners templates to model from.
evidence_detail: Agent body; note the prompt contradicts itself ('Note which approach is preferred' vs 'Don't recommend').
landing: A second custom agent beside the locator: 'find the closest existing slice implementation and its test' for new migrations/endpoints.

author: Dex
quote: You're a curator of insights, not a document summarizer.
claim: Notes are read through two agents: a locator that only lists thoughts/ documents by type, and an analyzer that extracts decisions, constraints, specs and open items while filtering superseded or exploratory content and assessing relevance now.
evidence_detail: Two agent prompts; analyzer output includes 'Status: still relevant/implemented/superseded'.
landing: Design input for the knowledge-store reader: locate by type, then extract decisions with a staleness/relevance verdict.

author: Dex
quote: Handle thoughts/searchable/ (read-only directory for searching)
claim: The thoughts store has shared/, per-user, and global areas (tickets, research, plans, prs), with a hard-linked read-only searchable/ copy for grep and a path-correction rule that strips only 'searchable/' from reported paths.
evidence_detail: Directory tree in the agent prompt.
landing: A filesystem layout for the knowledge store (typed folders, dated filenames, searchable mirror) that agents can grep without new infrastructure.

author: Dex
quote: Change as few files at a time as possible
claim: Rule to keep each change touching as few files as possible.
evidence_detail: One line, no rationale given.
landing: A per-phase diff-size guard in the ship-plan routine or reviewer prompt.

author: Dex+others
quote: Start with 2-3 well-crafted searches before fetching content
claim: The web researcher is capped: 2-3 searches, fetch only the 3-5 best pages, quote exactly with links, and note dates and gaps; the research command only uses it if the user explicitly asks.
evidence_detail: Search Efficiency section; web agents are opt-in in research_codebase.
landing: Budgeted search limits and 'gaps' section in any research agent the harness adds.

author: Dex
quote: come up with a prompt and session title for a new agent to pick up where you left off
claim: A personal command has the agent write a continuation prompt and session title, show it to the user, and on approval launch a new opus session in the same directory via the humanlayer CLI.
evidence_detail: 11-line command; includes a typo in the CLI name (humanalyer).
landing: A 'continue in a new session' command: prompt + title, human approval, then launch; shorter than the full handoff file.

author: Dex
quote: Can query directly with `sqlite3`
claim: A session-forensics command reconstructs what past agent sessions did by querying the orchestrator's SQLite database (raw_events with result events in the last 24 hours), its logs and git state, then writes a report of research, plan and implement sessions.
evidence_detail: Describes tooling for finding what was done where; no outcomes.
landing: The audit-from-outside idea behind W2: independent session records (transcripts, final-result events) checked against claimed phase compliance.

author: Dex
quote: Adopt the persona of legendary Programmer Uncle Bob
claim: The file opens with a persona line and ends with flattering 'you are different from other models' framing ('Other models partial-read... You're different') to motivate compliance.
evidence_detail: Persona/motivational prompting, no test.
landing: Not obviously adoptable; a data point on his personal CLAUDE.md style versus his published 'short, universally applicable' guidance (Kyle/Dex blog posts).

author: Dex
quote: Once you've done the 1500-line read, YOU HAVE COMPLETE CONTEXT. Don't second-guess yourself.
claim: After a full read the agent is told not to re-read or second-guess, trading verification for forward momentum.
evidence_detail: Prompt rule; tension with refute-by-default reviewing.
landing: A counter-example for the harness: his personal config trusts the implementer, while FixFlow's reviewers assume refutation.

author: Dex
quote: If a git operation fails like a `git push` stop immediately and tell me what happened
claim: On any failed git operation (his yubikey push) the agent must stop and report rather than retry or work around it.
evidence_detail: Rule with a concrete human-in-the-loop reason (physical key touch).
landing: A stop-and-report rule for failed push/deploy steps in the phase routine, matching the repo's deploy-trap list.

author: Dex
quote: After creating a worktree, you MUST run `make -C WORKTREE_DIR setup` to install deps etc
claim: Worktree creation is a fixed checklist: copy settings.local.json and .env, run make setup, run make thoughts, then launch the implementer with the single /implement_plan command.
evidence_detail: Five MUST steps in the file.
landing: A saved worktree-bootstrap script or skill; the repo's session-per-phase routine could script these steps instead of prose.

author: Dex
quote: Use `codelayer launch --model opus -w WORKTREE_PATH "/implement_plan"` (not cd + launch
claim: New sessions are launched via CLI with an explicit worktree path, always the opus model, and only the single /implement_plan command, so the handoff is a file and the fresh session starts clean.
evidence_detail: Rule in the 'Launching new sessions' section.
landing: Matches the one-phase-per-new-session defence; the pattern is 'launch carries one command, state lives in a file'.

author: Dex
quote: HUMAN_MESSAGE=$(echo "$CLAUDE_ANSWER" | npx humanlayer contact_human -m -)
claim: A headless loop runs `claude -p`, sends each answer to a human via a contact_human channel, feeds the reply back with --continue and routes permission prompts through an MCP approvals tool (--permission-prompt-tool).
evidence_detail: A 35-line shell prototype with an allowedTools variable; not production.
landing: A human-approval channel for headless runs; shows approval can be an external tool, not a prompt in the terminal.

author: Dex
quote: model="claude-3-5-haiku-latest"
claim: A tiny personal CLI streams a one-shot prompt to the small Haiku model with max_tokens 1024 for quick questions, i.e. cheap model on the command line as a default tool.
evidence_detail: 22-line script on an old Haiku (3.5) alias; no stated use.
landing: A cheap-model shell tool for classification or log-trimming steps that do not need the main agent.

author: Dex
quote: BLOCK=${expressions[$RANDOM % ${#expressions[@]}]}
claim: cblock prints a random block glyph after a label, a prompt-decoration script with no bearing on harness behaviour.
evidence_detail: 8-line script.
landing: None.

author: Dex
quote: super helpful for mental alignment with the agent (and with the team) before writing the actual plan
claim: Having the agent produce a component tree before planning a refactor aligns human and agent on structure and removes complex state and useEffects.
evidence_detail: Personal use; image of the tree not captured here.
landing: A pre-plan structural diagram step for the web manager's React Context state; could become a skill.

author: Dex
quote: swallow all test/build/lint output and replace it with a single ✓ if the stage passes
claim: Wrap test/build/lint commands so passing stages print one tick and only failing stages dump their full captured output.
evidence_detail: Used constantly at HumanLayer; a run_silent shell function is given; no numbers beyond a 'half a context window' estimate for their monorepo checks.
landing: A run_silent wrapper script used by the phase routine's check commands (backend ruff/mypy/pytest, web lint/test, mobile typecheck/jest); named in CLAUDE.md Commands.

author: Dex
quote: deterministic is better than non-deterministic. If you already know what matters, don't leave it to a model
claim: If you already know what matters in an output, a deterministic filter beats having the model churn through junk tokens.
evidence_detail: Closing principle.
landing: General design rule for the harness: prefer scripts over instructions where the check is knowable.

author: Dex
quote: every token you use is diminishing the results and moves you closer to "need to clear or compact
claim: Each token of context diminishes result quality and moves the session toward a forced clear or compaction.
evidence_detail: Assertion tied to the smart/dumb zone idea.
landing: Supports the one-phase-per-session defence; candidate rationale line in the phase routine.

author: Dex
quote: labs have to take big swings and the majority of their potential user base doesn't know how
claim: Recent models are RL-trained to be conservative about loading context, which compensates for context-inefficient codebases but hurts careful users.
evidence_detail: Speculation, explicitly flagged as opining.
landing: Explains why wrappers must be paired with an explicit no-truncation instruction; model-behaviour caveat for harness prompts.

author: Dex
quote: stay in the ~75k token "smart zone" for claude models
claim: Keep the working context under roughly 75k tokens (the smart zone) and treat every passing-test line as wasted context.
evidence_detail: Stated as a target number; no experiment given. Says a passing run wastes 2-3% of the window for under 10 tokens of information.
landing: A context budget rule in the phase routine (one phase per new session) with a ~75k reference figure; relates to compaction trigger.

author: Dex
quote: human time wasted on wrangling an agent in the dumb zone is likely more expensive by 10x
claim: Token cost and run time of checks are secondary; human time lost to an agent in the dumb zone costs 10x or more.
evidence_detail: Stated as likely; no data.
landing: Cost-model argument for effort routing and context discipline: optimise human time and context, not tokens.

author: Dex
quote: Rather than letting the model decide what to truncate, we like to take control of output deterministically.
claim: Decide truncation in a deterministic wrapper (success = tick, failure = full output) rather than leaving it to the model.
evidence_detail: Design principle, illustrated with an example output.
landing: Output caps in the harness are currently the model's choice or fixed caps; replace with exit-code-gated wrappers in scripts the routine calls.

author: Dex
quote: Enable failFast. pytest -x , jest --bail , go test -failfast . One failure at a time.
claim: Run test suites fail-fast so the agent sees one failure at a time instead of context-switching between several.
evidence_detail: Recommendation, no numbers.
landing: Check commands for backend (pytest -x) and web/mobile (jest --bail) in the routine's inner loop; full run only before PR.

author: Dex
quote: Strip generic stack frames that don't help your agent find the issue. Remove timing info.
claim: Filter failure output (stack frames, timings, framework parsing for counts) down to the assertion that failed.
evidence_detail: Recommendation; mentions a hacky run_silent.sh extracting counts from pytest, jest, go test, vitest.
landing: Failure-output filters for pytest/Vitest/Jest/ruff/mypy output in a shared script.

author: Dex
quote: we run these in a pre-push hook, and some subset of these projects for each plan phase.
claim: The same silent check wrappers run in a pre-push hook and as a per-plan-phase subset, giving a deterministic gate.
evidence_detail: Describes their own monorepo checks; would be half a context window without wrappers.
landing: Re-opens the skipped pre-commit/pre-push gate: a hook that runs the wrappers is also a non-self-reported compliance signal (mark: re-opens skipped hooks/pre-commit gate).

author: Dex
quote: Now your only job is to convince the model not to do its own truncation.
claim: After installing wrappers, the remaining work is instructing the model not to pipe output through head/tail or /dev/null itself.
evidence_detail: Suggests shouting in claude.md; no measure.
landing: One short universal line in CLAUDE.md Commands ('run checks via the wrapper; never pipe to head/tail').

author: Dex
quote: it ran a 5 minute test suite with head -n 50 and now it has to run it again
claim: Context-anxious models pipe output to head/tail or /dev/null, then rerun slow suites, burning more tokens and human time than they save.
evidence_detail: Reported complaints and a pytest | head -n 50 example; a trivial case where /dev/null guards cost more tokens (unofficial tokenizer).
landing: A known model failure mode to forbid in the routine for slow suites (backend integration tests against Postgres).

source_title: AITW Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents

claim: Run several agents in separate worktrees on the same spec, then synthesise the best answer into the feature branch by judgement or another agent.

source_title: AITW Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents

quote: File and Spec Management, in-tree vs out of tree

evidence_detail: Topic list only.

source_title: StartupHub.ai recap of No Vibes Allowed
author: other
quote: ship a week's worth of work in a single day
claim: A machine-drafted recap restates the talk's claims (300k-line Rust, a week's work in a day) and says implementation must adhere to the plan under 40% context; the 'week in a day' phrase is the recap's gloss of the 35k/7-hour story.
evidence_detail: Third-party summary; no new data; framing exaggerates (he said 1-2 weeks estimated in 7 hours, partly codegen).

author: Dex
quote: around the 40% line is where you're going to start to see some diminishing returns
claim: Quality degrades once a context window is roughly 40% full (the 'dumb zone'), a variable guideline depending on task complexity.

author: Dex
quote: the amount of lies you can find in any one part of your codebase

evidence_detail: Joke chart (audience answer 'slop'), no data.
landing: Knowledge store design: entries need freshness/verification-against-code; CLAUDE.md 'Keeping this file honest' section already addresses drift

author: Dex
quote: We prefer is on demand compressed context.
claim: Prefer generating a fresh research snapshot of the relevant code slice on demand (parallel subagents over vertical slices) over maintaining static onboarding docs: 'compressing truth'.
evidence_detail: Preference stated; no comparison data.
landing: A saved research workflow/skill that runs slice-wise explorers and writes a dated research doc; a candidate against growing CLAUDE.md

author: Dex
quote: Planning is about compression of intent.
claim: A plan file is a compression of intent: exact steps, file names, code snippets and a test after every change, so even a weak model cannot go wrong.
evidence_detail: Team practice; plans shown as slides.
landing: Plan @ <sha> draft PR body template: include file names, snippets and per-step verification command

author: Dex
quote: as your plans get longer, reliability goes up, readability goes down
claim: Plan length trades reliability against human readability; each team must find its sweet spot.
evidence_detail: Hand-drawn tradeoff curve; no data.
landing: Budget for plan length in the phase routine; owner one-page view is the readable side of this tradeoff

author: Dex
quote: how do we keep everybody on the team on the same page
claim: The key purpose of code review is mental alignment; reviewing plans and research (not only diffs) keeps technical leaders aware as code volume grows.
evidence_detail: Argument, credited to a Blake Smith article.
landing: Owner review should target the plan and decisions journal first; one-page owner view already approximates this

author: Dex
quote: putting his AMP threads on his pull requests
claim: Attach the agent thread, prompts and build-passed evidence to the PR so reviewers see the journey, not just a wall of diff (credited to Mitchell Hashimoto).
evidence_detail: Dex endorses a practice by another person; no data.
landing: Link the session transcript or journal from the draft PR; evidence folder with sha256 manifest is an adjacent mechanism

author: Dex
quote: a bad part of a plan is could be a hundred bad lines of code
claim: Leverage hierarchy: bad research causes thousands of bad lines, a bad plan hundreds, a bad line one; spend human attention at the top of the pipeline.
evidence_detail: Rule of thumb, no data.
landing: Reviewer effort allocation: refuter on research/diagnosis and plan before implementation, not only on final diff

author: Dex
quote: Do not outsource the thinking.
claim: AI can only amplify thinking already done; if you skip reading the plan the process does not work (tool spew of markdown files is a warning sign).
evidence_detail: Parquet Java Hadoop-removal failure story: they threw out plans and went to a whiteboard.
landing: Routine gate: a human-read checkpoint after plan; counter-signal against workflows that only generate artefacts nobody reads

author: Dex
quote: Specri development is broken. Not the idea, but the phrase.
claim: 'Spec-driven development' is semantically diffused (a spec may mean a better prompt, a PRD, or library docs) and so no longer useful as a term.
evidence_detail: Argument citing Fowler's semantic diffusion.
landing: Nowhere obvious; naming hygiene for harness docs (define 'phase', 'plan', 'verifier' precisely)

author: Dex
quote: If you don't onboard your agents, they will make stuff up.
claim: Without onboarding context the agent invents; onboarding must be supplied either via repo docs or generated research.
evidence_detail: Memento analogy.
landing: P1 cold-resume trial measures precisely whether the repository alone onboards a fresh agent

author: Dex
quote: if you have too many MCPs in your coding agent, you are doing all your work in the dumb zone
claim: Too many MCP tools consume the context budget so all work happens in the degraded zone.
evidence_detail: Assertion, no numbers.
landing: Audit enabled MCP servers and tool definitions for the phase sessions; keep tool surface minimal

author: Dex
quote: you don't always need a full research plan implement
claim: Scale the process to the task: a button colour needs just a prompt, medium cross-repo work needs research then plan; ceiling rises with more compaction.
evidence_detail: 2x2 sketch of task difficulty vs process weight.
landing: Phase routine tiering: light path for small phases versus full path; effort routing by phase size

author: Dex
quote: Pick one tool and get some reps.
claim: Do not min-max across Claude, Codex and other tools; calibrating how much context engineering a task needs takes repeated reps on one tool.
evidence_detail: Advice.
landing: Argues for running the routine repeatedly on one tool before judging it; relevant to the unrun phase routine

author: Dex
quote: a team of three. It took eight weeks. It was really freaking hard
claim: His team of three reached 2-3x throughput after an eight-week, difficult workflow rewrite that changed how they collaborate.
evidence_detail: Self-reported 2-3x throughput, team of three, eight weeks; the ai.engineer page notes it is team-specific, not guaranteed.
landing: Expectation setting: the phase routine may need weeks of iteration before it pays off

author: Dex
quote: we shipped 35,000 lines of code to BAML
claim: Seven hours on a Saturday produced about 35,000 lines in BAML, partly codegen and golden files, which the BAML CEO estimated as 1-2 weeks of work; one PR merged a week later.
evidence_detail: 35k lines / 7 hours / estimated 1-2 weeks; he notes some is codegen; the ai.engineer page says not controlled measurement.
landing: Caution on line-count as a productivity measure; do not use as target for FixFlow phases

author: Dex
quote: I'm going to try to oneshot a fix to your 300,000line Rust codebase
claim: He one-shot a fix to a 300,000-line Rust codebase (BAML) with research-plan-implement; the CTO merged it without realising it was a podcast bit.
evidence_detail: 300k-line Rust codebase, Monday-night work, merged by Tuesday; compared plans with and without research and discarded bad research.
landing: None directly; evidence that merged-PR acceptance is a proof used by him

author: Dex
quote: staff engineers don't adopt AI because it doesn't make them that much faster
claim: A growing rift: staff engineers skip AI, junior/mid use it and produce slop, seniors clean up; cultural change must come from the top.
evidence_detail: Observation, no data.
landing: Nowhere obvious (organisational, not harness config)

author: Dex
quote: There is no perfect prompt. There is no silver bullet.
claim: The three phase names are not essential; the durable idea is compaction and staying in the smart zone, and 'harness engineering' is a subset of context engineering.
evidence_detail: Assertion; early hint that RPI is provisional.
landing: Treat the phase routine as revisable; decide by observed cold-resume results rather than naming

source_title: AI Engineer talk page (No Vibes Allowed)
author: Dex
quote: documents matter only when they accurately compress relevant truth or intent
claim: Markdown artefacts are only valuable if they accurately compress truth or intent and improve execution; accumulating documents for their own sake does not help.
evidence_detail: Page's AI summary of the talk's argument (third-party paraphrase of Dex).
landing: Test for knowledge-store entries: does it compress verified truth and change a later action

author: Dex
quote: intentional compaction
claim: Instead of arguing on in a derailed session, have the agent compress the context into a reviewable markdown file and start a fresh session from it.
evidence_detail: Team practice; no measurement.
landing: Phase handoff artefact: the decisions journal / draft PR body as the compaction file that a new session onboards from (P1 cold-resume trial tests exactly this)

author: Dex
quote: The exact files and line numbers that matter to the problem that we're solving.
claim: A good compaction file names exact files and line numbers relevant to the task rather than narrative.
evidence_detail: Shown as an example slide, no numbers.
landing: Handoff template fields in the plan-@-sha draft PR body: file:line pointers, not prose

author: Dex
quote: the worst thing you can have is incorrect information, then missing information, and then just too much noise
claim: Context should be optimised for correctness, completeness, size and trajectory, ranked by harm: wrong info worst, then missing info, then noise.
evidence_detail: Framework stated without data.
landing: Principle for the knowledge store: a stale or wrong stored diagnosis is worse than none; verify before store

also.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
also.quote: Incorrect Information, Missing Information, Too much Noise
also.author: Dex
also.claim: Rank the worst context failures as incorrect information first, missing information second, noise third; optimise for correctness, completeness, size, trajectory.

author: Dex
quote: the next most likely token in this conversation is I better do something wrong
claim: Repeatedly correcting or yelling at an agent builds a bad trajectory that biases it to keep failing, so restart instead of steering in place.
evidence_detail: Mechanism explained informally; no experiment.
landing: Routine rule: after two failed corrections, restart the phase from the journal rather than continuing

author: Dex
quote: Sub agents are not for anthropomorphizing roles. They are for controlling context.
claim: Subagents exist to isolate expensive search/reading in a separate context and return a succinct finding, not to model job roles.
evidence_detail: Design principle with illustrative example.
landing: Custom agents under .claude/agents/: define by context-isolation job (locator, reader) not by role; extends the Haiku fixflow-explorer

author: Dex
quote: Frequent intentional compaction
claim: Build the entire workflow (research, plan, implement) around context management, with compaction between phases to stay in the smart zone throughout.
evidence_detail: Team practice credited with 2-3x throughput; no controlled measure.
landing: Ship plan section 0 phase routine (one phase per new chat) is a version of this

author: Dex
quote: you're going to pull in the root context and then you pull in the subcontext
claim: Progressive disclosure: root context file plus sub-context at each directory level so the agent loads only what its area needs.
evidence_detail: Described as an option; he then argues it goes stale.
landing: CLAUDE.md trim: split into root plus per-slice files or skills loaded on demand (slice folders exist per runtime)

author: other
quote: set up effective automated checks for linting, type checking, unit tests etc

author: other
quote: The solution is to simply have a bullet point in the CLAUDE.md file

evidence_detail: bastawhiz; reports it works for him and coworkers; counter from girvo that models still ignore the line sometimes so he re-checks manually.

author: other

author: other

author: other
quote: Claude rarely actually reads the other documentation files I point it to.

author: Dex
quote: the key here is "if X then Y syntax"
claim: Dex says writing pointers as 'if X then Y' conditions pierces the system-reminder's 'probably ignore this' framing by marking when an instruction is highly relevant.
evidence_detail: dhorthy reply to sothatsit, 2025-12-01; no numbers.
landing: Rewrite CLAUDE.md doc-map rows and skill descriptions as 'when doing X, read Y' triggers.

author: Dex
quote: injecting this file into the context window whenever an agent touches this directory
claim: Dex says CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md differ from README because the harness injects them deterministically, and managing every token in and how it is presented beats relying on public training data.
evidence_detail: dhorthy reply to _pdp_, 2025-11-30; argues for token-level context management in complex codebases.
landing: Supports directory-scoped CLAUDE.md files (backend/, technician-app/) so root stays small.

author: Kyle
quote: you shouldn't use an LLM to do a linter & formatter's job
claim: Post author Kyle says the durable principles are: don't make the LLM do a linter's job, LLMs are stateless and need onboarding, and deterministically injected instructions beat having the agent derive everything.
evidence_detail: 0xblacklight; also says the post is 'how to use this config point right now', expects some advice to age poorly, and that it targets hard brownfield problems where /init output is rarely enough.
landing: Pushes style/format rules out of CLAUDE.md into tooling; keep only non-derivable facts.
inventory_ref: Writing a good CLAUDE.md (2025-11-25 blog; thread itself not listed)

author: other
quote: I removed all my instructions and it basically never violates those points.
claim: A user says Opus 4.5 follows his coding-style preferences from reading the code alone, so he deleted his style instructions.
evidence_detail: nurettin; also Zerot: conventions already in surrounding code make CLAUDE.md copies pure context cost.
landing: Candidate trim: drop any rule the code or a linter already demonstrates; test by deleting and watching for violations.
inventory_ref: Writing a good CLAUDE.md (2025-11-25 blog; thread itself not listed)

author: other
quote: The more context you give the lower it's upper end of quality becomes.
claim: One commenter claims extra context and comments cap quality on hard problems and strips comments before sessions; others (xpe, Aurornis, stpedgwdgfhgdd) dispute generalising.
evidence_detail: johnsmith1840 uses custom scripts, no controlled test; xpe reports ~10k tokens of guidelines in CLAUDE.md helped across conversations, also unmeasured.
landing: Both directions are anecdote; supports measuring CLAUDE.md length effects in the knowledge-store pilot instead of assuming.
inventory_ref: Writing a good CLAUDE.md (2025-11-25 blog; thread itself not listed)

author: other
quote: Mr Tinkleberry
claim: A canary instruction (address me by a name) is used to detect when CLAUDE.md is no longer being followed; critics say it measures only the canary, and it may be ignored mid-conversation as low relevance.
evidence_detail: nico, dkersten (emoji prefix), homeonthemtn ('Purple fish' picked and chosen); chickensong saw adherence at start/end but not middle; isoprophlex says the canary reinforces itself in context.
landing: A cheap compliance signal for 'was the file loaded', but not proof rules were applied; relevant to telling skipped routine from unconsulted store.

author: other
quote: You could make a hook in Claude to re-inject claude.md.
claim: Commenters propose hooks to re-inject CLAUDE.md or a /bootstrap command to reload it when the agent drifts, since it can be lost mid-session.
evidence_detail: aqme28 (hook), jmathai (/bootstrap reading all CLAUDE.md, skills, commands; reports sessions not starting with them loaded), edf13 (proxy); Zerot says CLAUDE.md reloads on compaction.
landing: Re-opens the skipped hooks decision for compaction recovery and compliance logging.

author: other
quote: CLAUDE.md should only be for persistent reminders that are useful in 100% of your sessions
claim: Commenters say conditional content belongs in skills or subdirectory CLAUDE.md files that load on demand; but unshavedyak doubts skills reduce context if the agent loads them every time.
evidence_detail: jswny, stingraycharles (src/persistence/CLAUDE.md auto-loaded when reading files there), vaer-k (cites Anthropic docs on child-directory CLAUDE.md), unshavedyak.

inventory_ref: Writing a good CLAUDE.md (2025-11-25 blog; thread itself not listed)

author: other
quote: It seems to be 50/50 or LESS that Claude.md even reads/uses this file.
claim: A heavy user reports CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md rules (e.g. method under 50 lines) are routinely ignored, so he re-pastes instructions after resetting context.
evidence_detail: saberience; also AndyNemmity runs a very large but targeted CLAUDE.md with agents, hooks, skills and commands and says it works.

author: other
quote: If you're not benchmarking and systematically measuring the impact of your changes
claim: A commenter says without benchmarking and systematic measurement, CLAUDE.md tuning is not prompt engineering, just improving by feel.
evidence_detail: stingraycharles; related tsimionescu calls current practice closer to ritual than engineering; bird0861 notes prompts break on model changes ('prompt instability').
landing: Supports gating a CLAUDE.md trim on a measured trial (P1 cold-resume) and re-testing after model updates.

author: other
quote: Work through lists and constantly update status so you can clear context
claim: Commenters advise a short CLAUDE.md with pointers, status lists updated so context can be cleared and resumed, and one session per problem; also that Claude writes bloated CLAUDE.md files unless told one sentence per topic.
evidence_detail: chickensong, aiibe ('one session for one problem', never hit context limit), handoflixue (instruct 'one sentence per topic, be concise'), dkersten (refresh context often).
landing: Matches the one-phase-per-new-session routine and status-based resume; a concision instruction for agent-written docs.

author: Dex+others
quote: Turn any MCP server into a CLI for easy use with subagents
claim: MCP servers are wrapped as CLIs so sub-agents can call them through bash, instead of loading MCP tool schemas into context.
evidence_detail: One-line README; no mechanism or numbers given.
landing: Custom agents/skills: tool exposure for sub-agents via a CLI wrapper to keep tool definitions out of context

author: Kyle
quote: Frontier thinking LLMs can follow ~ 150-200 instructions with reasonable consistency.
claim: Frontier thinking models follow about 150-200 instructions consistently; smaller and non-thinking models fewer, and smaller models decay exponentially.
evidence_detail: Cites unspecified research 'not investigated in an incredibly rigorous manner'; no numbers on decay beyond the claim.
landing: Instruction budget for CLAUDE.md trim: count instructions, not lines (390 lines is well above).

author: Kyle
quote: Claude Code's system prompt contains ~50 individual instructions
claim: The Claude Code system prompt already uses about 50 instructions, nearly a third of the reliable budget, before CLAUDE.md, skills or user messages.
evidence_detail: Claimed from their analysis of the harness (logging proxy); no breakdown given.
landing: Budget arithmetic for CLAUDE.md plus skills: each new skill/agent description eats the same instruction budget.

author: Kyle
quote: As instruction count increases, instruction-following quality decreases uniformly.
claim: More instructions do not make the model ignore only the later ones; it ignores all of them uniformly, with bias toward the start and end of the prompt.
evidence_detail: Attributed to loose research; no source given.
landing: Argues against appending invariants to the bottom of CLAUDE.md; put the few critical ones first and last, move the rest out.

author: Kyle
quote: IMPORTANT: this context may or may not be relevant to your tasks.
claim: Claude Code wraps CLAUDE.md in a system reminder telling the model to ignore it unless highly relevant, so non-universal content gets ignored.
evidence_detail: Observed via a logging proxy on ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL; rationale for Anthropic's choice is speculation.
landing: Every non-universal line in CLAUDE.md lowers compliance with the rest; basis for moving phase-specific rules into skills. The proxy method is also a way to observe what the agent actually saw (marks: measurement pipeline skipped).

author: Kyle
quote: general consensus is that < 300 lines is best, and shorter is even better.
claim: CLAUDE.md should stay under 300 lines; HumanLayer's own root file is under sixty.
evidence_detail: Consensus claim plus their own file length.
landing: Target for the CLAUDE.md trim (390 lines now; <300 ceiling, ~60 as their example).

author: Kyle
quote: keeping task-specific instructions in separate markdown files with self-descriptive names
claim: Use progressive disclosure: an agent_docs/ folder of task-specific files, listed in CLAUDE.md with one-line descriptions for the agent to choose from.
evidence_detail: Recommendation with example file layout; compared to how Skills work.
landing: Move the invariant sections (outbox, bill freeze, dispatcher) to per-area docs or skills with descriptions; CLAUDE.md keeps an index.

author: Kyle
quote: Prefer pointers to copies . Don't include code snippets in these files if possible
claim: Reference file:line pointers to authoritative code rather than copying snippets, which go stale.
evidence_detail: Recommendation.
landing: Audit CLAUDE.md for stated facts (Alembic head, table counts) that duplicate code and rot; replace with pointers or a check script.

author: Kyle
quote: Never send an LLM to do a linter's job .
claim: Do not put code style rules in CLAUDE.md; use deterministic linters/formatters (ideally auto-fixing) and let in-context learning follow existing patterns.
evidence_detail: Recommendation; mentions Biome.
landing: Prune style rules from CLAUDE.md; rely on ruff/prettier/eslint already in CI.

author: Kyle
quote: consider setting up a Claude Code Stop hook that runs your formatter & linter
claim: A Stop hook that runs formatter and linter and feeds errors back to the agent replaces asking the agent to find formatting issues.
evidence_detail: Suggestion for those who feel strongly; slash command alternative separates implementation from formatting.
landing: Re-opens the skipped hooks decision: a Stop hook is both backpressure and an observable compliance record (mark: re-opens hooks).

author: Kyle
quote: A bad line of a research that misunderstands how the system works has the potential to result in a lot of bad lines
claim: Errors compound down the pipeline (bad research line, bad plan lines, bad code), and CLAUDE.md touches every phase, so every line deserves scrutiny.
evidence_detail: Argument; no data.
landing: Justifies review leverage at research/plan artefacts and a line-by-line CLAUDE.md audit.

author: Kyle
quote: we think you should spend some time thinking very carefully about every single line
claim: Do not auto-generate CLAUDE.md with /init; hand-craft it because it is the highest-leverage point of the harness.
evidence_detail: Recommendation.
landing: CLAUDE.md is hand-written already; guard against agent-appended additions in phase PRs (changes to CLAUDE.md need review).

author: Kyle
quote: Smaller models get MUCH worse, MUCH more quickly .
claim: Smaller models decay exponentially in instruction following, so avoid small models for multi-step tasks or complicated plans.
evidence_detail: Cited research, not named.
landing: Caution on the Haiku locator agent: keep its instruction set tiny and single-purpose; do not give small models multi-step plans.

author: Kyle
quote: CLAUDE.md onboards Claude to your codebase
claim: CLAUDE.md should cover WHAT (stack, map), WHY (purpose), HOW (build, test, verify) and not every possible command.
evidence_detail: Framework recommendation.
landing: Structure template for the trimmed CLAUDE.md: map, purpose, verification commands, index of deeper docs.

author: Dex
quote: walk through research/plan/impl with the legendary @vaibcode
claim: AITW #33 demonstrates the research/plan/impl flow inside CodeLayer by building three real features (AI session titles, summaries, Obsidian editor support).
evidence_detail: Announcement only; episode content not captured.
landing: Episode itself is the evidence of RPI in practice; this tweet is a pointer

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: if you don't come with opinions, the model will not
claim: You cannot outsource the thinking: if you know what you want (phase order, structure), state it; Dex overrode a model-written plan with his own phase order rather than iterating on it.
evidence_detail: Said when the co-host wanted to lean on the model more; Dex ties it to 12-factor: put the known workflow in deterministic code and let the model write code, tests and fixes.
landing: Principle for plan review: the human supplies phase order and unknowns
inventory_ref: (A4) CodeLayer; (B) June to December 2025 - 'Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer'

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: put your biggest unknowns as the first phase
claim: Order plan phases to retire the biggest unknown first (here: can the Haiku call be invoked and pulled through), before schema and wiring work.
evidence_detail: Said while explaining why the model's draft plan was wrong; the first phase was then validated by an integration test.
landing: Plan template: risk-first phase ordering

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: sprinting to as quickly as possible get to wired all the way through
claim: Models plan horizontally (database, service, API, front end) so nothing is testable until phase three; steer to vertical slices wired end-to-end early, and fix the create-plan prompt to say so.
evidence_detail: Observed in the draft plan: 'they're very horizontal ... only by the end of phase three can you run a curl'; says create-plan needs updating.
landing: Plan template / skill: vertical-slice requirement

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: you really want to iterate on the phases before you go write the file
claim: Make the model propose open questions and a phase outline before it writes the plan, since a few hundred tokens of outline are cheap to iterate whereas the written plan consumes much of the useful window.
evidence_detail: Observed the model writing the file before outline review, leaving Dex 'in the dumb zone or needing to rebuild all that context'.
landing: Plan step: outline gate before the plan document

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: eat the like 8% of the context window that is required
claim: Writing a ~600-line plan document costs about 8% of the context window, so steer as much as possible before it is written.
evidence_detail: Single stated figure, 'this 600 line markdown document'; not measured in an experiment.
landing: Context budget accounting per phase

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: even Opus 4.1 would skip steps all the time.
claim: Models skip the interactive steps of a prompt even when instructed; reinforce the key orders in the user message ('magic words') such as 'work back and forth with me, start with open questions, show the phase outline before writing the plan'.
evidence_detail: Dex says he has done 'thousands of these' and knows to notice a skipped questions step; novices will not notice; also says Opus 4.5 sometimes skips steps.
landing: Phase-routine opening prompt; relates to self-reported compliance (skips are invisible to novices)

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: You want a very easy way to convince yourself that the code itself is correct.
claim: Each phase needs a cheap human-checkable proof of correctness (shell command, integration test, one-off Go main) so the human does not have to read the logic; otherwise leverage is lost.
evidence_detail: Argued against the co-host's preference for reading code; 'I want to be able to hit that endpoint with a curl and it works'.
landing: Per-phase verification line in the plan; reviewer asks for the proof, not the diff

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: models are not good at evaluating whether code is correct
claim: Do not rely on the model (or on reading every line) to establish correctness; give it something validatable that is not model judgment.
evidence_detail: Short assertion during the testing debate; consistent with the later SlopCodeBench-era claims.
landing: Against review-agent-only verification; supports executable proof requirements

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: I guarantee it's going to like mock the things that we care about.
claim: Agent-written unit tests for a phase tend to mock the exact integration (here the CLI call) that matters; require a real, un-mocked integration test for the risky part.
evidence_detail: Prediction before reading the model's tests; he then judged the generated tests not useful.
landing: Reviewer checklist: fail-before/pass-after tests must hit the real boundary

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: have a little proof of concept script before you go into planning
claim: Run a throwaway proof-of-concept (a shell one-liner or script) before planning, and treat reverse-engineering a black box as a missing stage of research.
evidence_detail: Used to prove the Claude CLI could do a one-off text-in/text-out call and to probe whether Obsidian opens non-vault files; he says it is not yet baked into the methodology.
landing: Research step: optional PoC for unknown external behaviour (relevant to Railway/Expo/Supabase behaviour)

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: you want to keep the model objective as long as possible
claim: Keep research objective (how the system works today) separate from how it will work; models are good at explaining and bad at evaluating, and research questions should be things not discoverable from code, not implementation questions.
evidence_detail: A/B of two research runs (with and without the spec in the prompt): the no-spec run produced objective questions, the other produced implementation choices; models pick their first idea when implementation leaks in.
landing: Research prompt design; separation of fact-finding from planning

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: tell it the parts of the codebase that are going to matter
claim: In research, tell the agent which areas matter without telling it what you are building; stash the implementation ask in a text file for the planning step.
evidence_detail: Dex's stated practice, contrasted live with the co-host's spec-in-research approach; the co-host accepts it is a different style.
landing: Research/plan hand-off format in the phase routine

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: give me a bunch of boolean flags about like what is true
claim: Do not ask a model for a 1-10 score of how good something is; ask for boolean facts about the thing and let deterministic code decide.
evidence_detail: Recalled from an earlier AITW email-classification episode; applied here to why research should stay descriptive.
landing: Verdict schema for refuters and critics: structured true/false findings, verdict computed in code

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: doing the exact same work, but you're using smaller context windows to do the work
claim: A phase-implement command moves implementation into a sub-agent per phase that tests and validates, then reports to the parent which checks and asks for manual validation; all phases can run in one parent session using smaller windows.
evidence_detail: Dex insisted on it for a small change and argued 'worst case I waste five minutes'; the co-host's tests of it were mixed. Calls it a new CodeLayer capability.
landing: Workflow script: parent orchestrator with per-phase worker sub-agents; skill for phase implement

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: it dictates the amount of context engineering that you have to do
claim: Task size and difficulty dictate how much context engineering to apply; the only way to calibrate is to over- and under-do it repeatedly, and Dex tells people to try things they think will not work.
evidence_detail: Repeated across the stream (also 'binary search on either side'); co-host regularly pushes to 70% and the two disagree.
landing: Effort routing: scale process weight to task size; small changes skip the full routine

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: pick a dimension and then eval across that dimension for your own intuition
claim: Vary one dimension at a time (tools, amount of context engineering, repos) over a week and compare, locking the others; reset expectations when a new model ships.
evidence_detail: Dex describes rotating dimensions weekly ('still all vibes, but intentional'); the co-host instead snaps between workflows at each model release.
landing: A routing experiment protocol (medium vs xhigh) rather than a one-off switch

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: how do you edit a plan in flight when you realize something was wrong
claim: Open problem: how to re-steer a plan (back out, edit) when a defect is discovered after three phases of implementation; Dex's workaround was to fork back and give very specific instructions.
evidence_detail: Arose when the model silently edited both sides of the OpenAPI contract and then tried regenerating types needing Docker.
landing: Decisions journal / plan-amendment rule in the draft PR; re-plan procedure

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: figure out the contract between the front end and the back end
claim: Define the front/back contract, mock the backend side, get the front end right visually, then implement the backend, so debugging has a visual reference and the contract is known correct.
evidence_detail: Offered as an alternative tactic after the plan's phase order was discussed; not tried on stream.
landing: Plan tactic for mobile/web vs backend slices (technician-app and src/ against FastAPI schemas)

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: It'll just like edit both sides of the contract which is like very wrong.
claim: Agents sometimes edit the generated artifact and its consumer instead of the source contract (OpenAPI schema) so it technically works but is wrong; check that the contract source changed.
evidence_detail: Confirmed on stream: the session-title event type was added but the OpenAPI spec was not updated, so the new field never reached the client.
landing: Reviewer checklist item (schemas.py/models vs migration, API schema vs clients; drift checks already in CI)

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: actually sharing your prod database for your stable version
claim: A dev build of the app was silently sharing the stable version's database and daemon; separate the dev database path and verify which store a test hits before trusting results.
evidence_detail: Debugging detour of about 10 minutes; worktrees also lacked the untracked .env, so dev environments must be copied in.
landing: Worktree/environment setup checklist for phases; do not let verification touch shared state

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: controll X and fork it and just add that to your original instructions
claim: Rather than interrupting a running session with a correction, fork the conversation at an earlier turn and amend the original instructions; he also forks back to before the plan was written.
evidence_detail: Used repeatedly in the stream (fork command in CodeLayer) to retry with better wording without paying for the noisy branch.
landing: Context forking practice (his later 2026 forking post is by Kyle); fits correction-by-rewind in a phase

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: maybe that's a side effect of the fact that you're constantly pushing the context window
claim: Dex speculates that the co-host's distrust of plan execution may result from routinely running sessions to 70% of the window.
evidence_detail: Hypothesis only; the co-host defended long contexts ('people can push context windows further than they think').
landing: Context-budget policy debate (who is right is unmeasured)

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: one or two plan sessions and then one or two implementation sessions
claim: The natural unit of work is a task (one ticket or issue) with one or two research, plan and implementation sessions each, which the tool should group, rather than a vague 'project'.
evidence_detail: Product-design remark answering a viewer; reflects how his team shapes sessions.
landing: Ticket-per-phase mapping; how sessions are named and grouped in the PR

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: there's a lot of like oral tradition that goes into this stuff
claim: The method relies on unwritten instinct, so the product should add guard rails (fewer foot-guns) that work even for people without LLM intuition.
evidence_detail: Said while explaining CodeLayer's design aim; no evidence on whether it works.
landing: Encode tacit habits as prompts/skills/checks so a fresh agent (cold-resume trial) does not depend on them

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: used like thousands of tokens for a thing you could have told the model
claim: Pasting a screenshot to describe a UI change costs thousands of tokens when a sentence would do.
evidence_detail: Dex's criticism of the co-host pasting an image into the prompt; the co-host replied images are faster and help UI.
landing: Context-hygiene tip for prompts

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: all of these sub agents run with sonnet
claim: Research sub-agents are hard-coded to a cheaper model in the agent header while the parent runs the stronger model, and the sub-agent prompt can be inspected to verify what was passed.
evidence_detail: Shown by opening the sub-agent tool call; he also notes the model sometimes picks Haiku itself for a sub-agent.
landing: .claude/agents/ frontmatter model field; effort routing per agent

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: so there's no git or codebase context clouding the system prompt
claim: For a one-off model call (title generation) run it with a small model, an overridden system prompt, and in a temp directory so no repo context contaminates it, and keep it out of the normal tracked-session path.
evidence_detail: Design spec dictated for the title feature; the integration test ran it via the user's subscription rather than an API key.
landing: Pattern for cheap sub-calls (e.g. a verifier that starts with no repo context beyond the claim and the diff)

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: forget to check the like actual testing steps
claim: Everyone, including Dex, forgets to run the plan's manual testing steps; he walks the co-host through the manual verification that the implementation output itself stated.
evidence_detail: Live: the implementation report listed 'start the daemon and verify migration applies'; the co-host skipped it and the new column was missing until a dev-environment fix.
landing: Self-reported compliance gap: human-run steps in the plan are the most-skipped; make them explicit in the closing message

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: This took the plan for me from like 70% to 90%.
claim: Reading and steering a plan until it is about 90% right is enough; do not micromanage it, and time spent reading plans shrinks as you get reps.
evidence_detail: Subjective percentages, stated after one round of feedback on the phase order.
landing: Plan-review stopping rule (diminishing returns)

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex
quote: You got to let the tooling do the deterministic things
claim: Let the AI do what it is good at, let tooling do the deterministic things you want every time, and leave the human the high-leverage thinking, design and architecture; e.g. auto-inject a 'yes' when the model re-asks for an obvious go-ahead.
evidence_detail: Dex states the principle; the auto-yes idea was the co-host's and Dex agreed.
landing: Hooks/scripts for routine steps (re-opens skipped hooks idea) and saved workflows

source_title: Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer (AI That Works #33)
author: Dex+others
quote: the diff is like verifiably true
claim: To build a similar feature, hand the model the git diff/commit of an earlier small feature as the example instead of the plan, since the diff is verifiably what was done; teams keep generalizable sample PRs for this.
evidence_detail: Co-host proposed it; Dex agreed it gives better results for least effort and says his team does it all the time.
landing: Worked-example library of reference diffs in the repo or skills

source_title: AITW Using CodeLayer to Build CodeLayer
author: Dex
quote: Research / Plan / Implement to ship new features to CodeLayer itself.
claim: The team dogfoods the Research/Plan/Implement workflow inside CodeLayer.
evidence_detail: README is a one-paragraph stub.
landing: nowhere obvious

source_title: How three YC startups built their companies with Claude Code
author: other
quote: Don't make Claude do research while it's trying to plan, while it's trying to implement
claim: Separate research, plan and implement into discrete sessions, passing only distilled conclusions forward; Ambral's CTO says this was influenced by Horthy's work.
evidence_detail: Quote from Ambral CTO Stettner; Anthropic editorial; no numbers.
landing: Confirms one phase per new session; handoff must carry only distilled conclusions.

source_title: How three YC startups built their companies with Claude Code
author: other
quote: Opus 4.1 to do research and planning. Sonnet 4.5 has been absolutely killer
claim: Use the stronger model for research and planning and a cheaper model to implement each plan phase.
evidence_detail: One CTO's practice; not Dex's own claim.
landing: Model routing per phase type; compare to the xhigh-everywhere verifier setup.

also.source_title: AITW No Vibes Allowed live coding

source_title: How three YC startups built their companies with Claude Code
author: other
quote: it's generally due to a contradiction that I have in a prompt somewhere
claim: Unexpected low-quality output usually traces to a contradiction in the prompt; be deliberate about what enters context and when to start new conversations.
evidence_detail: Stettner's experience.
landing: Audit CLAUDE.md, skills and ship-plan prose for contradicting rules (e.g. doc drift vs CLAUDE.md).

source_title: How three YC startups built their companies with Claude Code
author: Dex
quote: after we spent 7 hours shipping what would normally be 1-2 weeks of work
claim: A 7-hour pairing session with Vaibhav shipped what would normally take 1-2 weeks, which convinced Horthy the workflow generalises.
evidence_detail: Dex's account, relayed by Anthropic; single session, unmeasured baseline.
landing: nowhere obvious (motivation, not a mechanism).

source_title: How three YC startups built their companies with Claude Code
author: Dex
quote: you have a completely different type of problem... a communication, collaboration, tooling, and management problem
claim: Once several people ship AI-written code, the bottleneck is team communication, collaboration, tooling and management, not individual use.
evidence_detail: Dex quote; Q4 2025 pilots claimed.
landing: Shared artefacts and a saved workflow library so the routine does not depend on one operator's chat habits.

source_title: How three YC startups built their companies with Claude Code
author: other
quote: Have your finger on the trigger to escape and interrupt any bad behavior.
claim: Watch the chain of thought and interrupt within the first few tool calls, since catching a wrong direction early saves more than letting a misguided run finish.
evidence_detail: Vulcan CEO advice; not Dex.
landing: An early checkpoint (first N tool calls) where the phase plan is confirmed before long runs; nowhere obvious in unattended workflows.

author: other
quote: Testing becomes deterministic - replay the same event log
claim: An append-only event log projected into prompt, UI and persistence lets you replay and assert deterministically.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav and guest Anders; Dex adoption not shown. Relevant to compliance auditing.
landing: append-only decisions journal as audit trail

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: The bash loop was nice because I started to see common failure domains
claim: Do not prompt the model to keep working; bound each run to one step and exit, and rerun it, so the work is bounded and the failure modes become visible and fixable.
evidence_detail: Episode README: 'One-loop, one-step. Exit. Rerun.' Dex's own 'models get anxiety and terminate early' framing.
landing: Phase routine: one bounded step per session instead of 'keep going'

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: The models get anxiety model, it will terminate early.
claim: Prompts that beg the model not to stop do not work; the way to get long work is short bounded runs repeated.
evidence_detail: Dex cites a community talk whose whole prompt was 'do not stop after one step'.
landing: Phase routine: avoid mega-prompts; rely on repo state for continuity

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: the more context you use the worse results you'll get
claim: Context budget plan: about 7% for specs, 7% for finding current state, 3% for the plan, 10-15% for base message and MCPs, leaving only roughly 10% for the work itself.
evidence_detail: Numbers attributed to Geoff, repeated by Dex as a model; no experiment.
landing: Per-phase context budget table in the ship plan

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: the most high performance range I found for the models is like before you hit this 30 to 40%
claim: Dex puts the high-performance range before about 30-40% of context fill; beyond it you are in the dumb zone, worse with many MCP tools loaded.
evidence_detail: Personal observation; he concedes newer models are less affected but says less context still wins.
landing: Session-length alarm / one-phase-per-session justification

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: No one will deny that you get better results if you use less
claim: Even as models support longer windows, less context still gives better results because attention is spread over less noise; the dumb-zone effect is weakening but not gone.
evidence_detail: Debate with Geoff and Vaibhav; Dex's counter-opinion is that long-context training is improving.
landing: Context policy that does not rely on a single dumb-zone percentage

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: The model will find something to do because you've invoked the cloud CLI
claim: When the desired and current state match, a looped model still invents new work, usually by changing the desired state (adding types nobody specified), so completion needs an external stop.
evidence_detail: Example: after ~100 loops it added types to the language implementation plan.
landing: Completion criteria in the plan; verifier that rejects scope growth

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: Don't mix the concerns.
claim: Appending unrelated tasks to one conversation (change colour, then SQL migration) degrades results; one item per context window gives good outcomes.
evidence_detail: Geoff's observation, Dex restates it as the reason Ralph works.
landing: One phase per new session

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: Back pressure is your governor. Strong typing or strong checks make the loop honest.
claim: Back pressure (types, tests, build, lint, scanners) is what stops bad generation; the weaker the checks, the more engineering is needed to wire them in, and the loop's speed is limited by the slowest check.
evidence_detail: README key idea; the C to Rust to Zig experience with the cursed compiler (C had none and went backwards).
landing: CI gates as backpressure: mypy, import-linter, alembic check; wire them into agent-visible commands

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: They'll spend three days designing the back pressure harness
claim: Dex repeats that the best agentic engineers spend days designing how the model will know it is working, then hand it over to run for ~48 hours.
evidence_detail: Said as a general claim about top practitioners; 50,000 lines is an illustrative figure.
landing: Phase 0 of any long task: design the verifier before the work

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: Note: This is a conceptual exploration. It's not 'do this for your production app today.'
claim: The episode frames Ralph as a mental model, not a production recipe; use when you have a crisp spec and fast checks, avoid when work needs long contiguous context with weak feedback or human review at every step.
evidence_detail: Episode README 'when to use it' lists; the quote is from the README, written by the episode team.
landing: Criteria for when a phase may run unattended

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: you can get into the high 70s 80s. Like there's going to be holes.
claim: Unattended loops reach roughly 70-95% of a spec; output cannot be trusted when it says done, and review is the new bottleneck.
evidence_detail: Geoff says 'high 70s, 80s' and 'when it says it's done, it's not really done'; Dex says 90-95% with steering.
landing: Treat self-reported completion as unverified; verifier required

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: Engineering has professional liability to it.
claim: Geoff's closing position that the engineer stays accountable for AI-generated code and cannot blame the tool; Dex does not dispute it.
evidence_detail: Closing remark.
landing: Owner view: the named human sign-off per phase

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: you're actually malicking and burning a lot of tokens so it can just do that one thing
claim: Re-allocating the same context each iteration is deliberately token-inefficient; the cost trade is accepted for determinism and smart-zone work, and a stable prefix could be cached.
evidence_detail: Dex notes @-mentioning the plan in the user message defeats prompt caching; cost not quantified here.
landing: Cost model for fresh-session-per-phase; keep the stable prefix first for caching

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: anything that was a minty allocation like cargo test
claim: Geoff: run noisy commands (cargo test) in sub-agents so only the exit code returns to the main context, comparable to garbage-collected green threads.
evidence_detail: Geoff's account; Dex does not push back.
landing: Run test and build commands via a subagent or quiet wrapper

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: you'd throw away the implementation plan continually because it was so easy to regenerate
claim: If a loop hill-climbs without arriving, discard and regenerate the plan rather than patching it; code and plans are disposable, ideas and specs carry the value.
evidence_detail: Geoff's practice; README states 'Code is disposable'.
landing: Plan lifecycle: regenerate the phase plan when the journal shows drift

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: for extremely extremely hard tasks what I need to worry about at all times is the model will not continue
claim: Weakness of the technique, stated by the co-host and accepted by Dex: tasks needing long context horizon suffer because the implementation plan lacks detail, so the loop is a poor fit there.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav's summary of the tradeoff; Dex and Geoff accept it.
landing: Gating rule: which phases are loop-suitable versus interactive

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: there's forward modes, there's research modes, and there's reverse modes.
claim: Loop modes: forward (specs to code), research (study the source versus specs to write a gap plan), and reverse (code to specs), each using the same desired-state versus current-state frame.
evidence_detail: Dex demonstrates a reverse-mode prompt for a Go to TypeScript port.
landing: Saved workflow variants: audit loop (research mode) writing a gap register

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: Ralph as control loops: desired state, current state, take one action
claim: Dex frames Ralph as a control loop (desired state, current state, one action, re-read) borrowed from Kubernetes controllers.
evidence_detail: Conceptual framing in the episode; reappears as Kyle's control-theory talk.
landing: Loop design vocabulary for the register-driven phase plan

source_title: AI That Works: Ralph Wiggum Under the Hood
author: Dex
quote: The best AI engineers constantly challenge their own worldview of what is happening.
claim: Vaibhav's remark that practitioners must keep re-testing what the model can now do; Dex sets up the topic on this basis. Counted only as Dex's framing for running the episode.
evidence_detail: Co-host statement; low weight.
landing: nowhere obvious

source_title: AITW Ralph Wiggum under the hood
author: Dex
quote: One-loop, one-step. Exit. Rerun.
claim: Do not convince the model to work longer; bound each loop to one meaningful step, exit and rerun.
evidence_detail: Conceptual demo (Next.js to-do app), explicitly not production advice.
landing: outer-loop workflow script per phase

source_title: AITW Ralph Wiggum under the hood
author: Dex
quote: Back pressure is your governor.
