claim: Tests, types and builds act as back pressure that keeps a looping agent honest.
evidence_detail: Key idea in notes.
landing: CI three jobs, import-boundary contracts as backpressure

source_title: AITW Ralph Wiggum under the hood
author: Dex
quote: One bad spec line can waste tens of thousands of tokens.
claim: Specs must be right before code is generated, because one bad line propagates through the whole loop.
evidence_detail: Key idea; no measurement.
landing: plan review before implementation

source_title: AITW Ralph Wiggum under the hood
author: Dex
quote: Code is disposable. Ideas, specs, and harness design carry the value.
claim: Value lives in specs and harness design, so regenerate code and plans rather than patch them.
evidence_detail: Key idea.
landing: durable plan/spec files; saved workflows

source_title: AITW Ralph Wiggum under the hood
author: Dex
quote: Context budgeting so you stay in the smart zone
claim: Budget context so the loop stays in the 'smart zone' rather than drowning the model.
evidence_detail: Topic list.
landing: context threshold in phase routine

source_title: AITW Ralph Wiggum under the hood
author: Dex
quote: Avoid when: the task truly needs long contiguous context with weak feedback
claim: Loop-style autonomy suits crisp specs plus fast checks and fails when feedback is weak or per-step human review is needed.
evidence_detail: Use/avoid lists.
landing: phase triage: which of the 40 phases may run unattended

source_title: AITW Ralph Wiggum under the hood
author: Dex
quote: Reverse mode: deriving specs first, then generating forwards
claim: Derive specs from existing code first, then generate forward; plan regeneration and resets are steering tools.
evidence_detail: Demo observed self-termination, resets and plan regeneration.
landing: cold-resume spec derivation; knowledge store

author: Dex
quote: self-forking agents is a cool new paradigm
claim: An agent that resets itself to a known checkpoint with a summary or instruction (kimi-cli's D-Mail) is a promising new context-management paradigm.
evidence_detail: Endorsement of a pattern shown by @darrenangle; no measurement.
landing: Mid-phase checkpoint-and-rewind instead of compaction; links to his Context Forking post.

author: Dex
quote: the mechanism under the hood is obfuscated from the driver
claim: Some compactors hide what they keep, which suits vibe coding but is bad for context engineering; explicit handoff documents (agent's 'last will') work better.
evidence_detail: Agrees with @schickling's experience; no numbers.
landing: Supports one-phase-per-session with written handoff over default compaction; the PR decisions journal is already a handoff.

author: Dex
quote: RPI is a more tactical/practical approach that is downstream from specification
claim: Spec-driven development is a broader category including making outcomes verifiable for feedback loops; RPI is a narrower tactic downstream of it and should not be folded under the label.
evidence_detail: Terminology argument.
landing: Phase routine vocabulary: separate the spec (with verifiable outcomes) from the research-plan-implement tactics.

author: other
quote: Every single token counts.
claim: Tool-output design (relative paths, truncation notices, rg over grep, timeouts, errors removed after correction) is context engineering; sub-agents get fresh contexts and cannot spawn more.
evidence_detail: Vaibhav live build; Dex adoption not shown; a 'no recursion' sub-agent rule.
landing: script output conventions for verifiers; sub-agent depth limit

source_title: The context-engineering continuum for harder features
author: Dex
quote: more context engineering == you can ship bigger features in spicier codebases
claim: The more context engineering applied, the bigger the feature and the harder the codebase an agent can handle.
evidence_detail: One-line claim, 77 likes, no data.
landing: Scale context effort to feature difficulty rather than one routine for every phase.

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: the less context you use, the better results you get
claim: Workflow is built on frequent intentional compaction: research produces a baked understanding so planning happens in the sweet spot of a fresh, small context window.
evidence_detail: Stated as the basic idea of the research/plan/implement workflow; demonstrated live on a BAML Rust feature (no measurement).
landing: Phase routine in ship plan section 0 (one phase per new chat); already largely present
inventory_ref: (B) June to December 2025 - 2025-10-16 'No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents'

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: you're setting the trajectory to be a little bit more towards your few-shot prompting
claim: Invoke the plan command with no arguments so the first turns are a user/agent back-and-forth, which makes the model more likely to ask questions and outline phases instead of just calling tools until done.
evidence_detail: Explained as trajectory few-shotting; co-host called it a micro-optimisation and Dex said experience with these prompts would convince him.
landing: Plan step of the phase routine (how the plan session is opened)

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: really focus on what is the incrementally testable thing
claim: Design plan phases around what can be run and verified at the end of each phase; if a verification cannot happen until phase three, merge those phases, and split phases that are too meaty.
evidence_detail: Applied live: phase one was split into parsing then client creation, error definitions moved before the timeout implementation.
landing: Plan template: each phase names its runnable check

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: the smaller you can make your phases, the more you can
claim: Smaller phases let you learn from the first implementation and revise the rest of the plan, and each phase should compile or test on its own.
evidence_detail: Dex moved composite-client work to its own later phase because he did not know how it would work; plans were revised twice mid-session.
landing: Phase sizing guidance in the ship plan

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: somewhere in between clear and compact
claim: At the limit, have the model write a handoff prompt that starts with the implement command and a plan-file reference, then launch the next session from it via a CLI; Dex preferred this to the auto-compaction summary.
evidence_detail: Done live after auto-compaction was about to fire; he says 'it already compacted itself ... we're still going to do a handoff and start over'.
landing: Handoff-prompt convention for the end of a phase/session (closing message could be a launchable prompt)

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: LLMs are bad at judging things, if you ask me
claim: Better tests give the model an objective measure; LLMs are poor judges but good at reading errors and fixing them, so do not obsess over a perfect plan, only a good-enough one that lets test errors drive the fix.
evidence_detail: Opinion offered while the model iterated on cargo test failures.
landing: Verifier design: prefer executable checks over judge-style review; reviewer cites test output

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: you almost never want that
claim: Keeping all historical research and plans visible to the model is usually wrong; give the model all artifacts for the current ticket only, plus a few hand-manicured 'golden research' files (for example how tests work) that are always findable.
evidence_detail: 'In the past we kept all historical research and plans ... what I'm finding more and more is you almost never want that.' Vaibhav says he never saves them in the repo at all.
landing: Knowledge-store design: scope retrieval per task; a small curated always-available set instead of everything

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: the research basically gives you on-demand up-to-date code-based documentation
claim: Dex is lukewarm on agent-maintained code documentation for other developers because when everyone ships a thousand lines every couple of days it goes stale; on-demand research (about 10 minutes) replaces it.
evidence_detail: Claim made when asked whether spec and code stay connected; no data.
landing: Argues against persistent generated docs in the knowledge-store pilot; favours regenerate-on-demand research

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: move it into your infrastructure
claim: Whenever you find you always want the model to do something one way (for example run parser tests with update-expect, or build primitives before streaming before composites), move it into the commands and agents rather than re-typing it each plan.
evidence_detail: Said while adding guidance to the create-plan command; co-host would not put such task-specific text in CLAUDE.md and suggested prompt snippets.
landing: Skills / command files; also supports keeping task-specific rules out of CLAUDE.md

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: I have a global cloud ND that steers it to make
claim: A stale global CLAUDE.md instruction (use make) kept overriding the plan's own test commands in a repo that does not use make, and he had to remove it.
evidence_detail: Happened twice live ('Read the damn plan, you nerd'); he later says 'this shouldn't be in my global thing anyways'.
landing: CLAUDE.md audit: always-loaded rules can silently conflict with phase-specific plan commands

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: we'll start a new context window for this one since we've already used about 30%
claim: Once the spec is correct, throw away the context spent perfecting it and reseed a new window with only the final spec, rather than carrying the history of edits.
evidence_detail: Done live at ~30% usage; the co-host explains it is not about cache but about the model not being confused by old vs new spec.
landing: Phase routine: new chat per phase seeded from the artifact (plan @ sha), not from conversation history

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: The first thing in your path should be something else.
claim: Prevent a wrong-tool habit deterministically by shadowing the binary (python shimmed to echo 'use uv') rather than relying on the model to follow an instruction.
evidence_detail: Co-host describes Dex's shim; Dex confirms the principle but had to remove it; also recounts a friend whose agent ran rm -rf on a tilde directory.
landing: Re-opens the skipped hooks idea (PATH shim or PreToolUse hook as a deterministic enforcement channel)

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: The best engineers I know like they don't use evals.
claim: The best engineers rely on judgment from about 70 hours a week with the model rather than evals; the best investment is a good vibe-checker in your own head.
evidence_detail: Dex says it once; the co-host extends it ('most prompting is all vibes'); no data.
landing: Counter to building a measurement pipeline (the skipped item); supports owner judgment as the check

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: the model will just keep rewriting it with the new stuff
claim: Hand-editing a plan while another session is still writing it fails: the model overwrites the edit and re-introduces the removed content, so edits go through the model or after it finishes.
evidence_detail: Observed live (a 10-minute max he removed came back); co-host notes he uses a prompt saying 'I sometimes make edits you don't have'.
landing: Plan-file ownership rule in the phase routine (single writer at a time)

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: we're paralyzing between phase one and also iterating on phase two
claim: Implement phase N in one session while refining the plan for phase N+1 in another, because each reviewed artifact has the same shape and you do not pay full context-switch cost.
evidence_detail: Done live; he also says parallel tasks work because everything you review is shaped the same.
landing: Workflow orchestration: pipeline plan-review ahead of implementation

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: you should almost always be using Opus
claim: For research over a large complex codebase use the strongest model and cancel a run on a weaker one; paying more avoids the cost of restarting after a wrong result.
evidence_detail: Cancelled a Sonnet research run and restarted on Opus; co-host argues speed and cheaper models are fine for most work, so the two disagree on routing.
landing: Effort/model routing for verifiers and researchers (note: Oct 2025 models, pre-dates the xhigh-vs-medium report)

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: my most my most important resource is my time
claim: Skip slow, low-risk checks (run the TypeScript tests only at the very end) when a cheaper proxy such as Python compiling is a good predictor, optimising for human time while still guaranteeing the full run happens eventually.
evidence_detail: Said when choosing which tests the plan's verification step should run.
landing: Verification step tiering (cheap checks per phase, full suite before close)

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: I try to keep the context under 40%.
claim: Dex's practical working budget is under 40% of the window, tolerating 40-50% only if the task is nearly finished, and being aggressive otherwise (restarting at ~60%).
evidence_detail: Stated while live coding; later in the same session he restarts at 63% and complains of 'context anxiety' near 60%.
landing: A context-budget line in the phase routine or closing message ('percent of window used at handoff')

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: You have to read this stuff.
claim: The workflow is not a magic prompt; the human must read the diff and research/plan documents, and the leverage comes from reading higher-level artifacts.
evidence_detail: Said right after opening the diff of the model's spec edit; co-host adds that not reading code is why his own vibe-coding got worse.
landing: Owner one-page view / reviewer step: what a human must actually read

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: I'm looking for approximate fuzzy matching
claim: Reviewing a research doc means checking file:line references are roughly right with an expert in the codebase present; chasing 100% correctness has diminishing returns, and the expert adds omissions the model missed.
evidence_detail: Live: the BAML expert caught a missed file (orchestrator/stream.rs), the stream-only nature of idle timeout, and irrelevant publishing timeouts.
landing: Cold-resume trial / research artifact review: someone who knows the repo skims for omissions, not correctness

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: of which parts of the system are relevant can tank your entire project
claim: Errors compound upward: a bad line of code is one bad line, a bad plan step is a hundred, and a research misunderstanding of what is relevant sinks the project, so review effort belongs on research and plan.
evidence_detail: Aside during plan reading; framed as the reason to read research/plan carefully.
landing: Reviewer weighting: refute plan and research artifacts first

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: The plan gives you 10x leverage. The research gives you 100x leverage.
claim: Do not delegate spec writing to the model too; accept being 100x faster rather than reaching for 1000x, because past that returns diminish and some manual reading/pruning is still worth it.
evidence_detail: Illustrative multipliers, no data.
landing: Where the human stays in the loop: spec/ticket authoring and artifact pruning

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: make sure you don't get into the details of how to make an implementation plan
claim: The research prompt is documentation-only: map relevant code, tests, integration tests and codegen, explicitly not plan or solve, so the next fresh agent starts from facts.
evidence_detail: Prompt typed live; the research prompt itself is described as 'its only job is to document and explain' with parallel sub-agents and front-matter.
landing: Research step / skill wording in the phase routine

source_title: No Vibes Allowed: Live Coding with AI Agents
author: Dex
quote: the code base locator, its job is to document the code base
claim: A small set of single-purpose sub-agents (locator = super grep, analyzer = trace data flow, pattern finder) is invoked by the research prompt, and can also be steered to by hand for pinpoint questions instead of writing a new research doc.
evidence_detail: Agent definitions shown from the humanlayer repo; 'use code base pattern finder' used live to find how errors and Python tests are written.
landing: .claude/agents/ (extends the single Haiku locator; add analyzer and pattern-finder roles)

author: Dex
quote: easier to read a couple of good black box integration tests
claim: A few black-box integration tests serving as the specification are easier for a human to read than reviewing all the code.
evidence_detail: Review-economy argument, no numbers.
landing: Owner view and cold-resume trial could lean on black-box tests as the readable spec.

author: Dex
quote: I don't care if the model reviews the code and says it's good.
claim: He distrusts LLM assessment of code and cares only whether tests pass; good deterministic feedback loops are a bar for design partners.
evidence_detail: Stated policy, no data.
landing: Argues against reviewer-agent-only gates; ties each PR claim to a failing-then-passing test (already fail-before/pass-after in the routine).

source_title: AITW No Vibes Allowed live coding
author: Dex
quote: Research is 100x leverage
claim: Thirty minutes documenting how the codebase works saves hours of implementation thrashing; research docs act as compressed context for planning.
evidence_detail: 30 min research, 400k-line codebase, feature shipped in about 3h versus 1-2 days estimated.
landing: phase 0 research doc / cold-resume artifacts

source_title: AITW No Vibes Allowed live coding
author: Dex
quote: Phases should mirror how you'd code manually
claim: Plans split into small independently testable and shippable phases (7 phases there), with incremental commits after each green phase.
evidence_detail: 7-phase timeout plan.
landing: ship plan 40-phase decomposition and per-phase commits

source_title: AITW No Vibes Allowed live coding
author: Dex
quote: Always read the code - This isn't magic, you're still responsible
claim: The human must still read the code and have domain experts review the plan; reading is not optional.
evidence_detail: Lessons learned list.
landing: owner view / reviewer step

source_title: AITW No Vibes Allowed live coding
author: Dex
quote: Specialized agents: Code locator, pattern finder, analyzer
claim: Research uses three specialised sub-agents (locator, pattern finder, analyzer) running on the stronger model.
evidence_detail: Tool list for the session.
landing: .claude/agents/ (add pattern-finder, analyzer beside the locator)

source_title: AITW No Vibes Allowed live coding
author: Dex
quote: Voice > typing for prompts
claim: Speaking prompts injects more context than typing.
evidence_detail: Stated as advice; Whisper used.
landing: nowhere obvious (operator habit)

source_title: AITW No Vibes Allowed live coding
author: Dex
quote: While one agent implements, another can research the next phase
claim: Parallelise by researching the next phase while the current one implements.
evidence_detail: Session practice.
landing: phase routine sequencing

source_title: AITW No Vibes Allowed live coding
author: Dex
quote: The less context you use, the better results you get.
claim: Build the workflow around frequent intentional compaction, restarting with fresh context per major phase.
evidence_detail: Session had 3 context restarts to stay under 40-60% usage.
landing: one-phase-per-new-session rule; compaction trigger

source_title: AITW No Vibes Allowed live coding
author: Dex
quote: 40% context usage is the sweet spot - restart before hitting limits
claim: Keep context usage around 40% (40-60% range) and restart before hitting limits.
evidence_detail: A number from one 3-hour session, not a benchmark.
landing: a context-usage threshold in the phase routine

source_title: AITW No Vibes Allowed live coding
author: Dex
quote: A bad part of a plan is a hundred bad lines of code.
claim: Review leverage is highest on the plan, so human review effort should concentrate there.
evidence_detail: Stated as heuristic.
landing: ship plan review stage; Opus reviewer on plan

author: other
quote: Use less context. I promise you, your pipelines will be more accurate.
claim: Less context gives more accurate results; long-context routing degraded smaller requests in Anthropic's incident (30% of Claude Code users affected).
evidence_detail: Stated by Vaibhav; the 30% figure is from Anthropic's post-mortem; Dex endorsement not shown in notes.
landing: context budget rule; CLAUDE.md trim

author: other
quote: Don't be a hero, roll back
claim: When something breaks after a change, roll back first and investigate later; 30 test cases is often enough for basic eval coverage.
evidence_detail: Episode notes (Vaibhav and guest Aaron); Dex adoption not shown. Notes also list a Research-Plan-Implement discussion at 54:03.
landing: deploy runbook; eval sizing

author: Dex
quote: get you a coding agent that lets you inspect and iterate on subagent prompts
claim: A coding agent should let the user inspect and iterate on the prompts it sends to subagents.
evidence_detail: One-line wish.
landing: Log delegated subagent prompts verbatim so they can be inspected and reused; helps tell whether a routine was followed.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: Agents __SHOULD NOT__ verify their own code.
claim: CuriouslyC argues for a separate red-team reviewer agent and a panel of narrowly focused reviewers (security, performance, correctness, architecture) given code context plus the diff, rather than one all-purpose reviewer.
evidence_detail: Says he has run this with Gemini 2.5 for about 6 months; catches line/module logic issues and anti-patterns but not big architectural ones. A commenter notes Codex /review runs in a subthread seeing only the git diff.
landing: Reviewer design: split the single Opus reviewer into focused reviewers (custom agents) with diff-only context.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: Importantly, this code critic is wrong about 60% of the time.
claim: iambateman reports an LLM plan critic produces false findings about 60% of the time, so a human must filter the critique before it is acted on.
evidence_detail: Self-reported rate from his /feature workflow (8-10 markdown plan files, then a critic step); not a controlled measurement.
landing: Supports refute-by-default and a refuter pass over reviewer findings; informs how much to trust unfiltered reviewer output.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: I find it hard to read unverifiable documentation.
claim: madcocomo critiques the research/plan stage: hours of planning with no running code to verify against is hard to trust, and a markdown file may not carry enough to the next stage; he prefers fresh sessions on small source-level problems.
evidence_detail: Personal experience only.
landing: P1 cold-resume trial: tests whether artifacts alone carry state across sessions.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: most of the shenanigans of manual context window managing with putting things in markdown files is kind of unnecessary.
claim: jgilias reports Cursor's automatic todos and summarising compaction made manual context management mostly unnecessary, challenging the frequent-intentional-compaction thesis (Dex replied elsewhere: never use /compact, stash context to markdown or a commit message and clear).
evidence_detail: Single user, Sonnet 4 in Cursor; plans and guided research still needed. Dex's reply in-thread: you want control and visibility over what is compacted.
landing: Phase routine rule 'one phase per new chat' versus tool-side auto compaction; decisions journal as the stash.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: You can have a huge codebase, but if the complexity goes up with size then you are screwed.
claim: philipp-gayret disputes the 'performance / size' framing (complexity, not size, matters) and doubts that one bad CLAUDE.md line is 100K bad lines; Dex replies that Claude Code wraps CLAUDE.md in a 'may not be relevant' system-reminder so a poor CLAUDE.md is probably survivable.
evidence_detail: Dex's reply quotes the injected system-reminder text ('this context may or may not be relevant... Most of the time, it is not relevant') and says if you do not know what is in your context window you cannot balance CLAUDE.md against commands.
landing: CLAUDE.md trim decision: the wrapper explains why long CLAUDE.md content is down-weighted; supports moving rarely-needed invariants out of always-loaded context.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: it always diverges into researching and proposing fixes as well as searching for root causes
claim: jarek83 reports Claude Code frequently ignores the research_codebase prompt's explicit prohibition (document only, do not propose fixes), succeeding only twice in many tries, i.e. prompted phase constraints are not reliably followed.
evidence_detail: Single user's tries; no Dex answer in the file we read (thread ends there).
landing: Evidence for hooks or checkable outputs rather than prompt-only phase rules; re-opens the skipped hooks decision.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: I find models try to write scripts/manual workflows for testing
claim: Exchange on why typed/compiled languages (Go) work better: compile steps plus LSP feedback improve agent output; Dex says Go is good for building the model's own feedback-loop harness via integration tests. Commenters (mholm, 0xblacklight) add stable idioms and richer types.
evidence_detail: Opinions from commenters; Dex points to humanlayer/hld integration tests as an example.
landing: Backpressure: mypy strict, import-linter and pytest are already gates; supports integration-test harness as agent feedback loop.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: You can have two, and intermittently three, parallel process at once
claim: OtherShrezzing (with scuff3d, noodletheworld) argues human spec/PR administration (about 8 minutes per ~20-minute agent block) caps parallel agent runs at 2-3, and context switching erodes the gains.
evidence_detail: Back-of-envelope arithmetic (3 min spec plus 5 min PR per 20 min of agent work); the_duke replies 10 parallel is possible but 'not a sustainable pace'.
landing: Workflow-tool fan-out sizing and owner-view budget: review capacity, not agent count, sets the limit.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: a 20k LoC PR is an actively hostile move
claim: Many commenters (ooopakaj, ActionHank, bak3y, sensanaty, wwweston) say giant AI PRs are unreviewable and should be closed in favour of small atomic PRs; yojo adds that LLM-written tests are often poor and 2k lines of test diff is itself too much.
evidence_detail: Opinion plus yojo's example (five 200ms-wait tests added a second to the suite). Dex's reply: the model can write the code but you still design it; engage more, iterate, work in small steps.
landing: PR size cap and test-quality check in the Opus reviewer prompt; fail-before/pass-after per register id already addresses tautological tests.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: LLMs are categorically not compilers.
claim: sothatsit, sarchertech and maltalex reject the 'specs are the new source, you stop reading code' claim: LLMs are non-deterministic, you must read code to confirm the right program was written, so it is delegation not abstraction (Dex later retracted the don't-read-the-code advice per DarkFactory).
evidence_detail: Argument by principle; sarchertech reports a Claude Sonnet 4 trial of a CSV prompt (90-line script, float multiplication, loads whole file, crashes on currency symbols); qcnguy replies with a GPT-5 spec-review-implement run that handled the edge cases.
landing: Owner-view and reviewer policy: code is still read at the gate; specs are not a substitute.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: Overall productivity boost at 15 - 20% IIRC.
claim: malfist and others challenge the productivity premise, noting studies show AI can make some people less effective; keeda/CharlesW cite the Stanford analysis at about 15-20% average gain with slowdowns concentrated in high-complexity tasks on legacy or low-popularity languages, and Dex confirms the Stanford video has a slide on slower-than-no-AI cases.
evidence_detail: Numbers are second-hand recollection of a Stanford video (average ~15-20%); not verified by the commenters, who say 'IIRC'.
landing: Nowhere obvious; background for measuring actual benefit per phase rather than assuming it.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: A 35k LOC change in a 350k codebase
claim: daxfohl and others press on cost and measurement: Dex answers that 2 BAML PRs cost about $650 in raw tokens, his team of three averages about $12k per month on Opus, and they moved to a Max plan after running out of credits; gloosx notes '7 hours' versus 40 commits over 7 days (one 'ignore some tests'); afro88 notes only 2 of 3 tasks shipped.
evidence_detail: Dex's own figures given in reply ($650 for two PRs, ~$12k/month for three people); critics' counts: 40 commits over 7 days, one PR still draft over a month later, sample of 3 tasks in 2 codebases.
landing: Cost per phase accounting in the closing message or owner view; claims of speed should state elapsed days, not hours of agent time.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: really specific documentations were almost as if I was 'over-fitting' my solution
claim: nzach argues detailed specs overfit and reduce quality (last 10-20% never right), preferring concise behaviour-focused prompts plus plan mode; boredtofears and apercu agree; Dex notes his create_plan prompt runs a 3+ phase clarifying-question exchange before writing the plan.
evidence_detail: Personal experience of several commenters; the 'ask me clarifying questions' tip (danielbln, BeetleB) is offered as a cheap alternative.
landing: Plan granularity in the phase routine: tension between detailed plan (R38-5) and over-specification; clarifying-question step before plan.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: The problem is the research phase will fail because you can't glean tribal product knowledge
claim: asdev argues research that only reads code cannot recover tribal product knowledge; Dex's own reply elsewhere admits a plan was wrong because research missed that types and SDKs were generated from an OpenAPI spec.
evidence_detail: Dex's anecdote: user story plus research plan existed, yet a missing fundamental detail surfaced only deep in implementation and the plan was wrong.
landing: P1 cold-resume trial and knowledge store: facts that code reading cannot recover must be written down; generated-code provenance as a frozen fact.

source_title: HN 45347532: Getting AI to work in complex codebases
author: other
quote: your 200k LoC project could be solved in only about 10k LoC
claim: LeafItAlone, jongjong and jwpapi argue agent output is needlessly complex and line-count claims are a bad metric; 'simplify the solution' is their most common instruction, and 35k lines of generated code is not a productivity measure.
evidence_detail: Commenters' impressions (10k vs 200k guess is an estimate, not a measurement); Dex concedes 'wrote' rather than 'shipped' and that it is uncertain when to let duplication sprawl versus DRY.
landing: Reviewer prompt: complexity/over-engineering check; avoid LOC as a progress metric in closing messages.

author: Dex
quote: "refactor AFTER patterns emerge". its a good policy
claim: None of the hot agent frameworks are used in the top coding agents, which are now adding framework-like features; abstract only after patterns emerge.
evidence_detail: Observation across opencode, Codebuff and Claude Code; no data.
landing: Policy for the workflow library: save a workflow only after the same script shape has recurred.

source_title: AITW Bash vs MCP - token efficient coding agent tooling
author: Dex
quote: Token efficiency isn't just about saving money - it's about preserving context space
claim: Token overhead of tool definitions matters for context budget, not only cost.
evidence_detail: Claude -p write-a-file: total cache creation 13225 tokens baseline vs 18957 with the Linear MCP config (about 5.7k extra).
landing: MCP/tool loadout audit; always-loaded surface including CLAUDE.md

source_title: AITW Bash vs MCP - token efficient coding agent tooling
author: Dex
quote: Writing your own drop-in replacements for MCP tools
claim: A small CLI wrapper documented in CLAUDE.md and allowed via Bash(prefix:*) can replace an MCP server at lower token cost.
evidence_detail: Side-by-side token counts, linear-cli vs Linear MCP, via a stream-json log inspector.
landing: skills or scripts instead of MCP servers

source_title: AITW Bash vs MCP - token efficient coding agent tooling
author: Dex
quote: Advanced tricks like .shims for forcing uv instead of python or bun instead of npm
claim: Use PATH shims to force the agent onto the project's preferred tool (uv, bun) rather than correcting it in prose.
evidence_detail: Listed as a trick; no numbers.
landing: mechanical enforcement instead of CLAUDE.md prose; a re-open of the hooks question

source_title: AITW Bash vs MCP - token efficient coding agent tooling
author: Dex
quote: Naming conventions matter more than you think.
claim: Tool and command names directly affect how accurately the model uses them.
evidence_detail: Highlight quote.
landing: naming of skills, agents and scripts

source_title: AITW Bash vs MCP - token efficient coding agent tooling
author: Dex
quote: Don't just blindly use MCP for everything.
claim: No one-size-fits-all: MCP helps people unfamiliar with APIs but costs tokens, so pick per need.
evidence_detail: Key takeaways.
landing: tool-loadout policy

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: keeping utilization in the 40-60% range
claim: Design the whole workflow around context management and keep context-window utilization at roughly 40-60%, depending on problem complexity.
evidence_detail: Stated as the working rule behind 'frequent intentional compaction'; no measurement of the band is given.
landing: Phase routine: a context-use ceiling per phase; one phase per new session already approximates it

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: Getting a subagent to return this is not trivial
claim: A subagent's return should look like a good compaction (file paths, line refs, key findings), and prompting it to do so takes real effort.
evidence_detail: Image-backed claim; no examples in text.
landing: Output format spec in .claude/agents/fixflow-explorer.md

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: The generic one works almost as well.
claim: A generic Task() research prompt with a general-purpose subagent works almost as well as custom named subagents.
evidence_detail: His own comparison across repos; no numbers.
landing: Whether more custom agents are needed versus prompts/skills driving generic subagents

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: sometimes we skip the research and go straight to planning
claim: Research/plan/implement is 'three-ish' steps: research may be skipped for simple work or repeated in several compacted passes before implementing.
evidence_detail: Describes team practice.
landing: Phase routine: which phases need a research step versus plan-only

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: being super precise about the testing / verification steps in each phase
claim: A plan names exact files to edit and how, and states the test/verification step for each plan phase.
evidence_detail: Describes the plan prompt; no results.
landing: Plan template: per-phase verification step; reviewer fail-before/pass-after per register id

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: I'll often compact the current status back into the original plan file
claim: During implementation, write status back into the plan file after each verified phase so the plan doubles as the resume record.
evidence_detail: Team practice for complex work.
landing: Decisions journal / plan file status updates after each phase; cold-resume trial

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: this is the only step that needs to be done in a worktree
claim: Only the implement step needs a git worktree; research and planning can run on main.
evidence_detail: Aside; no rationale beyond practice.
landing: Phase routine: worktree use limited to implementation phases

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: I threw that research out and kicked off a new one
claim: Read the research output yourself, discard it when wrong, and rerun with more steering; do not build a plan on bad research.
evidence_detail: BAML bug: first research wrongly called the bug invalid.
landing: Refute-by-default reviewers on research/diagnosis outputs; knowledge-store verified diagnoses

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: the one built with research fixed the problem in the best place
claim: Two plans for the same bug, one with research and one without, both worked, but only the research-backed one put the fix in the right place and matched codebase test conventions.
evidence_detail: Single paired example; research-backed PR approved by maintainer, other closed.
landing: Justifies a research step before planning in the phase routine

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: ran both plans in parallel and submitted both as PRs
claim: Run competing plans in parallel and keep the one that survives review.
evidence_detail: BAML bug example, one winner out of two PRs.
landing: Workflow-tool orchestration: parallel-plan then judge pattern

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: 7 hours (3 hours on research/plans, 4 hours on implementation) and shipped 35k LOC
claim: A 7-hour paired session split 3h research/plans and 4h implementation produced about 35k LOC (cancellation and WASM) estimated at 3-5 senior-engineer days each.
evidence_detail: 35k LOC, 7 h, estimate by Vaibhav of 3-5 days per PR; one PR merged, one still open at the time.
landing: Time split benchmark for phase effort (roughly 40% front-loaded)

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: designing your ENTIRE WORKFLOW around context management
claim: Frequent intentional compaction means the process itself (research, plan, implement) is shaped so each step ends in a compacted artifact and starts in a fresh window.
evidence_detail: Claims of 300k LOC Rust work, 6 PRs in a day, a week of work in a day; no controlled comparison.
landing: Ship plan §0 phase routine (one phase per new chat, decisions journal as the compaction artifact)

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: You have to engage with your task when you're doing this or it WILL NOT WORK.
claim: The method requires continuous human engagement; there is no magic prompt, and human review at the high-leverage points is what makes it work on hard problems.
evidence_detail: Argued from the BAML and parquet-java sessions.
landing: Owner-view and review gates in the phase routine

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: the research steps didn't go deep enough through the dependency tree
claim: A failure case: parquet-java hadoop removal failed in 7 hours because research did not go deep enough and nobody involved was a codebase expert.
evidence_detail: One failed 7-hour session; lesson is that an expert in the codebase is needed.
landing: Research depth check (transitive dependencies) and owner/expert review of research before planning

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: a bad line of a plan could lead to hundreds of bad lines of code.
claim: Review leverage rises as you move upstream: a bad line of research yields thousands of bad code lines, a bad plan line hundreds, so review research and plans before code.
evidence_detail: Orders-of-magnitude illustration, no measurement.
landing: Reviewer scope: plan and diagnosis reviews ahead of PR-diff review (Opus reviewer per PR)

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: I can't read 2000 lines of golang daily. But I can read 200 lines
claim: Humans cannot keep up with reading AI-generated code but can read a 200-line implementation plan, so plans and research become the shared artifacts for team understanding.
evidence_detail: Personal experience with 2000-line PRs every few days.
landing: One-page owner view; plan-sized review artifacts

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: the most important part of code review is mental alignment
claim: Code review's main job is mental alignment; with high AI output, much of the codebase becomes unfamiliar to every engineer, so the process must keep people on the same page and help them learn unfamiliar areas quickly.
evidence_detail: Adopts Blake Smith's framing; supported by team experience.
landing: Owner view and closing message content; research docs as onboarding for the owner

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: I still read the tests pretty carefully
claim: When he stopped reading every PR line, he still read tests carefully and treated specs as the source of truth.
evidence_detail: Personal practice after an 8-week transition.
landing: Reviewer focus on tests (fail-before/pass-after) over implementation lines

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: our team of three is averaging about $12k on opus per month
claim: Reported spend: a three-person team averages about $12k per month on Opus.
evidence_detail: Single stated figure, about $4k per person per month; no breakdown.
landing: Cost baseline for effort routing and verifier spend

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: Our intern shipped 2 PRs on his first day, and 10 on his 8th day.
claim: Onboarding claim: with the workflow an intern shipped 2 PRs on day one and 10 on day eight.
evidence_detail: Two numbers, one person; also: 8-week team transition, 6 PRs in a day, a 2-week race-condition failure.
landing: Cold-resume trial framing: a newcomer (or fresh agent) productive from repo artifacts

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: the specs became our source of truth for what was being built and why
claim: Adopt spec-driven development: commit the specs and prompts, not just final code, since discarding them is like checking in a binary and throwing away the source.
evidence_detail: Credits Sean Grove; his team's 8-week transition.
landing: Decisions journal and plan files kept in repo as the source of truth

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: I won't even try to convince you that research/plan/implement is the right approach
claim: Research/plan/implement is not claimed to suit most teams; the requirement is any process that keeps people aligned and lets them learn unfamiliar code fast.
evidence_detail: Stated caveat.
landing: Treat the phase routine as one instance of an alignment process, judged on that goal

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: Write everything we did so far to progress.md
claim: Intentional compaction: when context fills, have the agent write goal, approach, steps done and current failure to a file, then start a fresh window.
evidence_detail: Given as an example prompt; no results.
landing: Phase routine: draft-PR body and decisions journal; cold-resume trial (P1) tests exactly this

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: Subagents are not about playing house and anthropomorphizing roles.
claim: Against role-playing agent personas: split work by context need, not by job title.
evidence_detail: Stated with link to an X post.
landing: Guidance for designing custom agents and reviewer roles

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: how the "thoughts tool" works
claim: HumanLayer shares and manages the research/plan markdown files through a 'thoughts' tool (shared thoughts directory), left unexplained here.
evidence_detail: Pointer only; the example repo paths show thoughts/shared/research and thoughts/shared/plans.
landing: A durable research/plans directory in the repo (knowledge-store neighbour)

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: AI tools often lead to a lot of rework
claim: Cites the Stanford study of 100k developers: much AI-shipped code reworks last week's slop, and AI is often counter-productive on brownfield and complex tasks.
evidence_detail: Secondhand: commits of 100k developers analysed by Yegor's team; no figures in text (charts as images).
landing: Motivation for rework/slop tracking; FixFlow is brownfield

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: You can also use commit messages for intentional compaction.
claim: Commit messages can serve as the compaction artifact that carries state into the next session.
evidence_detail: One-line aside linking an X post; nothing else.
landing: Commit/PR conventions; the 'Plan @ <sha>' PR body

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: Searching for files / Understanding code flow / Applying edits / Test/build logs / Huge JSON blobs from tools
claim: The main context consumers are file search, code-flow understanding, edits, test/build logs and large tool JSON, and compaction distils them into structured artifacts.
evidence_detail: A listed taxonomy; no sizes given.
landing: Output caps on test/build logs and tool output; which verifier outputs are summarised before returning

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: the contents of your context window are the ONLY lever you have
claim: Because each agent turn is a stateless function of its context, context contents are the only lever for output quality and are worth obsessing over.
evidence_detail: Argued from the 12-factor-agents premise; no data.
landing: CLAUDE.md content policy (what is always loaded)

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: other
quote: you only have approximately 170k of context window to work with.
claim: Dex quotes Geoff Huntley that only about 170k tokens of context are usable and the more you use, the worse the outcomes; Dex does not dismiss the while-loop (Ralph) answer.
evidence_detail: Quoted number from Huntley; Dex says he is 'not entirely sure that it is dumb'.
landing: Context budget per phase; looping agents with simple prompt as an alternative to long sessions

source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
author: Dex
quote: Subagents are about context control.
claim: Subagents exist to keep the parent's window clean (fresh-window search and summarising), not to model roles or personas.
evidence_detail: Stated with a demo video; no numbers.
landing: fixflow-explorer Haiku locator agent; design rule for any new custom agent (context-control purpose, not role-play)

source_title: YC Root Access: Advanced Context Engineering for Agents
author: Dex
quote: our goal all the time is to keep context utilization under 40%
claim: In the implement phase update the plan file with done status after each phase and move to a new context window.
evidence_detail: Team practice; 40% target.
landing: Plan file doubles as progress tracker; each phase starts in a new session (matches harness)

source_title: YC Root Access: Advanced Context Engineering for Agents
author: Dex
quote: If I'm shouting at Claude, it's because the plan was bad.
claim: If the plan is good the implementer needs no correction; frustration in implementation signals a plan defect, not an implementation one.
evidence_detail: Experience.
landing: Failure triage rule: when a phase goes wrong, return to the plan and record it in the journal

source_title: YC Root Access: Advanced Context Engineering for Agents
author: Dex
quote: I can sure as heck read 200 lines of an implementation plan.
claim: Review a ~200-line plan instead of a 2,000-line PR to keep mental alignment (a teammate had delivered 20,000-line Go PRs he could not review).
evidence_detail: 200 vs 2,000-line comparison; 20,000-line PR every couple of days.
landing: Owner one-page view and PR plan section as the primary review object

source_title: YC Root Access: Advanced Context Engineering for Agents
author: Dex
quote: our cloud MD and our slash commands are like we basically like test those for weeks
claim: CLAUDE.md and slash commands are tested for weeks before anyone is allowed to change them because they are the highest-leverage lines.
evidence_detail: Team policy statement.
landing: Gate on CLAUDE.md trim and skills: test before merge, consistent with the knowledge-store pilot gating

source_title: YC Root Access: Advanced Context Engineering for Agents
author: Dex
quote: This is a team of three in a month. These are credits
claim: Heavy token spend was judged worth it for the time saved (three-person team, one month, on API credits rather than a max plan); goal list includes 'spend as many tokens as possible'.
evidence_detail: No figure stated.
landing: Cost context for effort routing; cheap-but-correct trade-off

source_title: YC Root Access: Advanced Context Engineering for Agents
author: Dex
quote: he's getting a shout out anyways
claim: Ralph Wiggum loop (same prompt looped overnight) is endorsed as a smart use of coding agents if you understand context windows; he links Geoff Huntley's article.
evidence_detail: 12-hour overnight loop on a live stream, per Huntley; Dex's remark that Huntley is being humble.
landing: Loop-style fresh-context-per-iteration as a pattern for mechanical tasks (later he limits this; see other readers)

source_title: YC Root Access: Advanced Context Engineering for Agents
author: Dex
quote: The challenge of like playing telephone
claim: Subagent hand-back is lossy 'telephone': how the parent prompts the child to return findings determines quality, so prompt the return format.
evidence_detail: Stated as an open challenge.
landing: fixflow-explorer agent file: specify output contract (paths, line numbers, confidence)

source_title: YC Root Access: Advanced Context Engineering for Agents
author: Dex
quote: ingested data from 100,000 developers
claim: Cites the Stanford study of 100,000 developers: AI use creates rework and can be counterproductive on complex brownfield work.
evidence_detail: Third-party study (Stanford, 100,000 developers) cited by Dex; he does not give figures here.
landing: Context for why brownfield FixFlow needs guardrails

source_title: YC Root Access: Advanced Context Engineering for Agents
author: Dex
quote: I still read all the tests, but I no longer read every line of code
claim: After switching to spec-first he reads tests and specs but not every code line; trust is placed in reviewed specs plus tests.
evidence_detail: Personal practice; later retractions are covered by other readers.
landing: Reviewer protocol reads tests first; owner view; note this was later revised so treat as a baseline claim

source_title: YC Root Access: Advanced Context Engineering for Agents
author: Dex
quote: the idea of sitting and talking to an agent for two hours
claim: Endorses Sean Grove's 'specs are the new code' view as an important idea (spec as source, not prompts thrown away), and names it a favourite AIE talk.
evidence_detail: Guest idea Dex endorses; in Nov 2025 he backs away from the phrase 'spec-driven development'.
landing: Nowhere obvious

author: Dex
quote: we can prompt our way around split brain for most things
claim: The split-brain problem of sub-agents can mostly be solved by prompting, though long context is sometimes needed in exceptional cases.
evidence_detail: Reply in a thread; head tweet only captured.
landing: Custom agent prompts (fixflow-explorer) and subagent handoff format

author: Dex
quote: user -> Claude -> task() input -> subagent behavior -> subagent response format
claim: Subagent use chains user, parent Claude, task input, subagent behaviour and response format, like a game of telephone where each hop can distort.
evidence_detail: Describes the 'triple pendulum' of context management.
landing: Specify subagent input and return format explicitly in agent files and Workflow scripts

author: Dex+others
quote: Don't use a framework.
claim: Own your agent architecture: a simple main loop checking input between steps, or threading, and the nuances you build are the agent's identity.
evidence_detail: Episode one-thing takeaway.
landing: own workflow scripts rather than a framework

source_title: AITW Decoding Context Engineering Lessons from Manus
author: Dex+others
quote: periodically re-inject relevant information or tasks to reinforce the context
claim: In long runs the model loses the goal, so re-inject goals or plans periodically (a todo or plan file read repeatedly).
evidence_detail: Takeaway from the Manus paper discussion; who said it is unclear.
landing: phase routine re-reading the plan at checkpoints

source_title: AITW Decoding Context Engineering Lessons from Manus
author: Dex+others
quote: keeping your system message consistent and placing dynamic variables at the end
claim: Keep the stable prefix identical and put dynamic content last to benefit from KV/prompt caching.
evidence_detail: Takeaway; no numbers in notes. The earlier Bash-vs-MCP episode shows a cache read versus cache create contrast.
landing: stable CLAUDE.md prefix; workflow prompt templates

author: Dex
quote: whenever an LLM tells me something is good or bad, I become immediately skeptical.
claim: Evaluative statements from the model usually come from accidental steering or sycophancy; the useful output is neutral statements of fact, and he clears context and restarts when he sees evaluations.
evidence_detail: Personal observation, no counts.
landing: Refuter/reviewer prompts: ask for neutral findings with evidence rather than good/bad verdicts; restart context on evaluative drift.

author: Dex
quote: Can you imagine if your REST API failed on 20% of requests?
claim: With AI, accuracy joins latency, uptime, cost and security as a performance dimension; an 80% agent is not production-ready, and context engineering is about reliability.
evidence_detail: Argument, framing 80% quality as an outage.
landing: Acceptance bar for harness claims: measured reliability, not a plausible-looking run

author: Dex
quote: This is more meaning dense. The LLM has to read less stuff
claim: Use XML-like traces in a single user message rather than verbose JSON/tool-message lists, for token efficiency and meaning density.
evidence_detail: Claimed benefit, no measurement.
landing: Format of handoff/journal and CLAUDE.md content: dense, tagged blocks

author: Dex
quote: before the output comes out, we're going to use a really small dumb model
claim: Insert a small, dumb model as a guardrail on tool output when you own the loop; safety comes from controlling every token in and out.
evidence_detail: Answer to a safety Q&A; no data.
landing: Cheap-model verifier/guardrail steps inside workflows (cost-routed verification)

author: Dex
quote: you can make assertions about the intent of the output
claim: Evals as deterministic assertions on the structured next-step intent of an agent trace, given a trace as input (BAML tests).
evidence_detail: Open-source Linear agent example with ~10 tools incl. 3 ways to contact a human.
landing: Assertable traces: have the phase routine emit a structured trace so compliance can be asserted rather than self-reported (soft alternative to hooks)

author: Dex
quote: There's no magic abstraction that solves the memory problem.
claim: There is no off-the-shelf memory abstraction; teams with good long-term agent memory built it from scratch for the use case.
evidence_detail: Example of AI math tutors with weeks/months of memory.
landing: Knowledge-store pilot: custom, task-specific store rather than a generic memory product

author: Dex
quote: Small focus agents, less than 100 tools, less than 20 steps.
claim: Keep agents small: under ~100 tools and under ~20 steps gives reliable results.
evidence_detail: Numeric rule of thumb, no data (AIEWF version says 3-10 step loops).
landing: Cap on tool count and steps per custom agent or workflow node

author: Dex
quote: one of the big takeaways there
claim: Constrained JSON generation hurts code quality (escaped newlines are poorly tokenised); let the model write code in its natural form.
evidence_detail: Mechanistic logit/tokenizer argument in Q&A.
landing: Nowhere obvious

author: Dex
quote: Put it in your slack, put it in your email. Your adoption will go up.
claim: Meet users in their existing channels (Slack, email) and design for asynchronous human contact by agents with stateful control flow.
evidence_detail: Observation from builders.
landing: Owner comms: draft PR and email-style closing message rather than a new dashboard; nowhere beyond that

author: Dex
quote: As they get smarter, there will always be a thing they're not good at.
claim: As models improve, the frontier of failure moves but never vanishes, so engineering principles keep paying off.
evidence_detail: Argument.
landing: Justifies keeping verifiers even as models improve

author: Dex
quote: I think slashcompact is trash. I never use it.
claim: Built-in /compact is generic and loses trajectory; do compaction manually into a file and start a fresh session ('clear' is the good primitive).
evidence_detail: Personal practice; he says /compact is designed to be general and gets you to about 80%.
landing: Hard rule for phase routine: no auto-compact reliance; write the handoff file and /clear

author: Dex
quote: we try to target like maximum 50% context
claim: Target at most about 50% context utilisation per session (in the YC talk this tightens to under 40%).
evidence_detail: Team target; he adds 'this doesn't always become true'. 50% in this episode, 40% in YC and Nov talks.
landing: Context budget number for phases; shows his own figure moved from 50% to 40%

author: Dex
quote: Once a model looks for something and finds a bunch of irrelevant stuff that's in the context window forever
claim: Irrelevant search results stay in context until compaction, so progress files should carry file paths and line numbers rather than letting the next agent search again.
evidence_detail: Mechanism explanation.
landing: Handoff format; also argues for locator agent (fixflow-explorer) returning paths only

author: Dex
quote: they are for exactly one thing, which is context control
claim: Subagents are mostly for read-only work; the parent should explicitly prompt 'use a sub agent' and tell it how to return; parallel subagents (e.g. one per test type) gave accuracy wins over one thread.
evidence_detail: Go unit-test example; no numbers (Vaibhav echoes accuracy).
landing: Agent file prompts that specify return format; use subagents for read-only research in phases

author: Dex
quote: A bad line of research can lead you to a thousand bad lines of code.
claim: Hierarchy of leverage including a fourth tier: the core prompt set that manages research and planning can cause 100,000 bad lines, so human attention goes upstream.
evidence_detail: Stated hierarchy 1 / 10-100 / 1,000 / 100,000 bad lines.
landing: Treat edits to CLAUDE.md, skills and agent files as the highest-risk change class needing verification (weeks of testing before change per YC talk)

author: Dex
quote: in our linear board we literally have like research in progress, research in review
claim: Review states exist for every artefact stage on the ticket board (spec needed, research in review, plan in review, code review, ready for deploy), so humans review research and plan before code.
evidence_detail: Linear column list shown.
landing: Observable phase states (draft PR status labels) make routine compliance visible from outside, a cheap W2 answer short of hooks

author: Dex
quote: What I read really closely in implementation is the tests.
claim: When reviewing implementation, read the tests closely; passing well-designed tests gives confidence in code; code review is skipped on well-tested areas but applied where tests are thin or algorithmically nuanced.
evidence_detail: Team policy; BAML merge queue merged the PR automatically when tests passed.
landing: Reviewer weights tests (fail-before/pass-after) over diff; risk-tiered review by test coverage

author: Dex
quote: I only do TDD with agents.
claim: Plans should make the first phase a failing test and then fix it, giving as many checkpoints as possible; the test commands must be trivial for the agent to run. (Stated by Vaibhav; Dex says he does the same and has a new plan prompt requiring failing test first.)
evidence_detail: Credited mainly to the co-host in this passage; Dex endorses and describes his own prompt change.
landing: Matches the reviewer's fail-before/pass-after requirement; plan template step 'write failing test first'

author: Dex
quote: you can literally give it the shell command
claim: Put exact verification shell commands after each file or step in the plan so the model runs them via its to-do list; 'automated verification' without a command is weak.
evidence_detail: Shown with a build-process plan.
landing: Plan template: each step carries the exact command and expected output

author: Dex
quote: Put it in your plan or better yet put it exactly directly in your prompt.
claim: CLAUDE.md is injected with a note that it may not be relevant, so instructions that must be followed should go in the plan or the prompt, not CLAUDE.md.
evidence_detail: He shows the injected reminder text in a captured trace of the request.
landing: Move must-follow routine steps out of CLAUDE.md into the phase prompt / skill; supports the CLAUDE.md trim

author: Dex
quote: A lot of what goes into the context window for claude is like system instructions.
claim: Inspect the actual request body via a proxy (system prompt, built-in tools, CLAUDE.md, MCP tools) to know what the budget is spent on before the user's message.
evidence_detail: Captured a real Claude call trace via a proxy and published it with the episode notes; no token counts spoken.
landing: Measurement: capture a trace of a FixFlow session to see how many tokens CLAUDE.md and tool definitions use; the skipped measurement pipeline would deliver this

author: Dex
quote: the research was wrong a couple times. I had to like delete it, throw it out
claim: Research output can be wrong (said the bug was already solved); read it, throw it out, add a failing test case to the spec, and restart; failed research can be compacted into a better prompt for the second attempt.
evidence_detail: BAML assert bug live demo; first research said no bug.
landing: Refuter on diagnoses; knowledge store entries must be verified and discardable

author: Dex
quote: you can prompt to say like, hey, here's what we're not doing
claim: Plans should state explicit non-goals to stop the implementer adding unrequested extras.
evidence_detail: Observed in live plan review.
landing: Plan @ sha template: 'not doing' section; reviewer checks diff against it

author: Dex
quote: The research one, You reject the PR and you would say do it this way.
claim: Plan-with-research vs plan-without-research comparison: both reached the same core fix but only the researched plan followed the repo's test convention; skipping research is fine for small issues but loses repo conventions.
evidence_detail: One-bug comparison; research plan shorter; two PRs, one closed.
landing: Rule of thumb for skipping research on small phases

author: Dex
quote: If you tell Claude to think deeply you get the thinking tokens. This can backfire.
claim: More thinking is not always better; ultrathink can make the model over-attend to earlier instructions and ignore later corrections.
evidence_detail: Personal experience, no data.
landing: Early precedent for the medium-beats-xhigh finding; supports effort routing for verifiers

author: Dex
quote: Even the prompts we write for Opus, we don't use them for Sonnet
claim: Prompts tuned for one model do not transfer; Opus prompts are not reused for Sonnet or o3 because attention differs.
evidence_detail: Team experience.
landing: Agent/skill files for Haiku or Sonnet workers need their own tuning separate from Opus phase prompts

author: Dex
quote: consider just making a script that does it exactly how you want it.
claim: Replace noisy MCP tool output with a script that returns context-optimised markdown (e.g. a Linear ticket with description and comments in one call).
evidence_detail: HumanLayer ticket-pulling tool; MCP JSON described as very noisy.
landing: Backpressure and fetch wrappers: run_silent-style scripts for gh/CI/Alembic output

author: Dex
quote: Open cloud code in the integrated terminal
claim: Run the agent in the IDE terminal with the extension so it receives LSP/type errors; enable Python type checking and select the right interpreter so feedback exists.
evidence_detail: Practical tip; no numbers.
landing: Mypy strict/Ruff/tsc as automatic feedback; ensure agent sessions can see typecheck errors

author: Dex
quote: it's guaranteed that the more files in a certain directory the worse it's going to be
claim: Codebase shape affects agents: identical file names (page.tsx) and inconsistent package scripts or naming make search harder; one team member spent over two weeks moving to Turbo so agents run uniform top-level commands.
evidence_detail: Two weeks of repo restructuring; Vaibhav also stresses consistent nomenclature.
landing: Single canonical command set (npm run, pytest, alembic) documented once; naming consistency checks

author: Dex
quote: you can add additional directories and then claude will be able to work
claim: Multi-repo work can be handled by granting additional directories in settings.json; symlinks may be skipped by search tools so hard links work better.
evidence_detail: Team practice for BAML plus cloud repo.
landing: Nowhere obvious (single monorepo)

author: Dex
quote: I shipped six PRs last Thursday and I haven't opened a nonmarkdown file
claim: He shipped six PRs in a day and had not opened a non-markdown file in an editor in over a month (almost two months by the YC talk).
evidence_detail: Self-report; also an engineer shipping 2,000 lines of Go per day that he could not review.
landing: None; motivates plan-level review

author: Dex
quote: everyone try cloud code for the first 10 minutes of a task
claim: Adoption heuristic: try the agent for 10 minutes; if no happy path within 30 minutes, fall back; and restart attempts quickly (the shoot-again-immediately analogy). (The 10-minute rule is stated by Vaibhav, Dex adds the restart tweak.)
evidence_detail: Time-boxed rule of thumb.
landing: Timebox in phase routine: abandon and restart a phase session after fixed attempts

author: Dex
quote: the research prompt. It's 300 lines of markdown.
claim: The research slash command is a 300-line prompt with subagent instructions and was tuned by a team member; slash commands are tested for weeks before anyone may change them.
evidence_detail: 300-line research prompt; 'test those for weeks' appears in the YC talk.
landing: Skills treated as tested artefacts with change control; counterweight to the CLAUDE.md length concern for command prompts

author: Dex
quote: don't forget to read everything the model outputs
claim: Closing takeaway: manage context via subagents and frequent compaction, steer, and read all output because research is the highest leverage and if wrong nothing else works.
evidence_detail: Summary of the episode.
landing: Human-read research/plan gates in routine

source_title: AITW #17 Advanced Context Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Dex
quote: CLAUDE.md > prompts > research > plans > implementation
claim: Human effort should be weighted to the highest-leverage pipeline stages, with CLAUDE.md first and implementation last.
evidence_detail: Episode takeaway list; no numbers.
landing: CLAUDE.md curation priority; ship plan phase review focus

source_title: AITW #17 Advanced Context Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Dex
quote: Use intentional compaction: actively manage and shrink your context
claim: Deliberately compact context (research and plan docs as compressed state) to keep the agent focused.
evidence_detail: Takeaway; no measurement.
landing: one phase per new session; phase handoff docs

source_title: AITW #17 Advanced Context Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Dex
quote: Review markdown docs to catch problems BEFORE implementation
claim: Humans should review the agent's research and plan documents to gain mental alignment before any code is written.
evidence_detail: Takeaway; linked to HumanLayer .claude/commands.
landing: ship plan phase routine: draft PR 'Plan @ sha' review gate

source_title: AITW #17 Advanced Context Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Dex
quote: Use sub-agents for complex tasks
claim: Decompose work into sub-agents with specialised prompts (find relevant files, plan, generate) rather than one monolithic prompt; sub-agents also protect the parent context (linked thread 'How not to use SubAgents').
evidence_detail: Takeaway plus whiteboards; no numbers.
landing: .claude/agents/ library beyond the Haiku fixflow-explorer

source_title: AITW #17 Advanced Context Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Dex
quote: Align language and naming
claim: Consistent naming across the codebase helps the agent see relationships between parts.
evidence_detail: Takeaway only.
landing: nowhere obvious (same-named slice folders across runtimes already do this)

source_title: AITW #17 Advanced Context Engineering for Coding Agents
author: Dex
quote: Phase 1 - Research: understanding how the system works today, including filenames
claim: Three-stage workflow: research (how it works today, with filenames), plan (step-by-step outline), implement (test as you go, expect surprises).
evidence_detail: Worked example resolving BAML issue 1252.
landing: phase routine in ship plan section 0

author: Dex
quote: Claude subagents are context management + prompt shortcuts. That is all.
claim: Using subagents to play house with anthropomorphised roles fails; they are for context management and prompt shortcuts only.
evidence_detail: Strong opinion; says engineers who do this well are 100x more effective, no data.
landing: Custom-agent design: define agents by context isolation and a reusable prompt (like the Haiku locator), not by role personas.

author: Dex
quote: type errors -> truth errors
claim: If specs are the code, debugging is finding the one line of incorrect context in research and plan markdown, and test suites should check truth and logical consistency of those documents.
evidence_detail: Conceptual argument building on @sgrove's idea.
landing: Consistency checks on plan/knowledge-store documents; a cold-resume trial that catches a wrong frozen fact is a truth-error test.

author: Dex
quote: you go upstream, fix the spec, and restart the *implementation*
claim: When a step-through of an implementation reveals a spec error, fix the spec upstream and restart the implementation rather than patching code.
evidence_detail: Debugging heuristic.
landing: Phase routine rule: a failed phase edits the plan at its sha and reruns in a fresh session, not patch-on-patch.

author: Dex
quote: more and more "compilation" will be unattended
claim: Spec compilation will increasingly run unattended, with less diff-by-diff watching and more spec in, code out.
evidence_detail: Prediction; he later argues against lights-off factories in July 2026 essays.
landing: Context for how much unattended running the plan permits; compare with his later 2-3x position.

author: Dex
quote: JSON vs XML for thread history (XML more token-efficient)
claim: Workshop notes record that XML-style thread serialisation was more token-efficient than JSON for the agent's history.
evidence_detail: One bullet in a learnings file; no counts.
landing: Context budget: format of state files and journals that agents re-read

author: Dex
quote: Debug artifacts - Test runs preserved in ./tmp/test_TIMESTAMP/ directories
claim: The workshop CLAUDE.md is a bullet file of implementation learnings, pitfalls avoided, chapter status with checkmarks and testing commands, including a script that simulates the Colab environment in a clean venv and keeps timestamped debug artifacts per run.
evidence_detail: Agent-maintained notes; shape is learnings + status + commands.
landing: Knowledge store / journal shape: pitfalls-avoided list and per-run preserved artifacts for a test-environment simulation

source_title: AITW Context Engineering and memory deep dive
author: Dex+others
quote: Treat RAG, memory, and prompts as a single, unified context engineering problem.
claim: All inputs (prompts, retrieval, memory, history) are one problem of assembling the final token set.
evidence_detail: Highlight; links to 12-factor-agents factor 3.
landing: knowledge-store design as context assembly

source_title: AITW Context Engineering and memory deep dive
author: Dex+others
quote: fetch it deterministically and inject it into the context yourself
claim: For information the agent always needs, inject it deterministically instead of relying on it to ask.
evidence_detail: Highlight.
landing: session-start injection of key facts in place of long CLAUDE.md; hooks (skipped, re-open)

source_title: AITW Context Engineering and memory deep dive
author: Dex+others
quote: Don't try to make your agent remember everything.
claim: Memory should be an engineered lossy process (Decaying Resolution Memory): recent detail, older material compressed; summarise with existing memory in view.
evidence_detail: Highlight; episode 07-15 implements DRM as code.
landing: knowledge-store design; journal compaction

source_title: AITW Context Engineering and memory deep dive
author: Dex+others
quote: semantically meaningful, human-like tools (e.g., 'check_calendar', 'search_inbox')
claim: Give agents narrow, purpose-named, sandboxed tools rather than a generic retrieve_memory function.
evidence_detail: Highlight.
landing: purpose-named skills/scripts for the knowledge store

source_title: AITW Context Engineering and memory deep dive
author: Dex+others
quote: Avoid solving complex, deterministic problems like timezone conversions inside a prompt.
claim: Do deterministic logic in code and hand the model a normalised format.
evidence_detail: Highlight.
landing: scripted checks over prompt rules

author: Dex
quote: **DO NOT PROCEED WITHOUT SELECTING A PERSONA.**
claim: The repo's CLAUDE.md uses a mandatory-persona gate in capitals (read one persona file before any work), which is the style the later improve-claude-md skill argues against.
evidence_detail: Template file; no adherence data. Shipped by the promptx tool.
landing: CLAUDE.md: counter-example of emphatic gating text; note the later reversal toward conditional blocks

author: Dex
quote: At any given point, your input to an LLM in an agent is "here's what's happened so far
claim: Own the context window: build a custom context format (events packed into one message as XML-ish tags, then 'what's the next step?') instead of default role-based messages, to maximize density and attention efficiency.
evidence_detail: Code example and screenshots of a token-count comparison, no benchmark.
landing: Context budget: how subagent prompts and phase handoffs are serialised

author: Dex
quote: Consider hiding errors and failed calls from context window once they are resolved.
claim: Resolved errors and failed calls should be removed from the context window, and the five benefits of owning it are density, error handling, safety, flexibility and token efficiency.
evidence_detail: Short list; no data.
landing: Context budget: strip resolved failures from handoffs and journals so cold-resume reads stay clean

author: Dex
quote: you want the flexibility to be able to try EVERYTHING.
claim: Explicit epistemic stance: he does not know the best way to hand context to a model and argues for keeping the structure flexible and experimenting, excluding temperature, fine-tuning and training from scope.
evidence_detail: Stated twice in the factor.
landing: Measurement posture: try-and-measure rather than fixed doctrine (cf. L1 effort routing evidence)

author: Dex+others
quote: focused agents with specific workflows, rules, and expertise areas
claim: multiclaude ships five role personas (developer, code-reviewer, rebaser, merger, multiplan-manager) as markdown files plus a staged CLAUDE.md to merge in, installed by `npx multiclaude init`, so roles are selected by telling the agent which persona file to adopt.
evidence_detail: README only; persona files not read, no usage data; date not in the file.
landing: Role persona files (reviewer, merger) as reusable library entries; each phase picks a persona rather than carrying all rules in CLAUDE.md.

author: Dex+others
quote: npx multiclaude launch branch-name plan-file.md
claim: A manager persona splits a large feature into worker plans and uses a launch command (branch + plan file) and a cleanup command to run coding agents in parallel, relying on Makefile setup and teardown targets that init creates.
evidence_detail: README description; no results.
landing: A branch+plan-file launch contract as the unit of parallel work; Makefile setup/teardown as the worktree interface.

also.quote: npx multiclaude launch branch-name plan-file.md
also.author: Dex
also.claim: A manager persona splits a feature into worker plan files and launches one agent per branch via a launch/cleanup CLI (using Makefile setup and teardown targets), then a merger persona consolidates the branches.
